Most Illustrious Gentlemen.

History of Mexico written by a Mexican, who seeks not

Aa protector to defend it but a guide to lead it and a master to enlighten it, must assuredly be dedicated to the most respectable learned body of that New World, as the one which, more than any other, is instructed in Mexican history, and therefore better fitted to decide on the merit of such a work and to point out the errors that may be in it.

> Io pur mi vergognerei di presentarvi un' opera così fconcia, e così diffettosa , se non fosfi sicuro, che la vostra prudenza, e la vostra umanità non fono punto inferiori alla vostra eminente dottrina . Voi sapete benissimo quanto arduo sia l’argomento della mia Storia, e quanto sia difficile di riuscirvi, massimamente per un uomo rifinito dalle tribolazioni, che s'è meslo a scrivere più di sette mila miglia lontano dalla sua patria, sprovveduto di molti documenti neceslarj, e privo anche di que’ riscontri, che potrebbe procacciarli per le lettere de’ suoi compatrioti . “Tosto dunque vi accorgerete in leggendo questa opera, ch’ efla anzichè una Storia, è un faggio, ‘un tentativo, uno sforzo, ma gagliardo, d'’ un Cittadino, che a dispetto delle sue calamità s' è adoperato per renderfi utile alla sua patria, ed in vece di rimproverare gli sbagli, compatirete l’ Autore, e gradirete :l servizio fattovi da lui nell'aver battuta una strada, che per nostra disgrazia s' è renduta malagevolilsfima.

I myself should be ashamed to present you with a work so crude and so defective, if I were not sure that your prudence and your humanity are in no way inferior to your eminent learning. You know very well how arduous is the subject of my History, and how difficult it is to succeed in it, especially for a man worn out by tribulations, who has set himself to write more than seven thousand miles from his homeland, deprived of many necessary documents, and lacking even those verifications which he might procure through the letters of his compatriots. You will therefore soon perceive, on reading this work, that it is not so much a History as an essay, an attempt, an effort, though a vigorous one, of a citizen who, in spite of his calamities, has labored to make himself useful to his homeland; and instead of reproaching its mistakes, you will make allowance for the author, and welcome the service he has done you in having beaten a path which, to our misfortune, has become exceedingly difficult.

(a) The University of Mexico was founded by order of the Emperor Charles V, and by the authority of Pope Julius III, in the year 1553, with all the prerogatives and privileges of that of Salamanca. Its first lecturers were most excellent, because they were chosen from among the men of letters of Spain, at a time when the sciences flourished there more [p. v] by a sacred awe on seeing in your schools the images of those most illustrious men who once adorned both New and Old Spain, or on hearing those immortal names of Veracruz, Hortigosa, Naranjo, Cervantes, Salcedo, Sariñana, Siles, Sigüenza, Bermúdez, Eguiara, Miranda, Portillo, etc., etc., which would do honor even to the most renowned Academies of learned Europe? (b) The mere remembrance of the names of your Doctors who are still living would be enough to make the author lose heart, and among others that of the most illustrious Chancellor and head of your University, whom, besides the distinction of his illustrious birth, a sublime intelligence, a supreme erudition in sacred and in human letters, and a solid piety have raised to the most brilliant offices of learning, and render most worthy of the sacred purple.

(b) Of the great men of the University of Mexico honorable mention is made by Cristóbal Bernardo de la Plaza in his Chronicle of the same University, carried from 1553 to 1683; by Dr. Eguiara in the Bibliotheca mexicana, and in the preface to his Theology; by Pinelo in the Biblioteca occidental; and by many other authors, European as well as American.

[p. vi]

But leaving aside now the praises due to you, since they will perhaps be thought flatteries by those who are unaware of your signal merit, I wish to complain to you in a friendly way of the indolence, or negligence, of our forebears with regard to the history of our homeland. It is indeed true that there were many worthy men who labored to illustrate Mexican antiquity, and left many most valuable writings on it. It is likewise true that there was already in that University a Professor of Antiquities, charged with explaining the characters and the figures of the Mexican paintings, since they were of the greatest importance for deciding in the courts the suits that arose over the ownership of certain lands, or over the nobility of certain Indian families. But this is precisely what grieves me. Why was that Professor, so necessary, not kept? Why let those writings, so precious, perish, and especially those of the most learned Sigüenza? For lack of a Professor of Antiquities there is at present no one who understands the Mexican paintings, and through the loss of the writings the history of Mexico has become most difficult, not to say impossible. Now, since such a loss cannot be repaired, let at least what remains to us not be lost. I hope that you, who are in that kingdom the guardians of the sciences, will seek to preserve the remains of the antiquity of our homeland, forming of them, in the very magnificent edifice of your schools, a museum no less useful than curious, in which may be gathered the ancient statues

A le [p. 2] le sentenzez © per la grandezza de' fatti” raccontati + ma bensì per la diligenza nelle ricerche, per la sincerità della narrazione, per la naturalezza dello stile, e_pel fervigio farro a’ Letterati vaghi di sapere le antichità messicane, presentando loro raccolto in questa operetta quanto di pregevole trovasi sparso quà e lì negli Autori, e davvantaggio parecchie cose non mai da eli pubblicate,

found myself condemned, to serve as best I could my homeland and my nation, and to restore to its splendor the truth obscured by an incredible swarm of modern writers on America, has been no less laborious and difficult for me than costly. For, to say nothing of the great expense incurred in procuring from Cadiz, from Madrid, and from other cities of Europe the necessary books, I have read and diligently examined almost everything that has been published thus far on such a subject; I have compared the accounts of the authors, and weighed their authority in the balance of criticism; I have studied a great many historical paintings of the Mexicans; I have made use of their manuscripts, already read when I was in Mexico; and I have consulted many men experienced in those countries. To such diligence I might add, to lend credit to my labors, that I lived thirty-six years in several provinces of that vast kingdom, that I learned the Mexican language, and that for some years I associated with the very Mexicans whose history I write. Yet I do not flatter myself that I can give a perfect work; for besides finding myself destitute of those endowments of talent, judgment, and eloquence which are required in a good historian, the lamentable loss of the greater part of the Mexican paintings, which I have mentioned and bewailed elsewhere, and the lack of so many valuable manuscripts, which are preserved in several libraries of Mexico, are insuperable obstacles for anyone who would undertake such a History, above all outside those countries. Nevertheless I hope that my labor will be welcome, not indeed for the elegance of the language, for the beauty of the descriptions, for the gravity of the [p. 2] maxims, or for the grandeur of the deeds recounted; but rather for the diligence in research, for the sincerity of the narration, for the naturalness of the style, and for the service done to men of letters eager to know the Mexican antiquities, by presenting to them, gathered together in this little work, whatever is valuable that lies scattered here and there among the authors, and moreover several things never published by them.

> Essendomi io prefisla la utilità de' miei nazionali , come fine principale di questa Storia, la fcrissi da principio in ispabieilt pe : indotto poi. da alcuai Letterati Iraliani, che mostra. vansi oltremodo bramolsi di leggerla nella lor propria lingua , mi addofiai .il nuovo, e faticoso impegno di rtraslatrarla in toscano ; ma coloro, ch’ ebbero la bontà di pregiar le mie fatiche, avranno pure quella di compiatirmi.

Having set before myself the usefulness of my countrymen as the principal end of this History, I wrote it at first in Spanish; then, induced by some Italian men of letters, who showed themselves extremely eager to read it in their own language, I took upon myself the new and laborious task of translating it into Tuscan; but those who have had the kindness to value my labors will have also that of making allowance for me.

Per l'opposto a quelli che son portati per lo studio della Natura, parrà questo medesimo faggio qual'in+ fatti È, troppo ristretto, e superfiziale; ma per soddisfare alla loro. curiosità sarebbe d’ uopo lo scrivere un’ opera assai diversa da quella , ch’ io ho intrapresa, Del resto io avreî rispar. miata una gran pena, se non fossi stato costretto a compiacere a’ suddetti amici, mentre per iscrivere convenevolmente quel poco di storia naturale, studiai l’opere di Plinio, di Dioscori. de, di Laet, di Hernandez , d' Ulloa, di Buffon , di Bomare, e d'altri Narturalisti; non contentandomi nè di ciò ,ch' io avea veduto co' miei. occhj, nè di ciò, che ho ayuto per informa+ zione d'uomini pratici di que’ pacsi, e bene intendenti .

Induced likewise by some friends, I wrote that essay on the natural history of Mexico which is read in the first book, which I myself believed unnecessary, and which many will perhaps think out of place; but in order not to depart wholly from my subject, I strove to bring back to ancient history what I say of natural things, noting the use that the ancient Mexicans made of them. On the other hand, to those who are drawn to the study of Nature, this same essay will seem, as it in fact is, too restricted and superficial; but to satisfy their curiosity it would be necessary to write a work quite different from the one I have undertaken. For the rest, I should have spared myself a great deal of trouble, had I not been constrained to humor the aforesaid friends, since in order to write properly that little natural history I studied the works of Pliny, Dioscorides, de Laet, Hernández, Ulloa, Buffon, Valmont de Bomare, and other naturalists; not content either with what I had seen with my own eyes, or with what I have had by information from men experienced in those countries and well informed.

> / ; Na > zione [p. 3] zione d' uno Rile brillante , e vezzoso, di riflesoni filosofiche ; e politiche, e di fatti inventati a capriccio , ficcome veggo farsi da non pochi Autori del nostro vantato secolo ; ma a me re, come quegli che fono nemico giurato d' ogni inganno, ugia , ed affettazione, tanto più bella dover comparir la verità, quatro più ignuda . Nel raccontar gli avvenimenti della conquista fatta dagli Spagnuoli mi sono ugualmente allontanato dal panegirico del Solìs, e dalle invettive di Monhgnor de Ias Casas ; poichè nè voglio adulare i miei Nazionali , nè ca. luoniarli. («) Metto i farti in quel grado di certezza, o di verisimiglianza , in cui gli rrovo : dove poi non poslo accertare qualche successo a cagione della discordanza degli Autori, ficcome intorno alla morte del Re Motezuma, espongo fincera» mente i lor diversì sentimenti, ma senza tralasciar quelle congetture, che detta la buona ragione, In somma ho avuto sem» pre mai d' avanti agl' occhj quelle due fante leggi della storia, di non ocsar dire il falso, nè rtemer di dire il vero, e mi lufingo di non avervi contravvenuto , -

In writing I have had nothing more at heart than the truth. I should have labored far less, and my History would perhaps be more welcome to many, if all the diligence I have employed in tracking down the truth I had put into embellishing my narration [p. 3] with a brilliant and charming style, with philosophical and political reflections, and with facts invented at will, as I see done by not a few authors of our vaunted century; but to me, who am a sworn enemy of all deceit, falsehood, and affectation, the truth seems bound to appear the more beautiful the more bare it is. In recounting the events of the conquest made by the Spaniards I have kept myself equally far from the panegyric of Solís and from the invectives of Monsignor de las Casas; for I neither wish to flatter my countrymen nor to calumniate them. (a) I set down the facts at the degree of certainty or verisimilitude at which I find them; where I cannot ascertain some occurrence because of the disagreement of the authors, as concerning the death of King Moctezuma, I set forth their different opinions candidly, but without omitting those conjectures which sound reason dictates. In short, I have always kept before my eyes those two holy laws of history, not to dare to say what is false, nor to fear to say what is true, and I flatter myself that I have not contravened them.

> Non dubito, che vi sieno de’ leggitori sì delicati, e lezio: fi , che non possano comportare la durezza di tanti nomi messicani sparsi per tutta la Storia; ma qnesto è un male, a cui non ho potuto rimediare senza espormi ad incorrere in un'altro diferto men tollerabile, ed aflai comune in quasi rutti gli Europsì , che hanno (critto dell America , cioè quello d' alterare in sì fatta maniera i nomt-per raddolcirli , che non fi possano più conofcere. Chi sarebbe capace d' indovinare, che 1il Solìs parla di Quaubnahuac dove dice Quarlabaca, di Huejorlipan dove mette Gualipar, e di Cuitlalpicoc dove scrive Pilparoe? Quindi ho stimato più ficuro l'imitar l’ esempio di molti scrittori moderni, i quali dovunque adducono nelle loro opere i nomi di persone, di luoghi, di‘ fiumi, ec. d’un'altra Nazione della Europa, gli scrivono rali, quali coral Nazione

I do not doubt that there are readers so delicate and fastidious that they cannot endure the harshness of so many Mexican names scattered throughout the History; but this is an evil for which I could not find a remedy without exposing myself to falling into another defect, less tolerable, and quite common in almost all the Europeans who have written of America, namely that of altering names in such a manner, in order to soften them, that they can no longer be recognized. Who would be capable of guessing that Solís speaks of Quauhnahuac where he says Quatlabaca, of Huejotlipan where he puts Gualipàr, and of Cuitlalpitoc where he writes Pilpatoc? Hence I have thought it safer to imitate the example of many modern writers, who wherever they cite in their works the names of persons, places, rivers, etc., of another European nation, write them just as that nation

> (x) Tornon pretendo far credar& adulatore il Solis, nè calunniatore Monsig. de las Casas, ma soltanto voglio dire. che ciò che scrisse il Solìs mosso dal deliderio d' ingrandire il fuo Eroé, è Monsignor de las Casas-trasportaro dal Pio zelo per gl' Indiani, iv non potrei scrivere senza adulare, o calunniare. [p. 4] gli usa: e pure vi sono de’ nomi presi dalla lingua tedesca ; & dalla illirica affai più duri all’ orecchie italiane pel maggior concorso-di consonanti forti , che tutte le veci messicane da me adoperate. Non però rifiuto que’ nomi già alterati , ne’ quali per efsere generalmente conosciuti, non v'è pericolo di sbagliare. Così scrivo Messico in vece di Mexico, Tlascalla in vece di Tlaexcallan, è Motezuma in vece di Moreuczoma. Rapporto alla Geografia d' Anahuac ho adoperato ogni mio studio per renderla esatta , prevalendomi or della notizia di que’ paeli presa da me medesimo ne' molti viaggj che vi feci, or dell’ informazioni , e degli scritti altrui; ma contuttociò non sono riuscito pienamente, mentre a dispetto delle più pre» murose diligenze non ho potuto procacciarmi quelle scarse ofservazioni astronomiche, che fi son fatte su' luoghi . Il fito pes rò , e le distanze da me accennate tanto nel corpo cella lo. ria, quanto nella carta geografica, non debbono credersì messe con quella precisione , ed esattezza, che fi richiede da un Geo- "

(a) I do not claim to make Solís out a flatterer, nor Monsignor de las Casas a calumniator, but I mean only to say that what Solís wrote, moved by the desire to magnify his Hero, and Monsignor de las Casas, carried away by pious zeal for the Indians, I could not write without flattering or calumniating. [p. 4] uses them; and yet there are names taken from the German language, and from the Illyrian, far harder on Italian ears, because of the greater concurrence of strong consonants, than all the Mexican words I have employed. I do not, however, reject those names already altered which, being generally known, leave no danger of mistake. Thus I write Messico in place of Mexico, Tlascalla in place of Tlaxcallan, and Motezuma in place of Moteuczoma.

With regard to the geography of Anahuac I have used every effort to make it exact, availing myself now of the knowledge of those countries that I gained myself in the many journeys I made there, now of the information and the writings of others; but for all that I have not fully succeeded, since in spite of the most earnest diligence I have not been able to procure those scanty astronomical observations that have been made on the spot. The position, however, and the distances that I have indicated, both in the body of the history and on the geographical map, must not be believed to be set down with that precision and exactness which is required of a geographer, but approximately, as may be done by a shrewd traveler who judges by eye. I have had in my hands innumerable geographical maps of Mexico, ancient as well as modern, and it would have been easy to copy the one that pleased me most, making a few slight changes to bring it to the ancient geography; but among so many I have not found even one that is not full of errors, as much with regard to the latitude and longitude of places as in what concerns the division of the provinces, the course of the rivers, and the direction of the coasts. To know what account is to be made of all the maps published thus far, it is enough to note the discrepancy that there is in them about the longitude of the capital, though it ought to be better known than that of any other city of Mexico. This discrepancy is no less than fourteen degrees, since by some geographers that city is placed at 264 degrees of longitude from the island of Hierro, by others at 265, by others at 266, and so on up to 278, or perhaps more.

No less to embellish my History than to facilitate the understanding of several things described in it, I have had engraved

> grafo ; ma a un dipresso, come può farsi da un viaggiatore accorto, che giudica ad occhio . Ho avute nelle mani innumerabili carte geografiche del Messico così antiche , come moderne , e sarebbe stato facile il copiare quella , che più mi piacesse , facendovi alcune lievi mutazioni per ridurla alla Geografia antica; ma fra tante non ne ho trovato neppure una , che non sia piena d' errori tanto rapporto alla latitudine, e alla longitudine de' luoghi y, quanto in ciò che riguarda la divisione delle Provincie, il corso de' fumi, e la direzione delle coste. Basta per conoscere il conto, che fi debbe fare di tutte le carte finora pubblicate, avvertire il divario, che in efse v' è intorno alla longitudine della Capirale , contuttocchè esser debba più conosciuta di quella di qualunque altra Città del Meisico. Questo divario nen è meno di quattordici gradi, mentre da alcuni Geografi è situata quella Città in 264. gradi di longitudine dalla isola del Ferro , da altri in 2655 da altri in 266,, e così fino a 278., o forse più. Non meno per abbellire la mia Storia , che per agevolare I' intelligenza di parecchie cose in effa delcritte, ho fatto inta[p. 5] 5 tagliare fino &@ venti rami. I caratteri messicani , e le figure delle Città, de’ Re, delle armadure , degli abiti, degli scudi, del secolo, «dell'anno, del mese, e del diluvio fono stare prese da varie pitture messicane . La figura del tempio maggiore è stata fatta sopra quella del Conquistatore Anonimo , correggendovi le misure da lui recate, ed aggiungendovi il resto giusta la descrizione d’ altri Autori antichi . L’ immagine dell'altro tempio è copia di quella, che pubblicò ‘il Valades nella sua Rerrorica Criftiana. Le figure de' fiori, e degli animali fono per la maggior arte copie di quelle dell’ Hernandez. Il ritratto di Motezuma pi staro fatto sulla copia, che pubblicò il Gemelli dell'originale, che aveva il Siguenza, I ritratti de' Conquistatori fono coje di quelli, che fi vedono nelle Decadi dell' Herrera, Tutte E abr figure sono itate disegnate sopra ciò, che abbiamo ve» duto co' nostri occhj, e-sopra ciò , che ne raccontano gli Sto; rici antichi .

[p. 5] as many as twenty copperplates. The Mexican characters and the figures of the cities, of the kings, of the armor, of the garments, of the shields, of the century, of the year, of the month, and of the flood have been taken from various Mexican paintings. The figure of the great temple has been made after that of the Anonymous Conqueror, correcting the measurements he gives and adding the rest according to the description of other ancient authors. The image of the other temple is a copy of the one that Valadés published in his Rhetorica christiana. The figures of the flowers and of the animals are for the most part copies of those of Hernández. The portrait of Moctezuma has been made after the copy that Gemelli published of the original which Sigüenza had. The portraits of the Conquerors are copies of those that are seen in Herrera’s Decades. All the other figures have been drawn after what we have seen with our own eyes, and after what the ancient historians relate of it.

> Oltracciò ho voluto premettere alla narrazione de’ fatti una breve notizia degli Scrittori della Storia antica del Meslico , così per far vedere i fondamenti della mia opera, come per far onore alla memoria d'’ alcuni illustri Americani, gli scritti de’ quali sono affatto {conosciuti nell’ Europa, Servirà altresì per additar le fonti della Storia Messicana a chi perfezionar volesse nell' avvenire questo mio imperfetto lavoro.

Besides this, I wished to put before the narration of the facts a brief account of the writers of the ancient History of Mexico; both to show the foundations of my work, and to do honor to the memory of some illustrious Americans whose writings are wholly unknown in Europe. It will serve likewise to point out the sources of Mexican history to anyone who might in the future wish to perfect this imperfect work of mine.

> ERDINANDO CORTE”S . Le quattro lunghissime lettere F scritte da questo famoso Conquistatore al suo Sovrano Car» lo V. contenenti il ragguaglio della Conquista, e molti preges voli riscontri intorno al Messico, e a' Messicani, sono state pubblicate în ispagnuolo , in latino, in toscano, ed in altre lingue. La prima di queste lettere fu stampata in Siviglia nel 1522, Sono tutte bene scritte, e vi fi scorge della modestia, e della fincerità ne' racconti, mentre nè vanta i suoi proprj farti, nè oscura gli altrui, S' egli avesse avuto l’ ardire d'’ ingannar il suo Re, i suoi nemici, che tante querele presentarono alla corte contro di lui, non avrebbono lasciato di rinfacciargli ua tal delitto.

> BERNAL DIAZ DEL CASTILLO, Soldato conquista» tore. La Storia vera della conquista della N. Spagna da lui scritta fa stampata ia Madrid nel 1632. in un tomo ia foglio, Malgrado la sconciatura de’ racconti, e la rozzezza del lioguaggio, questa Storia è stata assai stimata per la semplicità, e la sincerità dell’ Autore, che da per tutro fi scorge. Egli fu testimonio oculato di quasi rutto quanto ne racconta; ma talvolta non seppe spiegar le cose a cagione della sua idiortaggine, e talvolta ancora fi mostra dimentico de' fatti per avere scritto molti anni dopo la conquista,

> ALFONSO di MATA, e ALFONSO d'’ OJEDA, tutti e due Conquistatori, e Scrittori di Comentar} sulla Conquista del Messico , di cuì fi fervirono l’ Herrera, e il Torquemada . Quelli dell’ Ojeda sono più distesi , e più stimau. Egli ebbe più pratica degl' Indiani, e imparò la loro lingua, come quegli che fu incaricato di badar alla truppe ausiliarie degli Spagnuoli. s

I N T H E S I X T E E N T H C E N T U RY.

Hernán Cortés. The four very long letters written by this famous Conqueror to his sovereign Charles V, containing the account of the Conquest and many valuable particulars concerning Mexico and the Mexicans, have been published in Spanish, in Latin, in Tuscan, and in other languages. The first of these letters was printed at Seville in 1522. They are all well written, and there is seen in them modesty and sincerity in the narration, since he neither boasts of his own deeds nor obscures those of others. Had he had the audacity to deceive his King, his enemies, who brought so many complaints against him to the court, would not have failed to reproach him with such a crime.

Bernal Díaz del Castillo, soldier and conqueror. The True History of the Conquest of New Spain, written by him, was printed at Madrid in 1632, in one folio volume. Despite the clumsiness of the narratives and the roughness of the language, this History has been highly esteemed for the simplicity and the sincerity of the author, which are everywhere apparent. He was an eyewitness of almost everything he relates; but at times he did not know how to explain things because of his lack of education, and at times again he shows himself forgetful of the facts through having written many years after the conquest.

Alonso de Mata and Alonso de Ojeda, both Conquerors, and writers of commentaries on the Conquest of Mexico, which Herrera and Torquemada made use of. Those of Ojeda are fuller and more esteemed. He had more familiarity with the Indians, and learned their language, as one who was charged with looking after the auxiliary troops of the Spaniards.

[p. 7]

> Na IL CONQUISTATORE ANONIMO. Così chiamiamo

The Anonymous Conqueror. So we call the author of a short but very curious and estimable account, which is found in Ramusio’s collection under this title, Relazione d’un gentiluomo di Ferdinando Cortès. I have not been able to guess who this Gentleman was, because no ancient author mentions him; but whoever he may be, he is sincere, exact, and curious. Taking no heed of the events of the conquest, he relates what he observed in Mexico concerning the temples, the houses, the tombs, the arms, the garments, the food, the drink, etc., of the Mexicans, and lets us see the form of their temples. If his work were not so brief, there would be no other comparable to it in what concerns Mexican antiquities.

> Î’ Autore d’una breve, ma assai cuciosa, e stimabile relazione , che li trova nella raccolta del Ramusio sotto questo titolo, Relazione d' un Gentiluomo di Ferdinando Corrs, Non ho potuto indovinare chi fia stato questo Gentiluomo; perchè niun' Autore antico ne fa menzione ; ma chi che fia, egli è fincero, esatto, e curicso, Egli non curandoli degli avvenimenti della conqailsta, racconta ciò , che oflervò nel Messico intorno a’ tempj, alle case, a' fepolcri, all'armi, agli abiti, al mangia. re, al bere ec. de' Messicani, e ci fa vedere la forma de’ lor tempj. Se la sua opera non fosse cotanto ristretta , non sarebbe verun' altra con efla paragonabile in ciò, che riguarda le anti. chità Messicane.

Francisco López de Gómara. The History of New Spain, written by this learned Spaniard from information received by word of mouth from the Conquerors, and in writing from the first religious who were engaged in the conversion of the Mexicans, and printed at Saragossa in 1554, is well conceived and curious. He was the first to publish the festivals, the rites, the laws, and the manner the Mexicans had of reckoning time; but there are errors in it, because that first information was not altogether exact. The translation of this work into Tuscan, printed at Venice in 1599, has so many errors that it cannot be read without annoyance. (b)

Andrés de Olmos, Spanish Franciscan of holy memory. This tireless Preacher learned the Mexican, Totonac, and Huastec languages, and composed a grammar and a dictionary of all three. Besides other works prepared by him for the benefit of the Spaniards and of the Indians, he wrote in Spanish a treatise on Mexican antiquities, and in Mexican the exhortations which the ancient Mexicans used to give to their children, of which I give a specimen in bk. VII of this History.

> BERNARDINO SAHAGUN, laboriosn Francescano Spa: gnuolo . Essendo stato più di seflanta anni impiegato nella instruzione de' Meslicani, seppe colla maggior perfezione e la loro lingua, e la loro storia, Oltre ad altre opere da lui scritte tanto in messicano , quanto in ispagnuolo, compose in dodici grossi tomi in foglio un Dizionario universale della lingua mes+ ficana, contenente tutto ciò che apparteneva alla Geografia, alla Religione , e alla Storia politica, e naturale de' Messicani . Questa opera d'’ immensa erudizione e fatica fu mandata al Cronichista Reale dell’ America, residente in Madrid, dal Mars+ chele di Villamanrique Vicerà del Melslico, e nona dubitiamo , che finora fiali conservata in qualche librerìa di Spagna, Scriffe ancora la Storia generale della N. Spagna in quattro tomi , li quali fi conservano manoscritti nella librerìa del Convento de’ Francescani in Tolosa di Navarra, secondochè afferma Gio + vanni di S. Antonio nella sua Biblioreca Francescana

Bernardino de Sahagún, laborious Spanish Franciscan. Having been employed for more than sixty years in the instruction of the Mexicans, he came to know with the greatest perfection both their language and their history. Besides other works written by him both in Mexican and in Spanish, he composed in twelve large folio volumes a Universal Dictionary of the Mexican Language, containing everything that pertained to the geography, the religion, and the political and natural history of the Mexicans. This work of immense erudition and labor was sent to the Royal Chronicler of America, resident in Madrid, by the Marquis of Villamanrique, Viceroy of Mexico, and we do not doubt that it has been preserved up to now in some library of Spain. He wrote also the General History of New Spain in four volumes, which are preserved in manuscript in the library of the Convent of the Franciscans at Tolosa in Navarre, according to what Juan de San Antonio affirms in his Bibliotheca universa franciscana.

Alonso de Zorita, Spanish jurist and Judge of Mexico. After making, by order of King Philip II, diligent inquiries into the political government of the Mexicans, he wrote in Spanish A Compendious Account of the Lords Who Were in Mexico, and of Their Diversity; of the Laws, Usages, and Customs of the Mexicans; of the Tributes They Paid, etc. The original manuscript in folio was preserved in the library of the College

Juan de Tovar, a most noble Mexican Jesuit. He wrote on the ancient history of the kingdoms of Mexico, Acolhuacan, and Tlacopan, after making diligent inquiries by order of the Viceroy of Mexico, Don Martín Enríquez. Of these manuscripts Father Acosta made principal use in what he wrote concerning Mexican antiquities, as he himself declares.

Questo grand' uomo , dopo eflerk tratcenuto alcuni anni nell' una, e nell’ altra Americas e -informatosi da uomini pratici de' coltumi di quelle Nazioni, scrisse. in ispagnuolo la Storia naturale, e mora- Îe delle Indie , la quale fu itampata la prima volta in Siviglia Hel 1589., poi ristampata in Barcellona nel 1591., ed indi ortata in varie lingue dell’ Europa . José de Acosta, a most illustrious Spanish Jesuit, widely known in the world of letters for his writings. This great man, after staying some years in the one America and in the other, and informing himself from men experienced in the customs of those nations, wrote in Spanish the Natural and Moral History of the Indies, which was printed the first time at Seville in 1589, then reprinted at Barcelona in 1591, and thereafter translated into various languages of Europe. This work is very well written, especially in what concerns the physical observations on the climate of America; but being so very concise, it is lacking in many articles, and there are some mistakes in it about ancient history.

Fernando Pimentel Ixtlilxochitl, son of Coanacochtzin, last king of Acolhuacan, and Antonio de Tovar Cano Moctezuma Ixtlilxochitl, descendant of the two royal houses of Mexico and Acolhuacan. These two lords wrote, at the request of the Count of Benavente and of the Viceroy of Mexico, Don Luis de Velasco, letters on the genealogy of the kings of Acolhuacan, and on other points of the ancient history of that kingdom, which were preserved in the said College of the Jesuits.

[p. 10] Tadeo de Niza, a noble Tlaxcalan Indian. In the year 1548, by order of the Viceroy of Mexico, he wrote the history of the conquest, which was signed by thirty Tlaxcalan lords.

Gabriel de Ayala, a noble Indian of Texcoco. He wrote in Mexican historical commentaries containing the account of all the events of the Mexicans from the year 1243 of the common era to 1562.

Juan Buenaventura Zapata y Mendoza, a noble Tlaxcalan. He wrote in the Mexican language the Chronicle of Tlaxcala, containing all the events of the Tlaxcalans from their arrival in the country of Anahuac to the year 1589.

Pedro Ponce, a noble Indian, parish priest of Tzompahuacan. He wrote in Spanish An Account of the Gods and Rites of Mexican Heathenism.

The Lords of Colhuacan. They wrote the annals of the kingdom of Colhuacan. A copy of this work was in the aforesaid library of the Jesuits.

Cristóbal del Castillo, a Mexican mestizo (a). He wrote the History of the journey of the Aztecs or Mexicans to the country of Anahuac, the manuscript of which was preserved in the library of the College of the Jesuits of Tepotzotlán.

Diego Muñoz Camargo, a noble Tlaxcalan mestizo. He wrote in Spanish the History of the City and of the Republic of Tlaxcala. Torquemada made use of this work, and there are copies of it both in Spain and in Mexico.

Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, of Texcoco, descended in direct line from the kings of Acolhuacan. This noble Indian, most versed in the antiquities of his nation, wrote, at the request of the Viceroy of Mexico, several erudite and most valuable works, namely: 1. The History of New Spain. 2.

The History of the Chichimec Lords. 3. A historical summary of the kingdom of Texcoco. 4. Historical memoirs of the Toltecs and other nations of Anahuac. All these works, written in Spanish, were preserved in the library of the College of SS. Peter and Paul of the Jesuits of Mexico; and from them we have drawn some materials for our history. The author was so cautious in writing that, to remove every suspicion of fabrication, he had the conformity of his narrations with the historical paintings, which he had inherited from his most illustrious ancestors, legally attested.

Juan Bautista Pomar, a Texcocan, or Cholulan, descended from a bastard of the Royal House of Texcoco. He wrote historical memoirs of that kingdom, which Torquemada used.

Domingo de San Antón Muñón Chimalpahin, a noble Indian of Mexico. He wrote in Mexican four works highly esteemed by connoisseurs. 1. A Mexican chronicle containing all the events of that nation from the year 1068 to 1597 of the common era. 2. The history of the conquest of Mexico by the Spaniards. 3. Original accounts of the kingdoms of Acolhuacan, of Mexico, and of other provinces. 4. Historical commentaries from the year 1064 to 1521. These works, which I have greatly desired, were preserved in the library of the College of SS. Peter and Paul of Mexico, and the Chevalier Boturini had copies of them, as of almost all the works of Indians that I have mentioned. The Chronicle was found also in the library of the College of St. Gregory of the Jesuits of Mexico.

Fernando Alvarado Tezozomoc, a Mexican Indian. He wrote in Spanish a Mexican chronicle about the year 1598, which was preserved in the aforesaid library of SS. Peter and Paul.

Bartolomé de las Casas, famous Spanish Dominican, first Bishop of Chiapas, and supremely deserving of the Indians. The terrible writings presented by this venerable prelate to Kings Charles V and Philip II in favor of the Indians, and against the Spanish conquerors, printed at Seville,

> BARTOLOMEO de las CASAS, famoso Demenicano spagauola,.primo Vescovo di Chiapa, e-sommamente benemerito-d:gl" “Indiani . Lrterribili "scritti presentari da questo veneravile Prelats a’ Re Carlo V. e Filippo IL. in favor degl’ indianiy € contro gli Spagnuoli conquiltatori ; stampati in Sivt[p. 12] glia, ed indi tradoti , e ristampati a gara per odio degli Spa: gnuoli in varie lingue della Europa, contenzono alcuni punti della- storia antica de' Messicani, ma così esagerati ed alterati , che non polsliamo riposarci sulla fede dell' Autore, benchè per - altro assai ragguardevole. Il troppo fuoco del suo zelo tramandò della luce col fumo, cioè il vero frammischiato col falso: (a) non già- perchè egli cercasse a bella posta d’ ingannar il sua Re, e il mondo tutto, mentre il sospettar in lui una ral malvagità , farebbe far torto alla virtù di lui riconosciuta e riverita anche, da' suoi nemici; ma perchè non eflendo egli stato presente a ciò che racconta del Meslico, fi fidò troppo delle informazioni altrui : ciò che faremo vedere in alcuni luoghi della nostra Storia. Afai più forse ci gioverebbono altre due grandi opere dello stesso Prelato non mai pubblicate , cioè I, una Storia apologetica del clima e della terra de' paesi dell’ America , .e dell’ indole, de' costumi &c. degli Americani sors toposti al dominio del Re Cattolico. Questo manoscritto in 83zo. foglj fi conservava nella librerìa de' Domenicanidi Valladolid in Ispagna,, dove fu letto dal Remesal, siccome egli ne fa fede nella sua Cronica de' Domenicani di Chiapa e di Guatemala, 2. una storia generale dell’ America in tre tomi in foglio, una copia della quale era nella librerìa del Signor Conte di Villaumbrosa in Madrid , dove la vide il Pinelo, secondochè egli ‘aflerma nella (ua Biblioreca Occidenzale . Due romi di questa, storia vide il suddetto Aurore nell’ archivio celebre di Simancas, ch’ è stato Il sepolcro di molti pregevoli manoscritti dell’ America . Due tomi simlmente erano in Amsterdam nella librerìa di Giacomo Kricio .

B2 [p. 12] and thereafter translated and eagerly reprinted, out of hatred for the Spaniards, in various languages of Europe, contain some points of the ancient history of the Mexicans, but so exaggerated and altered that we cannot rely on the authority of the author, though otherwise very respectable. The too great fire of his zeal transmitted light together with smoke, that is, the truth mingled with the false: (a) not indeed because he sought on purpose to deceive his King and the whole world, since to suspect such wickedness in him would be to wrong his virtue, acknowledged and revered even by his enemies; but because, not having been present at what he relates of Mexico, he trusted too much in the information of others: which we shall show in some places of our History. Far more useful to us, perhaps, would be two other great works of the same prelate, never published, namely 1. an Apologetic History of the climate and the land of the countries of America, and of the character, customs, etc., of the Americans subject to the dominion of the Catholic King. This manuscript, in 830 folios, was preserved in the library of the Dominicans of Valladolid in Spain, where it was read by Remesal, as he attests in his Chronicle of the Dominicans of Chiapas and Guatemala. 2. a general history of America in three folio volumes, a copy of which was in the library of the Count of Villaumbrosa at Madrid, where Pinelo saw it, as he affirms in his Biblioteca occidental. Two volumes of this history were seen by the aforesaid author in the celebrated archive of Simancas, which has been the sepulcher of many valuable manuscripts of America. Two volumes likewise were at Amsterdam in the library of Giacomo Kricio.

On his voyage to Spain he composed in twenty cantos the History of the conquest of Mexico, and printed it at Madrid under the Spanish title of El peregrino indiano in 1599. This work must be counted among the histories of Mexico, because it has nothing of poetry but the meter.

> NEL:SECOLO XVII,

Antonio de Herrera, Royal Chronicler of the Indies. This sincere and judicious author wrote in four folio volumes eight Decades of the history of America, beginning from the year 1492, together with a geographical Description of the Spanish colonies in that New World, which work was printed for the first time at Madrid at the beginning of the last century, and then reprinted in 1730, as well as translated and published in other languages of Europe. Although the principal aim of the author was to relate the deeds of the Spaniards, he does not however omit the ancient history of the Americans; but in what concerns the Mexicans he for the most part copies the accounts of Acosta and of Gómara. His method, moreover, like that

[p. 14] of all the strict annalists, is displeasing to lovers of history, since at every step the narrative is seen to be interrupted, the account of some deed being broken off by the telling of other events quite different from it.

Enrico Martínez, a foreign author, though with a Spanish surname. After traveling through the greater part of Europe, and staying many years in Mexico, where he was most useful by reason of his great skill in the mathematics, he wrote the History of New Spain, which was printed in Mexico in 1606. In the ancient history he follows for the most part in the footsteps of Acosta; but it contains astronomical and physical observations that are important for the geography and for the natural history of those countries.

Gregorio García, a Spanish Dominican. His famous treatise on the origin of the Americans, printed in quarto at Valencia in 1607, and afterwards enlarged and reprinted at Madrid in 1729 in folio, is a work of immense erudition, but almost wholly useless, since it contributes little or nothing toward tracing the truth. The foundations of the opinions that he puts forward on the origin of the Americans are for the most part weak conjectures, drawn from the resemblance in some customs and in some words of the languages, which are often cited in altered form.

Juan de Torquemada, a Spanish Franciscan. The history of Mexico written by him under the title of Monarquía indiana, printed at Madrid about 1614 in three large folio volumes, and reprinted in 1724, is beyond doubt the most complete, with regard to Mexican antiquity, of all that have been published up to now. The author remained in Mexico from his youth until his death, knew the Mexican language very well, associated with the Mexicans for more than fifty years, collected a great number of ancient paintings and excellent manuscripts, and labored on his work more than twenty years; but in spite of his diligence and of such advantages, he often shows himself lacking in memory, in criticism, and in good taste, and in his history there are to be seen many gross contradictions, above all concerning chronology, several childish tales, and a great abundance of superfluous erudition; so that a good deal of patience is needed to read it. Nevertheless, there being very many things in it of great merit,

[p. 15] which will be sought in vain in other authors, I was obliged to do in such a history what Virgil did with the works of Ennius, that is, to search for gems amid the dung.

Arias de Villalobos, a Spaniard. His History of Mexico, carried from the founding of the capital down to the year 1623, written in verse and printed there in the same year, is a work of little merit.

Cristóbal Chaves Castillejo, a Spaniard. About the year 1632 he wrote a folio volume on the origin of the Indians and on their first colonies in the country of Anahuac.

Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora, a celebrated Mexican, professor of mathematics in the university of his native land. This great man was one of those who have deserved best of the History of Mexico; for at great expense he made a large and choice collection of manuscripts and ancient paintings, and he applied himself with the greatest diligence and assiduity to illustrating the antiquities of that kingdom. Besides many mathematical, critical, historical, and poetical works composed by him, some still in manuscript and some printed in Mexico from the year 1680 to 1693, he wrote in Spanish: 1. The Ciclografía mexicana, a work of great labor, in which, by calculating the eclipses and the comets noted in the historical paintings of the Mexicans, he adjusted their epochs to ours, and, making use of good documents, set forth the method that they had in counting the centuries, the years, and the months. 2. The Historia del imperio de los chichimecas, in which he set forth what he had found in the manuscripts and in the Mexican paintings concerning the first colonies that passed from Asia to America, and concerning the events of the most ancient nations settled in Anahuac. 3. A long and very learned dissertation on the preaching of the Gospel in Anahuac, made there, as he believed, by the Apostle St. Thomas, availing himself of the tradition of the Indians, of the crosses found and already venerated in Mexico, and of other monuments. 4. The Genealogy of the Mexican Kings, in which he deduced the series of their ancestors from as far back as the seventh century of the Christian era. 5. Critical annotations on the works of Torquemada and of Bernal Díaz. All these most erudite manuscripts,

> AGOSTINO di BETANCURT, Erancescano da Meslice; La sua storia antica , e moderna del Messico siampata in. quella Capitale nel 1698. in un/tomo in. foglio ' forro il titolo di Teatro Messicano , non è .in, ciò che riguarda alla storia, antica altro, che uan ristretto di «quella del Torquémada fatto in fretta, e scritto con poca accuratezza,

Agustín de Vetancurt, a Franciscan of Mexico. His history, ancient and modern, of Mexico, printed in that capital in 1698 in one folio volume under the title of Teatro mexicano, is, so far as the ancient history is concerned, nothing other than an abridgment of Torquemada’s, made in haste and written with little care.

> ANTONIO SOLIS, Cronichista-Reale dell’ America .. La. storia della Conquista della N. «Spagna scritta da questo pulitissimo, ed ingegnoso Spagnuolo , fembia più va panegirico , che una istoria. IL suo linguaggio è -puro ed: elegante , ma lo stile alquanto affettato, le sentenze troppo ricercate , € l'aringhe compolte a piacere ; © come quegli, che non badava tanto al vero , quanto al bello, contraddice sovente agli Autori, più degni di fede, ed anche al medesimo Cortès, il cui panegirico intraprese, Ne’ tre ultimi libri della noltra Storia accenniamo alcuni sbaglj di questo celebre Scrittore .

Antonio de Solís, Royal Chronicler of America. The history of the Conquest of New Spain written by this most polished and ingenious Spaniard seems more a panegyric than a history. His language is pure and elegant, but the style somewhat affected, the maxims too far-fetched, and the harangues composed at pleasure; and, as one who paid less heed to the truth than to beauty, he often contradicts the authors most worthy of belief, and even Cortés himself, whose panegyric he undertook. In the last three books of our History we point out some mistakes of this celebrated writer.

Lorenzo Boturini Benaducci, a Milanese. The museum that he formed of paintings and ancient manuscripts was the most copious and the most choice that has ever been seen in that kingdom, at least after that of the most illustrious Sigüenza; but before he could lay hand to his work he was stripped, by the excessive jealousy of that government, of all his literary property, and sent to Spain, where, having been wholly cleared of every suspicion against his loyalty and honor, though without recovering his manuscripts, he printed at Madrid in 1746, in one quarto volume, a sample of the great history that he was planning. In it are found some important pieces of information never before published; but there are also errors in it. The system of history that he had formed for himself was too grand, and therefore somewhat fanciful.

Besides these and other writers, both Spanish and Indian, there are also some anonymous ones whose works are worthy of being remembered for the importance of their subject, and these are: 1. certain annals of the Toltec nation, painted on paper and written in the Mexican language, in which an account is given of the migration and the wars of the Toltecs, of their kings, of the founding of Tollan, their metropolis, and of other events of theirs down to the year 1547 of the common era. 2. certain historical commentaries in Mexican on the events of the Aztec, or Mexican, nation from the year 1066 to 1316, and others likewise in Mexican from the year 1367 to 1509. 3. a Mexican history in Mexican brought down to the year 1406, in which the arrival of the Mexicans at the city of Tollan in 1196 is placed, as we say in our history. All these manuscripts were in the precious museum of the Chevalier Boturini.

We do not make mention here of those authors who wrote of the antiquities of Michoacán, Yucatán, Guatemala, and New Mexico; for although all these provinces are today believed by many to be comprised in Mexico, they did not belong to the Mexican empire, whose history we are writing. We do mention, however, the authors of the ancient history of the kingdom of Acolhuacan and of the republic of Tlaxcala, because their events [p. 18] are for the most part connected with those of the Mexicans.

If in enumerating the writers on Mexico we sought to make a show of erudition, we could set down here a very long catalogue of French, English, Italians, Dutch, Flemings, and Germans who have written, either on purpose or incidentally, of the ancient history of that kingdom; but having read very many of them in order to make use of them in my work, I have found none who could be of service to me, except the two Italians Gemelli and Boturini, who, by having been in Mexico, and by having procured from the Mexicans paintings and particular records concerning their antiquities, have in some manner contributed to the illustration of its history. All the others have either repeated what had already been written by the Spanish authors whom we have mentioned, or else have altered the facts to suit themselves, in order to rage all the more fiercely against the Spaniards, as M. de P. has lately done in his Recherches philosophiques sur les Américains, and M. Marmontel in his romance Les Incas.

Among the foreign historians of Mexico none is more celebrated by them than the Englishman Thomas Gage, whom I see cited by many as an oracle, and yet there is no writer on America more shameless in lying. Others are led to circulate fables by some passion, such as hatred, love, or vanity; but Gage lied only for the sake of lying. What passion, or what interest, could ever have induced this author to say that the Capuchins had a fine convent at Tacubaya; that at Jalapa a bishopric was erected in his time with an income of ten thousand ducats; that from Jalapa he went to the Rinconada, and thence in one day to Tepeaca; that there is in this city a great abundance of anone and of chicozapoti; that this fruit has a stone larger than a pear; that the Hermitage of the Carmelites lies northwest of the capital; that the Spaniards burned the city of Tinguez in Quivira, that, having rebuilt it, they were living there in his time, and that the Jesuits had a college there; and a thousand other gross falsehoods, which are found on every page, and which arouse in readers acquainted with those countries now laughter, now indignation?

Vesposti

Among the modern writers on the affairs of America the most famous and esteemed are M. Raynal and Dr. Robertson. M. Raynal, besides gross blunders made in what concerns the present state of New Spain, doubts all that is said of the founding of Mexico and of the whole ancient history of the Mexicans. “We are permitted to affirm nothing,” he says, “except that the Mexican empire was governed by Moctezuma when the Spaniards landed on the coasts of Mexico.” Here is language truly frank, and worthy of a philosopher of the eighteenth century. Are we then permitted to affirm nothing more? And why not doubt even the existence of Moctezuma? If we are permitted to affirm that, because it is found established by the testimony of the Spaniards who saw that king, we find in the same way attested by the same Spaniards a great many other things belonging to the ancient history of Mexico, seen by them, and further confirmed by the deposition of the Indians themselves. Such things, then, can be affirmed, such as the existence of Moctezuma, or else we shall have to doubt even that. If, moreover, there is reason to doubt the whole ancient history of the Mexicans, there will likewise be reason to call in question the antiquity of almost all the nations of the world, since it is not easy to find another history whose events have been attested by a greater number of historians than those of the Mexicans; nor do we know that among any other people so rigorous a law was ever published against lying historians as that of the Acolhuas in Book VII, which we have mentioned.

Dr. Robertson, though more moderate than Raynal in his distrust of history, and better supplied with Spanish books and manuscripts, fell likewise into more errors and contradictions, since he sought to go further in the knowledge of America and of the Americans. Then, to make us despair of being able to obtain even a moderate account of the institutions and customs of the Mexicans, he exaggerates the stupidity of the Conquerors and the destruction wrought upon the historical monuments of that nation by the superstition of the first missionaries. “In consequence,” he says, “of this fanatical zeal of the monks… whatever knowledge of remote events

C2 [p. 20] such rude monuments contained was entirely lost, and no information remained concerning the ancient revolutions and policy of the empire, but what was derived from tradition, or from some fragments of their historical paintings that escaped the barbarous researches of Zummaraga. From the experience of all nations it is manifest, that the memory of past transactions can neither be long preserved, nor be transmitted with any fidelity by tradition. The Mexican paintings, which are supposed to have served as annals of their empire, are few in number, and of ambiguous meaning. Thus amidst the uncertainty of the former, and the obscurity of the latter, we must glean what intelligence can be collected from the scanty materials scattered in the Spanish writers.” But in all this the author is mistaken; for, 1. the materials found in the Spanish historians are not so scanty that a reasonable, though not altogether complete, history of the Mexicans cannot be formed from them, as is manifest to anyone who consults them without partiality: it is enough to know how to make the choice, and to separate the grain from the chaff. 2. Nor, in order to write such a history, is there need to rely on the materials scattered among the Spaniards, since there are so many Histories and Memoirs written by the Indians themselves, of which Robertson had no knowledge. 3. Nor are the historical paintings that escaped the researches of the first missionaries few, except in relation to the unspeakable abundance that existed before, as may easily be seen in our history, and in that of Torquemada, and of other writers. 4. Neither are such paintings of ambiguous meaning, except to Robertson, and to all those who do not understand the characters and the figures of the Mexicans, nor know the method that they had for representing things, just as our writings are of ambiguous meaning to those who have not learned to read. When the lamentable burning of the paintings was carried out by the missionaries, there were living very many historians, Acolhuas, Mexicans, Tepanecs, Tlaxcalans, etc., who exerted themselves to repair the loss of such monuments, as in part they succeeded in doing, now by making new paintings, now by making use of our characters, already learned by them, now by instructing

their own preachers by word of mouth in their antiquities, so that they might preserve them in their writings, as did Motolinía, Olmos, and Sahagún. It is therefore absolutely false that whatever knowledge of remote events… was entirely lost. It is false likewise that no information remained concerning the ancient revolutions and policy of the empire, but what was derived from tradition, &c. In our history, and principally in our dissertations, we shall make plain some of the many errors that there are in the history of the aforesaid author, and in the works of other foreign writers, of whom large volumes could be made. Not content with vitiating the history of Mexico with the errors, absurdities, and lies written in their books, some authors have also spoiled it with lying pictures and figures engraved on copper, such as those of the famous Theodor de Bry. In Gage’s work, in M. Prévost’s general history of voyages, and in others, there is depicted a fine road built over the Mexican lake for going from Mexico to Texcoco, which is certainly the greatest absurdity in the world. In the great work entitled La Galerie agréable du monde there are depicted the ambassadors sent in ancient times to the court of Mexico mounted on horseback upon elephants. This is, without a doubt, a magnificent lie.

## Paintings

[p. 22]

## PAINTINGS

We do not pretend to make here a register of all the Mexican paintings that were saved from the burning by the first missionaries, or that were made afterward by the Indian historians of the sixteenth century, of which some Spanish authors made use, since such an enumeration would be no less useless than tedious to readers; but we wish only to make mention of some collections, the knowledge of which may be useful to anyone who would write the History of that kingdom.

I. The Mendoza Collection. So we call the collection of 63 Mexican paintings made by order of the first Viceroy of Mexico, Don Antonio de Mendoza, to which he had added, by persons who understood them, their interpretation in the Mexican and Spanish languages, in order to send them to the Emperor Charles V. The vessel on which they were sent was captured by a French corsair and taken to France. The Mexican paintings came into the hands of Thevet, geographer to the Most Christian King, from whose heirs Hakluyt, at that time chaplain to the English ambassador at the court of France, bought them at a great price. Thence carried to England, their Spanish interpretation was translated into English by Locke (not the same as the other famous metaphysician of the same name) by order of Walter Raleigh, and finally, at the request of the learned Henry Spelman, published by Samuel Purchas in the third volume of his collection. In 1692 they were printed anew at Paris, with the French interpretation, by Melchisédech Thévenot in vol. II of his work entitled Relations de divers voyages curieux. The paintings were, as we have already said, sixty-three: the first twelve containing the founding of Mexico, and the years and conquests of the Mexican kings; the thirty-six following representing the tributary cities of that crown, and the quantity and quality of their tributes; and the last fifteen indicating a part of the education of their children and of their political government. But it must be noted that Thévenot’s edition is deficient and defective, since in the copies of paintings XI and XII the figures of

[p. 23] the years are seen to be changed, the figures belonging to the reign of Moctezuma II being put in that of Ahuitzotl, and the reverse; the copies of paintings XXI and XXII are altogether missing, and for the most part the figures of the tributary cities. Father Kircher reprinted a copy of the first painting, made from that of Purchas, in his work entitled Oedipus Aegyptiacus. This Mendoza collection has been diligently studied by us, and has afforded us some advantage for the History.

Acosta fa menzione di cerri annali messicani dipinti, che erano al suo tempo nella librerìa del- Vaticano, Non dubitiamo , che vi siano tuttora, atteso la somma, e lodevole curiosuà de' Signori Italiani nel conservare sì fatte anticaglie, ma non abbiamo avuto agio di portarci a Roma per ricercarli e studiarli.

II. The Vatican Collection. Father Acosta makes mention of certain painted Mexican annals that were in his time in the library of the Vatican. We do not doubt that they are there still, in view of the great and praiseworthy curiosity of the Italian gentlemen in preserving such antiquities, but we have not had the opportunity to betake ourselves to Rome to seek them out and study them.

> Ill. La Raccolta di Vienna. Nella librerìa Imperiale di questa Corte fi conservano otto pitture messicane, ,, Da una » nora, dice il Dott. Robertson, in questo codice meslicanoap- 9 parisce, ch’ è stato un presente farto da Emmanuelle Re di » Portogallo a Papa Clemente VII. Dopo d' efler /passato in » mano di diversi illustri Proprietarj cadde in quella del Card. » di Saxe-Eisenach, il quale lo regalò all’ Imperatore Leopol- 9 do, y Lo stesso Autore ci da nella sua Storia dell’ America Ia copia d' una di tali pitture, nella prima parte della quale hi rappricicna un Re, che fa la puerra ad una Città , dopo averle mandata un’ ambasciata. Vi fi scorgono delle figure di tempj, ed alcune altresì d' anni, e di giorni ; ma del resto essendo questa copia da per se, e sfornita di colori, e mancandovi nelle figure umane que’ contrassegni, che in altre pitture messicane danno a conoscere le persone, è non che difficile, anche affatto impossibile I' indovinare il suo fignificato. Se il Dott. Robertson avesse insieme con esla pubblicate l' altre sertte copis a, lui mandate da Vienna, potremmo forle intenderle tutre.

III. The Vienna Collection. In the Imperial library of that court there are preserved eight Mexican paintings. “According to a note in this Codex Mexicanus,” says Dr. Robertson, “it appears to have been a present from Emmanuel King of Portugal to Pope Clement VII. After passing through the hands of several illustrious proprietors, it fell into those of the cardinal of Saxe Eisenach, who presented it to the emperor Leopold.” The same author gives us in his History of America a copy of one of these paintings, in the first part of which a king is represented making war on a city, after having sent it an embassy. Figures of temples are to be seen in it, and some also of years and of days; but for the rest, this copy being by itself and without colors, and the human figures lacking those marks which in other Mexican paintings make the persons known, it is not merely difficult but altogether impossible to guess its meaning. If Dr. Robertson had published along with it the other seven copies sent to him from Vienna, we might perhaps be able to understand them all.

[p. 24] purchased at a great price, and some left to him by will by the most noble Indian Don Juan de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, who had inherited them from the kings of Texcoco, his ancestors. Those images of the Mexican century and of the migration of the Aztecs, and those portraits of the Mexican kings, which Gemelli published in vol. VI of his Giro del mondo, are copies of the paintings of Sigüenza, then living in Mexico, when Gemelli came there. (a) The figure of the Mexican century and year is in substance the same that more than a century earlier Valadés had published in Italy in his Rhetorica christiana. Sigüenza, after having made use of the aforesaid paintings for his most erudite works, left them at his death to the College of SS. Peter and Paul of the Jesuits of Mexico, together with his very choice library and his excellent mathematical instruments, where I saw and studied in the year 1759 some volumes of such paintings, containing for the most part the penalties prescribed by the Mexican laws against certain crimes.

(a) Dr. Robertson says that the copy of the journey of the Mexicans, or Aztecs, was given to Gemelli by Don Cristóbal de Guadalajara; but in this he contradicts Gemelli himself, who declares himself indebted to Sigüenza for all the Mexican antiquities that he gives us in his account. From Guadalajara he had nothing else than the hydrographic chart of the Mexican lake. “But as it seems now,” adds Robertson, “to be a received opinion (founded I know not on what evidence) that Carreri was never out of Italy, and that his famous Giro del Mundo, is an account of a fictitious voyage, I have not mentioned these paintings.” If I did not live in the eighteenth century, in which the most extravagant ideas are seen to be adopted, I should be greatly astonished that such an opinion should be generally accepted. In fact, who could imagine that a man who had never been in Mexico would be capable of giving so minute an account of the smallest events of that time, of the persons then living, of their qualities and offices, of all the monasteries of Mexico and of other cities, of the number of their religious, and even of that of the altars of every church, and of other minutiae never published? Nay, in order to do justice to the merit of this Italian, I declare that I have never found a more exact traveler in what he saw with his own eyes, though not in what he had by the information of others. [p. 25] of these paintings, containing some events of the conquest, and some fine portraits of the Mexican kings. In 1770 there were published in Mexico, together with Cortés’s letters, the figure of the Mexican year and thirty-two copies of as many paintings of the tributes that several cities of Mexico paid to that crown, the one and the others taken from the Boturini Museum. Those of the tributes are the same as those of the Mendoza collection, published by Purchas and by Thévenot. Those of Mexico are better engraved, and have the figures of the tributary cities, which for the most part are lacking in the others; but for the rest, six copies of those belonging to the tributes are altogether wanting in them, and there are a thousand absurdities in the interpretation of the figures, caused by ignorance of antiquity and of the Mexican language. This must be noted, so that those who see that work printed in Mexico under a respected name may not for that reason trust it and stumble into some error.

Il piede Toledano, il quale è anconomasticamente lo Spagnuolo, e la terza parte d'’ una Vara Caitigliana , è al piede Reale come 1240. a 14492. cioè dalle 1440. parti, di cui si considera composto il piede Reale, ne ha il Toledano 1240, onde 7. piedi Toledani fanno a un dipresso 6. piedi Reali , o sia una pertica di Parigi* Nella carta geografica dell’ Imperio Messicano ci siamo contentati d' accennare le provincie ed alcuni pochi luoghi , trala-

Wherever we make mention of toises, feet, and inches without saying more, the measures of Paris are to be understood, which, being more generally known, are therefore less exposed to some equivocation. Now the toise of Paris (Toise) has six royal feet (Pie du Roi). Each foot has 12 inches (Pouces), and each inch 12 lines. The line, moreover, is considered to be composed of ten parts, or points, in order to be able to express more easily the proportion of this foot to the others. The Toledo foot, which is by antonomasia the Spanish one, and is the third part of a Castilian vara, is to the royal foot as 1240 to 1440; that is, of the 1440 parts of which the royal foot is considered to be composed, the Toledo foot has 1240; hence 7 Toledo feet make approximately 6 royal feet, or a toise of Paris.

The capital, Tzintzuntzan, called by the Mexicans Huitzitzilla, was situated on the eastern shore of the beautiful Lake Pátzcuaro. Besides these two cities there were others of great note, such as those of

Tiripetío, Zacapu, and Tarecuato: all this country was pleasant, rich, and well peopled.

The kingdom of Tlacopan, situated between those of Mexico and

Michoacán, was of so small an extent that, outside the capital of the same name, it comprised nothing else than a few cities of the

Tepanec nation and the villages of the Mazahuas situated in the western mountains of the Mexican valley. The court of Tlacopan was on the western shore of Lake Texcoco, four miles west of that of Mexico.

(b)

The kingdom of Acolhuacan, the most ancient, and at one time the most extensive, was afterward reduced to narrower limits by the conquests of the Mexicans. It bordered on the east on the republic of

Tlaxcala, on the south on the province of Chalco, belonging to the kingdom of Mexico, on the north on the country of the Huastecs, and on the west it ended at Lake Texcoco; and it was likewise hemmed in by several states of Mexico. Its length from south to north was a little more than two hundred miles, and its greatest breadth did not exceed sixty; but in so small a district there were very large cities and very numerous peoples. The court of Texcoco, situated on the eastern shore of the lake of the same name, fifteen miles east of that of Mexico, was justly celebrated no less for its antiquity and grandeur than

The celebrated republic of Tlaxcallan, or Tlascalla, bordered on the west on the kingdom of Acolhuacan, on the south on the republics of Cholula and of Huexotzinco, and on the state of Tepeyacac, which belonged to the crown of Mexico, on the north on the state of Zacatlán, and on the east on other states likewise subject to the same crown. Its length did not reach fifty miles, nor its breadth more than thirty. Tlaxcallan, the capital, from which the republic took its name, was situated on the slope of the great mountain Matlalcueye, to the northwest, and about seventy miles east of the Mexican court.

The kingdom of Mexico, though the most recent, nevertheless had a much greater extent than all the other aforesaid kingdoms and republics taken together. It extended to the southwest and south as far as the Pacific Ocean, to the southeast as far as the neighborhood of Cuauhtemallan, to the east, excepting the districts of the three republics and a small part of the kingdom of Acolhuacan, as far as the Gulf of Mexico, and to the north as far as the country of the Huastecs; to the northwest it bordered on the barbarous Chichimecs, and to the west it was confined by the dominions of Tlacopan and of Michoacán. The whole Mexican kingdom was comprised between 14° and 21° of north latitude, and between 271° and 283° of longitude, reckoned from the meridian of the island of Hierro. (c)

whose circumference, measured along the lower part of the mountains, is more than 120 miles. A good part of the valley is occupied by two lakes, the one upper, of fresh water, and the other lower, of brackish water, which communicate with each other by a good channel. Into the lower lake, because it lay in the lowest part of the valley, all the waters flowing down from the mountains used to run together; hence, whenever through the extraordinary abundance of the rains the water rose above the bed of the lake, it easily flooded the city of

Mexico, founded in that same lake, as was seen to happen no less under the dominion of the Mexican monarchs than under that of the

Spaniards. These two lakes, whose circumference was not less than ninety miles, represented in some manner the figure of a camel, whose head and neck were the fresh-water lake, or that of Chalco, the body the brackish lake, called that of Texcoco, and the legs and feet the streams and torrents that ran down from the mountains to the lake. Between the two lakes lies the small peninsula of

Iztapalapan, which separates them. Besides the three courts of

Mexico, Acolhuacan, and Tlacopan, there were in this delightful valley forty other considerable cities and innumerable villages and hamlets. The largest cities after the courts were those of Xochimilco,

Chalco, Iztapalapan, and Cuauhtitlan, which today scarcely preserve a twentieth part of what they then were. (d)

Mexico, the most renowned of all the cities of the New World, and capital of the empire (the description of which we shall give in another place), was built, after the fashion of Venice, on several islets of

The principal inland provinces were: to the north, that of the § 2.

Provinces of the Otomis; to the west and southwest, those of the Matlatzincas and the kingdom of Mexico. Cuitlatecs; to the south, those of the Tlahuicas and the Cohuixcas; to the southeast, after the states of Itzocan, Yauhtepec, Cuauhquechollan, Atlixco, Tehuacán, and others, the great provinces of the Mixtecs, the Zapotecs, and finally those of the Chiapanecs. To the east were the provinces of Tepeyacac, of the Popolocas, and of the Totonacs. The maritime provinces of the Gulf of Mexico were those of Coatzacoalco and of Cuetlachtlan, which the Spaniards call Cotasta. The provinces of the Pacific Ocean were those of Colima, Zacatula, Tototepec, Tehuantepec, and Soconusco.

The province of the Otomis began in the northern part of the Mexican valley and continued northward through those mountains as far as ninety miles from the capital. Above all the inhabited places, of which there were very many, there rose the ancient and celebrated city of Tollan (today Tula), and that of Jilotepec, which after the conquest made by the Spaniards was the metropolis of the Otomi nation. Beyond the places of this nation toward the north and northwest there were no other inhabited places as far as New Mexico. All this great tract of land, which is of more than a thousand miles, was occupied by barbarous nations, which had neither a fixed domicile nor obedience to any sovereign.

The province of the Matlatzincas comprised, besides the valley of Toluca, all the space that lies from there to Tlaximaloyan (today Taximaroa), the frontier of the kingdom of Michoacán. The fertile valley of Toluca is more than forty miles long from southeast to northwest, and as much as thirty wide where it broadens most. Toluca, which was the principal city

> ;imaloyan ( oggi T'aximaroa ) frontiera del regno di Michuacan. The Cuitlatecs inhabited a country that stretched more than two hundred miles from northwest to southeast, from the kingdom of

> A Levante de' Mixtechi erano Zapotechi , così chiamarci dalla loro. capitale Teorzapozlan . Nel loro distretto era la Valle di Huasyacar , dagli Spagnuoli detta Oaxaca, O Guaxaca «

Michoacán as far as the Pacific Ocean. Their capital was the great and populous city of Mexcaltepec on the coast, of which scarcely the ruins remain.

The capital of the Tlahuicas was the pleasant and strong city of

Quauhnahuac, called by the Spaniards Cuernabaca, about forty miles south of Mexico. Their province, which began at the southern mountains of the Mexican valley, extended almost sixty miles to the south.

The great province of the Cohuixcas bordered on the north on the

Matlatzincas and the Tlahuicas, on the west on the Cuitlatecs, on the east on the Yopis and the Mixtecs, and to the south it extended as far as the Pacific Ocean, in that part where at present are the port and city of Acapulco. This province was divided into many particular states, such as those of Zumpango, Chilapa, Tlapa, and Teoixtla (today

Tixtla), a land for the most part excessively hot and unwholesome.

Tlachco, a place celebrated for its silver mines, either belonged to the aforesaid province or bordered on it.

The Mixtecapan, or province of the Mixtecs, extended from

Acatlán, a place a hundred and twenty miles from the court toward the southeast, as far as the Pacific Ocean, and contained several cities and villages, well peopled and of considerable commerce.

To the east of the Mixtecs were the Zapotecs, so called from their capital Teotzapotlan. In their district was the valley of Huaxyacac, called by the Spaniards Oaxaca or Guaxaca.

To the north of the Mixtecs lay the province of Mazatlan, and to the north and east of the Zapotecs that of Chinantla, with their capitals of the same names, whence their inhabitants were called Mazatecs and Chinantecs. The provinces of the Chiapanecs, the Zoques, and the Quelenes were the last of the Mexican empire toward the southeast. The principal cities of the Chiapanecs were Teochiapan (called by the Spaniards Chiapa de Indios), Tochtla, Chamula, and Zinacantán; of the Zoques, Tecpantla; and of the Quelenes, Teopixca.

On the slope and in the surroundings of the famous mountain Popocatépetl, which is thirty-three miles to the southeast of the court, there were the large states of Amaquemecan, Tepoztlán, Yauhtepec, Oaxtepec, Chietla, Itzocan, Acapetlayoccan, Cuauhquechollan, Atlixco, Cholula, and Huexotzinco. These last two, which were the most considerable, having, with the help of their neighbors the Tlaxcalans, shaken off the yoke of the Mexicans, reestablished their aristocratic government. The cities of Cholula and of Huexotzinco were among the greatest, and the most populous, of all that land. The Cholulans had the small hamlet of Cuitlaxcoapan on the very spot where the Spaniards afterward founded the city of Puebla, which is the second of New Spain. (f)

(e) Some believe that anciently there was nothing else in the place of Huaxyacac than a mere garrison of the Mexicans, and that that city was founded by the Spaniards; but besides that we know from the register of tributes that Huaxyacac was one of the tributary cities of the crown of Mexico, we know also that the Mexicans were not wont to establish a garrison except in the most populous places of the conquered provinces. The Spaniards were said to found some city whenever they gave a Spanish name to some place of the Indians and established Spanish magistrates there; nor was it otherwise with the founding of Antequera in Huaxyacac, and that of Segura de la Frontera in Tepeyacac.
