These were the principal inland provinces of the Mexican empire, passing over for the moment several other lesser states in order to make the description less tedious.

Among the maritime provinces of the Pacific Ocean the most northerly was that of Colima, whose capital of the same name was situated in 19° of latitude and 272° of longitude. Continuing along the same coast toward the southeast there was the province of

Zacatula, with a capital called by the same name. Then came the coast of the Cuitlatecs, and next that of the Cohuixcas, in whose district lay Acapulco, today a port famous for its commerce with the

Philippine Islands, in 16° 40′ of latitude and 276° of longitude.

Bordering on the coast of the Cohuixcas was that of the Yopis, and next to this that of the Mixtecs, known in our times by the name of

Jicayán. Then followed the great province of Tehuantepec, and finally that of Soconusco. The city of Tehuantepec, from which the state took its name, was situated on a pretty islet formed by a river two miles from the sea. The province of Soconusco, which was the last and the most southerly of the empire, bordered on the east and southeast on the country of Xochitepec, which did not belong to the crown of Mexico, and on the west on that of

> Confinava colla costa dsi Gohuixchi quella dei Jopi, e con questa quella dei Mixtechi , conosciuta ai nostri tempi col nome di Xicayan. Indi seguiva la grande Provincia di Tecuantepec, e finalmente poi quella di Xoconochco. La Città di Tecuantepec, dalla quale fi derivò il nome allo stato , era situata in una bella isoletta, che forma un fiume due miglia dal mare . La Provincia di Xoconochco, ch' era l'ultima, e la più meridionale dell' Imperio, confinava a Levante e Scirocco col paese di Xochirepec, cha non appare teneva alla Corona di Messico, verso Poneate coa quello di [p. 35] : 35 di Tecuantepec , è verlo Mezzogiorno terminavasi nel mare, ===

Tehuantepec [p. 35] of Tehuantepec, and toward the south ended at the sea. Its capital, also called Soconusco, was situated between two rivers in 14° of lati‐ Bk. I. tude and 283° of longitude. On the Gulf of Mexico there were, besides the coast of the Totonacs, the provinces of Cuetlachtlan and of Coatzacoalco. The latter bordered on the east on the vast country of Onohualco, under which name the Mexicans included the states of Tabasco and of the peninsula of Yucatán, which were not subject to their dominion. Besides the capital, likewise called Coatzacoalco, founded on the bank of a great river, there were other well-populated places, among which special mention is due to Painala, as having been the birthplace of the famous Malintzin, one of the most effective instruments of the conquest of Mexico. The province of Cuetlachtlan, which had a capital likewise so called, comprised all that coast which lies between the Alvarado River, where the province of Coatzacoalco ends, and the Antigua (*), where that of the Totonacs began. In that part of the coast which the Mexicans called Chalchicuecan there now stand the city and port of Veracruz, the most renowned in all New Spain.

> La sua Capitale’, chiamata anche Xoconochco , era situata Liu. I. fca due fiumi in 14. gr. di latitudine , ed ia 283. di longitudine . Sopra il Golfo Mellicano v'erano , oltre la colta dei Totonachi , le Provincie di Cuerlachilan , e di Coa- . #xacualco .. Oltre la Capitale , chiamata anche. ella Coatzacualco ;fondata sulla riva d’ un gran fiume, v' erano alcri luoghi ben. popolati , tra .i quali merita particolar- menzione, quello: di Painallg , per eflere stato patria della famosa Malinzzin, uno dei più efficaci stromenti della conquista del Messico. In quella parte della Costa, ch: i Messicani chiamavano Chalchicuecan, v' è presen» temente la Cirrà, e il porro della Veracroce , il più rinomato di tutta la Nuova Spagna, '

The whole country of Anahuac was, generally speaking, well populated. In the History and in the dissertations we shall have occasion to mention several particular cities and to give some idea of the multitude of their inhabitants. Almost all the inhabited places survive still under the same ancient names, though in part altered; but all the ancient cities, except Mexico, Orizaba, and one or two others, are seen to be so diminished that they scarcely have the fourth part of the number of buildings and inhabitants that they once had; there are many that have only the tenth part, and some that do not preserve even the twentieth part. Now, speaking of the Indians in general, and comparing what is reported of their multitude

The river of Papaloapan, which the Spaniards call Alvarado, after the name of the first Spanish captain who sailed upon it, has its principal source in the mountains of the Zapotecs, and after making a circuit through the province of Mazatlan, and receiving other lesser rivers and streams, discharges itself by three navigable mouths into the

Gulf, at a distance of 30 miles from Veracruz. The river Coatzacoalco, which is likewise navigable, descends from the mountains of the

Mixes, and, crossing the province from which it takes its name, empties into the sea near the country of Onohualco. The river of Chiapan begins its course in the mountains called Cuchumatanes, which separate the diocese of Chiapas from that of Guatemala, crosses the province called after it, and then that of Onohualco, whence it goes to the sea. The Spaniards call it Tabasco, as they also called that tract of land which joins the peninsula of Yucatán to the Mexican continent. They also named it the River of Grijalva, out of regard for the commander of the first Spanish fleet, who discovered it.

Among the rivers that run to the Pacific Ocean, the most renowned is the Tololotlan, called by the Spaniards the river of

Guadalajara, or the great river. It takes its rise in the mountains of the valley of Toluca, crosses the kingdom of Michoacán and Lake

Chapala, then goes on to water the country of Tonalá, where the city of Guadalajara, capital of New Galicia, now stands, and after running a course of more than

There were also, and there still are, several lakes, which served no less to embellish the country than to facilitate the commerce of those peoples. The lakes of Nicaragua, of Chapala, and of Pátzcuaro, which were the most considerable, did not belong to the Mexican empire. Among the others, those most important to our history are the two of the Mexican valley, of which we have already made mention. That of Chalco extended fully twelve miles from east to west as far as the city of Xochimilco, and then, taking a direction toward the north for as many miles, was joined by means of a canal to the lake of Texcoco; but its breadth did not exceed six miles. The lake of Texcoco measured fifteen miles, and even seventeen, from east to west, and somewhat more from south to north; but its extent is now smaller, because the Spaniards have diverted many of the waters that flowed into it. All the water that runs into it is originally fresh, and becomes brackish only on account of the nitrous bed of the lake in which it is received. As for springs, there are so many in that land, and so diverse in quality, that they would deserve a separate history, especially if those of the kingdom of Michoacán had to be recorded. There are numberless sources of mineral waters, nitrous, sulphurous, vitriolic, and aluminous: some of which burst forth boiling, and so hot that in a few moments any fruit of the earth or any animal flesh is cooked in them.

The climate of the countries of Anahuac varies according to their

> najo , è cagionato dalla somma depressione delle coste rap. porro alle, terre mediterranee , o dai monti di rena ammasfari nelle spiaggie, come accade nella Veracroce , mia patria, La umidità proviene non men dal mare, che dalle acque, che dalle montagne , che dominano le coste, in abbondanza scendono. Nelle terre calde non v' è mai della brina, e moltissimi abitatori di corali regioni non hanno altra idea della neve, se non quella che fi procacciano per la lezione dei libri , o pel racconto dei forestieri. Le terre troppo elevate ,o troppo vicine alle altiisime montagne, che vi sono eternamente coperte di neve, fono fredde: ed io fono stato in montagna non più di venticinque miglia dalla Capitale discosta, dov è della brina e del ghiaccio anche nel canicolari . Tutti gli altri pacsi mediterranei, dov' era la maggior popolazione di quella terra, godono d'’ un clima così benigno , e così dolce, che nè sentono il rigore del Verno, nè gli ardorì della State . E' vero, che in molti di que’ paesi vi è frequentemente della brina nti tre mesi di Decembre, Gennajo, e Febbrajo, e talvolta ancora suol nevicare ; ma il lieve incomodo , che un tal freddo cagiona , non dura più che infin' allo spuntar del Sole: non è d' uopo di altro fuoco , che di quello dei suoi raggî per riscaldarli nell’ inverno , né d'altro refrigerio in tempo di caldo, che di quello della ombra. La medesima veste, che copre gli uomini nei canicolarì, gli difende nel Gennajo, e gli animali dormono tutto I’ anno a cielo scoperto.

§ 4. situation. The maritime countries are hot, and for the most part hu‐ Climate of Anahuac. mid and unwholesome. Their heat, which makes one sweat even in January, is caused by the extreme depression of the coasts relative to the inland regions, or by the hills of sand heaped up on the beaches, as happens at Veracruz, my native city. The humidity comes no less from the sea than from the waters that descend in abundance from the mountains that overlook the coasts. In the hot lands there is never any frost, and very many inhabitants of such regions have no other idea of snow than what they acquire by reading books or from the accounts of strangers. Lands that are too elevated, or too near the very high mountains that are eternally covered with snow there, are cold; and I have been on a mountain not more than twenty-five miles distant from the capital, where there is frost and ice even in the dog days. All the other inland countries, where the greatest population of that land was, enjoy a climate so mild and so gentle that they feel neither the rigor of winter nor the heats of summer. It is true that in many of those countries there is frequent frost in the three months of December, January, and February, and sometimes it even snows; but the slight inconvenience that such cold causes lasts no longer than until sunrise: there is no need of any other fire than that of the sun's rays to warm oneself in winter, nor of any other refreshment in time of heat than that of shade. The same garment that covers men in the dog days defends them in January, and the animals sleep the whole year under the open sky.

This mildness and pleasantness of the climate beneath the torrid zone is the effect of several natural causes entirely unknown to the ancients, who believed it uninhabitable, and not well understood by some moderns, by whom it is held to be little favorable

> s is. Il fuoco acceso nelle viscere della terra con le dette ma. Monti» terie zolfine, e bituminose si è fatti in alcune montagne de»

of the solar rays, and the longer stay of this planet above the horizon in winter, in comparison with other regions farther from the equator, combine to lessen the cold and to avoid all that horror with which

Nature is seen disfigured under other zones. One enjoys even at that season the beauty of the sky and the innocent delights of the countryside, whereas under the cold zones, and for the most part even under the temperate, clouds rob one of the prospect of the sky, and snow buries the fair productions of the earth. Nor are lesser causes at work to temper the heat of summer. The copious rains that frequently water the earth after midday from April or May to September and

October, the high mountains always laden with snow, scattered here and there throughout the land of Anahuac, the cool winds that then blow, and the shorter stay of the Sun above the horizon, in comparison with the regions of the temperate zone, transform the summer of those happy countries into a cheerful and cool spring.

But the pleasantness of the climate is offset by the thunderstorms, which are frequent in summer, especially in the neighborhood of

Matlalcueye, or the mountain of Tlaxcala, and by the earthquakes that are sometimes felt, though with more fright than damage. Both effects are caused by the sulphur and the other combustible materials deposited in great abundance in the bowels of the earth. As for hailstorms, they are neither more frequent nor greater there than in

Europe.

The Popocatépetl and the Iztaccíhuatl, near each other and thirty-three miles distant from Mexico toward the southeast, are also of astonishing height. The Popocatépetl, to which they give there by antonomasia the name of Volcan, has a mouth or vent of more than half a mile, through which in the time of the Mexican kings it often threw out flames, and in the last century many times hurled a great quantity of ashes over the neighboring places; but in this century hardly any smoke has been observed. The Iztaccíhuatl, known to the Spaniards by the name of Sierra nevada, has also at times thrown out smoke and ashes. Both mountains always have their summits crowned with snow, which is so abundant that from what tumbles down on the neighboring slopes the cities of Mexico, Puebla, and Cholula are supplied, and other neighboring places, even as far as forty miles distant from those mountains, in which an incredible quantity is consumed all the year in ices. Everyone knows by now that the celebrated chain of the Andes, or Alps of South America, continues across the Isthmus of Panama and through all New Spain until it is lost in the unknown countries of the north. The most considerable part of this chain is known in that kingdom by the name of Sierra

Madre, especially in Sinaloa and Tarahumara, provinces twelve hundred miles distant from the capital.

Huacana, and from that time on it has not ceased to throw out fire and burning stones, from which three lofty mountains have been formed, whose circumference was already about six miles, according to the report that in 1766 was made to me by the Chevalier Don Juan Manuel de Bustamante, governor of that province, and an eyewitness. In the eruption the ashes were hurled as far as the city of Querétaro, fully a hundred and fifty miles distant from Jorullo. A thing truly incredible, but nonetheless notorious and public in that city, where a gentleman showed me the ashes that he had collected on a sheet of paper. In the city of Valladolid, sixty miles distant, ashes rained in such abundance that the courtyards of the houses had to be swept two or three times a day. Silver was dug from the mines of Tlachco (celebrated even at that time), of Zumpango, and others; but it was not so highly prized by them as by other nations. After the conquest so many silver mines have been discovered in that country, especially in the provinces that lie to the northwest of the capital, that it is quite impossible to number them. Of copper they had two kinds, one hard, which they used in place of iron for making axes, hatchets, hoes, and other instruments of war and of agriculture, and the other common and pliant, for making basins, pots, and other vessels. This metal abounded more than elsewhere in the provinces of Zacatula and of the Cohuixcas, as it does today in the kingdom of Michoacán. They dug tin from the mines of Tlachco, and lead from those of Ixmiquilpan, a place in the country of the Otomis. Of tin they made money, as we shall say in its place, and of lead we know that it was sold in the markets; but we are wholly ignorant of the use they made of it. They had also iron mines in Tlaxcala, in Tlachco, and in other places; but either they did not discover the mines, or else they did not know how to take advantage of the metal. They had likewise in Chilapa mines of quicksilver, and in many places mines of sulphur, alum, vitriol, cinnabar, ochre, and of a white earth very much like white lead. As for the quicksilver and the vitriol, we do not know what use they made of them; of the other minerals they made use for their paintings and dyes. Of amber and of asphaltum, or bitumen of Judea, there was, and there still is, great abundance on the coasts of both seas, and several places of the empire paid tribute in both of them to the king of Mexico. The amber, which they set in gold, they used only for ornament and pleasure; of the asphaltum they made use in certain incensings, as we shall see elsewhere.

Among the precious stones there were, and there still are, diamonds,

F2 [p. 44] though few, emeralds, amethysts, cat's-eyes, turquoises, cornelians, Bk. I.

and certain green stones resembling emeralds and not much inferior to them, and of all these stones the provinces of the Mixtecs, of the

Zapotecs, and of the Cohuixcas, in whose mountains the mines of such gems are found, paid tribute to the king. Of their abundance, of the esteem in which the Mexicans held them, and of the manner in which they worked them, we shall speak more opportunely in another place. The mountains that lie on the coast of the Gulf of Mexico between the port of Veracruz and the river Coatzacoalco, as also those of Chinantla and of the province of the Mixtecs, supplied them with rock crystal, and the cities of Tochtepec, of Cuetlachtlan, of

Cosamaloapan, and others were obliged to contribute annually a certain quantity for the luxury of the court.

No less do those mountains abound in various kinds of stones valued for use in architecture, sculpture, and other arts. There are quarries of jasper and of marble of various colors in the mountains of

Calpulalpan east of Mexico, in those that separate the two valleys of

Mexico and of Toluca, now called Monte de las Cruces, and in those of the Zapotecs; of alabaster at Tecalco (at present Tecali), a place near the province of Tepeyacac, and in the country of the Mixtecs; of

Tetzontli in the same valley of Mexico, and in many other places of the kingdom. The stone Tetzontli is for the most part of a dark red color, quite hard, porous, and light; it binds lime and sand to itself very tightly, and for that reason is sought after more than any other stone for the buildings of the capital, whose soil is marshy and not very firm. There are also whole mountains of lodestone, and among others a very large one between Teoixtla and Chilapa in the country of the

Cohuixcas. Of the Quetzalitztli, commonly known by the name of nephritic stone, the Mexicans made various curious figures, some of which are preserved in several museums of Europe. The Chimaltizatl, which is a species of selenite, or ass's mirror, is a diaphanous whitish stone, [p. 45] and easily divisible into thin plates, which by means of calcination

> del Vangelo: fi fecero: delle pietre. sacre assai pregiate . (#)

Bk. I. yields a fine plaster, and the ancient Mexicans used it for the white of their paintings. There is also an infinite quantity of gypsum and of talc; but as to this stone we do not know the use they made of it. The Mezcuitlatl, that is, dung of the moon, is of the class of those stones which, because of their resistance to the action of fire, are called by the chemists Lapides refractarii. It is transparent, and of a reddish gold color. But no other stone was so commonly used among the Mexicans as the Itztli, of which there is abundance in many places of Mexico. The Itztli is semi-diaphanous, of vitreous substance, and for the most part black; but there is also found white and blue. Of this stone they made mirrors, knives, lancets, razors, and even swords, as we shall say where we treat of their military affairs, and after the introduction of the Gospel highly prized altar stones were made of it. Dr. Hernández, that is, the Pliny of New Spain, describes in his Natural History as many as twelve hundred plants proper to that land; but his description, being limited to medicinal plants, scarcely comprises a part, though a large one, of what provident Nature has produced there for the benefit of mortals. Of medicinal plants we shall say a word when we treat of the medicine of the Mexicans. With regard to the other classes of vegetables, there are some valued for their flowers, others for their fruits, others for their leaves, others for their root, others for their stem or their wood, and others finally for their gum, resin, oil, or juice. The Floripundio, which by its size deserves the first place, is a white flower, beautiful, very fragrant, and monopetalous, that is, of a single leaf, but so large that it measures eight inches and even more in length, and three or four in diameter at the upper part. Many hang together from the branches in the form of bells, but not quite round, since their leaf, or corolla (*), makes five or six angles in it at proportionate distances from one another. These flowers grow on a pretty little shrub, whose branches form a round crown in the manner of a dome. Its trunk is tender, its leaves large, angular, and of a dull green.

> IL Coarzontecoxochii! , o Fior di resta viperina, è d' una incomparabile vaghezza , (4) E composto di cinque periti , o fo-

The flowers are followed by round fruits, as big as oranges, which have almonds inside.

> (*) Le foglie colorite , delle quali è composto il fiore, chiamansi pani da Fabio Colonna, e corolla da Linneo per distinguerle dalle vere foglie .

The Jolloxochitl, or Flower of the Heart, is also large, and no less valued for its beauty than for its scent, which is so strong that a single flower suffices to fill a whole house with the sweetest fragrance. It has many glutinous leaves, white on the outside and reddish or yellowish within, and so arranged that when the flower is open and its leaves spread it has the shape of a star, but when closed it somewhat resembles a heart, and for that reason it was given such a name. The tree that bears it is quite large, and its leaves long and rough. (p)

The Oceloxochitl, or Tiger Flower, is large, composed of three pointed leaves, and red, but toward the middle variegated with white and yellow, and in some manner representing the spots of that beast, whence it took its name. The plant has leaves likewise resembling those of the flag, and a bulbous root.

> Il Cacaloxochisl, o Fior del Corvo è picciolo, ma odaorofissimo , e dipinto di bianco , roflo, e giallo. L'albero, che porta questi fiori lì vede da elli coperto da per tutto, formandovi nell’ estremità dei rami dei mazzetti naturali non men alla vista, che all’ odorato gratiffimi . Nor v' è cola più comune di questi fiori nelle terre calde: gli Indiani se ne servono per ornare gli altari, e gli Spagnuoli ne fanno delle conserve deliziose. (r)

The Cacaloxochitl, or Raven's Flower, is small, but very fragrant, and painted white, red, and yellow. The tree that bears these flowers is seen to be covered with them everywhere, forming at the ends of the branches natural bunches most pleasing both to the sight and to the smell. There is nothing more common than these flowers in the hot lands: the Indians use them to adorn their altars, and the Spaniards make delicious preserves of them. (r)

> L' Ixquixochirl è un piccolo fior bianco, somigliante per la figura al Cynorbodo, o fia rosa falvatica, e pel gusto alla rosa coltivata, ma molto ad efla superiore per la fragranza, Niene in alberi grandi.

The Izquixochitl is a small white flower, resembling in shape the dog rose, or wild rose, and in taste the cultivated rose, but far superior to it in fragrance. It grows on large trees.

> IL Cempoalxochiri , © Cempasucbil, come dicono gli Spagnuoli, è quel fiore traspiantato in Europa , che i Francelì appellano Eiller d' Inde, o fia Garofano d' India . E' comunissimo nel Messico, dove ancor Ì’ appellano Fior dei Morti , e ve ne sono parecchie spezie diverse nella grandezza , nella figura, € nel numero di foglie, di cui son composti.

The Cempoalxochitl, or Cempasuchil as the Spaniards say, is the flower transplanted into Europe that the French call Œillet d'Inde, or Indian pink. It is very common in Mexico, where they also call it Flower of the Dead, and there are several different species of it, differing in size, in shape, and in the number of leaves of which they are composed.

Bk. I.

ant, and about six finger-breadths long, springing from a round calyx quite like that of the acorn, but different in size, in color, and in substance. Of these lovely flowers some are all red and others all white, and the tree that bears them is also most beautiful.

The Macpalxochitl, or Hand Flower, resembles the tulip; but its pistil represents the shape of a bird's foot, or rather that of a monkey, with six fingers ending in as many nails. The Spanish common folk of that kingdom give to the tree that bears these so curious flowers the name of Arbol de manitas.

Besides these and other innumerable flowers peculiar to that country, in the cultivation of which the Mexicans delighted, the land of

Mexico was enriched with all those that were transplanted there from

Asia and from Europe, such as lilies, jasmines, pinks of various species, and many others, which now in the gardens of Mexico vie with the American flowers.

As for fruits, the land of Anahuac is indebted in part to the Canary

names from the abundance of vines found there, from which many vineyards were made, which today yield good wine. In the Mixteca there are two species of wild vines, native to that land: the one, resembling the common vine both in its shoots and in the shape of its leaves, bears red grapes, large, and covered with a hard skin, but of a sweet and pleasing taste, which would doubtless be improved if they were brought under cultivation. The grape of the other vine is hard, large, and of a very harsh taste; but quite good preserves are made of it. Canaries; (t) but knowing that many hold a different opinion, I do not wish to engage in a dispute which, besides being of no importance to me, would divert me from the course of the History. It is certain that these plants, and all the others brought there from elsewhere, have thrived happily in that country, and have multiplied as much as in their own. All the maritime lands abound in coconut palms. Of oranges there are seven very different species, and of lemons at least four. There are as many, and very different ones, of (u) Musa, or Platano, as the Spaniards call it. The largest, which is the Zapalote, is from fifteen to twenty inches in length, and up to three in diameter. It is hard, and little esteemed, nor is it eaten otherwise than roasted or cooked. The Platano largo, that is, long, is eight inches at most in length

(t) Oviedo in his Natural History testifies that the first to carry the Musa from the Canary Islands to Hispaniola in 1516 was Fr. Tomás de Berlanga, a Dominican, and that from there it was transplanted to the continent of America. Hernández, in bk. 3, ch. 40 of his Natural History, speaks thus of the coconut: It grows everywhere among the Eastern Indians, and now also among the Western Indians. Bernal Díaz, in his True History of the Conquest, ch. 17, says that he sowed in the land of Coatzacoalco seven or eight orange seeds: And these, he adds, were the first oranges that were planted in New Spain. As for the Musa, it may be believed that of the four species there, only one is foreign, namely the one they call Guineo.

(u) The Musa was not entirely unknown to the ancients. Pliny, citing the account that the soldiers of Alexander the Great gave of all that they saw in India, makes this description of it: Another tree is greater, and more excellent in its fruit and sweetness, on which the wise men of the Indians live. Its leaf imitates the wings of birds, three cubits in length, two in breadth. It puts forth its fruit from the rind, wonderful for the sweetness of its juice, so that one satisfies four. The name of the tree is pala, of the fruit ariena. Hist. Nat., bk. XII, ch. VI. Besides these characteristics proper to the Musa, it must be added that the name Palan, given to the Musa in those remote times, is preserved to this day in Malabar, as Garcia de Orta, a learned Portuguese physician who lived there many years, attests. It might be suspected that from the name Palan the name Platano has been derived, which so ill suits it. The name Bananas, which the French give it, is what it has in Guinea, and that of Musa, which the Italians give it, is taken from the Arabic language. By some it is called Fruit of Paradise, and there was no lack of those who persuaded themselves that this was precisely the fruit that made our first Fathers transgress. This species of Musa is cultivated in the public garden of Bologna, and we have tasted it; but we found it so poorly ripened and unpleasant, on account of the climate, that it might be taken for another species altogether different from that one. The Dominico is the smallest, but also the most delicate. The plant, too, is smaller than the others. There are in that land whole forests, and very large ones, of Musa no less than of oranges and lemons, and in Michoacán a considerable trade is carried on in dried plantain, which is much better than grapes and figs.

(v) Several European writers on the things of America confuse the Chirimoya with

the Anona and with the Guanabana: but these are three different species of fruit, though the first two resemble each other somewhat. One must also take care not to confuse the Ananas with the Anona, which are more different from each other than the watermelon and the melon. M. de Bomare, on the contrary, makes two fruits of the Chirimoya and the Cherimolia, whereas cherimolia is nothing other than a corruption of the first and legitimate name of that fruit. The Ate also, which some set down as a fruit altogether different from the Chirimoya, is only a variety of its species.

All the fruits comprised by the Mexicans under the generic name of Tzapotl are round, or approach roundness, and all have a hard stone. (x) The black Zapote has a thin rind, green, smooth, and tender, and the pulp black, soft, and sweetly flavored, which at first sight resembles that of cassia. (y) Inside the pulp it has flat blackish stones, no longer than a finger's breadth. It is perfectly spherical, and its diameter is from one and a half to four or five inches. The tree is of medium size, and dense, and its leaves small. The pulp of this fruit, iced and seasoned with sugar and cinnamon, is of a delicate taste.

> gusto. delicato ;.

The white Zapote, which for its narcotic virtue was called by the Mexicans Cochitzapotl, is somewhat like the black one in size, in shape, and in the color of the rind, though in the rind of the white the green is lighter; but in other respects it differs greatly, for the pulp of this one is white and delightful. Its stone, which is believed to be poisonous, is large, round, hard, and white. The tree is dense, and larger than the black one, and the leaves are larger still. Moreover, the black is proper to a hot climate, and the white, on the contrary, to a cold or temperate one.

(y) Gemelli says that the black Zapote has also the flavor of cassia; but this is very far from the truth, as all those who have eaten it know. He says further that this fruit, when it is unripe, is poison to fish; but it is surprising that such an effect should have been known only to the foreigner Gemelli, who did not stay ten months in Mexico. Europe. The tree is of medium size, its wood good for working, and its leaves round, and similar in color and consistency to those of the orange tree. It grows without cultivation in the hot lands, and in the

Mixteca, in the Huasteca, and in Michoacán there are woods of such trees twelve and fifteen miles long. (A)

The Capollino, or Capulin, as the Spaniards call it, is the cherry of

Mexico. The tree is hardly distinguishable from the cherry tree of

Europe, and the fruit is similar in size, in color, and in the stone; but not so in flavor.

The Nance is a small round fruit, yellow, aromatic, and savory, with very small seeds, which grows on trees proper to the hot lands.

The Chayote is a round fruit, and similar in the husk with which it is covered to the chestnut, but four or five times larger, and of a deeper green color. Its flesh is greenish white, and in the middle it has a large stone, white and similar to the flesh in substance. It is eaten cooked together with the stone. This fruit grows on a twining and perennial plant, whose root is also good to eat.

> (q de

The plant of the Tlalcacahuatl, or Cacahuate, as the Spaniards call it, is without doubt one of the rarest that are found there. It is an herb, but very bushy, and well furnished with roots. Its leaves are somewhat like those of purslane, but less thick. Its little flowers are white, and from them comes no fruit. Its fruit grows not on the branches or on the stem, as in other plants, but attached to the hairlike fibers of the roots, inside a white sheath, grayish, long, roundish, ridged, and rough, just as it is represented in our third figure among those of the flowers and fruits. Each sheath holds two, three, or four cacahuates, which have the shape of pine nuts, but are much larger and thicker, and each is composed, like so many other seeds, of two lobes, and has its germinating point. It is edible, and of good taste, not raw, but a little toasted. If they are toasted more, they take on a smell and a taste so like those of coffee that it is not difficult to deceive anyone. An oil is made from the cacahuates which is not of bad taste; but it is believed to be harmful, because it is too heating. It gives a fine light, but is easily put out. This plant would surely thrive in Italy. It is sown in March or in April, and the harvest is gathered in October or in November.

Hernández counts four species; but the Tlalcacahuatl, the smallest of all, was the one the Mexicans most commonly used in their chocolate and in other daily drinks, while the other species served them more as money for trading in the market than as food. The cacao was one of the most cultivated plants in the hot lands of that kingdom; and several provinces paid tribute in it to the Crown of Mexico, among others that of Soconusco, whose cacao is excellent and better not only than that of Caracas, but also than that of Magdalena. The description of this celebrated plant, and of its cultivation, is found in many authors of all the civilized nations of Europe.

Vanilla, or Vainiglia, so well known and so much used in Europe, grows without cultivation in the hot lands. The ancient Mexicans used it in their chocolate and in other drinks which they made of cacao.

There are two species, the one black and small, from which an excellent oil for painting is drawn, and the other white and larger, from which a refreshing drink is made. Bk. I. Of the tomato there are six species, distinct in size, in color, and in taste. The largest, which is the Xictomatl, or Xitomate, as the Spaniards of Mexico call it, is already very common in Europe: in Spain and in France under the name of Tomate (D), and in Italy under that of Pomo d’oro. The Miltomatl is smaller, green, and perfectly round. How much both were used by the Mexicans at their meals will be told later, when we come to speak of their foods.

The Xocoxochitl, commonly known by the name of Tabasco pepper because it abounds in that province, is larger than the pepper of Malabar. It grows on a large tree, whose leaves have the color and the luster of those of the orange tree; and the flowers are a fine red, and similar in shape to those of the pomegranate, and of a lively and most pleasing odor, in which the branches also share. The fruit is round and grows in clusters, which, being green at first, afterwards turn almost black. This pepper, already used by the ancient Mexicans, can take the place of that of Malabar.

Cotton was, by reason of its usefulness, one of the most considerable fruits of that country: for it took the place of flax (although this plant, too, was not lacking to them (E)), and of it the inhabitants of Anahuac for the most part clothed themselves. There is a white kind, and a tawny kind, commonly called coyote. It is a plant very common in the hot lands, but much more cultivated by the ancients than by the moderns.

(D) The Tomatl of the Mexicans is the generic name of all the fruits of that class. The Spaniards of Europe and the French adopted it to signify the Xictomatl, which is the species known to them, and the Spaniards of Mexico to signify the Miltomatl, which in that country is the most usual.

(E) Flax was in fact found in Michoacán, in New Mexico, and in Quivira in great abundance, and of excellent quality; but we do not know that those nations cultivated it or made use of it. The Court of Spain, aware of the lands in the kingdom of Mexico that are suited to the cultivation of flax and hemp, sent to that country last year (1778) twelve peasant families from the Vega of Granada, so that they might employ themselves in this branch of agriculture.

As for the grains and pulses properly so called, that land received from Europe wheat, barley, rice, chickpeas, peas, broad beans, lentils, and others; all of which throve happily in lands suited to their nature, and have multiplied there as much as we shall show in our dissertations. (F)

Among the grains the chief, the most useful, and the most usual was maize, called by the Mexicans Tlaolli, of which there are many species differing in size, in color, in weight, and in taste. There is a large kind and a small, white, yellow, blue, purple, red, and black. Of maize the Mexicans made their bread and several dishes, of which we shall speak elsewhere. Maize was carried from America to Spain, and thence to other countries of Europe, to the great advantage of the poor, although there is no lack in our day of an author who claims to make America indebted to Europe for maize. A notion truly the most extravagant and the most improbable that can enter a man’s head. (G)

that was found in Michoacán, and boasts of its prodigious fecundity; but the ancients either did not know how, or else did not wish, to make use of it, valuing more highly, as they still do today, their maiz, or maize. The first who sowed European wheat in that land was a Black slave of the conqueror Cortés, who had found three or four grains inside a sack of rice that was carried for the provisioning of the

Spanish soldiers.

The principal pulse of the Mexicans was that of the beans, of which there are several species, and much more varied than those of Bk. I. maize. The largest species is that of the Ayacotli, which is the size of a broad bean, and springs from a handsome red flower; but the most esteemed is that of certain small, black, heavy beans. This pulse, which in Italy is little esteemed, because poor, is in Mexico so good that it serves not only for the sustenance of poor people, but also for the delicacies of the Spanish nobility.

I. del Frumentone , La spezie più grande è quella del Ayacorli , il quale è della grandezza d'una fava, e nasce d'’ un bel fior roflo ; ma la più stimara è quella di certi fagiuoli piccoli, neri, e pesanti. Questo legume, il quale in Italia è poco stimato , perchè cattivo, nel Messico è ranto buono , che fserve non solo al sostentamento della gente miserabile , ma anche alle delizie della Nobiltà Spagnuola .

Il Dottor Hernandez ne descrive in» fin' a diciannove spezie , ancor più diverse nella sostanza in teriore , che nella forma, e nel colore delle loro foglie , Nel libro VII, della nostra storia avremo occasione d' esporre i grandi vantaggi, che i Messicani traevano da queste piante e l’incredibile ‘profitto, che òoggidì ne tirano gli Spagnuoli , L’' Jezorl è una spezie di palma montana ben alta, che per lo più' ha ‘il tronco raddoppiato, I suoi rami hanno la Sgura d' un ventaglio, e le sue foglie quella d' una spada, I suoi fiori fon bianchi, ed odorofi , dei quali fanno buone conserve gli Spagnuoli-, e il suo frutto è ‘simile a prima vi sta alla ‘musa, ma affatro inutile, ‘Delle Foglie facevano anticamente,e-fanno. ancor oggi_delle-stuoje fine , & i Mesh: cani ne cavavano del filo per le loro manifatture.

The Huacamote is the sweet root of a species of Jucca (H), which is Bk. I.

> Non è questa l'unica palma di quel pacle., 4 la al quia Sua ru TT n" ——

also eaten cooked. The potato, a root transplanted to Europe and much esteemed in Ireland and in Sweden, was also carried to Mexico from South America, its own country, just as there were brought thither from Spain and from the Canaries several other roots and salad plants, such as turnips, radishes, carrots, garlic, lettuces, asparagus, cabbages, and the like. Of onions, Cortés bears witness in his letters to Charles V that they were sold in the markets of Mexico: so that they had no need to have them brought from Europe. Moreover, the name Xonacatl, which they give to the onion, and that of Xonacatepec, by which a place has been known since the time of the Mexican kings, make us know that this plant was very ancient in that land, and not transplanted from Europe.

The Maguei, called Metl by the Mexicans, Pita by the Spaniards, and by many authors American aloe, since it is in fact very like the true aloe, is among the most common and most useful plants of Mexico.

Dr. Hernández describes as many as nineteen species of it, still more different in the inner substance than in the form and the color of their leaves. In Book VII of our History we shall have occasion to set forth the great advantages which the Mexicans drew from these plants, and the incredible profit which the Spaniards draw from them today.

The Iczotl is a species of mountain palm, quite tall, which for the most part has a doubled trunk. Its branches have the shape of a fan, and its leaves that of a sword. Its flowers are white and fragrant, of which the Spaniards make good preserves, and its fruit is like the

Musa at first sight, but quite useless. Of the leaves they made in ancient times, and still make today, fine mats, and the Mexicans drew thread from them for their manufactures.

This is not the only palm of that country. Besides the royal

> Il Quaubcojolls È una palma di mediocre grandezza, il cui tronco è inaccessibile al Quadrupediì , per esser tutto armato di pine lunghe, forti, ' ed acurissime.. 1 suoi rami hanoo la figura d'una vago pennacchio, fra i quali perder fi vedono in grofli grappi i suoi frutti , tondi , grandi quanto le noci comunali, e com’ elle di quatrro parti composti , cioé una scorza da principio verde, e dipni fosca , una polpa gialla tenacemente al nocciolo attaccata, un nocciolo rotondo e durissimo , e dentro il nocciolo una mandorla, o midolla bianca . :

The Quauhcojolli is a palm of middling size, whose trunk is inaccessible to quadrupeds, being entirely armed with long, strong, and very sharp spines. Its branches have the shape of a handsome plume, among which its fruits are seen hanging in large clusters, round, as large as common walnuts, and like them composed of four parts, namely a husk at first green and afterwards dark, a yellow pulp tenaciously attached to the stone, a round and very hard stone, and inside the stone an almond, or white marrow.

La sua scorza infino alla profondità di tre dita non è altro; che ua ammasso di membrane lunghe un- piede in circa, fortili, € flessibili, ma peralcro forti, dalle quali unendone molte insiems fanno ‘alcuni poveri i lor marerassi .

The palm Ixhuatl is smaller, and has no more than six or seven branches, for where a new branch sprouts, one of the old ones soon dries up. Of its leaves they made baskets and mats, and today they make hats also and other articles. Its bark, to the depth of three finger-breadths, is nothing but a mass of membranes about a foot long, thin and flexible, but otherwise strong, of which, by joining many together, some poor people make their mattresses.

The palm Teoiczotl is also small. The pith of its trunk, which is soft, is surrounded by certain leaves of a peculiar substance, round, thick, white, smooth, and shining, which look like so many shells piled one upon another, and which the Indians used anciently, and still use today, for the ornament of the arches of boughs that they make for their festivals.

As for the excellence, the variety, and the abundance of woods, that country yields to none in the world; for since no sort of climate is lacking there, neither are the trees proper to each lacking. Besides the oaks, the durmast oaks, the firs, the pines, the cypresses, the beeches, the elms, the walnuts, the poplars, and very many others common in Europe, there are whole forests of cedars and of ebonies, the two kinds of trees most esteemed by the ancients; there is a great quantity of agalloch, or aloes-wood, in the Mixteca, of Tapinzeran in

Michoacán, of Caoba in Chiapas, of Palo gateado, which we might call striped wood, in Zoncoliuhcan (today Zongolica), of Camote in the mountains of Texcoco, of Granadillo, or red ebony, in the Mixteca and elsewhere, of Mizquitl or true acacia, of Tepehuaxin, of Coptè, of Jabin, of Guayacan, or lignum vitae, of Ayaquahuitl, of Oyametl, of Zopilote wood, and of other innumerable woods valued for their incorruptibility, for their hardness and weight, (K) for their pliancy or ease of carving, for the beauty of their colors, or for their fragrance. The Camote has a most beautiful purple color, and the Granadillo a dark red; but still more beautiful are the Palo gateado, the Caoba, and the

Tzopiloquahuitl, or Zopilote wood. The hardness of the Guayacan is already well known in Europe, and that of the Jabin is no less. The aloes-wood of the Mixteca, although different from the true agalloch of the Levant, judging by the description that

Dr. Hernández describes in his Natural History about a hundred species of trees; but since he devoted his study principally, as we have already said, to medicinal plants, he leaves out the greater part of the trees which that most fertile land bears, and especially those most considerable for their size and for the preciousness of their wood. There are trees of a height and breadth so surprising that they are in no way inferior to those that Pliny boasts of as miracles of Nature.

Father Acosta makes mention of a cedar that was in Atlacuechahuayan, a place nine miles distant from Antequera, or Oaxaca, whose trunk had a circumference of sixteen brazas, that is, more than eighty-two Paris feet; and I have myself seen in a country house a beam a hundred and twenty Castilian feet long, or a hundred and seven Paris feet. In several houses of the capital, and of other cities of the kingdom, very large cedar planks of a single piece are to be seen. In the valley of Atlixco there is still preserved alive a very ancient fir (L), so large that in the cavity in its trunk made by

ably. A still greater idea of its breadth is given us by a testimony as authoritative as that of His Excellency Señor Don Francisco Lorenzana, formerly Archbishop of Mexico, and at present of Toledo. This prelate, in the annotations made by him on the Letters of the

Conqueror Cortés to Charles V, printed in Mexico City in 1770, bears witness to us that, having himself gone to observe that renowned tree, in company with the Archbishop of Guatemala and the Bishop of Puebla, he had as many as a hundred boys enter the aforesaid cavity of the tree.

Comparable also with this famous fir are the Ceibas which I saw in the maritime province of Jicayán. The breadth of these trees is proportioned to their prodigious height, and their prospect is supremely delightful in the season when they are seen adorned with new foliage, and laden with fruit, inside which is a certain kind of cotton, white, fine, and most delicate. Cloths could be made of it, and in fact have been made, as soft and delicate as those of silk, and perhaps even more so; (M) but it is hard to spin on account of the smallness of the threads, besides which the advantage would be less than the labor, since the cloth would have to be of little durability. Some use that cotton in cushions and mattresses, which have the peculiarity of swelling enormously in the heat of the sun.

Among very many trees worthy of memory for their singularity, which I am compelled to pass over, there is one I cannot omit, a certain kind of wild fig tree, which grows in the country of the

Cohuixcas his Natural History. I saw the fir of Atlixco as I passed through that city in 1756, but not so near that I could form a just idea of its size.

(M) M. de Bomare says that the Africans make of the thread of the Ceiba the veg‐

etable taffeta so rare and so esteemed in Europe. I do not wonder at the rarity of such a cloth, given the difficulty there is in making it. The name Ceiba is taken, like many others, from the language that was spoken in the island of Haiti, or Santo

Domingo. The Mexicans call it Pochotl, and many Spaniards Pochote. In Africa it has the name of Benten. The Ceiba, says the aforesaid author, is taller than all the trees hitherto known.

The Huitziloxitl, from which the balsam distills, is a tree of middling height. Its leaves are somewhat like those of the almond tree, but larger; its wood is reddish and fragrant, and the bark ashen, but covered with a reddish film. Its pale flowers come at the ends of the branches. Its seed is small, whitish, and curved, and comes likewise at the end of a thin husk a finger long. At whatever point an incision is made, especially after rains, there distills from it that most noble resin so greatly esteemed in Europe, and in no way inferior to the renowned balsam of Palestine. (O) Our balsam is reddish black, or else whitish yellow; for of the one color and of the other it flows from the incision; of an acrid and bitter taste, and of an intense but most agreeable odor. The balsam tree is common in the provinces of Pánuco and of Chiapas,

The abundance of these precious plants makes them disregard the loss of a great number of them, so as not to have to wait for the slowness of the distillation. Not only did the ancient

> P) Ti dell' HuitziloxitI un clio fimile nell’ odore e ne Hpore 4 quella di Fur e e amare, ma di. maggiore acrimania » e d un odor xe più intenso, il quale, È molto utile nella medicina n >

Mexicans gather the opobalsamum, or tear, distilled from the trunk, but they also obtained the xylobalsamum by the decoction of the branches. (P) From the Huaconex, and from the Maripenda (*) they obtained likewise an oil equivalent to balsam. The Huaconex is a tree of middling height, and of aromatic and hard wood, which keeps uncorrupted for years, even when buried in the earth. Its leaves are small and yellow, the flowers likewise small and whitish, and the fruit like that of the laurel. They drew the oil by distillation from the bark of the tree, after breaking it up, keeping it three days in ordinary water, and then drying it in the sun. They drew also from the leaves an oil of agreeable odor. The Maripenda is a shrub, whose leaves have the shape of a lance head, and the fruit is like the grape, and comes in clusters, at first green, then red. They drew the oil by the decoction of the branches mixed with some fruit.

The Xochiocotzotl, commonly called liquidambar, is the liquid storax of the Mexicans. The tree is large (not merely a small shrub, as

Pluche says); its leaves are somewhat like those of the maple, toothed, whitish on one side, dark on the other, and arranged in threes. The fruit is spiny and roundish, but polygonal, with black surfaces and yellow angles. The bark of the tree is in part green and in part tawny. From the trunk is drawn by incision that

(P) An oil is also drawn from the fruit of the Huitziloxitl, similar in odor and in

The Mexican name Copalli is generic, and common to all resins, but especially signifies those that serve for incense. There are as many as ten species of trees that yield these sorts of resin, differing among themselves not so much in name as in the form of the foliage and of the fruit, and in the quality of the resin. The Copal, by antonomasia, is a white and transparent resin, which distills from a large tree, whose leaves resemble those of the oak, but are larger, and the fruit is roundish and reddish. This resin is well known in Europe under the name of gum copal, and the use made of it both in medicine and in varnishes is also well known. The ancient Mexicans used it principally in the incensings which they made, now for the religious worship of their idols, now as homage to ambassadors and other persons of the first rank. Today they consume a great quantity of it in the worship of the true God and of his saints. The Tecopalli, or Tepecopalli, is a resin like the frankincense of Arabia in color, in odor, and in taste, which distills from a tree of middling size, that grows in the mountains, whose fruit is like an acorn containing a pine nut moistened with a mucilage, or viscous saliva, and inside it a little almond, which is usefully employed in medicine. Both these trees, and all the others of this class, in whose description we cannot linger, are proper to hot lands.

The Mizquitl, or Mezquite, as the Spaniards call it, is a species of true acacia, and the gum that distills from it is true gum arabic, as Dr.

> La Lacca o lia Gamma lacca ( come luol. chiamarsi dagli Speziali, ) scorre , in zanta abbondanza da \un albero al Mezquite somigliante, che ne restano coperti i rami . (R)

Hernández and other learned naturalists bear witness. The mesquite is a thorny shrub, whose branches are very irregularly arranged, and the leaves, thin, slender, and conjugate, that is, growing on one side and the other of the branches, resemble the feathers of birds; its flowers are similar to those of the birch. Its fruits are sweet and edible pods, and contain the seed, of which the barbarous Chichimecs anciently made a paste that served them for bread. Its wood is very hard and heavy. These trees are almost as common in Mexico as oaks in Europe, especially on the hills of the temperate countries. (Q)

Dragon’s blood distills from a large tree, whose leaves are broad and angular. This tree grows in the mountains of Huauchinango and in those of the Cohuixcas. (S)

The elastic resin, called Olin or Olli by the Mexicans, and Ule by the Spaniards of that kingdom, distills from the Olquahuitl, which is a tree of sufficient size, whose trunk is smooth and yellowish, the leaves quite large, the flowers white, and the fruit yellow and roundish, but angular, inside which there are almonds as large as hazelnuts, white, but covered with a yellowish skin. The almond has a bitter taste, and the fruit is always attached to the bark of the tree. The Ule, as it distills from the wounded trunk, is white, liquid, and viscous: then it becomes yellowish, and finally takes the color of lead, somewhat blacker, which it keeps from then on. Those who gather it have it take in various molds whatever form they wish, according to the use for which they intend it. This resin, condensed, is of all solid bodies the most elastic that we know.

The Mexicans made their balls of this resin, which, though heavy, bound higher than those of air. Today, besides this use, they use it, as wax is used in Europe, for making hats, boots, greatcoats, and cloaks

The Quauhxiotl is a tree of middling size, whose leaves are round, and the bark reddish. There are two subordinate species of it: one yields a white gum, which, put in water, tinges it a milky color; the other distills a reddish gum, both most useful for dysentery.

Sappiamo eflere quei boschi , quelle montagne, e quelle valli d' infiniti vegetabili utilisimi e preziosi ripiene , senza trovarsi alcuno, che volger voglia lo \guardo a riconoscergli . > s. 10. Non è meno sconosciuto il regno animale , malgrado la pedi del diligenza, che anche in questa parte adoperò il Dottor Herregno di nandez. La difficoltà , che v' è nel distinguere le spezie, € Messico, la meio

(a plant like the fig tree), and the ocote, a certain species of very aromatic pine, for the oil they yield; and brazil-wood, logwood or

Campeachy wood, indigo, and many others for their juices; but several of these plants are already known in Europe, and of others we shall have occasion to speak elsewhere.

That small part of the vegetable kingdom of Anahuac which we have so far set forth renews in us the sorrow we feel at seeing vanished, and for the most part lost, that exact knowledge of natural history which the ancient Mexicans had acquired. We know that those woods, those mountains, and those valleys are full of infinite plants most useful and precious, without finding anyone who is willing to turn his gaze to examine them. Whom will it not grieve that of the immense treasures drawn during the last two centuries and a half from those richest mines, no part has been set aside to found academies of naturalists, who, following in the footsteps of the most distinguished Hernández, might discover for the benefit of society those precious gifts which the Creator has so liberally bestowed upon them?

> Tra' Quadrupedi altri sono nuovi, ed altri antichi. I nuovi ( così appelliamo quelli, che nel secolo XVI. furono dalle Canarie, e dall’ Europa in quella terra trasportati ) sono i Cavalli, gli Afini , i Tori, le Pecore, le Capre, i Porci, i Cani, ed i Garti, tutti i quali fi sono così felicemente E cotanto moltiplicati , quanto faremo vedere nella nostra IV, diflertazione contro certi Filosofi del Secolo, che fi sono preso I’ impegno di persuaderci la degradazione di tutti i Quadrapedi nel nuovo Mondo.

Bk. I. the history of animals difficult and arduous. The first Spanish nomenclators, more versed in the art of war than in the study of nature, instead of retaining, as would have been better, the names which the Mexicans gave to their animals, called several animals of very different species tigers, wolves, bears, dogs, squirrels, etc., either from the similarity of the color of the skin, or of other features, or from conformity in certain operations and properties. Now I do not pretend to correct their errors, nor even to illustrate the natural history of that vast kingdom; but only to give my readers some idea of the quadrupeds, the birds, the reptiles, the fish, and the insects that live on the land and in the waters of Anahuac.

> Dei Quadrupedi antichi, cioè di quelli , che da tempo immemorabile in quella terra s' allevavano , altri erano comuni a tutti i due i continenti, altrì particolari del nuovo Mondo, ma pure comuni al Messico ed ad altri paesi dell’ America Settentrionale , o della Meridionale, ed altri finalmente propri soltanto del regno di Mellico.

Among the quadrupeds some are new, and others ancient. The new ones (so we call those which in the sixteenth century were carried to that land from the Canaries and from Europe) are the horses, the asses, the bulls, the sheep, the goats, the hogs, the dogs, and the cats, all of which have multiplied as happily and as greatly as we shall show in our Fourth Dissertation against certain philosophers of the age, who have taken it upon themselves to persuade us of the degradation of all the quadrupeds in the New World.

> I Quadrupedì antichi comuni al Messico, e all' antico «Continente , sono i Lioni, le Tigri, i Gatti salvatici , gl’ Orf, i Lupi, le Volpi, i Cervi così i comuni, come i bian- «chi (U) i Daini, le Capre falvatiche , i Tassi, le Faine , le

Of the ancient quadrupeds, that is, of those which from time immemorial have bred in that land, some were common to both continents, others peculiar to the New World, but yet common to Mexico and to other countries of North or South America, and others finally proper only to the kingdom of Mexico.

The ancient quadrupeds common to Mexico and to the old continent are the lions, the tigers, the wild cats, the bears, the wolves, the foxes, the deer, both the common and the white (U), the fallow deer, the wild goats, the badgers, the beech martens, the

weasels

(U) The white deer, whether of the same species or of a species distinct from the other deer, are undoubtedly common to both continents [p. 70] weasels, the martens, the squirrels, the polatouches, the rabbits, the Bk. I.

> Liu. I le Lepri, le Lodre, e i Sorcj. So bene, che il Signor de Buffon nega all’ America i Lioni , le Tigri, ed i Conigli ; ma siccome la sua opinione principalmente appoggiara sul debole fondamento della pretesa impossibilità del paslaggio al nuovo continente degli animali proprj delle terre calde dell’ antico mondo, è da noi nelle nostre dissertazioni abbastanza impugnata, non è d' uopo interrompere il corso della nostra itoria per ribatterla ,

hares, the otters, and the mice. I know well that M. de Buffon denies to America the lions, the tigers, and the rabbits; but since his opinion rests chiefly on the weak foundation of the alleged impossibility of the passage to the new continent of animals proper to the hot lands of the old world, and is sufficiently contested by us in our dissertations, there is no need to interrupt the course of our History to refute it.

The Miztli of the Mexicans is nothing other than the maneless lion mentioned by Pliny, (V) and quite distinct from the lion of Africa; and the Ocelotl is not different from the African tiger, as Dr.

Hernández, who knew both, bears witness. The Tochtli of Mexico is the same rabbit as that of the old continent, and at least as ancient in that country as the calendar of the Mexicans, in which the figure of the rabbit was the first character of their years. The wild cats, much larger than the domestic ones, are very fierce and feared. The bears are all black, and more corpulent than those that are seen in Italy, brought from the Alps. The hares are distinguished from the

European by having longer ears, and the wolves by having a larger head. Both species abound too much in that land. Polatouche we call, with M. de Buffon, the Quimichpatlan, or flying mouse of the

Mexicans. They called it mouse because it is like one in the head, though larger; and flying, because, having in its natural state the skin of the flanks loose and wrinkled, when it wants to make a violent leap from one tree to another, it stretches and

They were known to the Greeks and to the Romans. The Mexicans called them kings of the deer. M. de Buffon would persuade us that whiteness in deer is an effect of their servitude; but since there are found in the mountains of New Spain, as in fact there are, white deer that have never been slaves of men, such a thought no longer has any place.

The species of quadrupeds that were in the kingdom of Mexico, common also to other countries of the New World, are the Cojametl, the Epatl, several species of monkeys, comprised by the Spaniards under the generic name of Monos, the Ajotochtli, the Aztacojotl, the Tlacuatzin, the Techichi, the Tlalmototli, the Techallotl, the Amiztli, the Mapach, and the Danta (X).

The Cojametl, to which the Spaniards give, because of its resemblance to the boar, the name of Javali, or wild hog, is called in other countries of America Pecar, Saino, and Tayassù. (X) Several authors count among the animals of Mexico the Paco, or Peruvian sheep, the Huanaco, the vicuña, the taruca, and the sloth; but all these quadrupeds are proper to South America, and none of them to North America. It is true that Dr. Hernández makes mention among the quadrupeds of New Spain of the Paco, gives its portrait, and uses the Mexican name Pelonichcatl; but he did so on account of some individuals brought there from Peru, to which the Mexicans gave that name, as he also describes several animals of the Philippine Islands; yet they have never been bred in Mexico, nor are they found in any country of North America, unless perhaps some individual taken there out of curiosity, as one has been taken to Europe. Sarigua, and Opossum, has been described by many authors, and is quite famous for the doubled skin which the female has on her belly, from the beginning of the stomach to the orifice of the womb; it covers her teats and has in the middle an opening, where she receives her young after bearing them, to keep them well guarded and to suckle them. In walking, and in climbing the walls of houses, she holds the skin stretched out and the opening shut, so that the young cannot get out; but when she wishes to send them out, that they may begin to seek their own food, or to bring them in again, whether to suckle them or to snatch them from some danger, she opens the passage by loosening the skin, counterfeiting pregnancy while she carries them and birth every time she sets them out. This curious quadruped is the destroyer of poultry-yards.

South America. We find no reason to believe them four different species, but only four breeds of one and the same species. The names which the Mexicans give to the first two breeds are Izquiepatl and Conepatl, which breeds are distinguished only in size and color. The name Coaso or Squash, taken from the traveler Dampier, who affirms that it is common in New Spain, has never been heard in that whole land. The

Indians of Yucatán, where the said traveler stayed, call that quadruped Pai. [p. 73] for those bony plates with which it keeps its back covered, in imitation of the ancient armor of horses. The Mexicans gave it that name Bk. I. for the resemblance, though imperfect, which it bears to the rabbit when it puts out its head, and to the gourd when it takes shelter beneath its plates, or shells; (Z) but it resembles no other animal more than the tortoise, although in several features it is not a little unlike it: one might give it the name of testaceous quadruped. Whenever this animal finds itself pursued on some plain, it has no way of escaping from the hands of the hunter; but since it ordinarily inhabits the mountains, where it finds some slope, it curls up, makes itself into a ball, and, rolling down the hillside, leaves the hunter mocked.

The Techichi, which elsewhere had the name of Alco, was a quadruped of Mexico and of other countries of America, which, because it was like a small dog in shape, was called Perro, that is, dog, by the Spaniards. It was of a melancholy aspect and altogether mute: whence arose the fable, spread by several authors still living, that all the dogs carried over from the old world become mute in the new. The flesh of the Techichi was eaten by the Mexicans, and, if we give credit to the Spaniards who still ate it, was of good taste and nourishing. The Spaniards after the Conquest of Mexico, having as yet neither herds nor flocks, supplied their slaughterhouses with these quadrupeds; so that in a short time they consumed the species, although it was numerous.

The Tlalmototli, or ground squirrel, called the Swiss by M. de Buffon, resembles the true squirrel in the eyes, the tail, the swiftness, and in all its movements

(Z) Ajotochtli is a word composed of Ajotli, Gourd, and Tochtli, Rabbit. M. de Buffon counts eight species of it under the name of Tatous, taking their diversity from the number of plates and movable bands that cover them. I could not say how many species there are in Mexico, since I have seen few individuals, and at that time, as I was not thinking of writing on this subject, I was not curious to count the plates and bands, nor do I know whether anyone has taken this trouble. [p. 74] but it is very unlike it in color, in size, in dwelling, and in some propBk. I.

erty. The hair of its belly is all white, and elsewhere white mixed with gray. Its size is double that of the squirrel, and it does not live, as the squirrel does, in trees, but in the small burrows which it digs in the ground, or among the stones of the bulwarks that surround the fields, in which it does considerable damage because of the great quantity of grain that it steals from them. It bites furiously anyone who approaches, and is incapable of being tamed; but for the rest it has elegance of form and grace in its movements. The species of these quadrupeds is among the most numerous, especially in the kingdom of Michoacán. The Techallotl is hardly to be distinguished from the aforesaid animals, except in having a smaller and less hairy tail.

The Amiztli, or water lion, is an amphibious quadruped that lives on the shores of the Pacific Ocean and in some rivers of that kingdom. Its body is three feet long, and its tail two. Its muzzle is long, its legs short, and its claws curved. Its skin is valuable for the length and softness of the hair. (aa)

The Mapach of the Mexicans is, in the opinion of M. de Buffon, the very same quadruped as is known in Jamaica by the name of

Ratton. The Mexican one is the size of a badger, with a black head, a long and slender muzzle like that of the greyhound, small ears, a rounded body, hair variegated with black and white, a long and well-furred tail, and five toes on each foot. Above each eye it has a little white band, and, like the squirrel, it uses its paws to carry to its mouth what it wishes to eat. It feeds indifferently on grain, fruit, insects, lizards, and the blood of hens. It is easily tamed, and is very graceful in its play; but it

The Danta, or Anta, or Beori, or Tapir (for it has various names in various countries) is the bulkiest quadruped of all that were in the lands of the Mexican kingdom, (bb) and the one that comes nearest to the hippopotamus, not only in size but in certain features and in some properties. The Danta is as large as a middling mule. Its body is somewhat arched like that of the hog; its head is thick and long, with an appendage in the skin of the upper lip, which it widens or shortens at will; its eyes are small, its ears small and round, its legs short, its forefeet have four hooves and its hind feet three, its tail is short and pyramidal; its skin is very thick and clothed with dense hair, which in maturity is brown. Its dentition, made up of twenty molars and as many incisors, is so strong and sharp, and the bites it inflicts are so terrible, that it has been seen, as the historian Oviedo attests as an eyewitness, to tear away at one stroke of its teeth a span or two of skin from a hunting dog, and from another a whole leg with the thigh. Its flesh is edible, (cc) and its skin valuable, since it is so strong that it resists not only arrows but even musket balls. This quadruped inhabits the solitary woods of the hot lands, near some river or little lake, since it lives no less in the water than on land.

All the species of monkeys that are in that kingdom are known to the Mexicans under the general name of Ozomatli, and to the Spaniards under that of Monos. There are some of various sizes and shapes: small ones and singularly

The quadrupeds most peculiar to the land of Anahuac, whose species I do not know to be found in South America, nor in other countries of North America not subject to the Crown of Spain, were the Cojotl, the Tlalcojotl, the Xoloitzcuintli, the Tepeitzcuintli, the

Itzcuintepotzotli, the Ocotochtli, the Cojopollin, the Tuza, the Ahuitzotl, the Huitztlacuatzin, and others perhaps unknown to us.

[p. 77] the jackal; whence several historians of Mexico have assigned it now to one species, now to another; but it is nonetheless indubitably dif‐ Bk. I. ferent from all of these, as we demonstrate in our dissertations. It is smaller than the wolf, and as large as a mastiff, but leaner. It has yellow, sparkling eyes, small, pointed, erect ears, a blackish muzzle, strong legs, feet armed with thick, curved claws, a thick and hairy tail, and a skin variegated with black, dusky brown, and white. Its voice has something of the howl of the wolf and of the barking of the dog. The Coyote is among the most common quadrupeds in Mexico, (ff) and among those most harmful to flocks. It assails a herd, and where it finds no lamb to carry off, it seizes a sheep by the neck with its teeth, and, joined to it in this way and beating its rump with its tail, leads it where it wishes. It pursues deer, and sometimes even attacks men. In flight it commonly does nothing but trot; but this trot is so lively and so swift that a horse at the gallop can hardly overtake it. The Cuetlachcojotl seems to us a quadruped of the same species as the Coyote; for it is not distinguished from it except by having a thicker neck and hair like that of the wolf.

The Tlalcojotl, or Tlalcoyote, is the size of a middling dog, but stouter, and is in our opinion the bulkiest of all the quadrupeds that live underground. In the head it somewhat resembles the cat, and the lion in color and in the length of its hair. It has a long, bushy tail, and feeds on hens and other small animals, which it hunts in the darkness of the night.

The Cojopollin is a quadruped as large as an ordinary rat; but it has a thicker tail, and uses it in place of a hand. The muzzle and the ears are like those of a little pig; the ears are transparent, the legs and feet white, and the belly yellowish white. It lives and rears its young in trees. The young, when they are afraid, cling tightly to their mother.

The Tozan, or Tuza, is a quadruped equivalent to the mole of Europe, but very different. Its body, which is well formed, is seven or eight inches long. Its muzzle is like that of the rat, its ears small and round, and its tail short. Its mouth is armed with very strong teeth, and its feet furnished with strong, curved claws, with which it digs the earth and makes for itself the burrows where it lives. The Tuza is most pernicious to the fields because of the grain it steals, and to travelers because of the many burrows or holes it makes in the roads; for where, because of its poor sight, it does not find the first burrow, it makes another, thus multiplying the inconveniences and dangers for those who travel on horseback. It digs the earth with its paws and with two canine teeth, larger than the others, which it has in the upper jaw; in digging it puts the earth into two membranes made in the manner of pouches, which it has beneath the ears, furnished with the muscles necessary for their contraction and dilation. When it has filled the membranes, it empties them by shaking the bottoms of the membranes with its paws, and then returns to dig in the same manner, using in this labor the canine teeth, and the claws in place of a hoe, and the membranes

The Ahuitzotl is an amphibious quadruped, which for the most part lives in the rivers of the hot lands. Its body is a foot long, its muzzle long and pointed, and its tail large. Its skin is variegated with the colors black and brown.

The Huitztlacuatzin is the porcupine, or spiny hog, of Mexico. It is as large as a middling dog, which it resembles in the face, although its muzzle is flattened; its feet and legs are quite thick, and its tail is proportioned to the size of the body. Its whole body, except the belly, the hinder part of the tail, and the inner part of the legs, is armed with hollow, sharp quills or spines, four finger-breadths long. On the muzzle and the forehead it has long, erect bristles, which rise above the head in the manner of a plume. Its whole skin, even between the spines, is covered with soft black hair. It feeds only on the fruits of the earth. (ii)

The Cacomiztle is a quadruped very much like the beech marten in its manner of living. It has the size and form of a common cat; but its body is thicker, its hair longer, its legs shorter, and its aspect wilder and fiercer. Its voice is a shrill cry, and its food hens and other small animals. It lives and rears its young in the less frequented parts of houses. By day it sees little, and does not come out of its hiding place except at night to procure its food. Both the Cacomiztle and the

Tlacuatzin are found even in the houses of the capital. (jj)

of Mexico. form and character. Their abundance and variety, and their excellence, have led some authors to say that Mexico is the kingdom of birds, as Africa is that of wild beasts. Dr. Hernández in his Natural History describes more than two hundred species peculiar to that country, and yet he leaves out several worthy of record, such as the Cuitlacochi, the Zacua, and the Madrugador. We shall content ourselves with running through a few classes, pointing out some particular feature where occasion calls for it. Among the birds of prey there are kestrels, goshawks, and several species of eagles, falcons, and sparrowhawks. To the birds of this class the aforesaid naturalist grants superiority over those of Europe. Because of the well-known excellence of the Mexican falcons, Philip II, king of Spain, ordered that a hundred of them be brought to his court every year. Among the eagles the largest, the handsomest, and the most renowned is the one the Mexicans call Itzquauhtli, which hunts not only the largest birds and hares, but attacks even men and wild beasts. Of the kestrels there are two species: the one called Cenotzqui is very handsome.

South America by the name of Gallinazos, by others by that of Auras, and by some, finally, by the most improper one of ravens. (kk) There are two species of these birds, very different from each other: that of the true Zopilote, and that of the Cozcaquauhtli. Both are larger than the raven. These two species agree in having a curved beak and claws, and on the head, instead of feathers, a wrinkled membrane with a few curly hairs. In flight they rise to such a height that, though so large, they pass out of sight, and especially when a hailstorm is about to come they are seen wheeling in great numbers beneath the high clouds until they vanish in the distance. They feed on carrion, which they see with their most keen eyes, or else sense with their very lively sense of smell, from the greatest height, and then descend, forming with majestic flight a great spiral line down to the carcass on which they wish to feed. Both are almost mute. The two species are distinguished in size, color, number, and some property. The true Zopilotes have black feathers, and the head, beak, and feet brown; they often go in troops, and spend the night together in the trees. (ll) Their species is very numerous, and common to all climes. The species of
