(mm) That bird which now has in New Spain the name of King of the Zopilotes seems different from the one we describe. That modern King of the Zopilotes is as large as a common eagle, robust, and of a majestic air, with strong talons, lively and handsome eyes, and fine black, white, and tawny feathers: the most singular thing is that fleshy growth of scarlet color which surrounds the neck like a collar, and covers the head like a little crown. So it was described to me by a capable and trustworthy person, who says he has seen three individuals of that species, and in particular the one that in 1750 was sent from Mexico to the Catholic King Ferdinand VI. He says besides that the portrait of a bird published in the work entitled Il Gazzettiere americano is true to life. The Mexican name Cozcaquauhtli, which means eagle with a collar, really suits this one more than the other. The image of this bird, which is seen among our figures, is a copy of that in the Gazzettiere americano. [p. 84] as those of the Philippine Islands and of other eastern regions. Bk. I.

> Lis orientali .

Among the water birds we wish to count not only the web-footed birds (palmipedes), which swim and commonly live in the water, but also the long-shanked waders (himantopodes), and other fishers, which live for the most part on the shores of the sea, the lakes, and the rivers, and find their food in the water. In this order of birds there is a prodigious number of geese, at least twenty species of ducks, several kinds of herons and egrets, very many swans, gulls, moorhens, cormorants, halcyons, kingfishers, pelicans, and others. The multitude of the ducks is so great that at times they cover the fields, and seen from some distance they look like flocks of grazing sheep. Among the egrets and herons there are gray ones, wholly white ones, and others which, having the feathers of the body white, have the neck, the extremities, the front part of the wings, and a part of the tail adorned with a vivid scarlet color or a beautiful blue. The pelican, or onocrotalus, known to the Spaniards of Mexico by the name of Alcatraz, is well known for that enormous pouch, or belly, as Pliny calls it, which it has under the beak. There are two species of it in Mexico: one has the beak smooth, and the other has it toothed. I do not know whether, as this bird is known to Europeans, so is known its rare property of succoring the disabled individuals of its species, which some

Americans make use of to provide themselves with fish without labor.

They take a pelican alive, break one of its wings, and, tying it to a tree, lie in ambush in a place nearby, where they wait for the arrival of the other pelicans with their provision, and when they have seen them throw the fish from the pouch, they run up at once, and, leaving the prisoner a part of it, carry off the rest.

But if the pelican is worthy of admiration for its providence toward others of its species, no less admirable is the Toalquachilli for the arms with which the Creator has furnished it for its defense. This is a small water bird with [p. 85] a long, slender neck, a small head, a long yellow beak, long legs, feet, and claws, and a short tail. The color of its legs and feet is ash-gray, Bk. In the other classes of birds there are some valued for their flesh, others for their feathers, others for their song or their voice, and others finally for their instinct, or for some notable property of theirs which may interest our curiosity.

As to the birds whose flesh is wholesome and pleasant nourishment, I have counted more than seventy species. Besides the common hens carried from the Canary Islands to the Antilles, and thence to Mexico, there were and are hens proper to that country, which, because they are in part like the common hens and in part like peafowl, were called Gallipavos by the Spaniards, and Huexolotl and Totolin by the Mexicans. These birds, carried to Europe in return for the hens, have multiplied excessively, particularly in Italy, where, in view of their character and their size, they were given the name of turkeys; (*) but the multiplication of the European hens in Mexico has been far greater. There are also in great abundance wild turkeys, everywhere like the domestic ones, but larger, and in many countries of more savory flesh. There are partridges, quails, pheasants, cranes, turtledoves, doves, and very many others esteemed in Europe. The prodigious number of the quails may be known from what we shall say when we come to speak of the ancient sacrifices. The birds known there by the name of pheasants are of three species different from the

size of a goose and with a crest on the head which they spread and fold at will, are distinguished from each other in color and in some property. The Coxolitli, called royal pheasant by the Spaniards, has tawny feathers, and its flesh is more delicate. The Tepetototl grows so tame that it takes food from its master’s hand, comes to meet him when it sees him enter the house, making demonstrations of joy, learns to knock at the door with its beak, and in all things shows itself more docile than might have been expected of a bird native to the woods. I saw one of these pheasants which, having been for some time in a poultry yard, learned the manner of fighting of the cocks, and fought with them raising the feathers of its crest, as the cocks raise those of the neck. It has black, shining feathers, and the legs and feet ashen. The pheasants of the third species, called Gritones by the Spaniards, that is, Criers, are smaller than the others, and have the tail and wings black, and the rest of the body brown. The

The noise that these birds make in the woods with their cries is incredible; though similar to those of hens, they are louder, more continuous, and more annoying. Of turtledoves and doves there are several species, some common to Europe and others proper to those countries.

The birds valued for their feathers are so many, and so beautiful, that we should give our readers great pleasure if we could represent them to their eyes with all the colors that adorn their feathers. I have counted as many as thirty-five species of Mexican birds exceedingly beautiful, of which some will have to be mentioned by us.

The Huitzitzilin is that marvelous little bird so celebrated by the historians of America for its smallness, its mobility, the singular beau‐ Bk. I. ty of its little feathers, the slightness of its food, and the length of its sleep in winter. This sleep, or rather this immobility, caused by the stiffness or numbness of its limbs, has been judicially established several times to convince the incredulity of some Europeans: an incredulity in truth caused by ignorance; for the same immobility is seen in several countries of Europe in dormice, hedgehogs, swallows, bats, and other animals whose blood is equally cold, although in no other is it perhaps so long as in the Huitzitzilin, since this little bird remains in some countries deprived of all movement from October until April. As many as nine species of Huitzitzilin are counted, differing in size and in colors. (pp)

The Mezcanauhtli is a wild duck, the size of the moorhen, but of singular beauty. It has a moderately long and broad beak, blue above and black beneath; the feathers of the body white, but spotted with many black points. Its wings are white and brown beneath, and above variegated with black, white, blue, green, and tawny. Its feet are reddish yellow, its head partly brown, partly tawny, and partly purple, with a beautiful white spot between the beak and the eyes, which are black. Its tail is blue above, brown beneath, and white at the tip.

The Tlauhtototl is very like the Tlacuiloltototl in its colors, but smaller. The macaws and the cardinals, so prized by Europeans for their most beautiful colors, are very common in those countries.

All these beautiful birds, and others native to Mexico, or else brought to Mexico from other neighboring countries, were highly esteemed by the Mexicans for their singular works of mosaic, of which we shall make mention elsewhere. From the old continent peafowl were brought there, but through the carelessness of those peoples they have multiplied very little.

Several authors who grant the Mexican birds superiority in the beauty of their feathers deny them that of song; but we who have heard both the one and the other are quite certain that such an opinion was dictated not by fairness but by ignorance; for it is harder for

Europeans to hear the Mexican birds than to see them.

There are also in Mexico the goldfinches and the renowned [p. 89] nightingales, and besides at least twenty-two other species of songbirds, little or in no way inferior to those; but far surpassing all those Bk. I. we know is the most celebrated Centzontli, a name given to it by the Mexicans to express the surprising variety of its voices. (qq) It is impossible for us to give a complete idea of the sweetness and softness of its song, of the harmony and variety of its tones, and of the facility with which it learns to express whatever it hears. It imitates to the life not only the song of other birds, but even the different voices of quadrupeds. It is the size of a common thrush. The color of its body is white beneath and gray above, with some white feathers, especially near the tail and the head. It eats anything; but it takes particular delight in flies, which it takes with demonstrations of pleasure from the fingers of whoever offers them. The species of the Centzontli is everywhere among the most numerous; but although these birds are so common, they are so prized that I have seen twenty-five scudi paid for one. Attempts have often been made to carry it to Europe; but I do not know whether any has ever succeeded; and I am persuaded that even if it arrived alive in Europe it could never be without great detriment to its voice and its instinct, because of the discomforts of the voyage and the change of climate.

Gorriones by the Spaniards, resemble true sparrows only in size, in hopping as they walk, and in making their nests in holes in walls. The

> (*) Ho sentito dite, che i Gorioni della tech rossa sono i maschi, e quelli della testa gialla le femmine.

Mexican ones have the lower part of the body white and the upper gray; but when they reach a certain age, some have the head red and others yellow. (*) Their flight is laborious, perhaps because of the smallness of their wings or the weakness of their feathers. Their song is very sweet and quite varied. There is a great abundance of these singers in the capital and in other cities and villages of Mexico.

No less abundant in the country of Anahuac are the talkative birds, or imitators of human speech. Among the songbirds themselves there are some that learn a few words, such as the renowned

Centzontli, and the Acolchichi, that is, red-shouldered bird, to which, for such a badge, the Spaniards gave the name of Commendatore. The

Cehuan, which is larger than a common thrush, mimics the human voice, but in a tone that seems mocking, and follows travelers for a long stretch. The Tzanahuei resembles the magpie in size, but differs in color; it learns to speak, steals cautiously whatever it can, and in all things shows an instinct superior to that commonly observed in other birds.

Bk. I. rots, of which four principal species are counted in Mexico: the Huacamaya, the Toznenetl, the Cochotl, and the Quiltototl. (rr)

The Huacamaya is more valued for its most beautiful plumage than for its voice. It pronounces words indistinctly, and its voice is coarse and disagreeable. This is the largest of all the parrots. The Toznenetl, which is the best of all, is the size of a dove; the color of its feathers is green, but on the head and the front part of the wings it is red in some and yellow in others. It learns as many words and songs as they teach it, and pronounces them clearly; it imitates to the life the laughter and the mocking tone of men, the weeping of children, and the voices of various animals. Of the Cochotl there are three subordinate species, differing in size and in colors, which in all are beautiful, and among which green predominates. The largest of the Cochotl is almost the size of the Toznenetl; the other two species, called catarinas by the Spaniards, are smaller. All learn to speak, though not so perfectly as the Toznenetl. The Quiltototl, which is the smallest, is also the least fit for speaking. These little parrots, whose feathers are dyed a most beautiful green, always go in numerous flocks, now making a great noise in the air, now ravaging the grain. When they are in the trees they are confused, because of their color, with the foliage. All the other parrots go for the most part in pairs, male and female.

feathers or for the excellence of their song, are nonetheless worthy of particular mention for their habits. The Awakeners are, among the diurnal birds, the last to take their rest in the evening and the first to leave it in the morning and to announce the return of the Sun. They do not cease their song and their games until an hour after sunset, and long before dawn they resume them, nor do they ever show themselves so cheerful as during both twilights. About an hour before dawn one of these birds, from the branches of a tree where it spent the night in company with many others of its species, begins to call them in a high and sonorous voice, and in a cheerful tone repeats the call many times, until it hears first one and then another answer.

On the journeys I made through the kingdom of Michoacán, where they are most abundant, they were useful to me; for they woke me in good time to make my departure at the break of day. These birds are as large as sparrows.

The Tzacua, a bird resembling the aforementioned Calandra in size, in colors, and in the building of its nest, is still more wonderful.

IL La solita visita dei nidi, Queste cose sulle Tzacue oflervatefi da un uomo perspicace, erudito , e fincero, (*) ci fanno credere , che trovar se ne potrebbero delle più sorprendenti, fe reiterate sì foflero le oflervazioni; ma lasciando adeflo questi obbietti tanto piacevoli , volgiamo lo sguardo ad altri terribili.

These birds live in society, and every tree is for them a village composed of a great multitude of nests, which are seen hanging from the branches. A Tzacua that acts as Chief, or Guard of the Village, sits in the middle of the tree, whence it often flies now to one nest, now to another, and after singing a little returns to its post, and thus visits all the nests, all the others meanwhile remaining silent. If it ever sees some bird of another species coming toward the tree, it goes to meet it, and with beak and wings strives to drive it off; but if it sees a man approaching (and perhaps any other animal of formidable size), it flies away crying to another tree nearby, and if meanwhile some Tzacuas of the same village arrive from the fields, it goes to meet them [p. 93] and, changing the tone of its voice, it forces them to withdraw; but as soon as it sees the danger cease, it returns cheerfully to its customary Bk. I. visit of the nests. These things observed of the Tzacuas by a man who is perspicacious, learned, and truthful, (*) lead us to believe that still more surprising ones might be found, if the observations were repeated; but leaving now these objects so pleasing, let us turn our gaze to others, terrible ones.

The reptiles of Mexico may be reduced to two orders or classes, §Reptiles

> I Coccodrilli messicani sono rali, quali fono gli affricani nella’ grandezza, nella figura , nella voracità , nella maniera di vivere, ed in tutte l'altre proprietà appartenenti al lor carattere . Abbondano in parecchj fiumi e laghi delle terre calde, & sono petniciosi ad altri animali, ed anche agli vomini ,: Sarebbe superfiua -la descrizione di questi feroci anfib}, mentre fi trova tanto d' essi ‘scritto,

of Mexico. namely four-footed reptiles and apodal reptiles, or those without feet. (ss) In the first class are the crocodiles, the large lizards, the lizards, the frogs, and the toads, and in the second all the species of serpents.

The Mexican crocodiles are such as the African ones are in size, in shape, in voracity, in manner of living, and in all the other properties belonging to their character. They abound in several rivers and lakes of the hot lands, and are destructive to other animals, and even to men. A description of these fierce amphibians would be superfluous, since so much is found written of them.

Among the large lizards we count the Acaltetepon and the Iguana: the Acaltetepon, known to the Spanish common people by the very improper name of Scorpions, are two large lizards similar to each other in color and in shape, but different in size and in the tail. The smaller is about fifteen inches long, and has a long tail, short legs, a broad, cleft, red tongue, a gray and rough skin with little white bumps scattered everywhere, which look like pearls, a slow gait, and a fierce look. From the muscles of the hind legs to the tip of the tail it has the skin crossed

> L' Iguana è un Lucertone innocente assai conosciuto nell’ Europa per le relazioni d egli Storici dell’ America + Abbondano nelle terre calde, e ve ne fono due spezie, l' una terrestre, e l’altra acfibia , Alcune fono così grandi, che hanno fino a tre piedi di lunghezza. Sono velocifslime nel loro corso, ed agilissime nel montar sugli alberi. La loro carne , e le loro uova sono commestibili , e lodate da parecchi Autori; ma la carne è perniciosla per quelli, che sono dal mal francese infettati.

The Iguana is an innocent large lizard, well known in Europe from the accounts of the historians of America. They abound in the hot lands, and there are two species of them, one terrestrial and the other amphibious. Some are so large that they reach as much as three feet in length. They are extremely swift in their course, and extremely agile in climbing trees. Their flesh and their eggs are edible, and praised by several authors; but the flesh is pernicious to those who are infected with the French disease.

> Di Lucertole vi sono innumerabili spezie differenti nella grandezza ,' nei colori , e nelle qualità; poichè altre sono velenose, ed altre innocenti. Fra le innocenti fì debbe il primo luogo al Camaleonte dai Meslicani appellato Quara palcarl . Questo è quali in tutto somigliante al Gamaleonte volgare; ma differisce nell' esser privo di cresta, e nell' aver dell’ orecchie, le quali sono grandi, tonde, e troppo aperte, Fra l’ altre Lucertole innocenti non ve n' è niuna degna di rammemorarsi , se non la T'apayaxin , (O) così per la sua figura , come per altri riguardi , E' perfettamente orbicolare , catrtilaginosa , e fi fente molto fredda nel toccarla. Il diametro del suo corpo è di sei dita. La sua testa è durissima, e di colori diversi macchiata . E’ tanto lenta & pigra , che neppure scofsa fi muove. Se le percuotono la testa, o le compae gli occhj, lancia da essi fino a due o tre passi “in ontananza alcune pocciole di sangue; ma per altro è ani. male innocente, e mostra compiacerlì d' eflere mareggiata :

Of lizards there are innumerable species, differing in size, in colors, and in qualities; for some are venomous and others innocent.

Among the innocent ones the first place is due to the chameleon, called by the Mexicans Quatapalcatl. This is almost wholly like the common chameleon; but it differs in being without a crest, and in having ears, which are large, round, and too open. Among the other innocent lizards there is none worth recording, except the Tapayaxin,

(*) both for its shape and for other respects. It is perfectly orbicular, cartilaginous, and feels very cold to the touch. The diameter of its body is six finger-breadths. Its head is very hard, and spotted with various colors. It is so slow and sluggish that even when shaken it does not move. If they strike its head, or press its eyes, it squirts from them, to a distance of two or three paces, a few drops of blood; but otherwise it is an innocent animal, and shows pleasure in being handled.

Among the venomous lizards the worst appears to be the one which, for its rarity, received from the Mexicans the name of Tetzauhqui. This one is very small, and of a gray color, which on its body is yellowish, and on its tail bluish. There are still others reputed venomous, and known to the Spaniards by the name of Salamanquesas, or by that of Scorpions (since the ignorant common people have given this name to several reptiles); but I have assured myself, after many observations, that such lizards are either wholly without venom, or, if perhaps they have any, it is not as active as is believed.

> Delle Rane vi sono nel lago di Chalco tre numerosissime spezie differenti nella grandezza e nei colori , ed asflai comuni nelle ravole della Capitale . Quelle della Huaxte- ca sono eccellenti, e così grofle , che pesano una libbra Spagnouola, Ma ron vidi , nè fentii mai in quel regno le Ranette d' alberi, che fono tanto volgari così in Italia, come in altri paesi della Europa,

What we say of the lizards may also be said of the toads; for we have never seen or heard of any misfortune caused by their venom, although in several countries too hot and humid the ground is covered with them. In such lands are found toads so large that they measure as much as eight inches in diameter.

> La varierà delle Serpi è molto maggiore di quella dei suddetti rettili , mentre ve ne sono delle prandi e delle piccole , delle versicolori, e di quelle d’ un sol colore , delle velenose, e delle innocenti .

Of frogs there are in the lake of Chalco three very numerous species, differing in size and in colors, and very common on the tables of the capital. Those of the Huasteca are excellent, and so large that they weigh a Spanish pound. But I never saw or heard of tree frogs in that kingdom, which are so common both in Italy and in other countries of Europe.

The variety of serpents is much greater than that of the aforesaid reptiles, for there are large ones and small, many-colored ones and ones of a single color, venomous ones and innocent ones.

The one the Mexicans called Canauhcoatl seems to have been the most considerable in thickness. It was as much as three Paris perches long, and as thick as a man of ordinary size. A little smaller was one of the Tlilcoa, or black serpents, seen by Dr. Hernández in the mountains of Tepoztlán; for, having such a thickness, it was also ten Spanish cubits

I sonagli possono considerarsi come un appendice delle vertebre, e son degli anelli sonori di soitan+za cornea , mobili , e dipendenti gli uni dagli altri per mezzo delle articolazioni o giunture , ognuna di tre osserti com posta . Morde con due canini, che - ha nella mascella superiore, i quali sono ficcome nella Viperò» e in altre spezie di Serpi, mobili, cavi, e forari vero la punta. Il veleno, cioè quel liquido gialliccio, cristals lizzabile, e tanto pernicioso , è contenuto dentro’ le glandole, che vi sono sopra Il’ origine di quei due deati . Queste glandole compresse nel mordere , [anciano ‘per i canali deî denti il fatal liquore, e l’ introducono per li fori nella fe rita, e nella massa del sangue. [p. 96] long, or more than sixteen Paris feet; but nowadays serpents of such Bk. I.

bulk will hardly be found, unless it be in some solitary wood, very far from the capital.

The most notable venomous serpents are the Ahueyactli, the

Cuicuilcoatl, the Coral, or Coralline, the Teixminani, the Cencoatl, and the Teotlacozauhqui.

The Teotlacozauhqui, of whose kind there are several species, is the famous rattlesnake. Its size is varied, as are its colors; but ordinarily it is three or four feet long. The rattles may be considered as an appendage of the vertebrae, and are sonorous rings of horny substance, movable, and dependent on one another by means of articulations or joints, each composed of three small bones. (tt) These rattles sound every time the serpent moves, especially when it is agitated to bite. It is very swift in its motion, and therefore it also received from the

Mexicans the name of Ehecacoatl, or Air Serpent. Its bite causes death infallibly, unless one runs promptly to its remedies, among which it is esteemed effective to keep the wounded part inside the earth for some time. It bites with two canine teeth which it has in the upper jaw, which are, as in the viper and in other species of serpents, movable, hollow, and perforated toward the point. The venom, that is, that yellowish liquid, crystallizable and so pernicious, is contained in the glands that are above the root of those two teeth. These glands, compressed in biting, shoot the fatal liquor through the channels of the teeth, and introduce it through the holes into the wound and into the mass of the blood. We would gladly communicate to the public several other observations made on this subject, if the condition of this history allowed us. (uu)

The Ahueyactli is little different from the one already described, but it has no rattles. This serpent communicates, according to what Bk. I. Hernández says, that kind of venom which was called by the Ancients Hemorrhoos, by which the wounded man discharges blood through the mouth, the nose, and the eyes, although such an action can be prevented with certain antidotes.

> La Cuicuzlcoazi , così appellata per la varietà dei suoi colori , è lunga appena otto oncie , e grofla come il dita mignolo; ma il tuo veleno è tanto attivo, quanto quello della Teotlacozaubqui.

The Cuicuilcoatl, so called for the variety of its colors, is barely eight inches long, and as thick as the little finger; but its venom is as active as that of the Teotlacozauhqui.

> La Teinminansi è quella sorte di Serpe , che Plinio chiama Jaculum , E' lunga, e dottile ,, ed ha il dorso bigio, e il ventre paonazziccio . Muovelsi lempre per linea diritta, e mai non s' aggira, Lanciali dagli alberi ai viandanti, e da ciò ebbe il nome. (vv) }

The Teixminani is that sort of serpent which Pliny calls jaculus. It is long and slender, and has a gray back and a purplish belly. It always moves in a straight line, and never turns about. It darts from the trees at travelers, and from this it took its name. (vv)

> Vi sono di queste serpi nelle montagne di Quaubnahuac , ed in altre terre calde ; ma eslendo io itato tanti anni in quel regno, non seppi mai, che una, tal disgrazia ad alcun viandante accadesle, e lo sitello poslo dire dei terribili efferci che ne cagiona l' Abueyactli .

There are some of these serpents in the mountains of Cuauhnahuac, and in other hot lands; but although I was so many years in that kingdom, I never learned that such a misfortune befell any traveler, and I can say the same of the terrible effects which the Ahueyactli causes.

> La Cencoar!, (*) ancor efla velenosa , ha cinque piedi in» circa di lunghezza , e otto oncie: di circonferenza , dov' è più grofla . The Cencoatl, (*) also venomous, is about five feet in length, and eight inches in circumference where it is thickest. The most singular thing about this serpent is that it shines in the dark. Thus the provident author of nature awakens our attention in various ways to defend ourselves from harm, now through hearing with the noise of the rattles, now through the eyes with the impression of light.

Among so many species of serpents as are found in the little-frequented woods of that kingdom, I know of none so far discovered to be viviparous, except the Acoatl, or water serpent, of which this is believed, but not known. This one is about twenty inches long, and one inch thick. Its teeth are very small: the upper part of its head is black, the sides blue, and the lower yellow; the back streaked with black and blue, and the belly entirely blue.

> Se dalla terra poi volgiamo lo sguardo all' pile dei u-

The ancient Mexicans, who delighted in raising every kind of animal, and who by familiarity had driven the natural horror from their minds, used to take in the fields a green and innocent little serpent to raise at home, where, well fed, it would usually grow as thick as a man. They kept it inside a tub, from which it did not come out except to take its food from its master's hand, and to climb onto his shoulder, or else to wind itself about his feet.

The shark belongs to that class of marine beasts which were called by the Ancients caniculae. Its voracity is very well known, as also its size, its strength, and its speed. It has two, three, and sometimes more rows of teeth no less sharp than strong, and swallows whatever is presented to it, whether it be edible or not. There has been found at times in its belly a whole sheep's skin, and even a large butcher's knife. It often accompanies ships, and there have been sharks that, according to what Oviedo attests, accompanied for as much as five hundred miles a ship that was going with the wind astern and sails swollen, circling it often for love of the refuse that was thrown into the sea.

The manatee, or Lamentino as it is called by some, is of a disposition very different from that of the shark, and surpasses it in size.

Oviedo himself testifies that manatees were at times caught so large that to transport one a cart with two pairs of oxen was needed. It is viviparous, like the shark; but the female bears at each birth no more than one little manatee, though a very large one. (zz) Its flesh is delicate and resembling that of veal.

Some in naming them these rules. 1. To the known fish I give their own Tuscan name, as whale, dolphin, sand sole, ray, shad, sphyraena, pike, stingray, mullet, plaice, anchovy, etc. 2.

To those fish which, although they have no proper name in the Tuscan language, can nevertheless be expressed by a Tuscan name equivalent to the Spanish or Mexican, I give such a name: thus I say blonde for Vermejuela, little dove for Palometa, toad for

Sapo, goldfinch for Sirguero, old wife for Vieja, parrot for Cochomichin (a Mexican name), etc. 3. For those, then, that have neither a proper name nor can be expressed by an equivalent Tuscan name, I use the same Spanish names, but conforming some of them to the Tuscan manner, as Pampano, Roballo, Pargo, Bobo, Botetto for Botete, Ciuccio for Chucho, etc.

The manta is that flat fish so dangerous to the pearl fishers, of which Ulloa and other authors make mention, and I do not doubt that it is the same one recorded by Pliny, but not well understood, under the name of Cloud, or Mist. (Bb) It may be believed that it passed from the seas of the old continent to those of the new, as other fish appear also to have passed. So great is the strength

> Ti dell'antico Continente a quei del nuovo, siccome pare , che fieno ancor passati altri pesci. E' così grande la forza, che

which be believed that the same happens to the female manatee as to woman, namely, that while ordinarily she has one fetus, extraordinarily she bears two or three. Dr. Hernández describes the coupling of such animals thus: It couples in the human manner, the female lying on her back, almost entirely on the shore, and the male coming upon her with a certain swiftness. We do not count the manatee, though viviparous, among the quadrupeds, as several modern naturalists do; because all the world understands by the name of quadruped an animal that goes on four feet, and the manatee has only two, and those shapeless.

(Aa) M. de la Condamine confirms what we say with regard to the manatee's living always in the water, and the same had been said two centuries earlier by Oviedo and Hernández, eyewitnesses both. It is true that Hernández seems to say quite the opposite; but it is an evident misprint, which anyone who reads the text can perceive. It should also be noted that the manatee, though properly marine, is frequently found in the rivers.

(Bb) The divers themselves report that a kind of cloud thickens over their heads, like flat fish, pressing upon them and preventing them from coming up again, and that for this reason they carry very sharp stilettos attached to lines; for unless it is pierced it does not withdraw, this being, as I think, the effect of darkness and terror. For no one has found among the animals any one called a cloud or mist (the name by which they call this evil). Pliny, Natural History, bk. 9, ch. 46. The account which these divers, or “cormorants,” gave of their Cloud is not different from what the divers of the seas of America say of their Manta, and the name of Cloud suits it, since it really looks like a cloud to those who are in the water beneath it, and even today swimmers carry long knives, or sharp sticks, to free themselves from such a beast. This observation, which escaped all the interpreters of Pliny, was made by my compatriot and friend the Abbé José Rafael Campoy, a person highly praiseworthy no less for his morals and his honor than for his eloquence and his erudition, especially in Latinity, in history, in criticism, and in geography. His death, which touches us too deeply, occurring on December 29, 1777, did not allow him to complete several works already begun, which would have been very useful. Of the two species of sawfish that are in those seas, one is the common one known to Pliny and described by many naturalists; the other, no longer than a foot, has on its back a row of teeth, or spines, that looks like a saw, whence it received from the Mexicans the name of Tlateconi, and from the

The robalo is one of the most numerous species, and its flesh is one of the most delicate foods, especially that of the river kind. Dr. Hernández believed it to be the Lupus of the Ancients, and Campoy the Asellus minor; but these are mere conjectures; for the marks that the Ancients left us of those fish are so scanty that it is impossible to establish the identity.

The humpback (among the Spaniards Corcobado) was so called on account of a hump, or prominence, which it has from the beginning of the head to the mouth, which is very small. The sphyraena likewise received the name of

Picuda (which we might call Long-beak) because it has the lower jaw longer than the upper.

The toadfish is a fish horrible to look at, black, perfectly round, and without scales, whose diameter is three or four inches. Its flesh is tasty and wholesome.

Il Barbo di fiume, conosciuto col nome di Bagre, è della grandezza del Bobo,e d'’ un gusto anche elquisito, ma nocevole, se prima non fì purga la sua carne con sugo di limone , o qualche altro acido di una certa bava o liquido viscoso, che ha, I Bobi per quel che sappiamo, fi pescano soltanto nei fiumi, che sboccano nel Golfo Messicano, e i Barbi in quelli, che fi scaricano nel mar Pacifico , o in qualche lago, Il gusto di queste due spezie di pesci quantunque delicato, non arriva pure a quello dei Pampani, e delle Colombelle, che sono , non senza ragione, i più stimati di rutti, - La Curvina è lunga un piede e mezzo , ma sottile, ed attondata, e d’ un colore paonazzo nericcio, Nella testa di uesto pesce trovansi due pietruzze bianche , che sembrano "alabastro’, lunghe un' oncia e mezza , larghe quattro lince incirca , le quali credonsi efficaci contro la ritenzione dell’ orina , prendendone tre grani in acqua .

Among the needlefish there is one called by the Mexicans Huitzitzilmichin, [p. 103] three feet long, but very slender. Its body is covered with certain little plates instead of scales. Its snout is eight inches long, and is longer in Bk. I. the upper part, the opposite of the other needlefish, which it surpasses no less in the taste of its flesh than in the size of its body.

> Il Bogerzro È un piccolo pesce lungo otto oncie incirca , ma \proporzionatamente groflo, Il suo fegato è tanto velenoso, che in mezz'ora cagiona la morte a chi il mangia, con ‘forti dolori e convulboni . Quando è ancor vivo lulla spiaggia, dove si sente toccare, si gonfia enormemente, ed i ragazzi prendono piacere nel farlo scoppiare d' un colpo di piede .

The bobo is a most noble fish, and much esteemed for the excellence of its flesh, about two feet long, and four or six inches wide where widest. The river barbel, known by the name of Bagre, is of the size of the bobo, and of an exquisite taste too, but harmful unless its flesh is first purged with lemon juice, or some other acid, of a certain slime or viscous liquid which it has. The bobos, as far as we know, are caught only in the rivers that empty into the Gulf of Mexico, and the barbels in those that discharge into the Pacific Ocean, or in some lake. The taste of these two species of fish, though delicate, does not quite reach that of the pámpanos and of the little doves, which are, not without reason, the most esteemed of all.

> L' Occhiane (*) è un pesce piano e tondo , che ha otto, o die-

The corvina is a foot and a half long, but slender and rounded, and of a blackish purple color. In the head of this fish are found two little white stones that look like alabaster, an inch and a half long, about four lines wide, which are believed effective against retention of urine, taking three grains of them in water.

The botete is a small fish about eight inches long, but disproportionately thick. Its liver is so poisonous that in half an hour it causes death to him who eats it, with severe pains and convulsions. When it is still alive on the beach, where it feels itself touched, it swells up enormously, and boys take pleasure in making it burst with a stamp of the foot.

The Iztacmichin, or white fish, has always been famous in Mexico, and is no less common today on the tables of the Spaniards than anciently on those of the Mexicans. Three or four species of it are distinguished. The Amilotl, which is the largest and the most prized, is more than a foot in length, and has five little fins, two on the back, two at the two sides of the belly, and another under the belly itself.

> (Cc) IL Campoi fi persuase esser l' Occhione l' Uranorcopos , @ Callionymos di Plinio : ma Plinio non ci lasciò i contrafsegni di questo pesce . The Xalmichin, a little smaller than that, seems to me to be of the same species. The Jacapitzahuac, which is the smallest, is no more than eight inches in length, and an inch and a half in width. All these fish are scaly, savory, and very wholesome, and the lakes of Chalco, of

Pátzcuaro, and of Chapala are full of them. The other species is that of the Xalmichin of Cuauhnahuac, which is without scales, and is covered with a soft, white skin.

The Axolotl, or Axolote (*), is an aquatic large lizard of the Mexican lake. Its form is ugly, and its aspect ridiculous. Its length is ordinarily eight inches; but there are some twice as large. Its skin is soft and black, its head long, its mouth large, its tongue broad, small, and cartilaginous, and its tail long. From the middle of the body to the end of the tail it tapers. It swims with its four feet, which are like those of the frog

Uranoscopos, which has been the whole foundation of that opinion, suits equally all those fish which, having their eyes on the top of the head, look at the sky, like the rays and other flat fish.

As for shells, there are infinite species, and among them some of a beauty never seen, especially in the Pacific Ocean. Along all the coasts of this sea there was at various times the pearl fishery. The Mexicans fished for them on the coast of Tototepec, and on that of the Cuitlatecs, where they now fish for tortoiseshell. Among the starfish there is one furnished with five rays, and with an eye in each. Among the sponges and lithophytes there are rare and strange species. Dr. Hernández presents us with the portrait of a sponge sent to him from the Pacific Ocean, which had the shape of a human hand, but with ten or more fingers, clay-colored with black dots and red streaks, and was more callous than ordinary ones.

Finally, descending to the smallest animals, in which the power and Insects of Mexico. wisdom of the Creator shine forth the more, we may reduce the innumerable species of insects that are in Mexico to three orders, namely flying, terrestrial, and aquatic, although there are terrestrial and aquatic ones that afterward become flying, and must be considered now in the one state, now in the other.

The Cucujo, or luminous beetle, which is the most worthy of consideration, has been mentioned by several authors, but by none, so far as I know, described. It is more than an inch long, and furnished with double wings, like the other flying beetles. It has on its head a movable little horn, which is very useful to it; for when, having turned over and resting on its back, it finds itself hindered in its motion, it restores itself to its natural position by the action of this little horn, sheathing and pressing it into a membrane made in the manner of a pouch, which it has on its belly. Near the eyes it has two little membranes, and another larger one on the belly, thin, transparent, and filled with a matter so luminous that its light suffices to read a letter comfortably, and to light the road for those who walk at night; but it never gives a greater light than in flying. When it sleeps, it does not send it forth; for it covers it with other, opaque membranes. This luminous matter is a white, mealy, viscous substance, which preserves its illuminating virtue for some time after it has been drawn from the body of the Cucujo, and with it some people write luminous characters on hats. There is a great abundance of these flying phosphors on the sea coasts, and at night they are wont to form charming and brilliant spectacles in the nearby mountains. To catch them boys do nothing but whirl a firebrand in the evening: attracted by this light the Cucujos come into the hands of the hunters. There has not been lacking some author who confounded these marvelous insects with fireflies; but these are much smaller, and much less luminous, common in Europe, and very frequent in that country.

As agreeable as the sight of the Cucujo is, so disagreeable is [p. 107] that of the Temolin. This is a large beetle, of a reddish chestnut color,

Bk. I. furnished with six hairy feet, and with four toes on each. There are two species of Temolin: the one has its forehead armed with a horn, or antenna, and the other with two.

Of bees there are at least six different species. The first is that of the common bees of Europe, with which they agree no less in size, form, and color than in nature, habits, and the quality of the honey and wax which they make. The second species is of others like them, but entirely without a sting. Of this species are those of Yucatán and of Chiapas, which make the famous honey of Estabentun, which is clear, aromatic, and of a taste superior to that of all the other kinds of honey that we know. The harvests of this honey are six, one every two months; but the best is that which is gathered in November, because the bees make it from a white flower like jasmine, and very fragrant, which comes in September, and is called in that country Estabentun, whence the honey took its name. (Ee) The third species is of certain bees similar in form to winged ants, but smaller than the common bees, and without a sting. These insects, proper to hot and temperate countries, build combs similar in size and shape to the large sugar loaves, and sometimes much larger than they, hanging from the rocks or from the trees, especially from oaks. The population of these combs is much more numerous than that of the combs of the common bees. The nymphs of these bees are white and round like pearls, and are edible too. Their honey is grayish, but of a delicate taste. The bees of the fourth species are yellow, smaller than the common ones, and like them armed with a sting. Their honey is inferior to the aforesaid. Those of the fifth species are small and stingless; they build round combs in underground cavities, and their

species, is black and yellow, as large as the common ones, but stingless.

The species of wasps are at least four. The Quetzalmiahuatl is the common one of Europe. The Tetlatoca, or vagabond, is so called because it often changes its dwelling, and is always seen occupied in gathering the materials for building it. It has a sting; but it makes neither honey nor wax. The Xicotli, or Xicote, is a large wasp, black except for the belly, which is yellow. It makes a very sweet honey in the holes that it opens in the walls. It is armed with a strong sting, and its wound is very painful. The Cuicalmiahuatl likewise has its sting, but we do not know whether it makes honey.

The Quauhxicotli is a hornet, all black save the tail, which is red. Its sting is so large and so strong that with it it not only pierces a sugar cane through from one side to the other, but even bores through the trunks of trees.

Among the flies, besides the common ones, which are neither in so great a number nor so importunate as those of Italy in summer, (Ff)

there are luminous ones, like the fireflies. The Axayacatl is a marsh fly of the Mexican lake. From the innumerable eggs that these flies lay on the rushes and on the flag, or iris, of the lake, thick crusts are made, which the fishermen gather to sell in the market. This caviar, called Ahuauhtli, was eaten by the Mexicans, and today is a very familiar dish to the Spaniards, and has almost the same taste as the caviar of fish. But the ancient Mexicans ate not only the eggs, but even the flies themselves, reduced to a mass and cooked with nitre.

There are also in the hot lands certain midges, which make no noise in flying, but whose sting causes a violent itching, and if, to rid himself of it, the person bitten scratches the affected part, a sore is easily made.

In the same hot lands, especially in certain coastal ones, cockroaches abound, which are large, winged insects, loathsome and harmful, because they infest food, and sweet things especially, but otherwise useful to dwellings, because they purge them of bedbugs. It has been observed that the ships which on the voyage from Europe to New Spain go laden with bedbugs are on the return voyage entirely free of these stinking insects, because of the cockroaches. (*)

The species of butterflies are far more diverse, and more numerous, in Mexico than in Europe. Their variety and their beauty cannot be worthily depicted; nor are the best brushes capable of expressing the excellence of design and of colors which the author of nature employed in adorning their wings. Several notable authors have celebrated them in their writings, and Dr. Hernández had some of them drawn to give Europeans some idea of their beauty.

But butterflies are not comparable in number with the locusts, which at times fall upon the maritime lands, darkening the air with the dense clouds which they form, and utterly destroying all the vegetation that is in the countryside, as I saw in 1738 or 39 on the coast of Jicayán.

Of the worms some are useful and others harmful: some served as food for the ancient Mexicans, and others as medicine, like the Axin and the Pollin, of which we shall speak elsewhere. The Tleocuilin, or burning worm, has the properties of cantharides. Its head is red, its breast green, and the rest of its body tawny. The Temahuani is a worm entirely armed with small yellow and poisonous spines. The Temictli resembles the silkworm in its operations, no less than in its transformations. Silkworms were brought over from Europe and multiplied successfully. Abundant harvests of good silk were gathered, especially in the Mixteca, (*) where it was a considerable article of commerce; but when the Mixtecs were afterward compelled to give it up for political reasons, the raising of silkworms was likewise neglected, and today few there are who engage in it. Besides this common silk there is another, very valuable, white, soft, and strong, which is found on the trees in several forests of the coastal countries, especially in those years when the rains are scanty; but only some poor people make use of it, because of the little economy of those peoples, or rather because of the burdens that anyone would have to suffer who wished to undertake such a trade. Centipedes are found sometimes in temperate countries, and more often in hot and humid ones. Dr. Hernández says that he saw some so large that they were two feet long and two fingers thick; but such insects must have been seen by that author in some country too humid and uncultivated, for we, although we have lingered in many places of every sort of climate, have never found any of so immense a size.

Scorpions are common throughout that kingdom; but in the cold and temperate countries they are for the most part few and not very harmful. In the hot lands, and in those where the air is too dry, however moderate the heat may be, they are more abundant, and their venom is such that it suffices to bring death to children and to cause terrible agonies to adults. It has been observed that the venom of the small yellowish scorpions is more active than that of the large brown ones, and that their sting is more deadly at those hours of the day when the sun is hottest.

Among the many species of spiders found there, we cannot pass over two remarkable ones, the tarantula and the Casampulga. (*) The name of Tarantola is given in that country, improperly, to a very large spider, whose back and legs are covered with a blackish down, soft and fine, like that of chicks. It belongs to the hot lands, and is found not only in the fields but also in houses. It is thought venomous, and it is commonly believed that a horse which in walking treads on one of them immediately loses its hoof; but I have never heard of any particular occurrence that might confirm this common opinion, although I spent five years in a very hot country where such spiders abounded. The Casampulga is small, and has short feet,

The most common ants in that country are of three species. The first is that of the small black ones common on both continents.

> Oltre a queste spezie ve n' è un alcra singolare in Michuacan, e forse ancora in altre provincie . Quelta è più grande dell’ altre formiche, ed ha il corpo bigio, e la resta nera, Nella parte deretrana porta un sacchetto pieno d'’ un li quore assai dolce, del quale sono molto ghiotti i ragazzi , € credono che sia mele fabbricatco dalle formiche, come l’ altro -comune dalle api; ma a ‘noi pare che sieno fin uova . Il Sig. della Barrere nella Storia Naturale della Francia. Equinoziale fa menzione di sì fatte formiche trovate nel la Cajenna ; ma queste sono alate, e le nostre senz' ale,

Others are large and red, and armed with a sting with which they inflict painful bites; the Spaniards call them bravas, that is, fierce. Still others are large and brown, and have from the Spaniards the name of

Harrieras, that is, carriers, because they are continually occupied in carrying off grain for their provision, much more than the common ants do; for which reason they are more destructive to the fields. In some countries they have multiplied excessively through the negligence of the inhabitants. In the province of Jicayán black bands are seen on the ground for several miles, formed by the ants as they go and come.

Besides these species there is another, a remarkable one, in

Michoacán, and perhaps in other provinces as well. This one is larger than the other ants, and has a gray body and a black head. In its hind part it carries a little sack full of a very sweet liquor, of which the boys are very fond, and they believe that it is honey made by the ants, like the common sort by the bees; but to us it seems rather to be eggs. M. de la Barrère, in his Natural History of Equinoctial France, makes mention of such ants found in Cayenne; but those are winged, and ours are wingless.

The Nigua, called Pique in other countries, is a very small insect not altogether unlike the flea, which in some hot lands breeds in the dust. It attaches itself to the feet, and, breaking the cuticle imperceptibly, nests between it and the skin; and if it is not removed at once, it breaks the skin also and passes on to the flesh, multiplying with incredible quickness. For the most part it is not felt until, in piercing the skin, it causes an intolerable itching. These insects, because of [p. 113] their surprising multiplication would be enough to depopulate those countries, if it were not so easy to avoid them, and if the inhabitants Bk. I. were not so quick in removing them before they multiply. God, for His part, that the harm done us by them might be less, not only denied them wings, but also withheld from their legs that conformation, and those vigorous muscles, which He granted to fleas for leaping; but among the poor, who by reason of their misery are condemned to live in the dust and to a habitual neglect of their persons, such insects usually multiply so greatly that they make wide cavities in their flesh and cause them dangerous sores.

What the Nigue do in dwellings, the Garrapate, or ticks, do in the country; of which there are two species, or rather two classes. The first is of those lice, no less common in the new than in the old continent, which attach themselves to the skin of sheep, horses, and other quadrupeds, and get into their ears, and even sometimes into those of men.

At the beginning it seems nothing but a little black dot; but with the blood that it sucks it swells in such a way, and so quickly, that in a very short time it becomes as large as a broad bean, and then takes on the color of lead. The cochineal at its greatest growth has the size and shape of a bedbug. The female is misshapen and sluggish. Her eyes, her mouth, her little horns, or antennae, and her feet are so hidden among the wrinkles of her skin that they cannot be distinguished without the aid of the microscope; and so several Europeans persisted in believing that it was some kind of seed, not a true animal, against the testimony of the Indians who raised it, and of Hernández, who observed it as a naturalist. The male is rarer, and one serves for three hundred females or more. He is also smaller and thinner than the female, but nimbler and more active. He has on his head two jointed little horns, and in each joint four bristles arranged with perfect symmetry.

His

(Ii) The Chronicler Herrera says, in Dec. 4, bk. 8, ch. 8, that although the Indians

had the cochineal, they made no account of it until they were instructed by the

Spaniards. But what did the Spaniards teach them? To raise cochineal? How could they teach what they knew nothing whatever of, and what, instead of an insect, they took for a seed? Did they teach them, perhaps, to use it for dyeing? But if the Indians did not use it for dyeing, why did they take so much trouble in raising it? Why were

Huaxyacac, Coyolapan, and other places obliged to pay the King of Mexico twenty sacks of cochineal every year, as appears from the tribute roll? How can it be believed that those nations, so given to painting, were ignorant of the use of cochineal, and did not know how to employ such insects, when they knew how to make use of the achiote, the indigo, and very many stones and mineral earths?

(Jj) The cochineal that comes every year from the Mixteca to Spain exceeds two

thousand five hundred sacks, as some authors testify. The commerce that the city of

Oaxaca carries on in it amounts annually to two hundred thousand scudi. M. de

Bomare says that a certain cochineal is given the name of mesteca cochineal because it is raised in Meteque, in the province of Honduras; but this is an error. It is called

Misteca because it comes from the Mixteca, a province farther from Honduras than

Rome is from Paris.

La maniera di moltiplicardki , che hanno questi prezioli insetti, la economia degl” Indiani nell’ allevargli, e le diligenze , che adoperano per difendergli dalla pioggia troppo-ad essi nocevole, e dai molti nemici, che li oveldizitane s' esporranno quando parleremo dell' Agricoltura dei Messicani. His feet are six, each composed of three parts. From the hinder part of his body rise two hairs, two or three times longer than the body. Bk. I. He is furnished with two large wings, of which the female is entirely deprived. These wings are strengthened by two muscles: one external, which extends along the whole circumference of the wing, and the other internal and parallel to the first. The internal color is red, but darker in the female, and the external a whitish red. In the wild cochineal the internal color is darker still, and the external whitish or ash-colored. The cochineal is raised on a species of nopal, or opuntia, or Indian fig, which rises to a height of about eight feet, and whose fruit is similar to the tunas or figs of other opuntias, but not, like them, edible. It feeds on the leaves of this opuntia, sucking the juice with a trunk that it has in its breast between the first two pairs of feet. There it attains its full growth, and produces a numerous offspring. The manner of multiplying that these precious insects have, the economy of the Indians in raising them, and the pains they take to defend them from the rain, which is too harmful to them, and from the many enemies that persecute them, will be set forth when we speak of the agriculture of the Mexicans. (Kk)

Among the aquatic insects the Atetepitz is a marsh beetle, resembling in size and shape the flying beetles. It is furnished with four feet, and covered with a hard crust. The Atopinan is a marsh grasshopper of a dusky color, six fingers long and two wide. The Ahuihuitla is a worm of the Mexican lake, four fingers long, and as thick as the quill of a goose, tawny in the

(Kk) Don Antonio de Ulloa says that the nopal on which the cochineal is raised has no spines; but this is not so, for I, who spent five years in the Mixteca, always saw it on spiny nopals. M. Raynal persuaded himself that the color of the cochineal is owed to the tuna, or red fig, on which it feeds; but this author was not well informed; for the cochineal feeds not on the fruit but on the leaf, which is entirely green, nor does that nopal bear red figs but white ones. It is true that it can also be raised on that of the red fig; but that is not the plant proper to the cochineal. [p. 116] upper part of the body, and white in the lower. It stings with its tail, Bk. Finally, passing over other insects, whose names alone would furnish a very copious list, I wish to end this account with a kind of zoophytes, or plant-animals, which I saw in 1751 in a country house ten miles distant from Puebla toward the southeast. These were three or four fingers long, furnished with four very slender feet, and armed with two little horns; but their body was nothing other than the ribs of leaves of the same shape, size, and color as those seen in the other leaves of the trees where these insects were found. Dr. Hernández makes mention of them under the name of Quauhmecatl, and Gemelli describes another not altogether unlike them, found in the neighborhood of Manila. (Ll)

From the little that we have so far set forth of the natural history of that kingdom, the difference may be recognized that exists between the hot lands, the cold, and the temperate, of which the vast country of Anahuac is composed. In the hot lands Nature is more prodigal, in the cold and the temperate more benign. In the hot lands the mountains are more abundant in minerals and springs, the plains more pleasant, and the woods more leafy. In these lands are found the plants most useful to life, (Mm) the largest trees, the most precious woods, the most beautiful flowers, the

(Ll) I know well that modern naturalists give the name of Zoophytes, for the most

part, only to certain marine bodies which, having the appearance of vegetables, nevertheless have the nature of animals. Nevertheless I give that name to those land insects, because it suits them with as much propriety, and perhaps more, than those marine bodies. In my Physics I believe I have set out, with the greatest verisimilitude, the mechanism of nature in the generation of such insects.

are several European fruits produced, such as apples, peaches, pears, and others; but what is the lack of these few vegetables when compared with that unspeakable abundance and variety of plants, as fruit-bearing as medicinal, which are found in such countries? [p. 117] the most delicious fruits, and the most aromatic resins. There the species of animals are more varied and more numerous, and their in‐ Bk. I. dividuals handsomer and larger, the birds of more beautiful plumage and of sweeter song; but all these allurements are counterbalanced by as many inconveniences; for in such countries are found the most terrible wild beasts, the most venomous reptiles, and the most harmful insects. The land does not suffer the dismal symptoms of winter, nor is the air subject to the tiresome vicissitude of the seasons. On the land a perpetual spring reigns, and in the air a continual summer, to which the inhabitants readily accustom themselves; but the incessant sweating of their bodies, and the abundant and savory fruits with which the bountiful earth regales them at all times, expose them to several maladies unknown in other countries. The cold lands are not so fertile or so beautiful; but they are healthier, and their animals less harmful to man. In the temperate countries (at least in many, such as the valley of Mexico) one enjoys the advantages of the cold countries without their inconveniences, and several delights of the hot countries without their discomforts. The most common maladies in the hot countries are intermittent fevers, the spasm, and consumption, and in the port of Veracruz, for some few years past, the black vomit. (Nn) In the other countries, catarrhs, defluxions, pleurisy, and acute fevers, and in the capital diarrhea. Besides these ordinary maladies, certain epidemic diseases are wont to be felt at times, which seem periodic, although their period is not fixed and regular, such as those that occurred there in 1545, in 1576, and in our own days in 1736 and in 1762. The smallpox, brought there by the Spanish conquerors, is not seen in that country as frequently as in Europe, but after a certain number of years it comes, and then attacks all those who have not suffered it before, making in one stroke all that slaughter that it makes successively in Europe.

Character of the Mexicans, and of the The physical and moral qualities of the Mexicans, their disposition

other nations of

Anahuac. and their inclinations, were the same as those of the Acolhuas, the

Tepanecs, the Tlaxcalans, and the other nations, without any difference save that which comes from a different education; wherefore what we shall say of the one we wish to be understood likewise of the others. Several authors, ancient and modern alike, have undertaken the portrait of these nations; but among so many I have not found even one who is everywhere exact and faithful. Passions and prejudices in the case of some authors, and want of enlightenment, or else of reflection, in the case of others, have made them use colors very different from those they ought to have used. What we shall say, on the other hand, is founded on a serious and lengthy study of the history of those nations, on an intimate acquaintance of not a few years with them, and on the most minute observations made on their present condition, both by ourselves and by other impartial persons.

For the rest, I find nothing in myself that could incline me for or against them: for neither does the claim of a fellow countryman bend my judgment in their favor, nor is love of my nation, or zeal for the honor of my countrymen, capable of engaging me to condemn them; so that I shall say sincerely and frankly the good and the bad that I have recognized in them.

The Mexicans are, then, of middling stature, from which they depart more by excess than by defect, and of just proportion in their limbs; of good complexion, narrow forehead, and black eyes, with teeth even, firm, white, and clean, and hair thick, black, coarse, and straight; their beard is scanty, and for the most part they have no hair on their legs, thighs, and arms. Their skin is of an olive color.

> Non fi troverà forse veruna Nazione sulla terra, nella quale fieno più rari i deformi . E più difficile di trovare un gobbo , uno storpio , un guercio fra mille Messicani , che fra cen[p. 119] cento individui d' altre Nazioni . La spiacevolezza del low colore , la strattezza della loro fronte, la scarsezza della lo- Lu. IL ro barba , e la groflezza della loro capigliatura s' equilibrano in tal maniera colla regolarità ,e colla proporzione delle loro membra , che tengono 1l .mezzo fra la bellezza , e la detor.

Perhaps no nation on earth will be found among whom deformed persons are rarer. It is harder to find a hunchback, a cripple, or a squinter among a thousand Mexicans than among [p. 119] a hundred individuals of other nations. The unpleasantness of their color, the narrowness of their forehead, the scantiness of their beard, Bk. I. and the coarseness of their hair are so balanced by the regularity and proportion of their limbs that they hold the middle ground between beauty and deformity. Their aspect neither attracts nor offends; but among the young Mexican women many are found who are fair and quite beautiful, whose beauty is made the more lovable by the sweetness of their speech, the pleasantness of their manners, and the natural modesty of their countenances.

> mirà .. IL loto asperto nè alletta, nè offende; ma fra le gio.

Their senses are very keen, above all that of sight, which they keep entire to extreme old age. Their constitution is sound, and their health robust. They are found entirely free from many infirmities that are frequent among the Spaniards; but in the epidemic diseases to which the country is subject from time to time, they are the principal victims: among them such diseases begin, and among them they end. One never perceives from the mouth of a Mexican that foul breath which in others is wont to be caused by the corruption of the humors or by the indigestion of food. They are of a phlegmatic constitution; but the pituitous evacuations of their heads are very scanty, and they seldom spit. They turn gray and grow bald later than the Spaniards, and those who reach the age of a hundred are not very rare among them; almost all the others die of an acute disease.

> vani Messicane se ne trovano molte bianche, ed affai belle, la cui beltà rendesi più amabile per la dolcezza del loro parlare, per la piacevolezza delle loro maniere, e per la natu.

They are at present, and have always been, very sober in eating; but their passion for strong liquors is nonetheless most vehement. In ancient times they were held to their duty by the severity of the laws; today the abundance of such liquors and the impunity of drunkenness make half the nation lose its wits; and this is without doubt the principal cause of the slaughter that epidemic diseases make among them, besides the misery in which they live, more exposed to malignant influences and more deprived of the means of correcting them.

Among the few Mexicans who have devoted themselves to the study of letters, the rest of the nation being employed in public and private labors, we have known good geometers, excellent architects, and learned theologians.

There are many who grant the Mexicans great ability for imitation, but deny them that of invention. A vulgar error, which is belied by the ancient history of this nation.

would have us believe that the Spaniards at the arrival of the Phoenicians were more polished than the Mexicans at the arrival of the Spaniards; but this paradox has been sufficiently refuted by the very learned authors of the Literary History of Spain. It is true that the Spaniards in those remote centuries were not so barbarous as the

Chichimecs, the Californians, and other savage nations of America; but neither had they their government so well regulated, nor their arts so advanced, nor had they made, so far as we know, so much progress in the knowledge of Nature, as the

Mexicans at the beginning of the sixteenth century.

Bk. II. these do not act upon them with that impetuosity or that fury that they do in others. One does not ordinarily see among the Mexicans those transports of anger, or those frenzies of love, that are so frequent in other nations.

> —{Rr) L'esperienza ciha fatto conoscere quanto grati fieno i Messicani ai benefizj , che ricevono, qualora ficuri sono della benevolenza e Hella- fiticerità del benefattore. They are slow in their operations, and have an incredible phlegm in those works that require time and lengthy labor. They are likewise most patient of injuries and hardships, and very grateful for any benefit done them, provided they have no cause to fear some harm from the beneficent hand; but some Spaniards, not knowing how to distinguish tolerance from indolence, or distrust from ingratitude, say proverbially that the Indians neither feel injuries nor appreciate benefits. (Rr) This habitual distrust, in which they stand toward those who are not of their nation, often leads them to falsehood and to perfidy; whence good faith has not been held among them in all the esteem that it deserves.

They are also naturally serious, taciturn, and severe, and show themselves more zealous for the punishment of crimes than for the reward of virtue.

Liberality and detachment from any interest whatever are among the principal attributes of their character. Gold does not have among the Mexicans all the esteem that it enjoys among others. (Ss) They give without regret what they procure with the greatest labor. This detachment of theirs from interest, and the little love they bear toward those who govern them, make them refuse those labors to which they are compelled by them, and this

(Rr) Experience has shown us how grateful the Mexicans are for the benefits they receive, whenever they are sure of the benevolence and sincerity of the benefactor. Their gratitude has often been made manifest by public and noisy demonstrations, which make plain the falsity of that proverb.

The respect of children toward their parents, and that of the young toward their elders, are innate in that nation. Fathers love their children very much; but the love that husbands bear their wives is less than that which wives bear their husbands. It is common, though not general, among the men to be less attached to their own wives than to those of others.

he history of the primitive peopling of Anahuac is so ob‐

T         scured, and so enveloped in fables (as is that of the other

peoples of the world), that to find the truth is not merely difficult but altogether impossible. Certain it is nevertheless, as much from the venerable testimony of the holy books as from the constant and universal tradition of those peoples, that the first inhabitants of Anahuac descended from those few men whom Divine Providence snatched from the waters of the Flood to preserve the human species on earth. Nor can it be doubted that the nations that anciently peopled that land came to it from countries farther north in America, where their ancestors had settled many years and centuries earlier. On these two points I find all the Toltec, Chichimec, Acolhua, Mexican, and Tlaxcalan historians in agreement; but it is not known who the first inhabitants were, nor the time of their passage, nor the events of their journey and of their first settlements. Several historians, wishing to penetrate this chaos armed with feeble conjectures, vain combinations, and certain suspect paintings, have become lost

(b) I know well that many philosophers of Europe, who laugh at the asserters of giants, will mock me too, or at least pity my too great credulity; but I must not betray the truth to avoid censure. I know that among the civilized peoples of America the tradition ran of the existence in those countries of certain men of immense height and corpulence, and I do not recall that among any American nation there is a memory either of elephants, or of hippopotami, or of other quadrupeds of such size. I know that human skulls and entire skeletons of surprising size have been found, on the deposition of innumerable authors, and especially of two eyewitnesses above all exception, Dr. Hernández and Father Acosta, who lacked neither learning, nor criticism, nor sincerity; and I do not know that so far, among so many excavations made in New Spain, the skeleton of a hippopotamus has ever been uncovered, or, what is more, even a tooth of an elephant. I know that some of those bones are found in tombs built expressly; and I do not know that tombs are built to bury hippopotami or elephants. All this, and still more, ought to be considered, before deciding, by those authors who affirmed without hesitation that all the bones discovered in America belonged to those, or to I know not what other immense animals.

(c) Several historians of Mexico say that the giants were treacherously killed by the Tlaxcalans; but this report, besides having no other support than certain poems of those same Tlaxcalans, does not agree with the chronology of the aforesaid historians, since they make the giants too ancient, and the Tlaxcalans too modern in the country of Anahuac.

The nation of the Toltecs is the first of which some notices remain to us, Bk. II. though very scanty. These men, exiled, as they said, from their homeland

Huehuetlapallan, a place, as we conjecture, in the kingdom of Tollan, (d) from which they took their name, situated to the northwest of New Mexico, began their migration in the year I Tecpatl, that is, 596 of the common era. They stayed in every place where they came, for as long a time as their fancy suggested, or the need of providing for the preservation of life. Where they thought it advisable to make a longer stay, they built houses, and cultivated the land, sowing maize, cotton, and other plants, the seeds of which they carried with them in order to procure what was necessary. In this fashion they went wandering, always making their way toward the south, for the space of

Tulancingo, more than 50 miles to the northeast of the site where, some centuries later, the famous city of Mexico was founded. Throughout their whole journey they marched under the orders of certain captains, or lords, who were seven in number when they arrived at Tulancingo. (e) In this country, although of mild climate and fertile soil, they would not settle, but when scarcely twenty years had passed they withdrew forty miles to the west, along the bank of a river, where they founded the city of Tollan, or Tula, after the name of their homeland. This city, the most ancient, so far as is known, of the land of Anahuac, and one of the most celebrated in the history of Mexico, was the metropolis of the Toltec nation and the court of their kings. It is no wonder that only eight monarchs reigned in little less than four centuries, since a strange law of that nation ordained that none of their kings should reign either more or less than one Toltec century, which (as we shall explain elsewhere) consisted of fifty-two years. If the king completed the century on the throne, he at once left the government, and another was put in his place; but if the king failed before the century was out, the nobility succeeded to the government, and governed the rest of the century in the name of the deceased king. This was seen to happen in the case of Queen Xiutzaltzin: she died in the fifth year of her reign, and the nobility governed for the forty-eight remaining years.

§ 2.

Most celebrated among all the nations of Anahuac were the Toltecs, Civilization of the both for their civilization and for their excellence in the arts; whence in Toltecs. later centuries the name of Toltecs was given as a mark of honor to the most distinguished artisans. They always lived in society, gathered in well-regulated cities under the dominion of sovereigns and the direction of laws. They were little warlike, and more devoted to the cultivation of the arts than to the exercise of arms. The later nations acknowledged themselves indebted to their agriculture for maize, cotton, chili pepper, and other most useful fruits. And they practiced not only the arts of primary necessity, but also those that serve luxury. They knew how to smelt gold and silver, and to give them every sort of figure in casting. They worked skillfully every species of gem, and this was precisely the art that made their name most famous; but nothing could make them more esteemed among us than their having been the inventors,

many observations and exact knowledge of astronomy.

The Chevalier Boturini (*), on the authority of the ancient histories of the

Toltecs, says that these people, observing in their ancient homeland

Huehuetlapallan the excess of almost six hours of the solar year over the civil year that was in use among them, regulated it by the intercalary day that they inserted every four years; which they did a hundred and more years before the

Christian era. He says further that in the year 660, Ixtlilcuechahuac reigning in Tula, Huematzin, a celebrated astronomer, with the approval of the king convoked the sages of the nation, and with them painted that famous book which they called Teoamoxtli, that is, Divine Book, in which, with well-distinguished figures, were set forth the origin of the Indians, their dispersion after the confusion of tongues at Babel, their migration in Asia, their first settlements on the continent of America, the founding of the empire of Tula, and their progress up to that time. The heavens, the planets, the constellations, the Toltec calendar with its cycles, the mythological transformations (in which they enclosed their moral philosophy), and the secrets of popular wisdom wrapped up among the hieroglyphics of their gods, together with everything that belonged to religion and to customs, were described there. The said Chevalier adds, moreover, that there was seen noted in their paintings the solar eclipse that occurred at the death of our Redeemer, in the year VII
