Whatever may be said of these curious anecdotes of the Chevalier Boturini, which I leave to the free judgment of prudent readers, it is certain and indubitable among all those who have studied the history of those nations that the Toltecs had a clear and distinct knowledge of the universal Flood, of the confusion of tongues, and of the dispersion of peoples; indeed, they named their first ancestors, who separated from the rest of the families in that universal dispersion. It is likewise certain, as we shall show elsewhere (though it may seem an incredible thing to the critics of Europe, accustomed to believe all Americans cut to one measure), that the Mexicans and all the other civilized nations of Anahuac had their civil year as well adjusted to the solar by means of intercalary days as the Romans had it after the ordinance of Julius Caesar, and that such exactness was owed to the enlightenment of the Toltecs. As regards religion, they were idolaters, and, so far as appears from history, were the inventors of the greater part of the Mexican mythology; but we do not know that they had in use those barbarous and bloody sacrifices which afterward became so frequent among the other nations. The Texcocan historians believed the Toltecs to be the authors of that most famous idol representing the god of water, placed on Mount Tlaloc, of which we shall speak later. It is certain indeed that they built, in honor of their beloved god Quetzalcoatl, the very lofty pyramid of Cholula, and probably also the famous ones of Teotihuacan, in honor of the Sun and the Moon, which, though disfigured, still subsist. (h) The painting alleged by the Chevalier Boturini represented the pyramid of

Cholula, with this Mexican inscription, Toltecatl Chalchihuatl onazia Ehecatepetl, which he interprets thus: Monument, or precious stone of the Toltec nation, which with its neck went searching out the region of the air; but disregarding the incorrect manner of writing and the barbarism Chalchihuatl, anyone at all instructed in the Mexican language will at once perceive that a more fantastic interpretation could not be made. At the foot of the painting, the said Chevalier says, the author set a note, in which, speaking to his countrymen, he admonished them in this fashion: Nobles and lords, behold your writings, the mirror of your antiquity, and the history of your forefathers, who, urged by fear of the flood, built this refuge as a fitting shelter, in case they should again be overtaken by such a calamity. But

to tell the truth, the Toltecs would have been entirely devoid of sense if, for fear of the flood, they had undertaken with so much expense and toil the building of that portentous pyramid, when they had in the lofty mountains not far from Cholula a safer refuge against inundations, and much less danger of dying of hunger. On the same canvas was represented, says Boturini, the baptism of Ilamatecuhtli, queen of Cholula, conferred on her by the deacon Aguilar on August 6, 1521, together with the apparition of the Madonna to a certain Franciscan religious who was in Rome, ordering him to set out for Mexico, where on a mountain made by hand (that is, the pyramid of

Cholula) he was to place her image. But this is nothing other than a tissue of dreams and lies: for neither were there ever kings in Cholula, nor could that baptism, of which no writer speaks, have been celebrated on August 6, 1521, because at that time

Aguilar was with the other Spaniards in the greatest heat of the siege of the capital, which seven days later was to surrender to the victors. Of the alleged apparition of the

[p. 131] side into many large cities; but the stupendous calamities that befell them in the first years of the reign of Topiltzin overturned their pow‐ Bk. II. er and their happiness. For some years heaven denied them the rain necessary for their fields, and the earth the fruits on which they sustained themselves. The air, infected with mortal corruption, filled the land each day with corpses, and with consternation the minds of those who survived the ruin of their fellow countrymen. Thus a great part of the nation died of hunger and of contagion. Topiltzin also died in the year II Tecpatl, the twentieth of his reign, which was probably 1052 of the common era, and with him ended the monarchy of the Toltecs. The wretched remnants of the nation, thinking to escape the common calamity, sought in other countries a fitting remedy for their ills. Some made for Onohualco, or Yucatán, others toward Guatemala; meanwhile there remained in the kingdom of Tula various families scattered here and there in the great valley, where Mexico was afterward founded, in Cholula, in Tlaximaloyan, and in other places, and among them the two princes, sons of King Topiltzin, whose descendants in the course of time became related by marriage to the royal families of Mexico, of Texcoco, and of Colhuacan.

Their native country, whose situation we do not know, was called

Amaquemecan, where, by their own account, several monarchs of their nation ruled for many years. (k)

The character of the Chichimecs was indeed singular, as is seen from their history; for to a certain kind of civility they added many traits of barbarism. They lived under the command of a sovereign, and of chiefs and governors entrusted with the supreme authority, with as much submission as is commonly seen among the most civilized nations. There was distinction between the commoners and the nobility, and the commoners were accustomed to revere those whom birth, merit, or the favor of the prince raised above their condition.

They lived gathered in places composed, as one must believe, of wretched huts; (l) but they practiced neither agriculture nor those arts that

(k) Torquemada names three Chichimec kings of Amaquemecan, and to the first

gives 180 years of reign, to the second 156, and to the third 133. See what we say in our Dissertation II concerning the preposterous chronology of this author. The same author undoubtedly affirms that Amaquemecan was six hundred miles distant from the site where the city of Guadalajara is today; but in more than twelve hundred miles of populated country that lies beyond that city, there is found no trace, nor any memory, of the kingdom of Amaquemecan: whence we believe it to be a country not yet discovered, and much farther north than Torquemada imagined.

Their religion was reduced to the simple worship of the Sun, to whose alleged divinity they offered grass, and the flowers they found growing in the fields. As for their customs, they were certainly less unpleasing, and less coarse, than the temper of a hunting people would lead one to expect.

Anahuac. between his two sons, Achcauhtli and Xolotl. The latter, either because he ill endured, as often happens, the division of his own authority, wished to try whether fortune destined other lands for him, where he might command without a rival; or because, seeing that the mountains of his kingdom were not sufficient to provide sustenance for a number of inhabitants perhaps grown too large, he determined to remedy the necessity by a timely departure. Having therefore taken such a resolution, for the one motive or the other, and having first had a good part of the southern lands reconnoitered by his scouts, he set out from his homeland with a large army of his subjects, who chose, whether from affection or from interest, to accompany him. Informato Xolotl dellà condizione del paese, prese la risoluzione di itabilirs in Tenayuca , luogo dal fito di Messico sei miglia verso Tra» montana discosto, e distribuì nelle vicine terra tutta la. sua gente; ma per essere stata la maggior popolazione verso Tramontana, & verso Greco, ebbe poi quel tratto di terra il nome di Chichimecarlalli, cioè Terra dei Cicimechi. Gli Storici dicono, che in Tenayuca fi fece la rivista della gente, e però gli fu ancora dato il nome di Nepobualco , che vale , luogo della numerazione; ma &È affatto incredibile quel che aggiunge Torquemada, cioè essere stato trovato nella « €Tivista più d'un milione di Cicimechi , ed esser durati fino + ai suoi tempi dodici mucch} fatti dei fasi, che andavano gettando nel passar la rivista» Impertiocchè nè è verisimile, che. un efercito tanto groflo sì mettessè in istrada per un viaggio così lungo, nè pare possibile , che un distretto tanto piccolo sostentar potesse un milione di cacciatori . (n)

(m) Several authors have labored to divine the etymology of the name Chichimecatl. Torquemada says that this name is derived from Techichinani, which means Sucker, because the Chichimecs sucked the blood of the animals they hunted. But this etymology is forced, especially among those peoples who did not alter names in such a fashion in their derivation. Vetancurt believed that it was derived from Chichime, that is, Dogs, because by that name they were called in contempt by the other nations; but if it had been so, they would not glory, as in fact they did glory, in the name of Chichimecatl. > Stabilito il Re nel luogo: di Tenayuca, che fin d" allo. ra destinò per la sua Corte, e dati gli ordini opportuni per la formazione delle altre Città o Villagg}, comandò: ad un suo Capîtano chiamato Achiroma:l,, che andass2 a riconoscere l'origine di certi fumi, che il Principe avea osservato nella fua spedizione . Tula, where they arrived after eighteen months. From this place they headed toward those of Cempoala and Tepepulco, about forty miles distant to the northeast of the site of Mexico. Thence Xolotl sent his son, Prince Nopaltzin, to observe the country. The prince traversed the shores of the lakes and the mountains that surround the delightful valley of Mexico, and having surveyed the rest of the country from the top of a high mountain, he shot four arrows toward the four winds as a sign of the possession that in the name of the king his father he was taking of all that land. Informed of the condition of the country, Xolotl took the resolution to settle in Tenayuca, a place six miles distant from the site of Mexico toward the north, and distributed all his people in the neighboring lands; but because the greater part of the population was toward the north and toward the northeast, that tract of land afterward took the name of

Chichimecatlalli, that is, Land of the Chichimecs. The historians say that in Tenayuca a review of the people was held, and that for this reason the name of Nepohualco was also given to it, which means place of the counting; but altogether incredible is what Torquemada adds, namely that more than a million Chichimecs were found in the review, and that twelve heaps made of the stones they kept throwing down as they passed in review lasted down to his own times. For it is neither likely that so great an army would set out on so long a journey, nor does it seem possible that so small a district could have sustained a million hunters. (n)

Once the king was settled in the place of Tenayuca, which from that time he designated for his court, and the appropriate orders given for the formation of the other cities or villages, he commanded one of his captains, called Achitomatl, to go and reconnoiter the origin of certain smokes that the prince had observed on his expedition.

This humane conduct helped the Chichimecs greatly; for through contact with that industrious nation they began to taste maize and other fruits of industry, they learned agriculture, the manner of extracting metals and the art of smelting them, as well as those of working stone and of spinning and weaving cotton, and others, by which they improved their sustenance, their clothing, their dwellings, and their customs.

A few years later there arrived also three princes with a large army of the Acolhua nation, natives of Teoacolhuacan, a country near, or not very far from, the kingdom of Amaquemecan. These princes were called Acolhuatzin, Chiconcuauhtli, and Tzontecomatl, and were of the most noble house of Citin. The nation was the most civilized and polished of all that were in that country after the Toltecs. One may well understand how great must have been the stir that so great a novelty made in that kingdom, and the disquiet into which so great a multitude of unknown people threw the Chichimecs; nor does it seem likely that the king would have allowed them to enter the country without first having informed himself of their condition and of the motive of their coming. The king was then in Texcoco, whither he had moved his court, either weary of the site of Tenayuca, or else attracted by the advantageous situation of that new place. Here the three princes arrived, and, presented to the king, after a deep bow and that ceremony of veneration so familiar to those peoples, of kissing the hand after touching the earth with it, they said to him in substance these words: “We have come, great King, from the kingdom of

Chichimecs enjoy under the rule of so humane a king, we have set aside the comforts we had in our homeland for the glory of being your subjects. We beg you therefore to give us a place in your happy land, where we may live dependent on your authority and subject to your commands.” The Chichimec was gratified, more than by the lordly air and the courtly manners of those most noble youths, by the flattering vanity of seeing humbled in his presence three princes attracted by such distant [p. 137] countries by the fame of his power and of his clemency. He replied pleasantly to their expressions, and offered to comply with their Bk. II. wishes; but while he was deliberating on the manner of doing so, he ordered his son Nopaltzin to lodge them and to take care of them.

The king had two unmarried daughters, whom at first he thought to marry to the two elder princes; but he would not disclose his thought until he should have informed himself of their character and been certain of the will of his subjects. When he was then sure of the one and of the other, he called the princes to him, who were somewhat anxious about their lot, and made known to them his resolution not only to grant them establishments in his kingdom, but also to marry them to his daughters, complaining that he had not another, so that none should be excluded from the new alliance. The princes thanked him with singular expressions of gratitude, and offered to serve him with the greatest fidelity.

The day appointed for the wedding having arrived, so great a crowd of people flocked to Tenayuca, the place destined for that great ceremony, that the city not being sufficient to hold it, many people remained in the countryside. Acolhuatzin married the elder of the two princesses, called Cuetlaxochitl, and Chiconcuauhtli took the other. The third prince had Coatetl, a maiden born in Chalco of most noble parents, in whom Toltec blood had been mingled with Chichimec. The public rejoicings lasted as long as sixty days, in which there was wrestling, racing, and combats with wild beasts, exercises suited to the genius of the Chichimecs, and in all of them Prince Nopaltzin distinguished himself. Following the example of the royal persons, those two nations went on knitting themselves together with marriages, until of both one was made, which, taking its name from the nobler part, was called Acolhua, and the kingdom Acolhuacan, the name of Chichimecs remaining then for those men who, prizing the exercise of the chase more than the labors of agriculture, or else impatient of subordination, went off to the mountains that are toward the north [p. 138] and toward the northwest of the Mexican valley, where, giving them‐

These barbarians, mingled with the nation of the Otomis, who followed the same system of life, occupied a tract of land of more than three hundred miles, and by their descendants the Spaniards were for many years greatly harassed after the conquest of Mexico.

When the rejoicings of the wedding were over, Xolotl divided his

§ 7. kingdom into several states, and gave the investiture of them to his

Division of the states, and rebellions. sons-in-law and to other nobles of the one nation and of the other.

He granted to Prince Acolhuatzin the state of Azcapotzalco, eighteen miles west of Texcoco, and from him descended the kings under whose yoke the Mexicans remained for more than fifty years. To

Chiconcuauhtli he conferred the state of Xaltocan; and to

Tzontecomatl that of Coatlichan.

The population increased every day, and with it the civilization of the peoples; but there were awakened together in their minds ambition and other passions, which lie asleep for want of ideas in the time of savage life. Xolotl, who during the greater part of his government had ruled his subjects with gentleness, and had found in them the greatest docility, was then seen, in the last years of his life, compelled to use severity to repress the restlessness of some rebels, now stripping them of their offices, now punishing the most guilty with death.

These just punishments, instead of frightening them, so exasperated them that they formed the detestable design of taking the king’s life, nor did a ready occasion for carrying it out fail them. The king had shortly before made known his wish to increase the water of his gardens, where he was accustomed to divert himself, and often also went to sleep there, weighed down by years, or enticed by the freshness and the pleasantness of the place. Aware of this, the rebels, having made a dam in the stream that crossed the city, opened a trench [p. 139] to conduct the water to the gardens; but to do so they waited for the time when the king was accustomed to sleep there, and then, the dam Bk. II. having been removed on the side of the trench, they sent all the water at once into the gardens, so that he should be drowned. They flattered themselves that their crime would never be discovered, since the misfortune of the king might be ascribed to some accident, or to measures ill taken by subjects who sincerely desired to serve their lord; but they deceived themselves, and their blow did not succeed; for the king had secret warning of the conspiracy, and, dissembling that he knew of it, he went at the accustomed hour to the garden and lay down to sleep in an elevated spot, where he would not be in danger. When he then saw the water enter, although the treachery was already evident, he continued his dissimulation in order to mock his enemies: “I,” he then said, “was well persuaded that my subjects loved me; but now I see that they love me far more than I thought. I wanted to increase the water of my gardens, and behold, my subjects have brought it to me without any expense. We must therefore make a feast of my good fortune.” Then he ordered rejoicings to be held in the court, and when they were over he departed for Tenayuca, full of grief and indignation, and determined to give a rigorous punishment to the conspirators; but there he was seized by a mortal illness, which calmed his anger.

Now, feeling the nearness of death, he called to him Prince § 8.

Death and funeral of Nopaltzin, his daughters, and Acolhuatzin his son-in-law (since the Xolotl. other two princes were already dead), and to them he commended peace among themselves, the care of the peoples entrusted to them, the protection of the nobility, and kindness toward all their subjects; and then, a few hours later, amid the tears and sobs of his children, he ceased to live, at a very advanced age, and after having reigned in that country, as it seems, more than forty years. He was a robust and courageous man, but of a most tender heart toward his children, and very kind toward his subjects. His reign would have been happier had it been shorter. (o)

The news of the king’s death spread at once throughout the king‐

> » mente e la morte nostra, e la wita-

Bk. II. dom, and prompt notice was given to the principal lords, so that they might be present at the funeral. They adorned the royal corpse with several small figures of gold and silver, which the Chichimecs, instructed by the Toltecs, had already begun to make, and placed it on a seat made of copal gum and other aromatic materials; and so it remained five days, while the lords summoned to the obsequies were arriving. When all had assembled amid an infinite throng of people, the corpse was burned, according to the custom of the Chichimecs, and the ashes gathered in an urn of very hard stone. This urn was kept on display for forty days in a hall of the royal house, where every day the nobility came to render to their dead lord the homage of tears, and afterward the urn was carried to a cave near the city with the same demonstrations of grief.

§ 9.

As soon as the funeral of Xolotl was over, they celebrated the exalNopaltzin, second tation to the throne of Prince Nopaltzin with acclamations and re‐

king of the

Chichimecs. joicings for another forty days. As the lords were then taking leave of the new king to return to their respective states, one of them made this brief address: “Great King and Lord, we, as your subjects and servants, go to obey your commands, to govern the peoples that you have entrusted to our care, bearing in our hearts the pleasure of having seen you on the throne, owed no less to your virtue than to your birth. We protest that the good we have in serving so lofty and so powerful a lord is incomparable; and we beg you to look upon us with the eyes of a true father, and to protect us with your power, that we may be secure beneath your shadow. You are at once a restoring water and a devouring fire, and in your hands you hold equally both our death and our life.”

Bk. II. Apopozoc. To Tlotzin, who was the first-born, he conferred the government of Texcoco, that he might go on learning the difficult art of ruling men, and to the other two he gave the investiture of the states of Zacatlán and of Tenamitic. (p)

For a year the king remained at the court of Tenayuca, setting in order the affairs of the state, which was no longer so tranquil as at the beginning. Thence he went to Texcoco to treat with his son about the most suitable means to be taken to restore the kingdom to its former tranquillity. Being there, he once entered the royal gardens with his son and with other lords of his court, and while he was conversing with them, he burst unexpectedly into violent weeping, and being asked the cause: “Two,” he replied, “are the causes of my tears: one is the memory of my dead father, which is revived in me by the sight of this place, where he used to divert himself; and the other is the comparison I make of those happy times with these bitter days. When my father planted these gardens, he had subjects more peaceable, who served him with sincerity in those offices that he conferred on them, and they accepted them with humility and with gratitude; but today ambition and discord reign everywhere. It grieves me to be compelled to treat as enemies those subjects whom once I treated in this very place as friends and brothers. You, my son,” he added, speaking to Tlotzin, “keep ever before your eyes the image of your mighty grandfather, and strive to imitate the examples of prudence and of justice that he left us. Fortify your heart with all that you will afterward need for ruling

Prince Acolhuatzin, who was still living, thinking the limits of his state of Azcapotzalco too narrow, resolved to take possession of that of Tepotzotlán, and in fact took it by force, in spite of the resistance made by Chalchiuhcua, lord of that state. It is to be believed that

> ci A] n i —

Acolhuatzin would not have undertaken such violence without the express consent of the king, who perhaps wished in that way to avenge some offense received from Chalchiuhcua.

Somewhat more bloody was the contest which broke out a little later over an interest of a very different nature. Huetzin, lord of

Coatlichan, son of the late Prince Tzontecomatl, (q) wished to marry

Atotoztli, a beautiful and noble maiden, and a niece of the queen. The same pretension was held by Yacazozolotl, lord of Tepetlaoztoc; but he, either because he was more in love with the maiden, or because he was of a more violent character, not content with asking for her from her father, wished to make himself master of her beauty by arms, and to this end gathered a small army of his subjects, to whom was joined Tochintecuhtli, who had been lord of Cuahuacan, and for his misdeeds had been stripped of it and confined to Tepetlaoztoc. Aware of this attempt, Huetzin came to meet him with a larger number of troops, and offered him battle in the neighborhood of Texcoco, in which some of Yacazozolotl’s people perished along with him, and the rest of the army was routed. Tochintecuhtli saved himself by flight, taking refuge in the city of Huexotzinco beyond the mountains.

Huetzin

(q) Torquemada makes Huetzin the son of Itzmitl, and this one the son of

Tzontecomatl, in ch. 36 of bk. 1; but in ch. 40 he says that Itzmitl was one of those who came with Xolotl from Amaquemecan; so that he makes him born before his father Tzontecomatl, who was still young when he came to Anahuac; and he did not come before the 47th year of the reign of Xolotl, as the same author affirms. Besides this, in one place he makes Itzmitl a pure Chichimec, and in another the son of an

Acolhua: but who will be able to point out all the contradictions and anachronisms of Torquemada?

[p. 143]

Huetzin, freed from his rival, took possession, with the consent of the king, of the maiden and of the state of Tepetlaoztoc.                Bk. II.

After these little wars among the feudatories, another, more considerable, was set in motion by the crown against the province of Tulancingo, which had rebelled. The king himself went there in person with a large army; but as the rebels were in great number and well trained in arms, the royal army at times had the worse of it in the nineteen days that the war lasted, until, reinforced with new troops sent by Prince Tlotzin, the rebels were routed, and the leaders of the rebellion punished with the extreme penalty. Their bad example, imitated by other lords, met likewise with the same fate.

Nopaltzin had already restored tranquillity to the kingdom, when the celebrated Prince Acolhuatzin, first lord of Azcapotzalco, died, leaving the state to his son Tezozomoc. His funeral was celebrated with great magnificence, the king attending with the nobility of both nations, Acolhua and Chichimec.

It was not long before the king himself also died, after thirty-two § 10. years of reign, having previously declared as his successor to the Tlotzin, third king of crown his first-born, Tlotzin. The obsequies were held in the same the Chichimecs. court, and with the same apparatus and ceremonies as those of King Xolotl, to whom he was like no less in character than in robustness and courage.

Among the other lords who attended the exaltation of the new king were his two brothers Cuauhtequihua and Apopozoc, whom he kept for a year in his royal house. Tlotzin was of so benign and loving a temper that he was the whole delight of his vassals. All the nobles sought pretexts to visit him and to enjoy the pleasantness and sweetness of his manner. Notwithstanding this disposition so inclined to peace, he took great care of the affairs of war, causing his subjects to exercise often in arms, and he himself delighted in the chase; but we know nothing in particular of his actions, nor of the events of his reign in the thirty-six years that he occupied the throne of Acolhuacan. § 11.   There succeeded Tlotzin in the kingdom his son Quinatzin, (*) Quinatzin, fourth king of the born of Cuauhcihuatzin, daughter of the lord of Huexotla. His exalta‐

Chichimecs. tion was celebrated with greater solemnity than that of his predecessors, not in Tenayuca, but in Texcoco, where he established his court, and from then until the conquest by the Spaniards that city was always the capital of the kingdom of Acolhuacan. To pass from the old to the new court he had himself carried in an open litter on the shoulders of four principal lords, and under an umbrella, which four others bore. Until that time all the lords had always walked on foot.

This king was the first to whom vanity suggested such a kind of magnificence, and this example was imitated by his successors, and by all the kings and magnates of that country, each striving to surpass the others in pomp: an emulation too pernicious no less to the states than to the princes themselves.

The beginnings of his government were quite tranquil; but a little later the states of Metztitlan and of Totoltepec, situated in the mountains which lie to the north of that capital, rebelled. As soon as the king had notice of it, he marched with a large army, and sent word to the leaders of the rebellion that if their courage was equal to their perfidy, they should descend within two days to the plain of

Tlaximalco, where in a battle their fate would be decided; if not, he was determined to put their cities to fire and flame, sparing neither women nor children. The rebels, as they were already well prepared, came down before the appointed time to that plain to show off their courage. The signal for battle having been given there, they fought furiously and obstinately on both sides, until night separated the armies

Thus they continued for forty days in frequent fights, the rebels never losing heart in spite of the Bk. II. advantages which the royal troops won every day; but perceiving at last, from the slaughter and the diminution of their soldiers, their imminent ruin, they surrendered to their sovereign, who, punishing the leaders of the rebellion severely, pardoned the peoples their crime. He did the same with the state of Tepepulco, which had also rebelled.

> Quetto spirito di ribellione a guisa di contagio andavasi per tutto il regno diffondendo : poichè appena suggetrato Tepepolco , fi dichiararono ribelli Huehuetoca , Mizquic, Torcolapa , ed altre quattro Città. Volle il Re andar in persona con un buon corpo di truppe contro Totolapa, è mandò contro l'altre lei Città altrettanti corpi sotto il comando di bravi e fedeli Generali: e fu tanta la sua felicità , che infra pochissimo nempo , e senza perdita considerabile rimise sorto la sua ubbidienza tutte le sette Città. Quelte vittorie si celebrarono con grandi allegrezze. per otto. dì nella Corte, e furono premiati i Generali, ed i Soldati ,che più s'erano segnalati. Siccome il - cattivo esempio d' alcuni stati altri avea spinti alla ribellione, così .l’infelice riuscita servì loro nel avvenire d'esempio per non macchinar più novità contro la dovura- subordinazione al: lor Sovrano: onde nel resto del suo governo, che per quel che dicono gli Storici, fu di seffaora anni, godette ,Quinatzio d' una gran tranquillità ,

This spirit of rebellion went spreading through the whole kingdom like a contagion: for scarcely was Tepepulco subdued when Huehuetoca, Mixquic, Totolapan, and four other cities declared themselves in rebellion. The king wished to go in person with a good body of troops against Totolapan, and sent against the other six cities as many bodies under the command of brave and faithful generals: and so great was his good fortune that in a very short time, and without considerable loss, he brought all seven cities back under his obedience. These victories were celebrated with great rejoicings for eight days at the court, and the generals and the soldiers who had most distinguished themselves were rewarded. Just as the bad example of some states had driven others to rebellion, so the unhappy outcome served them as a lesson for the future not to plot any more novelties against the due subordination to their sovereign: whence in the rest of his government, which, according to what the historians say, lasted sixty years, Quinatzin enjoyed great tranquillity.

> Quando venne a morte questo Re, si fecero verso di lui alcune dimostrazioni , che non .s' erano mai fatte verso i fuoi + antecessoci ; poichè aperto il cadavero, e cavategli le viscere, il prepararono con non .so .che camposizione d' aromi, acciocchè fi prefervasse per qualche tempo dalla corruzione . Collocaronto poi in. una gran seggia vestito degli abiti reali, ed armato d'arco. e di sreccie, è gli posero ai piedi un'aquila di legno, ed addietro una tigre, per fignificare l'iotre- Pidezza e bravura di lui. When this king came to die, there were made toward him certain demonstrations that had never been made toward his predecessors; for his body having been opened, and the viscera removed, they prepared it with I know not what composition of aromatics, so that it might be preserved for some time from corruption. They then placed him in a great seat, clad in the royal garments, and armed with bow and arrows, and put at his feet a wooden eagle, and behind him a tiger, to signify his intrepidity and bravery. In this posture they kept him on public display for forty days, and after the customary weeping they burned him [p. 146] and buried the ashes in a cave of the mountains near Texcoco. Bk. II.

We cannot state the year in which the first five kings began to reign, because we do not know how long Xolotl and Techotlalatzin reigned; we judge it, however, probable that the Chichimec monarchy had its beginning in

Anahuac toward the end of the twelfth century, and lasted about 330 years, until 1521, in which it ended together with the kingdom of Mexico.

The Acolhuas arrived in the country of Anahuac after the thirteenth century had begun. As for the other nations, the diversity of opinions, and the confusion of the historians, about their origin, their number, and the time at which they came into Anahuac, is incredible. The very great study that I have made to trace out the truth has served me for nothing else than to increase my uncertainty and to make me lose altogether the hope of knowing in the future what up to now has been unknown. Passing over, then, the fables, we shall say only what is certain, or at least very probable.

Nothing is known of their origin (r), nor do the ancient paintings of those peoples tell us anything else, except that they inhabited the country surrounding the great mountain Matlalcueye, and that, driven out from there by the Teochichimecs, or Tlaxcalans, they moved to the coasts of the Gulf of Mexico. Bk. II.

ing scattered in the caves of the mountains, and sustaining themselves by the chase, in which they were most skillful. They occupied a tract of land of more than three hundred miles from the mountains of Ixmiquilpan toward the northwest, bordering on the east and on the west on other nations likewise savage. In the fifteenth century they began, as we shall say elsewhere, to live in society, subject to the crown of Acolhuacan, either compelled by force or else stimulated by the example of the other nations. They founded in the country of

Anahuac, and even in the very valley of Mexico, countless places: the greater part of them, and especially the largest, such as those of

Jilotepec and of Huitzapan, in the neighborhood of the country which they had occupied before; others scattered among the

Matlatzincas and the Tlaxcalans, and in other provinces of the kingdom, preserving down to our times without alteration their primitive language even in the isolated colonies, surrounded everywhere by other nations. It is not, however, to be thought that the whole nation was then reduced to civil life, since a great part, and perhaps the greatest, remained still together with the Chichimecs in savage life.

The barbarians of both nations, confounded by the Spaniards under the name of Chichimecs, made themselves famous by their raids, and were not wholly subjugated by the Spaniards until the seventeenth century. The Otomis have always been reputed the coarsest nation of

Anahuac, as much because of the difficulty that all find in understanding their language as because of their servile life; since even in the time of the Mexican kings they were treated like slaves. Their language is very difficult, and full of aspirations, which are formed partly in the throat and partly in the nose; but otherwise it is sufficiently copious and expressive. Anciently they were renowned for their skill in the chase; today they trade for the most part in coarse cloths, with which they clothe the other Indians.

[p. 149] of the Mexicans, and had frequent wars with them. Their artisans either surpassed or equaled those of the other nations: at least after the Bk. II. conquest of Mexico the best works of mosaic were made in Michoacán, and there alone down to our times has this so precious art been preserved. The Tarascans were idolaters, but not so cruel in their worship as the Mexicans. Their language is abundant, sweet, and sonorous. They often use the soft R: their syllables consist for the most part of a single consonant and a vowel. Besides the natural advantages of their country, the Tarascans had the good fortune to have as first bishop Don Vasco de Quiroga, one of the most distinguished prelates that Spain has produced, truly worthy of being compared with the ancient Fathers of Christianity; whose memory has been preserved alive down to our times, and will be preserved eternally among those peoples. The country of Michoacán, which is among the most valuable of the New World, was annexed to the crown of Spain by the free and spontaneous cession of its legitimate sovereign, without costing the Spaniards even a drop of blood, although it is to be believed that the fear instilled in him by the recent ruin of the Mexican empire impelled that monarch to such a cession. Bk. II. had come from the north, and that when they arrived at Soconusco they separated, some going to live in the country of Nicaragua, and the others remaining in that of Chiapas. This nation, according to what the historians say, was not governed by a king but by two military chiefs elected by the priests. So they continued until they were subjected to that crown by the last Mexican kings. They made the same use of paintings as the Mexicans and had the same way of reckoning time; but the figures with which they represented the years, the months, and the days were altogether different.

As for the Cohuixcas, the Cuitlatecs, the Yopis, the Mazatecs, the Popolocas, the Chinantecs, and the Totonacs, we know nothing of their origin or of the time when they arrived in Anahuac. Of their particular customs we shall say something, wherever it may serve the history of the Mexicans.

But among all the nations that peopled the country of Anahuac, § 15. the most renowned, and those that figure most in the history of The Nahuatlacas. Mexico, are those that were commonly called Nahuatlacas. This name, whose etymology we set out at the beginning of this History, was given principally to those seven nations, or rather to those seven tribes of one and the same nation, which arrived in that country after the Chichimecs, and peopled the islets, the shores, and the neighborhood of the Mexican lakes. These tribes were those of the Xochimilcas, the Chalcas, the Tepanecs, the Colhuas, the Tlahuicas, the Tlaxcalans, and the Mexicans. The origin of all these tribes was the province of Aztlan, whence the Mexicans came out, or else another one contiguous to it and peopled by the same nation. All the historians represent them as originating in one and the same country: all spoke the same language. The various names by which they are known were taken from the places they founded or those in which they settled.

It is beyond doubt that these tribes did not all arrive in that country together, but at different times and in the order we have indicated; but there is a great variety of opinion among the historians about the precise time at which they came into Anahuac. The Tlaxcalans, called Teochichimecs by Torquemada and other au‐ § 16. thors and considered as a tribe of the Chichimec nation, (y) settled at The Tlaxcalans. first in Poyauhtlan, a place situated on the eastern shore of the Lake of Texcoco, between this capital and the village of Chimalhuacán. There they lived for some time in great misery, sustaining themselves only on game for want of arable land; but having multiplied, and wishing to enlarge the bounds of their territory, they drew upon themselves the resentment of the neighboring nations.

(y) Torquemada not only says that the Tlaxcalans were Teochichimecs, but even affirms in bk. 3, ch. 10, that these Teochichimecs were Otomis. If the Tlaxcalans were Otomis, why did they not speak the Otomi language? And if they ever spoke it, why did they abandon it for the Mexican? Where has a free nation ever been seen to abandon its native speech in order to adopt that of its enemies? It is no less incredible that the Chichimecs were Otomis, as the aforesaid author supposes here, although in bk. 1, ch. 11, he affirms the opposite. Who compelled the Chichimecs to abandon their primitive speech? Only one who is unacquainted with the character of those nations, and does not know how constant they are in retaining their national tongue, could be persuaded that the Chichimecs, through intercourse and alliance with the Acolhuas, would have left Otomi for Mexican. If the true Otomis have not altered their idiom in so many centuries, neither under the domination of the Mexicans nor under that of the Spaniards, how can it be believed that the Chichimecs entirely changed their language, being masters of that country, and always occupying the throne of Acolhuacan from Xolotl, founder of that kingdom, down to the conquest of the Spaniards? I, however, do not doubt that the proper language of the ancient Chichimecs was the same as that of the Acolhuas and Nahuatlacas, that is, the Mexican. The same seems to me true of the Toltecs, whatever other authors may say, nor can I be persuaded of the contrary after the most diligent study of history. We know, too, that the names of the places whence the Toltecs and the Chichimecs came out, and of those which they founded in Anahuac, of the persons of both nations, and of the years they used, were Mexican. We know that the Toltecs and the Chichimecs, and the Chichimecs and the Acolhuas, from the very beginning communicated with one another and understood each other reciprocally without an interpreter. The finding of the Mexican language spread as far as Nicaragua cannot be ascribed to anything but the dispersion of the Toltecs, who spoke it, since it is not known that the Nahuatlacas advanced beyond Chiapas. Finally, we do not find even an argument to confirm the opposite opinion, although common among our historians.

[p. 154]

The Xochimilcas, the Colhuas, the Tepanecs, and in all likelihood the Bk. II. Chalcas too, who, being their neighbors, were likewise the most

harmed, formed a confederacy and raised a considerable army to drive such pernicious settlers out of the Valley of Mexico. The

Tlaxcalans, whom the consciousness of their usurpations kept ever on the watch, came out well drawn up to meet them. The battle was one of the bloodiest and most memorable that are read in the history of

Mexico. The Tlaxcalans, though inferior in number, made such slaughter of their enemies that they left the field full of corpses and a part of the lake, on whose shore the fight took place, stained with blood. Although they came out of this battle so glorious, they nevertheless resolved to abandon that site, well persuaded that as long as they were there they would be forever harassed by their neighbors; and therefore, after having surveyed the whole country by means of their scouts, and not having found a place where they could all settle together, they agreed to separate, one part of them going toward the south and the other toward the north. The latter, after a short journey, settled, with the permission of the Chichimec king, in

Tulancingo and in Huauchinango. The others, going around the great volcano Popocatépetl by way of Tetela and Tochimilco, founded in the neighborhood of Atlixco the city of Cuauhquechollan, and some, passing farther on, founded Amaliuhcan and other villages, and so extended as far as the Poyauhtecatl, or Mount Orizaba, to which they probably gave that name in memory of the place in the Valley of

Mexico that they had left.

But the greater and more considerable part of the tribe made its way by Cholula to the foot of the great mountain Matlalcueye, whence it drove out the Olmecs and the Xicalancas, ancient inhabitants of that country, and put to death their king Colopechtli. There they settled under a chief called Colhuacatecuhtli, endeavoring to fortify themselves so as to be better able to resist the neighboring peoples, should they ever attack them. In fact it was not long before the

Huexotzincas and other peoples, aware of the bravery and the strength of their new neighbors, fearing that in the future [p. 155] they might prove harmful to them, raised a large army to drive them Bk. II. out altogether from the whole country. The blow was so violent that the Tlaxcalans were forced to abandon the place and retire to the summit of that great mountain. Finding themselves there in the greatest consternation, they implored through their ambassadors the protection of the Chichimec king, and obtained from him a large body of troops. The Huexotzincas, not having forces sufficient to withstand the royal army, called the Tepanecs to their aid, believing that they would not refuse so fine an occasion for revenge; but these, remembering the tragic event of Poyauhtlan, although they sent troops, gave these too the order to do no harm to the Tlaxcalans, and the Tlaxcalans themselves were warned by them, lest they should take them for enemies, and be assured that those people were sent only to deceive the Huexotzincas and so as not to disturb the harmony that existed between them and the Tepanecs. With the help of the Texcocans, and through the perfidious laziness of the Tepanecs, the Huexotzincas were defeated and forced to return in ignominy to their own state. The Tlaxcalans, delivered from so grave a danger, and peace made with their neighbors, returned to their first settlement to continue the peopling already begun.

This was the origin of the famous city and republic of Tlaxcala, eternal rival of the Mexicans and the cause of their ruin. At the beginning they all obeyed one chief; but their population having afterward considerably increased, the city was divided into four quarters called Tepeticpac, Ocotelolco, Quiahuiztlan, and Tizatlan. Each quarter was under its own lord, to whom were likewise subject all the places dependent on that quarter; so that the whole state was composed of four petty monarchies; but these four lords together with other nobles of the first rank formed a kind of aristocracy with respect to the common concerns of the state. This diet or senate was the arbiter of war and of peace; it fell to it to prescribe the number of troops that were to be armed, and the general who was to command them.

The Tlaxcalans were warlike, courageous, and very jealous of their honor and their liberty. They preserved the splendor of their republic for a long time, despite the opposition they had to suffer from their enemies, until, having allied themselves with the Spaniards against the Mexicans, their ancient rivals, they were involved in the common ruin. They were idolaters, and as superstitious and cruel in their worship as the Mexicans. Their favorite god was Camaxtle, the very one revered by the Mexicans under the name of Huitzilopochtli. Their arts were those of the other neighboring nations. Their commerce was principally in maize and in cochineal. From the abundance of maize the capital was given the name of Tlaxcallan, that is, place of bread.

Bk. II. same that other nations had. But whatever it was, it will not be altogether useless to set before the free judgment of readers what the Mexican historians themselves relate of the origin of this resolution.

There was, they say, among the Aztecs a personage of great authority called Huitziton, to whose opinion all deferred in great measure. He had taken it upon himself, I know not for what motive, to persuade his countrymen to a change of country; and while he was turning this thought over, he happened to hear a little bird singing on the branches of a tree, whose voice imitated the Mexican word Tihui, which means, Let us go. This seemed to him a fine occasion to obtain what he wanted from his countrymen. Calling therefore another notable person, named Tecpaltzin, he led him to that tree, where the little bird was wont to sing, and said to him thus: “Do you not perceive, friend Tecpaltzin, what this little bird is telling us? That Tihui, Tihui, which it ever repeats to us, what does it mean, if not that we must leave this country and find another? This without doubt is a warning from some hidden deity who watches over our good. Let us obey his voice, then, and not draw his displeasure upon ourselves by our refusal.” Tecpaltzin fully assented to Huitziton’s interpretation, either from the opinion he had of his wisdom, or because he too had been struck by the same thought. These two authoritative personages being now in agreement, it was not long before they drew the body of the nation to their side.

Although I do not trust such a narration, it does not seem to me otherwise altogether improbable; for it is not hard for

he most wishes, to an ignorant and superstitious people. It would be much harder for me to be persuaded of what the Spanish authors commonly say, namely, that the Mexicans undertook that journey by express command of the Devil. The good historians of the sixteenth century, and those who have copied them, assume as altogether beyond doubt the continual and familiar intercourse of the Devil with all the idolatrous nations of the New World, and scarcely relate any event of history of which they do not make him the author. But although it is certain that the malice of those spirits strives to do men all the harm it can, and at times they have shown themselves to them in visible form in order to seduce them, especially those who have not entered by regeneration into the bosom of the Church; nevertheless it cannot be believed that such apparitions were so frequent, nor their intercourse with the aforesaid nations so free, as these historians believe; for God, who watches with loving providence over his creatures, does not grant to such enemies of mankind so much liberty to do harm. Readers ought not, however, to wonder if several events of this History which they have read in other authors they find in this one little in conformity with their credulity. I, in truth, am not disposed to ascribe any effect to the Devil on the sole testimony of some

Bk. II. which empties into the Gulf of California at 32½° of latitude, since this is the most considerable of all that are found on the road they took. Having crossed the Red River, then, beyond the 35th degree, they went southeast as far as the river Gila, where they halted for some time; for to this day are seen remains of large buildings made by them on the banks of that river. Then, resuming their road toward the south-southeast, they stopped at a latitude of about 29 degrees, in a place that is distant more than 250 miles from the city of Chihuahua, to the north-northwest. This place is known by the name of Casas Grandes, on account of a vast edifice, still standing, which, according to the universal tradition of those peoples, was built by the Mexicans during their migration. This edifice is made on the plan of those of New Mexico, that is, composed of three stories, with a terrace above them, and without a door in the lower story. The door for entering the building is in the second story, so that a ladder is needed. So do the inhabitants of New Mexico, in order to be less exposed to the assaults of their enemies, putting out the ladder only for those whom they permit to enter their houses. The Aztecs doubtless had the same motive in making the edifice in that form; for in it are observed the marks of a fortress, defended on one flank by a high mountain, and for the rest surrounded by a wall about seven feet thick, whose foundations still exist. In that fortress are seen stones as large as millstones; the beams of the roofs are of pine, and well worked. In the

They say that the division took place by express command of their god; but we are persuaded that some discord separated them. The situation of Chicomoztoc, where the Mexicans stayed nine years, is not known; but it seems to me that this place is twenty miles south of the city of Zacatecas, where to this day are seen the remains of a very vast edifice, which is indubitably the work of the Aztecs on their journey; for, besides the tradition of the Zacatecos, ancient inhabitants of that country, who, being altogether barbarous, neither had houses nor knew how to build them, that building found there by the Spaniards can be ascribed to no one but the Aztecs. That they were then reduced to a smaller number by the dismemberment of the other tribes will probably have been the reason why the Mexicans did not undertake such buildings in the rest of their migration.

In spite of this discord both parties continued to travel together, on account of the imaginary interest of the protection of their god. (E)

It should cause no wonder that the Aztecs made so many circuits and traveled more than a thousand miles beyond what was needed to arrive at Anahuac; since they had set themselves no goal, seeking here and there a country where they could enjoy to advantage all the comforts of life. Nor is it any less to be wondered at that in some places they made large buildings, thinking, as is to be believed, every place where they stopped to be the end of their migration. Several sites seemed to them at first suitable for their settlement, which they afterward abandoned through the experience of unforeseen inconveniences. Wherever they stopped they erected an altar to their god, and on departing they left the infirm, and probably some others who looked after them, and

At Tula they stayed nine years, and then eleven in other places not far off, until in 1216 they arrived at Zumpango, a considerable city of the Valley of Mexico. Tochpanecatl, lord of this city, received them with singular kindness, and, not content with granting them a comfortable lodging and with giving them abundant gifts, being attached to them through long and familiar acquaintance, asked the chiefs of the nation for some noble maiden to be the wife of his son Ilhuicatl. The Mexicans, obliged by so great a benevolence, gave him Tlacapantzin, whom that illustrious young man promptly married, and from them descended, as we shall see, the Mexican kings.

After they had stayed seven years in Zumpango, they went away together with the young Ilhuicatl to Tizayuca, a city not far from that one, where Tlacapantzin gave birth to a son, who was named Huitzilihuitl, and at the same time they gave another maiden to Xochiatzin, lord of Cuauhtitlan. From Tizayuca they passed to Tolpetlac and Tepeyac, where at present there is the town and the most renowned Sanctuary of Our Lady of Guadalupe, places all on the shores of the Lake of Texcoco and very near the site of Mexico, in which they stayed twenty-two years.

ticularly from the one of Xaltocan, made them, after seventeen years, abandon it to find a safer refuge in Acocolco, a place of several islets at the southern extremity of the lake. There they led for the space of fifty-two years the most wretched life in the world. They sustained themselves on fish and every sort of insect and on marsh roots, and covered themselves with the leaves of the plant amoxtli, which grows abundantly in that lake, since their garments were quite worn out and they found there no way of procuring new ones. Their dwellings were very poor huts, made of the canes and rushes that the lake produces. It would be altogether incredible that for so many years they could have survived in so inconvenient a place and in so hard a life, if it were not verified both by the testimony of their historians and by subsequent events.

§ 18.  But here at least, in the midst of misery, they were free; and liberty someSlavery of the

Mexicans in what sweetened their hardships; but in 1314 there came upon their other

Colhuacan. misfortunes that of slavery. There is variety among the historians concerning this event. Some say that the petty king of Colhuacan, a city not far from that site, not being able to endure that the Mexicans should maintain themselves in his district without paying him tribute, made open war on them, and having conquered them, made them slaves. Others affirm that that petty king sent them an embassy saying that, taking compassion on the wretched life that they led in those islets, he granted them a better place, where they might live more comfortably; that the Mexicans, who desired nothing more, accepted the favor at once and gladly left that site; but scarcely had they left it when they were assailed by the Colhuas and made prisoners. Whether it was in one way or in the other, it is certain that the Mexicans were led as slaves to

Tizapan, a place belonging to the state of Colhuacan.

After and much more if the chronology of Torquemada were adopted, who supposes Quinatzin reigning from the time when the Mexicans entered the Valley of Mexico. See our dissertations.

After some years of their slavery war broke out between the

Bk. II. Colhuas and the Xochimilcas, their neighbors, to the great disadvantage of the former, who in all the engagements always had the worst of it. Afflicted by so many losses, the Colhuas saw themselves compelled to make use of their prisoners, whom they ordered to prepare for war; but they did not furnish them with the necessary arms, either because those they had had been used up in the earlier battles, or because they left them at liberty to make them as they wished. The Mexicans, persuading themselves that this was a fine occasion to win the favor of their lord, determined to exert the utmost effort of their courage. They all armed themselves with long, strong staves, whose points they hardened in the fire, not so much to use them against their enemies as to help themselves in the leaps to be made from one thicket to another, should it be necessary, as in fact it was, to fight in the water. They made knives of itztli and targets or shields of crushed cane. They agreed not to delay, as they were wont, in taking prisoners, but to content themselves with cutting off one of their ears, letting them go without any other harm. With these arrangements they took the field, and while the Colhuas and the Xochimilcas were fighting, now on land on the shores of the lake, now on the water in boats, they hurled themselves impetuously upon the enemy, using the staves in the water: from all they met they cut off an ear and put it in the baskets which they carried for this purpose; but when they could not do so because of the enemy’s resistance, they killed him. The Colhuas obtained with the help of the Mexicans a victory so complete that the Xochimilcas not only abandoned the field, but, their courage not sufficing even to remain in their city, fled to the mountains.

This action having ended with such glory, the Colhua soldiers presented themselves with their prisoners to the general, according to the custom of those nations; for among them the bravery of soldiers was not estimated by the number of enemies they left dead on the field, but by that of the prisoners that they presented

[p. 166] alive to the general. It cannot be doubted that this was a reasonable Bk. II.

sentiment and a practice quite in conformity with humanity. If the prince can vindicate his rights and repel force without killing his enemies, humanity requires that their life be preserved. If we wish to consider utility, a dead enemy cannot do harm, but neither can he serve; and from a prisoner much advantage can be drawn without receiving any harm. If we look to glory, greater effort is required to deprive an enemy merely of his liberty than to take his life in the heat of the fray. The Mexicans too were called upon to make a showing of their prisoners; but presenting none (for the four whom alone they had taken they kept hidden for the purpose we shall tell), they were held in contempt as cowardly men by the general and the Colhua soldiers. Then the Mexicans, setting out the baskets full of ears, said:

“Behold, from the number of ears that we present to you, you can gather that of the prisoners we could have brought you, had we wished; but we did not wish to lose time in binding them, in order to anticipate your victory.” The Colhuas were left somewhat frightened at such an answer, no less by the cunning than by the courage of their slaves.

The Mexicans, having returned to the place of their residence

(which, as appears, was then Huitzilopochco), erected an altar to their protecting god; but wishing in the dedication to offer him something precious, they asked it of their lord. He sent them in contempt, wrapped in a dirty rag of coarse cloth, a vile dead bird with certain filth, which the Colhua priests carried, and having put it on the altar withdrew without a word. Great as was the indignation of the

Mexicans at so unworthy a jest, yet reserving vengeance for another time, they placed on the altar, in place of that filth, a knife of itztli and a fragrant herb. When the day of the dedication had arrived, the

This inhuman sacrifice, the first of this kind that we know to have been made in that country, caused such horror among the Colhuas that, having returned at once to Colhuacan, they determined to send away those slaves so cruel, who in the future might be very pernicious to the state; wherefore Coxcox (this was the name of the petty king) sent them the order to leave that district at once and go wherever they pleased. The Mexicans gladly left their slavery, and, setting out toward the north, went to Acatzitzintlan, a place situated between the two lakes, afterward called by them Mexicaltzinco, whose name is almost the same as that of Mexico, and was doubtless imposed for the same reason for which they imposed it, as we shall shortly see, on their capital; but not finding in that place the comfort they sought, or wishing to move farther from the Colhuas, they passed to Iztacalco, always drawing nearer to the site of Mexico. At Iztacalco they made a little mound of paper, in which probably they represented Colhuacan, (*) and spent a whole night dancing around it, singing their victory over the Xochimilcas, and thanking their god for having delivered them from the domination of the Colhuas.

The dedication of that sanctuary, miserable though it was, was not made without the shedding of human blood; for a bold Mexican, having gone out to seek some animal to sacrifice, came upon a Colhua called Xomimitl, and coming after a few words to blows because of their enmity, the Mexican overcame him, and, having bound him, carried him to his countrymen, who sacrificed him at once, and with great rejoicing presented on the altar the heart torn from his breast, this cruelty serving no less to vent their wrath against the Colhuas than for the bloodthirsty worship of that false deity. Around the sanctuary they went on building their very poor huts of canes and rushes, having at that time no other materials. This was the beginning of the great city of Tenochtitlan, which in time to come was to be the court of a great empire, and the greatest and most beautiful city of the New World. It was also called

Ma di che non è capace l' industria umana spinta dalla neceslicà ? La più grande, che ivi sentivano Ì Messicani, era quella della mancanza di suolo per le loro abitazioni , mentre la isoletta di Tenochtitlan non era bastevole-a tutti gli abitatori. Rimediaronvi facendo degli steccati in quelle parti, dov'era più bassa l'acqua, i quali terrapienarono con pietra e cespugli , unendo alla isoletta principale parecchie altre più picciole, e poco discoste, Per provvedersi poi di pietra, di legni, di pane, e di tutto il bisognavole alla loro abitazione, ed al lor vestire e mangiare, s'applicarono con fomma diligenza alla pesca non solo del pesce bianco, di cui abbiamo altrove parlato, ma eziandia d' alcri pescerti, e di parecchj insetti palustri , che fecero commestibili, ed alla caccia delle innumerabili spezie d’ uccelli , che’ cercando il loro cibo nelle acque, vi concorrevano. Pel commercio di questa cacciagione ‘coi luoghi sicuari sulle rive del lago, acquistavano tutto quello, che lor mancava,

The founding of Mexico took place in the year II Calli, corresponding to 1325 of the common era, the Chichimec Quinatzin Bk. II. reigning in that country; but not by having changed site did the Mexicans at once improve their fortune: for, isolated in the middle of the lake, without lands where to sow, or garments to cover themselves, and in perpetual distrust of all their neighbors, they led there a life as miserable as in the other places where they had been, sustaining themselves only on aquatic animals and vegetables. But of what is human industry, spurred by necessity, not capable? The greatest necessity that the Mexicans felt there was that of the lack of ground for their dwellings, since the islet of Tenochtitlan was not sufficient for all the inhabitants. They remedied it by making palisades in those parts where the water was shallower, which they filled in with stone and brushwood, joining to the principal islet several other smaller ones not far off. Then, to provide themselves with stone, timber, bread, and everything needful for their dwelling and for their clothing and food, they applied themselves with the greatest diligence to the fishing not only of the white fish, of which we have spoken elsewhere, but also of other little fish, and of several marsh insects, which they made edible, and to the hunting of the innumerable species of birds that, seeking their food in the waters, flocked there. By the trade in this game with the places situated on the shores of the lake, they acquired all that they lacked.

> Ma dove fece l'ultimo sforzo la loro industria fu nel fare dei cespugli, e del fango medesimo del lago degli orti

But where their industry made its utmost effort was in making, from the brushwood and from the very mud of the lake, gardens

Il nome Mexicaltzinco, vale il luogo della Casa 0 sia tempio del Dio Mexiti: siccchè fignificano în sostanza lo fesso Huitzilopochéo . Mexicaltzinco , e Mexico , nomi dei tre luoghi. che succesivamente abitarono i Messicani. [p. 170] e > lleggianti . full’ acqua ‘(la cui struttura e forma al fu6 Lis. 1L luogo esporremo , ) dove seminavano del Maiz, © frumen» tone, del peverone , della Chia, dei fagiuoli, e delle zucche, Così passarono i Meslicani i tredici primi anni, ordis nando nel modo possibile la loro Città , e rimediando alla loro miseria colla industria, e colla fatica. Sin' a questo tem. do s'era conservata sempre unita tutta la tribù , malgrado la discordia delle due fazioni , che fi erano formate nel tempo del loro pellegrinaggio. Questa discordia , ch' era stara dai padri ai figliuoli trasmessa , venne finalmente a scoppiare nel 1338. Una delle fazioni non potendo più sopporcar l’altra , prese la-risoluzione di separarsi; ma non potendo allontanarki tanto, quanto le suggeriva la sua rabbia, se ne andò verso Tramontana a stare in un’ altra isoletta poco distante, la quale, per aver ivi trovato, un gran mucchio d'a» rena, appellarono Xalzilolco , e poi pel. terrapieno, che vi fecero, chiamarono Tlatelolco , nome che finora ha conservato. (1) Quelli, che fi stabilirono in questa isoletta ,'la quale poscia fa unita a quella: di Tenochrtitlan , ebbero allora il nome di Tlarelolchi, e quei che restarono nel primo sito, s'ap» pellarono Tenochchi; ma noi gli chiameremo Messicani, sic» come gli chiamano rutti gli Storici . Maguei, or plants of Mexican aloe; but by the study of history I was undeceived, and now I am quite sure that Mexico signifies the Place of Mexitli or Huitzilopochtli, that is, the Mars of the Mexicans, on account of the sanctuary built for him there: whence Mexico means among the Mexicans the same as Fanum Martis among the Romans. The Mexicans drop from names of this kind the final syllable tli. The co added to it is our preposition in. The name Mexicaltzinco means the place of the House or temple of the god Mexitli: so that in substance they signify the same thing: Huitzilopochco, Mexicaltzinco, and Mexico are names of the three places which the Mexicans successively inhabited. beans, and gourds.

Thus the Mexicans passed their first thirteen years, arranging their city as best they could and remedying their misery by industry and toil. Until that time the whole tribe had always remained united, in spite of the discord of the two factions that had been formed during the time of their wandering. This discord, which had been handed down from fathers to sons, finally broke out in 1338. One of the factions, unable to bear the other any longer, resolved to separate; but being unable to withdraw as far as its anger suggested, it went north to settle on another islet not far away, which, because they found there a great heap of sand, they called Xaltilolco, and afterward, from the embankment they made there, Tlatelolco, a name it has kept to this day. (I) Those who settled on this islet, which was later joined to that of Tenochtitlan, then took the name of Tlatelolcas, and those who remained on the first site were called Tenochca; but we shall call them

Mexicans, as all the historians call them.

A little before or a little after this event the Mexicans divided their wretched city into four quarters, assigning to each its protecting god, besides that of the whole nation. This division survives at present under the names of San Pablo, San Sebastián, San Juan, and Santa María.

In homage to this wicked deity they performed at this time a hor‐

§ 21. rible sacrifice, which cannot be heard of without horror. They sent an Inhuman sacrifice. embassy to the petty king of Colhuacan, begging him to give them one of his daughters, that she might be consecrated Mother of their protecting god, and explaining to him that this was an express command of their god, in order to exalt her to so great an honor. The petty king, either enamored of the glory he hoped for in having a deified daughter, or else frightened by the misfortunes he foresaw if he should refuse the request of a god, at once granted what they asked, especially as he could not suspect what was about to happen. The Mexicans led that noble maiden with great jubilation to their city; but scarcely had she arrived when the Devil, according to what the historians say, commanded that she be sacrificed to him, and after her death flayed, and that one of the most valiant young men of the nation be clothed in her skin. Whether this was an order of the Devil or, what is more likely, a cruel invention of the barbarous priests, everything was punctually carried out. The petty king, invited by the Mexicans to be present at the apotheosis of his daughter, went to be one of the spectators of that great ceremony and one of the worshippers of that new deity. He was brought into the sanctuary, where beside the idol stood upright the young man clothed in the bloodied skin of the victim; but the darkness of the place did not let him see what was there. They put into his hands a censer and a little copal, that he might begin his worship; but having seen, by the light of the flame the copal made, the horrible spectacle that lay before him, he was moved to the depths by grief, and, carried away by violent emotions, rushed out crying like a madman, ordering his people to avenge so barbarous an outrage; but they did not dare undertake it, since they would infallibly have been overwhelmed by the multitude: so the disconsolate father returned to his house to bewail his misfortune for the rest of his life. His

Y2 [p. 172] unhappy daughter was created a goddess, and honorary Mother not Bk. II.

only of Huitzilopochtli but of all their gods, and this is precisely what the name Teteoinan signifies, by which she was known and revered from that time forward. Such were, in that new city, the specimens of a barbarous system of religion, which we shall set out elsewhere.

It is to be suspected that the Tlatelolcas, in making this request of that king, both to flatter him and to irritate him against the Mexicans, their rivals, exaggerated to him the insolence of those who had made a king without his permission; for a few days later the same king of Azcapotzalco convoked his councilors and spoke to them thus: “What do you think, noble Tepanecs, of the Mexicans’ attempt? They have made their way into our dominions, and are increasing considerably their city and their commerce; and, what is worse, they have had the audacity to create a king from among their own countrymen without waiting for our permission. Now if they do this in the beginnings of their settlement, what may be believed they will do when they have multiplied and their forces have grown? Is it not to be feared that in the future, instead of paying us the tribute we have imposed on them, they will claim that we pay it to them, and that the petty king of the Mexicans will want to be monarch of the Tepanecs as well? I, however, think it necessary to increase their burdens in such a way that, wearing themselves out in paying them, they may be consumed, or else, by not paying them, may be afflicted by us with other evils, and finally compelled to leave our state.” All applauded this resolution, nor could anything else be hoped for, since a prince who makes his inclination plain in seeking counsel looks more for §Burdens

3.

imposed on panegyrists who will second his wishes than for councilors who will the Mexicans. enlighten his mind. The king therefore sent word to the Mexicans that, the tribute they had paid him until that time having been so small, he wished them from then on to double it; that besides this they must bring him I do not know how many thousands of willow and fir cuttings to be planted in the streets and gardens of Azcapotzalco, and together with these convey to that court a great garden, in which all the seeds usual in Anahuac should be sown and already sprouted.

[p. 176]

The Mexicans, who until that time had paid no other tribute than Bk. III.

a certain quantity of fish and a certain number of aquatic birds, were greatly distressed at these new burdens, fearing that they would go on increasing from hour to hour; yet they did everything that was prescribed to them, bringing at the appointed time, together with the usual fishing and fowling, the cuttings and the floating garden.

Whoever has not seen the most beautiful gardens that to this day are cultivated in the midst of the water, and the ease with which they are transported wherever one wishes, will not be able without difficulty to persuade himself that such an event was true; but whoever has seen them, as I have and all those who have navigated that lake, where the senses find the sweetest recreation in the world, will have no reason to doubt the truth of this History. Having received the aforesaid tribute, the same king ordered them to bring him the next year another garden, and in it a duck and a heron, each brooding her eggs, in such a way that on arriving at Azcapotzalco the chicks would begin to hatch. The Mexicans obeyed, and took their measures so well that the foolish prince had the pleasure of seeing the chicks come out of the eggs. He then ordered that for the following year they bring him, besides the garden, a live deer. This new order was in truth harder to carry out, since to hunt the deer it was necessary to go to the mountains of the mainland, in evident danger of falling in with their enemies; nevertheless they carried it out, to avoid graver wrongs. This harsh oppression of the Mexicans lasted no less than fifty years. The historians of Mexico affirm that the Mexicans in all their afflictions implored the protection of their god, and that he made the execution of the orders easier for them; but we are of another opinion.

The poor king Acamapichtli had, besides these vexations, that of the barrenness of Queen Ilancueitl; and so he married

Tezcatlamiahuatl, daughter of the lord of Tetepanco, by whom he had several sons, among them Huitzilihuitl and Chimalpopoca, his successors on the crown. He took the second wife without leaving the first; indeed they lived, both [p. 177] of them in such concord that Ilancueitl took charge of the education of Huitzilihuitl. He had besides, though not honored with the title of Bk. III. queens, other wives, and among them a slave, of whom was born to him Itzcoatl, one of the best and most renowned kings that there were in Anahuac. Acamapichtli governed his city, which was then his whole kingdom, peacefully for the space of thirty-seven years. In his time the population increased, some stone buildings were erected, and the canals were begun, which served no less for the embellishment of the city than for the utility of the citizens. The Interpreter of the Mendoza Collection ascribes to this king the conquest of Mixquic, Cuitláhuac, Cuauhnahuac, and Xochimilco. But who can persuade himself that the Mexicans were capable of undertaking the conquest of four such large cities, when they could hardly sustain themselves in their own settlement? Hence the painting of this collection, which represents those four cities as conquered by the Mexicans, must be understood of them in so far as they were auxiliary troops of other states, as a little later they served the king of Texcoco against the people of Xaltocan.

Shortly before his death Acamapichtli convoked the magnates of the city and made them a short speech, commending to them his wives and his children and zeal for the public good. He said that, having received the crown from their hands, he returned it to them, that they might give it to the one whom they judged would be more useful to the state; and he declared the grief he felt in dying and leaving his nation tributary to the Tepanecs. His death, which occurred in 1389, was deeply felt by the Mexicans, and his obsequies were celebrated with as much solemnity as the wretchedness of the nation allowed.

From the death of Acamapichtli until the election of the new king there was, according to Dr. Sigüenza, an interregnum of four months; which did not happen again afterward, since from then on hardly a few days had passed after the death of a king when another was elected. This time the election could be delayed, the nobility being occupied in the [p. 178] regulating the number of the electors and establishing the ceremonial

The electors chosen from the nobility having therefore assembled, the oldest of them spoke in this manner: “My age gives me courage to speak first. Great indeed, O noble Mexicans, is the misfortune we have suffered in the death of our king; nor is there anyone who ought to mourn it more than we, who were the feathers of his wings and the eyelids of his eyes. Such a misfortune becomes greater by reason of the calamitous state in which we find ourselves under the dominion of the Tepanecs, to the disgrace of the Mexican name. You, therefore, to whom the remedy of the present calamities is so pressing, think of electing a king who shall be zealous for the honor of our powerful god
