§ 4. orphans, the widows, and the aged.” This brief address ended, they Huitzilihuitl, second king of Mexico. gave their votes, and there was elected Huitzilihuitl, son of the late king Acamapichtli. Then they went out in order, and, betaking themselves to the house of the elect, they took him in their midst, led him to the Tlatocaicpalli, that is, the royal seat, or throne, and having seated him, anointed him in the form that we shall set out elsewhere; they put on his head the Copilli, or crown, and one by one paid him obedience. Then one of the most distinguished personages raised his voice among them all, and spoke thus to the king: “Be not discouraged, O generous youth, by the new burden that has been laid upon you, of being head of a nation shut in among the reeds and rushes of this lake. It is truly a misfortune to have so small a kingdom established in another’s territory, and to govern a nation which, being free at the beginning, became tributary to the Tepanecs. But console yourself, for we are under the protection of our great god Huitzilopochtli, whose image you are, and whose place you hold. The dignity to which you have been raised by him must not serve you as a pretext for idleness and softness, but rather as a spur to toil. Always keep before [p. 179] your eyes the clear examples of your great father, who spared no toil

Huitzilihuitl was not yet married when he ascended the throne; so it was soon thought to give him a wife, and the nobles wished her to be a daughter of the same king of Azcapotzalco; but in order not to expose themselves to so ignominious a refusal as that which they had had to suffer in the time of Acamapichtli, they agreed to make the request this time with the greatest demonstrations of submission and respect. So some nobles went to Azcapotzalco, and, presenting themselves to the king and kneeling, set out their claim thus: “Behold, great lord, at your feet the poor Mexicans, awaiting from your kindness a favor far above their merit; but to whom shall we turn, if not to you, who are both our father and our lord? Behold us hanging upon your lips, and ready at all your nods. We beg you with the most profound respect to take pity on our master and your servant Huitzilihuitl, shut in among the thick reeds of the lake. He is without a wife, and we without a queen. Deign, lord, to let slip from your hands one of your gems, or of your precious feathers. Give us one of your daughters, that she may come to reign in your land.”

These expressions, which are singularly elegant in the Mexican language, so bent the mind of Tezozomoc (this was the king’s name) that he at once granted his daughter Ayauhcihuatl, to the unspeakable delight of the Mexicans, who conducted her in pomp to Mexico, and the longed-for marriage was celebrated with the usual ceremony of tying the edge of the bride’s garment to that of the bridegroom. The king had by her in the first year a son, to whom they gave the name of Acolnahuacatl; but eager to ennoble

§ 5.     There reigned at that time in Acolhuacan Techotlalatzin, son of Techotlalatzin, king

of Acolhuacan. King Quinatzin. The first thirty years of his reign were quite peaceful; but then Tzompan, lord of Xaltocan, rebelled against the crown, and, seeing that his forces were not sufficient to oppose his sovereign, called to his aid the states of Otompan, Metztitlán, Cuahuacan,

Tecomic, Cuauhtitlan, and Tepotzotlán. King Techotlalatzin promised him pardon, provided that he lay down his arms and submit. It is to be believed that he used such clemency out of regard for the most noble blood of the offender, since he was the last descendant of Chiconcuauhtli, one of the three Acolhua princes. But he, proud of the number of troops he had, rejected the grace with contempt. The king, indignant, sent against the rebels an army, to which were joined the Mexicans and the Tepanecs, summoned by him. The war was obstinate, nor could it be ended in less than two months; but victory having at last declared for the king, Tzompan and all the chiefs of the rebel cities were punished with the extreme penalty, the most illustrious line of Chiconcuauhtli ending in Tzompan himself.

This war, waged by the Mexicans as auxiliaries of the king of

Acolhuacan against Xaltocan and the other confederated states, is seen represented in the third painting of the Mendoza Collection; but the Interpreter of these paintings was mistaken, believing those cities to have been conquered for the crown of Mexico.

Con tali provvedimenti aumentò lo \plendore della corte, e raflodò il trono d’ Acolhuacan , benchè non potesse impedir le rivoluzioni , che fra poco esporremo. Questi , ed altri simili rratti di politica , che nel corso di questa Storia s' andranno scoprendo, faranno conoscere. il torto, che fecero agli Americani quelli Europei , che gli stimarono ani» mali -d' un’ altra spezie, e quelli ancora, che gli credono incapaci di miglioramento.

When the war was over the Mexicans returned in glory to their city, and King Techotlalatzin, to avoid new rebellions in the future, divided his kingdom into sixty-five states, giving each a lord to govern it in subordination to the crown. From every state he drew off some people to settle them in another, though they remained subject to the lord of the state from which they came, wishing thus to keep the peoples in check by means of foreign people, dependent on others, whom [p. 181] he placed in each. A policy truly useful for preventing rebellion; but injurious to innocent subjects, and troublesome for the lords who Bk. III. governed them. Besides this he honored several nobles with distinguished offices. He made Tetlato general of the army, Yolqui Quartermaster and Introducer of Ambassadors, Tlami Steward of the royal palace, Amechichi Superintendent of the cleanliness of the royal houses, and Cohuatl Director of the Goldsmiths of Ocolco. No one worked in gold and silver for the king’s service except the director’s own sons, who had, however, learned the art. The Quartermaster of Ambassadors had under him several other Colhua officials, the Steward had a certain number of Chichimecs, and the superintendent of cleanliness a similar number of Tepanecs. By such measures he increased the splendor of the court and strengthened the throne of Acolhuacan, though he could not prevent the revolutions that we shall presently set forth. These and other similar strokes of policy, which will be discovered in the course of this History, will show the wrong done to the Americans by those Europeans who thought them animals of another species, and by those too who believe them incapable of improvement.

> La nuova alleanza contratta dal Re di Messico con quello d' Azcapozalco, e la gloria acquistara dai Mellicani nella guerra di Xalcocan contribuirono assai non meno al vigore del loro piccolo stato, che al miglior trattamento delle loro persone; imperciocchèé avendo . già maggior libertà ed estensione nel loro commercio, cominciarono in questo tempo a vestirli di cotone, del quale erano innanzi affatto privi. per la loro mileria, nè d'altro, vestivansi,. se non delle tele groffe di filo di maguei, o di palma salvatica . Ma appooé cominciavano a respirare; che dalla stessa famiglia rea» 2 d' Azcapozalco uscì contra loro un nuovo nemico , ed un sanguinolento persecutore .

The new alliance contracted by the king of Mexico with the king of Azcapotzalco, and the glory the Mexicans had won in the war of Xaltocan, contributed greatly, no less to the vigor of their little state than to the better treatment of their persons; for, having now greater freedom and extension in their commerce, they began at this time to clothe themselves in cotton, of which they had before been entirely deprived by their poverty, and they wore nothing else than coarse cloths of maguei thread or of wild palm. But scarcely had they begun to draw breath when from the same royal family of Azcapotzalco there arose against them a new enemy and a bloodthirsty persecutor.

Maxtla, lord of Coyoacán and son of the king of Azcapotzalco, an ambitious, untamed, and cruel man, and therefore feared even by his own father, had taken offense at the

§ 6. Enmity of Maxtla tothe tenth year of the reign of Huitzilihuitl he went to Azcapotzalco ward the Mexicans. and convoked the nobility in order to set before them his complaints

against the Mexicans and their king. He represented to them the growth of the population of Mexico, exaggerated the pride and arrogance of that nation and the fatal effects that were to be feared from its present dispositions, and above all complained of the very grave wrong done him by the Mexican king in having taken his wife from him. It must be known that Maxtla and Ayauhcihuatl, though children of Tezozomoc, were born of different mothers, and perhaps such marriages were then permitted among the Tepanecs. Whether, then,

Maxtla truly wished to marry his sister, or whether this was, as is more likely, a mere pretext for carrying out his cruel designs, he took in that assembly the resolution of summoning Huitzilihuitl to reproach him with his alleged rashness. The Mexican king did indeed go to Azcapotzalco; nor should this cause wonder, since it was not unusual at that time for lords to visit one another; besides which,

Huitzilihuitl had the particular reason of being a feudatory of that crown; for although, from the birth of Acolnahuacatl, the queen of

Mexico had obtained from her father Tezozomoc the relief of the

Mexicans from the burdens to which they had been subjected for so many years, Mexico nevertheless remained in the condition of a fief of Azcapotzalco, and the Mexicans had to present to the Tepanec king two ducks every year in acknowledgment of his overlordship.

Maxtla received Huitzilihuitl in a hall of his palace, and after dining with him in the presence of the courtiers, who flattered him on his projects, he gave him a most severe reprimand for the injury he claimed to have been done him in the marriage with Ayauhcihuatl.

The Mexican king protested his innocence with the greatest humility, saying that he would never have asked for the princess, nor would the king her father have granted her to him, if she had been [p. 183] promised to another. But in spite of the sincerity of his excuses and the efficacy of his reasons, Maxtla replied to him indignantly: “I could Bk. III. well, without hearing you further, put you to death here on the spot: thus your rashness would be punished and my honor avenged; but I do not wish it to be said that a Tepanec prince treacherously killed his enemy. Go now in peace: time will furnish me with some occasion to take a more honorable vengeance.”

The Mexican went away full of grief and rage, and it was not long before he felt the effects of the enmity of his cruel brother-in-law. The true cause of this enmity was the fear that Maxtla conceived that the lordship of the Tepanecs might perhaps at some time fall to his nephew Acolnahuacatl, since he was born of a daughter of King Tezozomoc, whereby his nation would be made subject to the Mexican. To free himself, then, from such a fear, he took the barbarous resolution of putting his nephew to death, as in fact happened, at the hands of certain men who wished by so cruel a deed to win the favor of their master; for there never lack among the powerful venal men who are ministers of their passions. (*) Tezozomoc did not consent to this crime; but neither did he show, so far as we know, any displeasure. In the course of this History it will be seen that the pride, ambition, and cruelty of Maxtla, tolerated, indeed favored by his indulgent father, were the cause of his ruin and of the destruction of his nation. Huitzilihuitl bore so painful a blow very unwillingly; but he did not find himself with forces sufficient to avenge himself.

(*) There is no author who sets forth the circumstances of the tragic death of the little Prince Acolnahuacatl, nor can it be understood how the Tepanecs could carry out such an attempt in Mexico; yet we cannot doubt the fact, since it is attested to us by the native historians, although among the Spaniards there is someone, such as Father Acosta, who is mistaken, confusing this death with that of Chimalpopoca, third king of Mexico.

In the same year (1399) in which this tragedy occurred in Mexico, the

Bk. III. first king, Cuacuauhpitzahuac, died in Tlatelolco, leaving that city considerably enlarged with good buildings, beautiful gardens, and greater civiliza‐

§ 7. Tlacateotl, second tion. In his place was elected Tlacateotl, of whose origin the historians speak king of Tlatelolco.

variously, since some believe him a Tepanec, like his predecessor, and others an Acolhua, appointed by the king of Acolhuacan. The rivalry that existed between the Mexicans and the Tlatelolcas contributed greatly to the growth of both cities, each side seeking to surpass the other in everything. The

Mexicans for their part had formed family ties with the neighboring nations, had increased their agriculture by multiplying the floating gardens in the lake, and had also a greater number of boats, with which their fishing and their commerce had grown: so that they were able to celebrate their secular year I Tochtli, corresponding to 1402 of the common era, with greater display than all the other four that had passed since their departure from the country of Aztlan.

Techotlalatzin was still reigning at this time in Acolhuacan, already decrepit; so, foreseeing the approach of death, he called his son and successor

Ixtlilxochitl, and among the other instructions he gave him advised him to win the minds of the lords who were his feudatories; for it might happen that Tezozomoc, an old, crafty, and ambitious man, who until that time had been restrained by fear, would wish to conspire against the empire. The fears of Techotlalatzin were not vain, as we shall shortly see. Finally this king died in 1406, after a long reign, though not so long as some authors have said. (c)

[p. 185] there was the king of Azcapotzalco, who soon made plain how well he had been known to the late King Techotlalatzin; for without paying Bk. III. obedience to the new king, he went off to his own state to incite the minds of other feudatories to rebellion. He convoked the kings of Mexico and of Tlatelolco and told them that, Techotlalatzin, who for so many years had tyrannized that country, being dead, he wished to set at liberty all the individual lords in such a manner that each should rule his state with absolute independence of the king of Acolhuacan; that to attain so glorious an end he had need of their help, and trusted in their courage, already known to all nations, that they would share in the glory to which he aspired: and so that the blow might be surer, he would bring into the confederation other lords whom he knew to be animated by the same thoughts. Both kings, whether from fear of Tezozomoc’s overbearing power or to increase the glory of their arms, offered to serve him with their troops, and the same answer was given by other lords whom he solicited.

Meanwhile Ixtlilxochitl was trying to put the affairs of his court in order and to win the minds of his subjects; but he recognized, not without grave sorrow, that many had already withdrawn from his obedience to submit to the perfidious Tezozomoc; so, to check the progress of his enemies, he ordered the lords of Coatlichan, of Huexotla, and of other states near the court to arm without delay as many troops as they could. The king himself wished to command the army in person; but he was dissuaded by his courtiers, who thought his presence more necessary at court; since in that turbulence some hidden enemies, or men of equivocal loyalty, might take advantage of his absence to seize the capital and hurl him from the throne. Tochintecuhtli, son of the lord of Coatlichan, was therefore appointed general of the army, with Cuauhxilotl, lord of Iztapalocan, as his substitute in case of death or of some other accident. They chose as the theater of the war the plain of Cuauhtitlan, fifteen miles north of Azcapotzalco. The rebel troops were more

> » di, ed ;a facrificar la mia vitavalla mbbidienza , che vi n dabbo < Noa ignorate:zquanto! fiensi:da voi alienati gli wm Otompanesi per aderire alcyostté nemica" Tutta / la terra

Bk. III. before going to Cuauhtitlan, laid waste six states of rebel lords, both to weaken the enemy and so as not to leave behind anyone who might do them harm. The war was one of the most obstinate, the discipline of the Texcocans being balanced against the numbers of the

Tepanecs, who would soon have been wholly vanquished had they not constantly been reinforced with fresh troops. The confederates of the rebels frequently detached large bodies and sent them to make raids in the loyal states, sure of finding little resistance there, because nearly all the forces of the Texcocans were gathered at Cuauhtitlan.

Among the many evils they caused, they killed Cuauhxilotl, lord of

Iztapalocan, who, having returned from the camp of Cuauhtitlan, died in glory defending his city courageously. The king of Acolhuacan saw himself therefore compelled to divide his forces, assigning as a garrison for the cities a good part of the people who came to his aid from many distant places. Tezozomoc, seeing that instead of the advantages he expected his forces were diminishing every day, and that his people were weary of the fatigues and dangers of the war, after three years of continual fighting asked for peace, with the intention of ending by secret treachery what he had begun by open force. The king of Acolhuacan, although he could not trust in the good faith of the Tepanec, nevertheless consented without demanding of him any condition that would make him safe for the future, because his troops were as weary as those of his enemy.

§ 9.     Scarcely was this war finished, or shortly before it ended, when Chimalpopoca, third Huitzilihuitl died in 1409, after twenty years of reign, having pub‐

king of Mexico.

lished some laws useful to the state and leaving the nobility in possession of the liberty it had of electing the successor. His brother

Chimalpopoca was therefore elected, and from then on the law seems to have been established of making the election from among the brothers of the deceased king, and, if there were no brothers, from among his nephews. This law [p. 187] was constantly observed, as we shall see, until the ruin of the

Bk. III. Mexican empire.

While Chimalpopoca was trying to establish himself on the throne of Mexico, Ixtlilxochitl was wavering on that of Acolhuacan. The peace that Tezozomoc had asked of him was a mere pretext to let him fall asleep, and meanwhile to promote his negotiations more effectively. Every day he saw his own party grow larger, while that of the Texcocan was diminishing. This unfortunate king found himself reduced to such an extremity that, no longer thinking himself safe in his court, he wandered about the neighboring mountains, escorted by a small army and accompanied by the lords of Huexotla and Coatlichan, who remained constantly faithful to him. The Tepanecs, in order to press him harder, seized the provisions that were being carried to his camp: so that he came to such need that he was forced to ask for provisions from his own enemies. So easy is it to be hurled from the summit of human happiness into the abyss of misery!

He sent therefore a nephew of his named Cihuacuecuenotzin to § 10. Otompan, one of the rebel cities, to beg those citizens to succor their Memorable deed of

Cihuacuecuenotzin. king with provisions, of which he was in want, and to admonish them to abandon the party of the rebels, remembering the fidelity they had sworn to him. Cihuacuecuenotzin well knew the danger of the enterprise; but the nobility of his sentiments, the strength of his spirit, and his fidelity to his sovereign prevailing over his fear, he was ready to obey: “I go, lord,” he said to him, “to carry out your commands and to sacrifice my life to the obedience I owe you. You are not unaware how far the people of Otompan have been alienated from you in order to adhere to your enemy. All the land is occupied by the Tepanecs and full of dangers: my return is too uncertain. But if I perish in your service, and if the sacrifice I make to you of my life is worthy of some recompense, I beg you to protect my two tender little sons whom I leave.” These words, accompanied by tears, softened the heart of the king, who, on dismissing him,

Il Signor d’ Otompan, ed i primi uomini della Nobiltà risposero , che ubbidivano volentieri ‘ all'ordine del Re: d' Azcapozalco, e s' esibirono a far quanto potessero per fecondare le sue intenzioni. Die»

Aa2 [p. 188] said to him: “May our god accompany you and bring you back safe. Bk. III.

Ah! perhaps on your return you will find done to me what you fear for yourself; for there are so many enemies who seek my death.”

Cihuacuecuenotzin went without delay to Otompan, and before entering it learned that there were then in that city some Tepanecs sent by Tezozomoc to publish a proclamation; yet he was not discouraged, but with an intrepid spirit went on to the square, where the Tepanecs had assembled the people to publish the proclamation, and after courteously saluting them all, set forth his embassy freely.

The people of Otompan made sport of him and mocked his request; but none of them dared go further, until a base fellow threw a stone at him, urging the others to put him to death. The Tepanecs, who had been quiet and silent to observe what the people of

Otompan would do, now seeing them openly declared against the king of Acolhuacan and against his ambassador, cried out, saying, Let him die, let him die, the traitor, accompanying their cries with stones.

Cihuacuecuenotzin at first faced his enemies, but seeing himself overwhelmed by the crowd, and trying to save his life by flight, was killed by a shower of stones. A man truly worthy of a better fortune! A memorable example of fidelity, which would be celebrated by historians and poets, if the hero, instead of being an American, had been a

Greek or a Roman.

The Tepanecs became boastful over a deed so inhuman and so contrary to the law of nations, and declared to the multitude the great pleasure they had in being able to inform their master, as eyewitnesses, of the inviolable fidelity of the people of Otompan. They said further that they had been sent precisely to give them the order not to give aid to the king of Texcoco under pain of proscription, and to exhort them to take up arms against that king, and in defense of their own liberty. The lord of Otompan and the first men of the nobility answered that they willingly obeyed the order of the king of

Azcapotzalco, and offered to do all they could to second his intentions.

Tezozomoc. possible a good army and to station it in ambush on a mountain near the camp of the king of Texcoco: that they should then send to the royal camp two captains, of the shrewdest and the bravest, who, under the pretext of communicating to the king some most important secret, should try to draw him as far as possible from his people, and then without delay kill him. Everything happened as the malicious prince had planned. The king was then in the neighborhood of Tlaxcala; he had no suspicion of the two captains who came to him, and fell incautiously into the snare. The deed was carried out in sight of the royal army, though at some small distance. They ran at once to punish the rashness of those two wicked captains; but the army of the conspirators coming up, which was more numerous, they were quickly routed. The royal corpse could scarcely be saved to have its obsequies performed, and the heir prince, who was a witness of the tragic end of his father, had need to hide among some bushes to escape the fury of the enemies. Thus ended the unfortunate king Ixtlilxochitl, after seven years of reign, in 1410.

The perfidious Tezozomoc had prepared large bodies of troops, so that, once the premeditated blow against the person of the king had been struck by the people of Otompan and the Chalcas, they might fall upon the cities of Texcoco, Huexotla, Coatlichan, Coatepec, and

Iztapalocan, which had been the most faithful to their lord, and put them to fire and flame. The inhabitants of those cities who were able to save themselves by flight went from there over the mountains to take refuge among the Huexotzincas and the Tlaxcalans; all the others died defending their country; but they sold their lives dear, for infinite was the blood shed on both sides. If one wishes to seek the cause of so many evils, no other will be found than the ambition of a prince. Would to God that the ravages of the passions were rarer in the world and less violent! The ill-governed passion of one prince, or of one minister, is enough to flood the fields with human blood, to ruin cities, to overturn kingdoms, and to turn the whole earth upside down.

The cruelty of the Tyrant being at last sated with the oppression of his enemies, he had himself sworn king of Acolhuacan in the city of

Texcoco, granting to all those who had taken up arms against him a general pardon and freedom to return to their homes. He gave the city of Texcoco in fief to Chimalpopoca, king of Mexico, and that of

Huexotla to Tlacateotl, king of Tlatelolco, as a reward for the great services they had rendered him in the war. He set governors loyal to himself in other places, and declared Azcapotzalco the court and capital of the whole kingdom of Acolhuacan.

Nezahualcoyotl. The grief and rage that the latter [p. 191] felt at it aroused in him youthful ardor, and were on the point of hurling him into a rash action against his enemies, had not a confidant of Bk. III. his who accompanied him deterred him, representing to him the fatal consequences of his rashness, and showing him how much better it would be to wait for time to bring some more opportune occasion of recovering the crown and of avenging himself on his enemies: that the Tyrant was already decrepit, and that his death, which could not be long in coming, would change the state of affairs altogether: that the very peoples would come to submit to their lawful lord, compelled by the injustice and cruelty of the usurper. On this same occasion a Mexican officer of considerable standing (probably Itzcoatl, brother of the king and general of the Mexican armies), either on his own authority or by order of King Chimalpopoca, climbed up on the temple which the Toltec nation had in that court, and spoke thus to the immense crowd that was there: “Hear, Chichimecs, hear, Acolhuas, and all of you who are gathered here: let no one dare do any harm to our son Nezahualcoyotl, nor allow another to do it to him, unless he wishes to submit to a rigorous punishment.” This proclamation served greatly for the safety of the heir prince, no one wishing to bring upon himself the anger of a nation that was beginning to make itself respected.

Not long afterward many of the nobles who, to escape the fury of the Tepanec troops, had taken refuge in Huexotzinco and in Tlaxcala, assembled in Papalotla, a place near Texcoco, to deliberate on the course they should take in the present circumstances, and all agreed to submit to the new lords whom the Usurper had set over them in their cities, both to free themselves from so many hostilities and to be able to attend quietly to their homes and families.

for clothing, they should pay him another in gold and precious stones, without perceiving how much he would embitter by such burdens the minds of his subjects, whom he ought rather to have conciliated by moderation and gentleness, in order to make more secure the possession of a throne established upon injustice and cruelty. The Toltec and Chichimec nobles replied to the criers that they wished to present themselves in person to the king to speak to him about this matter. The Tyrant’s haughtiness seemed to them excessive, and his conduct too different from the moderation of the ancient kings from whom he descended. They therefore agreed to send him two orators, the ablest there were, a Toltec and a Chichimec (*), so that each of them, in the name of his nation, might make strong and effective remonstrances to him. Both went to Azcapotzalco, and, being introduced to an audience with the Tyrant, after making a very deep bow, the Toltec spoke first, out of regard for the greater antiquity of his nation in that country, and set before him the humble beginnings of the Toltecs, and the hardships they endured before arriving at the splendor and glory which they enjoyed for some time, and the misery to which they were reduced after their overthrow; he described the lamentable dispersion in which they were found by Xolotl when he came to that land, and, running through the two centuries that followed, he made a pathetic enumeration of the hardships they suffered, to move the Tyrant to compassion and to spare his nation the new burden.

Chichimecs, your forefathers, took no account of gold and gems. They put no other crown on their heads than a garland of herbs and Bk. III. wild flowers, nor did they adorn themselves with any other bracelets than the rough leather against which the bowstring struck in shooting. Their food at first was reduced to raw flesh and insipid herbs, and their clothing to the skins of deer and of wild beasts which they themselves hunted. Once they had learned agriculture from the Toltecs, the kings themselves tilled the earth, to encourage their subjects to labor by their example. The opulence and glory to which fortune afterward raised them did not make them any prouder. They made use of their subjects, it is true, as kings; but as fathers they loved them, and were content to be acknowledged by them with the humble gifts of the earth. I present to you, lord, these illustrious examples of your forefathers for no other reason than to beg you most humbly not to wish to exact from us more than those men exacted from our ancestors.” The Tyrant listened to the one address and the other, and although the comparison made with the ancient kings vexed him, he nevertheless concealed his displeasure, and contented himself, in dismissing the orators, with confirming the order published concerning the new burden.

Meanwhile Nezahualcoyotl kept going about, ever anxious, through several cities, seeking to win over minds in order to restore himself to the throne. But although his subjects loved him, and wished to see him in possession of the kingdom, they did not dare to favor his party openly, for fear of the Tyrant. Among the subjects most closely related to him who abandoned him were the lord of Chimalpan, his uncle, and Tecpanecatl, brother of his second wife Nezahualxochitl, of the royal line of Mexico. Persevering in such negotiations, he arrived one evening at a country estate in the province of Chalco, belonging to a widow lady named Tziltomiauh. He observed that there was a plantation of maguei there, from which the widow drew wine not only for the use of her household but also to sell, which was strictly forbidden by the Chichimec laws. He was inflamed

He dreamed that Nezahualcoyotl, transformed into an eagle, opened his breast and ate his heart; and another time, that the same, transformed into a lion, licked his body and sucked his blood. He was so frightened by such tragic imaginings, formed in him by the very consciousness of his injustice and tyranny, that, calling his three sons

Tayatzin, Teuctzintli, and Maxtla, after relating the dreams to them he charged them to put Nezahualcoyotl to death as soon as possible, provided they did it so secretly that no one could suspect the author of such a death. He survived these dreams by scarcely a year. He was already so old that, being unable to keep warm or to sit up any longer in a chair, it was necessary to keep him wholly covered with cotton inside a large osier basket made in the fashion of a cradle; but from this cradle, or rather sepulchre, he tyrannized over the kingdom of

Although it belonged to Tayatzin, as successor to the crown, to give the appropriate orders for the funeral of his father, nevertheless his brother Maxtla, being bolder and more active, assumed the right to himself, and then began to command with as much authority as if he were already in possession of the kingdom to which he aspired, thinking it quite easy to oppress his brother, who was a man of little account and not at all versed in government. Maxtla had the kings of Mexico and of Tlatelolco and the other lords notified, so that they might honor with their presence and their tears the obsequies of their common lord. Nezahualcoyotl, though not summoned, chose nevertheless to be present, in order to observe, as may be believed, with his own eyes the disposition of the court. He went accompanied by an intimate confidant of his and by some attendants, and, having entered the hall of the royal palace where the body lay exposed, he found there the kings of Mexico and of Tlatelolco, the three princes, sons of the Tyrant, and other lords. He saluted them all one by one, in the order in which they were seated, beginning with the king of Mexico, and presented them with bunches of flowers according to the custom of that country. The compliments being over, he sat down beside King Chimalpopoca, his brother-in-law, to keep him company in his mourning. (e) Torquemada makes Tezozomoc the immediate son of the first Acolhua prince, and so makes him reign 160 or 180 years; but from the very address made by the Chichimec orator it is clear to us that Tezozomoc was a descendant of Xolotl, of Nopaltzin, and of Tlotzin. Now the sister of Nopaltzin married Prince Acolhuatzin, so that their children were cousins of Tlotzin, son of Nopaltzin. In all this Torquemada agrees with us. Who, then, was ever called a descendant of his cousin? Whoever will read the genealogy of the Chichimec kings in Torquemada’s work will at once perceive the blunders made by this author. It may be that there were two or three lords of Azcapotzalco named Tezozomoc; but the one who tyrannized over Acolhuacan was at most a great-grandson of Prince Acolhuatzin. The next day the kings of Mexico and of Tlatelolco returned to their cities, and Maxtla began at once, with less dissimulation, to reveal his ambitious design of making himself master of the kingdom, showing by his arrogance and boldness that where his arts did not suffice he would use force. Tayatzin had not the courage to oppose it, knowing the bold and violent temper of his brother, and his advantage in having subjects accustomed to obey him. He therefore took the course of going to Mexico to confer with King Chimalpopoca, to whom he had been chiefly commended by his father, on so arduous a matter. He was received by the king with singular demonstrations of esteem, and after the usual compliments Chimalpopoca said to him:

Of all this conversation there was a witness, a retainer of Tayatzin, who had stayed in a place from which he could listen at his ease, and who, hoping to make his fortune by a betrayal, left that evening secretly for Azcapotzalco, went straight to the palace, and, having obtained an audience of Maxtla, revealed to him what he had heard. His mind was in an instant torn by the anger, the fear, and the grief that this report aroused in him; but being a politician, and practiced in concealing his feelings, he pretended to despise it, and severely reproached the informer for his boldness and rashness in slandering such distinguished persons; he called him drunk, and sent him home to sleep off the wine. He spent the rest of the night deliberating on the course to be taken, and determined at last to forestall his brother and to make him fall into his own nets.

[p. 198] business, he had to come from his state of Coyoacán, he wished them Bk. III.

to show him the love they bore him by the very speedy construction of such a building. So great was the diligence of the people of

Azcapotzalco, and so great the multitude of workmen who flocked to it, that Tayatzin, who had stayed in Mexico no more than three days, found on his return to Azcapotzalco the building already begun.

Astonished at such a novelty, and asking Maxtla the reason, he was told that, since he had to leave him the royal house so as not to prejudice his rights, he was building himself another, in which he might lodge whenever he came to court. The good Tayatzin was satisfied with such an answer, and easily persuaded himself that Maxtla no longer thought of the usurpation of the crown. The building being finished after a short time, Maxtla invited to a banquet his brothers, the kings of Mexico and of Tlatelolco, and other lords. Tayatzin, being wholly ignorant of the treachery of his retainer, did not perceive the snare that was being laid for him; but Chimalpopoca, who was shrewder and more cautious, must have suspected the treachery, and courteously excused himself from attending. When the day appointed for so great a function arrived, the invited guests gathered at the new house, and when they were most absorbed in the merriment of the banquet, and perhaps still more heated by the wine, which is the most opportune occasion for such crimes, armed men entered suddenly and fell with such violence upon the unfortunate Tayatzin that he scarcely opened his eyes to look at his murderers before they were closed by death. The whole company was thrown into confusion by so unexpected a tragedy; but Maxtla quieted it, laying bare the treachery contrived against him, and protesting that in this he had done nothing else than forestall the blow that hung over him. With these and like speeches he so changed their minds that, instead of avenging the death of their lawful lord, they acclaimed the perfidious Tyrant king; but if injustice raised him to the throne, it was only to cast him down from a greater height.

Much greater was Maxtla’s indignation against the king of Mexico; but it did not seem to him fitting to make an attempt [p. 199] against his life until he should see himself well secured on the throne. Meanwhile he vented his rage in insults against his person and in out‐ Bk. III. rages offered to his dignity. Soon after his intrusion into the kingdom,

§ 15. there was sent to him by the king of Mexico the present that it was Insults offered by the the custom to make every year in token of acknowledgment of the Tyrant           to the king of

Mexico. overlordship of the king of Azcapotzalco. This present, consisting of three baskets of fish, of shrimps, and of frogs, and of some vegetables, was carried by persons of rank of the court of Chimalpopoca with a fair speech and with singular expressions of submission and respect. Maxtla showed himself pleased with it; but, since according to the custom of those nations he had to reciprocate with some gift, and wishing besides to take revenge, after consulting his confidants he had delivered to the Mexican ambassadors for their king a Cueitl, that is, a kind of skirt, and a Huepilli, which was a woman’s shift, signifying by this that he held him effeminate and cowardly: an insult the most vexing to those peoples, since there was nothing they prized so much as the reputation of being courageous. Chimalpopoca’s displeasure was also very great, and he would have wished to avenge the outrage; but he could not.

Such a scorn was soon followed by a most grievous offense against honor. The Tyrant learned that among the wives of the Mexican king there was one singularly beautiful, and, inflamed by this mere report with wicked desires, he determined to sacrifice honesty and justice to his passion. To attain his end he made use of certain Tepanec ladies, charging them that when they visited, as they were wont to do, that Mexican lady, they should invite her to come to them at Azcapotzalco to divert herself for some days. Such visits being at that time quite frequent even among persons of the first rank and of different nations, it was not difficult for the villainous prince to seize the occasion he so much desired to satisfy his guilty passion, neither the tears nor the efforts used by that honest lady in defense of her honor sufficing to restrain him: whereupon she returned to Mexico full of ignominy,

[p. 200] and pierced by the keenest grief, to complain to her husband. This

Bk. III. unfortunate king, either so as not to survive his dishonor, or so as not to have to die in the hands of the Tyrant, resolved to put an end to his bitter life, dying sacrificed in honor of his god Huitzilopochtli, as certain so-called heroes of his nation had done; believing that such a death must wipe out the infamy received, and free him from the ignominious end which he feared from his enemy. He communicated this resolution to his courtiers, and they praised it, for the extravagant ideas they had in matters of religion, and some of them even wished to be made sharers in the glory of so barbarous a sacrifice.

§ 16.     When the day assigned for the religious tragedy came, the king apImprisonment and peared dressed as they represented their god Huitzilopochtli, and all

death of King

Chimalpopoca. the others who were to accompany him likewise put on the best garments they had. The ceremony began with a solemn dance; and while it lasted, the priests went on sacrificing one by one those unfortunate victims, reserving the king for the last. It was not possible that so strange a novelty should be unknown to the Tyrant: he learned of it in advance, and in order that his enemy might not by a voluntary death escape his vengeance, he sent a body of troops to surprise him before the sacrifice. They arrived, in fact, when barely two victims remained, after whom the king himself was to be sacrificed. This unhappy prince was seized by the Tepanecs and taken at once to Azcapotzalco, where he was put in a strong wooden cage, which was, as we shall say elsewhere, the prison used by those nations, under a strong guard. In this event there are certain circumstances that make assent a little difficult; but I give the account just as I find it among the historians of Mexico. And it is indeed to be wondered at that the Tepanecs had the boldness to enter that city and to make so perilous an attempt, and that the Mexicans did not arm in defense of their king; but the power of the Tyrant could without doubt embolden the Tepanecs and frighten the Mexicans.

[p. 201]

With the imprisonment of Chimalpopoca Maxtla’s desire revived to seize also Prince Nezahualcoyotl, and in order to obtain him more Bk. III. easily he had him summoned under the pretext of wishing to make an agreement with him about the crown of Acolhuacan. The shrewd prince at once perceived the malign intention of the Tyrant; but the ardor of his age, and the courage, or rather the rashness, of his spirit made him present himself intrepidly to the gravest perils. In passing through Tlatelolco he visited a confidant of his called Chichincatl, who let him know that the Tyrant was not only plotting against his life and that of the king of Tlatelolco, but would even, if he could, annihilate the whole Acolhua nation. Nevertheless, without being frightened, he betook himself to Azcapotzalco in the evening, and went straight to the house of a friend of his. Early in the morning he went to find Chachaton, a great favorite of the Tyrant, by whom the prince himself was loved, and commended himself to him, that he might dissuade Maxtla from doing anything against his person. The two went together to the palace, and Chachaton went in first to inform his lord of the prince’s coming and to speak to him in his favor. Then the prince entered, and after his compliments said to him thus: “I know, lord, that you have imprisoned the king of Mexico, and I do not know whether you have already put him to death, or whether he still lives in prison. I have also heard it said that you wish to put me to death too. If it is truly so, here I am before you: kill me with your own hands, so that your anger may be vented against a prince no less innocent than unfortunate.” As he said these words, the remembrance of his misfortunes drew some tears from his eyes. “What do you think?” said Maxtla then to his favorite. “Is it any wonder that a young man who has scarcely begun to enjoy life should seek death so intrepidly?” And turning to the prince, he assured him that he was plotting nothing against his life: that the king of Mexico was not dead, nor would he ever have him put to death, and he sought at the same time to justify himself in regard to the imprisonment

Chimalpopoca, informed of the arrival at the court of the prince, his brother-in-law, sent to beg him to come and see him in the prison.

> Tosio che Maxtlaton seppe la morte del suo illustre ri-, 5. 16, gione, montando in collera per essere stati frastornati i suoi vece “all progetti, e temendo che ancor NezahualcojotlI sottrarsi potesse è morte alla sua vendetta, rilolvette anticipargli in qualunque manie- > ra. potesse la: morte, che finora non gli avea dato, o per non popoca . averla potuto eseguire nella maniera da suo Padre ordinaragli, O perchè s' era impaurito, come affermano: altri Storici , da Ccz certi

The prince went to him, having first obtained Maxtla’s consent, and on entering the prison embraced him, both showing great tenderness in their looks and in their expressions. Chimalpopoca set before him the series of his misfortunes, made clear to him the malign intentions of the Tyrant against them both, and begged him never to return to the court; for his cruel enemy would infallibly put him to death, and the Acolhua nation would be left wholly abandoned. “Finally,” he said to him, “since my death is inevitable, I beg you earnestly to take care of my poor Mexicans. Be to them a true friend and father. And in token of the love I bear you, accept this pendant, which was once my brother Huitzilihuitl’s.” And taking from his lip a gold pendant that he had, he gave it to him, together with earrings and other gems that he kept in the prison, and to a retainer who accompanied the prince he gave other things. Then, with great sorrow, they took leave of each other, so that a longer stay in the visit might not cause some suspicion. Nezahualcoyotl, following the advice given him, left the court at once, and never returned to present himself to the Tyrant. He went to Tlatelolco, and, having taken there a boat and good rowers, hastened to Texcoco.

> Nan ff

Chimalpopoca remained in his bitter solitude, turning over thoughts of affliction. Each day the imprisonment became more intolerable to him: he had no hope of recovering his liberty, nor of being useful to his nation in the little time of life that remained to him.

“If I must at last die,” he said, “how much better, and more glorious, will it be for me to die by my own hands than by those of a perfidious and cruel Tyrant! Since I cannot take any other vengeance on him, at least I will not leave him the pleasure that [p. 203] he would then have in the choice of the time and of the kind of death with which I must end my unhappy days. I wish to be master of my Bk. III. life, to choose the time and the manner of dying, and to be also the executor of my own death, so that there may be so much the less ignominy in it, the less influence the will of my enemy has upon it.” (*) With such a resolution, so conformable to the ideas of those nations, he hanged himself from a beam of the cage, making use, as is to be believed, of his own girdle.

With an end so tragic the third king of Mexico finished his calamitous life. We have no more precise accounts either of his character or of the progress which the nation made in the time of his reign, which lasted about thirteen years, having ended in 1423, about a year after the death of Tezozomoc. All that is known of him is that in the eleventh year of his reign he had a great stone brought to Mexico, to serve as an altar for the ordinary sacrifice of prisoners, and another, round and larger, for the gladiatorial sacrifice, of which we shall speak elsewhere. In the fourth painting of the Mendoza Collection are represented the victories gained by the Mexicans in the reign of Chimalpopoca over the cities of Chalco and of Tequixquiac, and the naval engagement which they had with the Chalcas, with the loss of some men and of some boats overturned by the enemy. The Interpreter of that collection adds that Chimalpopoca left many sons born of his concubines.

to be restrained by motives of religion; so he gave four of the bravest captains the order to seek that prince everywhere and, without fail, to take his life wherever they should find him. The Tepanec captains set out with few men, so that the noise might not make the prey escape, and went straight to Texcoco, where on their arrival

> Sam

Nezahualcoyotl was playing ball with a retainer of his called Ocelotl.

This prince, in every place where he went to draw minds to his party, occupied himself in dances, games, and other amusements, so that the governors of those places, who by order of the Tyrant watched over his conduct and observed his steps, seeing him employed in pastimes, might persuade themselves that he no longer thought of the crown, and neglect to observe him. Thus he carried on his negotiations without causing the slightest suspicion. On this occasion, before the captains entered his house, the prince learned that they were

Tepanecs and that they came armed; whence, suspecting what it might be, he left the game and withdrew to the innermost rooms.

Then, informed by the porter that the Tepanecs were asking for him, he ordered Ocelotl to receive them and to tell them that he would be with them after they had dined and rested. It did not seem to the

Tepanecs that they ought to lose the opportunity by putting off the blow, and perhaps they did not yet dare to carry out the commission until they had made sure that there was inside the house no one capable of offering resistance; so after resting they sat down to table, and while they were dining the prince escaped by a secret door, and, going out of the city, walked more than a mile to Coatitlan, a small place of weavers, all of them people faithful and attached to him, where he remained hidden for the time. labyrinth, which he had had made with so many turns and intricacies that the way out was impossible to anyone who did not know its arrangement, whose secret [p. 205] having waited a good while after dinner, and seeing that neither the prince let himself be seen nor his retainer Ocelotl, they searched for Bk. III. him through the whole house without finding in it any person who could give them word of him. Assured, therefore, of his flight, they went out at once to look for him everywhere, and having learned from a peasant on the road to Coatitlan that he had taken refuge in that place, they entered it with an armed force, threatening the inhabitants with death if they did not reveal the fugitive prince; but, by a rare example of fidelity, there was not in the whole place anyone who would betray him, although some were killed for this reason. Among those who sacrificed their lives to fidelity were Tochmantzin, overseer of all the looms of Coatitlan, and Matlalintzin, a noble lady. The Tepanecs, unable to find the prince there in spite of their diligence and of the cruelty they had used against the inhabitants, went out to look for him through the countryside; and Nezahualcoyotl also went out by another way, and took a road opposite to that of his enemies; but as they were searching for him everywhere, he found himself in great danger of falling into their hands, had he not been hidden by certain peasants inside a heap of the herb chian that was on the threshing floor.

Safe from such a danger, the prince went to spend the night at Tetzcotzinco, a pleasant country house built by his ancestors for their recreation. There six lords were waiting for him, who, outside their states, were wandering through the cities of the kingdom. There they §Negotiations

Cholulans, who offered to help him in the war against the Tyrant. There also two lords of his party joined him with the sad news of the death of

Huitzilihuitl, one of his favorites, who had been put to the torture by the

Tyrant that he might reveal certain secrets, and who, being faithful to his master, would not disclose them to him, and ended his life in the torments. With this grief he passed from Apan to Huexotzinco, whose lord was a relative of his, who received him with singular affection and compassion, and promised also to aid him with all his forces. From there he went to Tlaxcala, where he was magnificently received, and in this city they agreed upon the time and the place at which the troops of Cholula, of Huexotzinco, and of Tlaxcala should assemble. When he left this last city to go to Calpulalpan, a place situated midway on the road from

Tlaxcala to Texcoco, he was accompanied by so great a nobility that he seemed more a king going out on a pleasure trip with his court than a fugitive prince seeking the means of getting possession of the crown usurped from him. In Calpulalpan he received the reply of the Chalcas, in which they declared themselves ready to serve their lawful lord against the wicked usurper. It is to be believed that the cruelty and insolence of the Tyrant alienated many peoples from him, besides which the Chalcas were too inconstant and too ready to adhere now to one party, now to another, as will be seen in the course of this history.

§ 19. Itzcoatl, fourth king Mexicans, finding themselves without a king and afflicted by the of Mexico. Tepanecs, deliberated on putting at the head of the nation a man capable of repressing the insolence of the Tyrant and of avenging the very grave injuries received from him. Having assembled, therefore, for the election of the new king, an authoritative old man spoke thus to the other electors: “You have lost, O noble Mexicans, in the death of your king the light of your eyes; but you still have that of reason with which to elect a worthy successor. The Mexican nobility has not ended in Chimalpopoca; there still remain several excellent princes, [p. 207] brothers of his, from among whom you can choose a lord who will govern you and a father who will welcome you. Imagine that for a Bk. III. short time the sun has been eclipsed and the earth darkened, and that now the light returns to us in the new king. What matters is that, without lingering in long conferences, we elect a prince who will restore the honor of our nation, avenge the affronts done to it, and set it again in its primitive liberty.” They proceeded at once to the election, and Prince Itzcoatl was elected by common consent, half-brother on the father’s side of the two preceding kings, and natural son of Acamapichtli, born of a slave woman. As much as he might lose in esteem by the unfortunate condition of his mother, so much was he worthy by the nobility and renown of his father, and far more by his own virtues, of which he gave many examples in the post of general of the Mexican armies, which he had held for more than thirty years. He was esteemed the most prudent, upright, and valiant man of the whole nation. Placed upon the Tlatocaicpalli, or royal seat, he was saluted as king by all the nobility with singular acclamations. Then one of the orators made him an address on the obligations of a sovereign: “All of us, O great king and lord,” he said to him among other things, “all of us now hang upon you. On your shoulders are borne the old, the orphans, and the widows. Will you have the heart to lay down this burden? Will you allow the children who crawl on the ground to perish at the hands of our enemies? Come, lord, begin to spread out your mantle to carry on your back the poor Mexicans, who flatter themselves that they live secure beneath the cool shade of your kindness.” This ceremony over, the exaltation of the new monarch was celebrated with public dances and games. It was no less applauded by Nezahualcoyotl and by his whole party: for no one doubted that the new king would be a constant ally of the prince his brother-in-law; and they hoped for great advantages from his prowess and from his military skill; but to the Tepanecs and their allies, and above all to the Tyrant, such an election was very displeasing.

All the time that the prince had been in Calpulalpan he had employed in making preparations for the war. When it seemed to him that it was now time to put his great designs into execution, he set out with his people and with the auxiliary troops of Tlaxcala and of

Huexotzinco, with the resolve to take the city of Texcoco by assault and to punish its inhabitants for their disloyalty toward him in his bad fortune. He halted with the whole army within sight of the city, in a place called Oztopolco. There he passed the night, arranging the troops and giving the necessary dispositions for the assault, and the next morning he marched toward the city; but before he reached it, the Texcocans, frightened by the severe punishment that hung over them, came humbly to meet him, asking pardon and presenting to him, to move him to compassion, the old and infirm, the pregnant women, and the mothers with their tender children in their arms, who, with bitter weeping and other demonstrations of grief, said to him: “Have pity, O most clement lord, on these your servants so afflicted. In what have these wretched old men, these poor women, and these innocent children offended you? Do not wish to destroy along with the guilty those who have no part in the offenses you wish to avenge.” The prince, softened at the sight of so many wretched people, granted pardon at once to the city; but at the same time he detached some of the troops, and ordered their captains to enter it and to kill the governors and the other officials established there by the

Huexotzinca troops, detached from the army, assailed with indescribable fury the city of Acolman, killing all they met as far as the house of the lord of the city, who was a brother of the Tyrant, and who, having no forces sufficient to defend himself, was slain by his enemies. On the same day the Chalca auxiliaries of the Prince fell upon the city of Coatlichan and took it without much resistance, with the death of the governor, who had taken refuge on the top of the great temple; so that in a single day the Prince brought under his obedience the court and two considerable cities of the kingdom of Acolhuacan.

Huitzilihuitl, called Moteuczoma (commonly Moctezuma), a young man of great bodily strength and invincible courage, to whom, for his immortal deeds, they gave also the name of Tlacaelel, that is, a man of great heart, and that of Ilhuicamina, that is, the Archer of Heaven; and to designate him in the ancient paintings they represented over his head the sky pierced with an arrow, as may be seen in the seventh and eighth paintings of the Mendoza collection, and as we shall show elsewhere among the figures of the kings of Mexico. This is that Mexican hero whom Father Acosta, or rather Father Tovar, from whom that author took the eulogy, so greatly celebrates under the name of Tlacaelel, although in several of the deeds attributed to him he has fallen into error. (g) Father Acosta, or rather Father Tovar, erred not only in the account of some deeds of our hero, but even in what concerns his person; for he believed Tlacaelel to be different from Moctezuma, whereas in fact he is a single personage, called by two and even three names. He makes Tlacaelel also a nephew of Itzcoatl and at the same time an uncle of Moctezuma, which is evidently false, since it is known that Moctezuma was the son of Huitzilihuitl, brother of Itzcoatl; whence he could not be the nephew of the nephew of Itzcoatl. His embassy happily concluded, he took leave of the Prince to return to Mexico; but on the road he fell into an ambush that his enemies had laid for him; he was taken prisoner with all his retinue, led to Chalco, and presented to Toteotzin, lord of that city and a mortal enemy of the Mexicans. The latter at once had them shut up in a narrow prison under the care of Cuateotzin, a person of consequence, ordering him to furnish the prisoners no other food than what he himself prescribed, until it should be determined what kind of death they were to end their days with. Cuateotzin, thinking such an order too inhuman, provided for them abundantly at his own expense. But the cruel Toteotzin, thinking to do a great service to the Huexotzincas, sent them the prisoners, so that, if it seemed good to them, they might sacrifice them in Huexotzinco with the assistance of the

Chalcas returned to Toteotzin, who, being determined to make some [p. 211] friends by means of those prisoners, informed the Tyrant Maxtla, leaving to his will the fate of those unfortunates, and hoping by such Bk. III. flattery to calm the anger caused in him by his perfidy and by his inconstancy in abandoning the Tepanec party for that of Prince Nezahualcoyotl. Meanwhile, while he awaited Maxtla’s reply, he had the prisoners shut up in the same prison and under the custody of the same Cuateotzin. The latter, grieved at the misfortune of a young man so illustrious and so brave, summoned on the evening before the day on which the reply from Azcapotzalco was expected a servant of his in whom he greatly trusted, and ordered him to set the prisoners at liberty that very night, and to tell Moctezuma on his part that he had resolved to save his life at the evident risk of losing his own; that if on this account he should have to die, as was to be feared, he should not forget to show his gratitude in the protection of the children he was leaving; and, finally, that he should not go by land to Mexico, because he would again be taken by the guards who were on the road, but should make his way by Iztapalocan to Chimalhuacan, and there embark to be carried to his city.

The servant carried out the order, and Moctezuma followed the counsel of Cuateotzin. They left the prison that night and cautiously made their way toward Chimalhuacan, where they kept hidden the whole following day, and, having nothing else to eat, fed on raw herbs; at night they embarked, and with the greatest speed were carried to Mexico, where they were received with singular rejoicing, since they were already believed dead there.

As soon as the barbarous Toteotzin was informed of the flight of the prisoners, he fell into a rage, and since he did not doubt that Cuateotzin had been the author of their liberty, he had him put to death at once and quartered, together with his wife and his children, of whom a son and a daughter were saved. The latter took refuge in Mexico, where she was much honored out of regard for her father, who by the sacrifice of his own life had rendered so important a service to the Mexican nation.

the help given to Nezahualcoyotl and for the slaughter they had made at Coatlichan, sent Toteotzin a most severe reprimand, calling him a double-dealer and a traitor, and ordering him to set the prisoners at liberty without delay. A reward worthy of a perfidious flatterer! Maxtla did not take this resolution in order to favor the Mexicans, whom he hated mortally, but only to show contempt for Toteotzin’s homage and to oppose his wishes. So far was he from favoring the Mexican nation that he had never been so intent as he was then on its ruin, and had already made ready troops to strike a decisive blow at Mexico, and then to go on and recover all that Nezahualcoyotl had taken from him. This

Prince, aware of Maxtla’s designs, went to Mexico to confer with that prudent king on the order they were to observe in that war and on the measures to be taken to thwart the Tyrant’s projects, and they agreed to unite the Texcocan troops with those of Mexico for the defense of that city, on whose fate the outcome of the war seemed to depend.

At the rumor of the imminent war the Mexican commoners were so greatly disturbed that, thinking themselves incapable of resisting the power of the Tepanecs, whom until then they had acknowledged as their superiors, they went in crowds to the king to beg him, with cries and with tears, not to undertake so perilous a war, which would infallibly bring about the overthrow of their city and of the nation. What would you have us do, then, said the king, to deliver ourselves from so many calamities? Let us ask for peace, replied the commoners, of the king of

Moctezuma happened to be present, and, unable to endure that a nation which boasted so much Bk. III. of honor should adopt so ignominious a course, he spoke thus to the commoners: “Ah, what are you thinking of, O Mexicans? Have you lost your wits? How has such cowardice entered into your hearts? Have you perhaps forgotten that you are Mexicans, and descendants of those heroes who founded this city, and of those valiant men who have preserved it in spite of the opposition of our enemies? Either change your sentiment, then, or renounce the glory that you have inherited from your forefathers.” And turning then to the king: “How, my lord,” he said to him, “can you permit so great an ignominy in your people? Speak to them once more, and tell them to let us adopt another course before putting ourselves so foolishly and so shamefully into the hands of our enemies.”

The king, who desired nothing more than this, spoke to the commoners, recommending the counsel of Moctezuma, which was well received. “Well, then,” said the king, addressing the nobility, “which of you, who are the flower of the nation, will have the courage to carry an embassy to the lord of the Tepanecs?” They all began to look at one another, and there was none among them who dared to face the danger, until Moctezuma presented himself with youthful intrepidity, saying: “I will go; for if after all I must die, it matters little whether it be today or tomorrow, nor can a better occasion be found for dying with glory, sacrificing my life to the honor of my nation. Here I am, my lord, ready to obey your commands. Command me, then, whatever you please.” The king, pleased with so great a courage, ordered him to go and propose peace to the Tyrant, but without consenting to ignominious conditions. The brave young man set out at once, and meeting the Tepanec guards, persuaded them to let him bear to their lord an embassy of the highest importance. Presented to the Tyrant, he asked him for peace in the name of his king and of his nation, but under honorable conditions. The Tyrant

asked of him a safe-conduct, he gave him no other than what he might procure by his own industry; whereupon the latter went off at once to

Mexico, promising to return the next day. The little confidence and security he had in that court, and the convenience of the journey, which was no more than four miles, were doubtless the reasons why he did not wait there for the Tyrant’s decision. He returned, then, to Azcapotzalco on the following day, as he had promised, and having heard from the

Tyrant’s own mouth the resolution of war, he performed with him the ceremonies customary among lords when they challenged one another, that is, he presented him with certain defensive arms, anointed his head, and attached feathers to it in the manner in which they did so with the dead; and besides this he protested to him in the name of his king that, by refusing to accept the peace offered him, he would without doubt be ruined together with the whole nation of the Tepanecs. The Tyrant, without showing displeasure at these ceremonies or at the threats made to him, gave him also some arms to present to the king of Mexico, and warned Moctezuma, for the safety of his person, to return in disguise by a little door of that palace. The Tyrant would not this time have paid so much heed to the law of nations, if he had foreseen that this same ambassador, whose life he was taking care of, was to be the principal instrument of his ruin. Moctezuma profited by the warning; but as soon as he saw himself out of danger, he began to insult the guards, reproaching them with their negligence and threatening them with their speedy destruction. The guards rushed upon him to kill him; but he defended himself so courageously that he killed one or two men, and others coming up, he retired precipitately to Mexico, bringing the news that war was already declared and that the leaders of both nations had been challenged.

At such news the commoners were again thrown into confusion, and had recourse to the king to ask of him permission to abandon [p. 215] the city, because they believed their ruin inevitable. The king tried to

Bk. III. comfort and encourage them with the hope of victory. But if we should ever be defeated, replied the commoners, what shall we do? If that hap‐

§ 21. pens, answered the king, from this moment we bind ourselves to put our‐ War against the selves into your hands, to be sacrificed by you, if you please. So be it, said the Tyrant. commoners again, if you are defeated; but if you gain the victory, from this moment we also bind ourselves, we and our descendants, to be your tributaries, to till your lands and those of the nobles, to build your houses, and to carry for you, every time you go to war, your arms and your baggage. This agreement having been made between the nobles and the commoners, and the command of all the Mexican troops having been committed to the brave Moctezuma, the king gave prompt notice to Prince Nezahualcoyotl to come at once with his army to Mexico, as he did one day before the battle.

It cannot be doubted that causeways on the lake had already been built by the Mexicans at this time for the more convenient communication of their city with those of the mainland; for otherwise the movements and skirmishes of both armies cannot be understood; indeed, we know from history that these causeways were cut by ditches, over which they had drawbridges; but no historian indicates the time at which they were built. (h) For my part, I truly wonder that in the midst of a life so calamitous the Mexicans had spirit enough to undertake and to carry out a work so great and so difficult.

On the day following the arrival of Prince Nezahualcoyotl in Mexico, the army of the Tepanecs showed itself in the field, very numerous and brilliant, no less for the little plates of gold with which they went adorned than for the handsome plumes they wore on their heads, with which they seemed to wish to enlarge their stature. They accompanied their march with great shouts,

general called Mazatl. The Tyrant Maxtla, although he had accepted the challenge, nevertheless would not stir from his palace, either because he thought it degrading to himself to have to fight with the king of Mexico, or, what is more likely, because he feared the fortune of war. As soon as the Mexicans were warned of the movements of the Tepanecs, they went out in good order to receive them, and the signal of battle having been given by King Itzcoatl with the sound of a little drum which he carried on his shoulder, both armies attacked with indescribable fury, each side being fully persuaded that that battle was to decide its fate. For the greater part of the day it could not be known to which side victory was inclining, since what the

Tepanecs gained they lost again a little later. But a little before sunset, the Mexican commoners, seeing the forces of the enemy continually increasing with fresh reinforcements, began to lose heart and to complain of their leaders. What are we doing, O Mexicans! they said to one another; will it be well to sacrifice our lives to the ambition of our king and of our general! How much more salutary will it not be to surrender, humbly confessing our rashness, in order to obtain pardon and the grace of life?

The king heard these words with the greatest grief, and seeing that with them his people were losing heart more and more, he summoned to council the Prince and the general to ask their opinion on what ought to be done to encourage the commoners, so dismayed.

What? replied Moctezuma, fight to the death. If we die with arms in hand defending our liberty, we shall have done our duty. If we survive defeated, we shall remain covered with eternal confusion. Let us go, then, let us go and die.

The clamors of the almost vanquished Mexicans were already beginning to prevail, among whom there were some so base that, calling to their enemies, they said: O mighty Tepanecs, lords of the mainland, restrain your anger; for we now surrender. If you please, [p. 217] here, before your very eyes, we will kill our chiefs, to deserve from you pardon

> Maxalacron‘afsai afflicco e dalla morte del'/suo Generale, e dalla sconfitta delle sue truppe } passò quella notte ( l’ ul+ tima della sua vità ) animando i ‘suoi Capitani , e ad essi rappresentando da: una parte la ‘gloria del trionfo, e dall'altra i mali , a cui soggiacerebbero, se mai fossero. vinti : poi» ché i Meshcadi ; ché insin' a-quel tempo verano starti tributarj dei Tepanechi , dove restassero vittoriosi, costrignerebbono i Tepanechi a pagar tributo a loro . Bk. III. for the rashness into which their ambition has led us. So great was the indignation which the king, the prince, the general, and the nobility felt at such clamors that they would on the spot have punished with death the baseness of their cowardly soldiers, had it not been in order not to make the enemy’s victory easier; and so, dissembling their displeasure, they all cried with one voice, Let us go and die with glory, and threw themselves with such impetus upon the enemy that they drove them back from a ditch which they had occupied and made them retreat. With this advantage the king began to animate his people, while the Prince and the general worked wonders of courage. In the hottest of the fray Moctezuma met the Tepanec general, who came on proud of the terror his soldiers had caused among the Mexican commoners, and dealt him so fierce a blow on the head that he stretched him lifeless at his feet. The rumor of victory spread at once through the whole field, whereby the Mexicans took great courage; but the Tepanecs were so dismayed by the death of their brave general Mazatl that they immediately fell into disorder. The night coming on prevented the Mexicans from continuing their advance: whereupon both sides withdrew to their cities, the Mexicans full of courage and impatient at not being able, because of the darkness of the night, to complete their victory, and the Tepanecs disconsolate and melancholy, though not wholly without hope of avenging themselves on the following day.

Maxtla, greatly afflicted both by the death of his general and by the defeat of his troops, spent that night (the last of his life) encouraging his captains, and representing to them on the one hand the glory of triumph, and on the other the evils to which they would be subject if they should ever be defeated: for the Mexicans, who until that time had been tributaries of the Tepanecs, should they remain victorious, would force the Tepanecs to pay tribute to them. Bk. III.

Both armies went out to the field and began the battle with extraordinary fury, which was maintained in full vigor until midday. The

§ 22.

Conquest of Mexicans, encouraged both by the advantages gained the day before Azcapotzalco, and death of the Tyrant and by a firm hope of conquering, made so great a slaughter of their

Maxtla.

enemies that they covered the field with corpses, routed them, put them to flight, and pursued them even into their city of

Azcapotzalco, carrying terror and death everywhere. The Tepanecs, seeing that not even in their houses could they escape the fury of the victors, fled to the mountains, ten and twelve miles distant from

Azcapotzalco. The proud Maxtla, who until that day had despised his enemies and considered himself superior to all the reverses of fortune, now seeing the Mexicans in his court, hearing the weeping of the vanquished, his strength failing him for resisting, and fearing to be overtaken in flight if he attempted it, resolved to hide himself in a temazcalli, or hypocaust, of which we shall speak elsewhere; but as the victors sought him everywhere, so at last they found him, and neither the entreaties nor the tears with which he implored their clemency being enough to move them, he was killed with cudgel blows and stones, and his corpse was thrown into the field to be food for the birds of prey. Such was the tragic end of Maxtla, who had not yet completed three years of his tyranny. Thus ended the injustice, the cruelty, the ambition, and the perfidy of this man, and the most grievous injuries done by him to the lawful heir of the kingdom of

Acolhuacan, to his brother Tayatzin, and to the kings of Mexico. His memory is odious and execrable in the annals of those nations.

> La notte seguente s' occuparono i vincitori nel saccheg. giar la Cirrà , nel rovinar le case, e nel bruciar i tempj, lasciando in- tale stato quella :Corte già ranto celebre , che non potesse rimetterlì in molti anni. Mentre i Messicani, e gli Acolhui raccolgevano i frutti della loro vittoria, i Tlascallesi , e gli Huexotzinchi distaccati dall' esercito presero per affalto la Corte antica di Tenajuca , e nel piorno se» guente vennero ad unirl a coloro, per prendere la Città di Cuerlachtepec . ‘

The following night the victors busied themselves in sacking the city, in demolishing the houses, and in burning the temples, leaving that court, once so celebrated, in such a state that it could not recover in many years. While the Mexicans and the Acolhuas were gathering the fruits of their victory, the Tlaxcalans and the Huexotzincas, detached from the army, took by assault the ancient court of Tenayuca, and on the following day came to join them, in order to take the city of Cuetlachtepec.

The fugitive Tepanecs, finding themselves reduced to the greatest misery in the mountains, and fearing to be overtaken there too by the victors, thought of surrendering and imploring their clemency; and to obtain it they sent to the king of Mexico a distinguished personage accompanied by other nobles from several places of the Tepanec nation. This ambassador humbly asked the king for pardon in the name of his fellow countrymen, offered him obedience, and promised that all the Tepanecs would acknowledge him as their lawful lord and serve him as vassals. He congratulated himself on their fortune, in the midst of so great an overthrow, in having to submit to a king so worthy and endowed with the most excellent qualities, and finally concluded his speech by earnestly begging him to be willing to grant them the grace of life and the liberty to return to their houses. Itzcoatl received them with the greatest kindness, granted all they wished, and declared that he would receive them not as subjects but as sons, and offered to perform toward them all the offices of a true father; but at the same time he threatened them with utter extermination should they dare to violate the fidelity they had sworn to him. After this favor the fugitives returned to their homes to rebuild their houses and to attend to the interests of their families; and from that time they remained always subject to the king of Mexico, adding by their misfortune to the examples of vicissitude that we constantly observe
