King Itzcoatl, after this famous conquest, had the commoners ratify the agreement already made by them with the nobility, whereupon they remained perpetually obliged to serve it, as they always did in the future; but those who by their clamors and laments had disheartened the others in the battle, were cut off from the body of the nation and from the Mexican state, and, as base and cowardly, perpetually banished. To Moctezuma then, and to the others who had most distinguished themselves in the war, the king gave the ownership of a part of the conquered lands, and assigned another part to the priests for their sustenance; and after giving the orders suitable to make his dominion firmer and more stable, he returned with his army to

Acolhuacan. Acolhuacan. If the king of Mexico had set aside fidelity and justice in favor of ambition, he would not have lacked pretexts to take possession of that kingdom also. The Tyrant Tezozomoc had placed Chimalpopoca in possession of Texcoco, and the latter, as lord, had commanded in that court. Itzcoatl, who had entered into all the rights of his predecessor, could consider that state as incorporated for some years past into the crown of Mexico. whence it is to be believed that the Tyrant Maxtla took it from him in order to give it to Huitznahuatl. [p. 223] declaring their rebellion they began to maltreat the Mexican women who went to their market, and even the men who for any reason hap‐ Bk. IV. pened to come to that city. Whereupon King Itzcoatl commanded that no Mexican should go to Coyoacán until the insolence of those rebels should be punished. The expedition of Huexotla being therefore ended, he marched against them. In the first three battles he fought he scarcely gained any other advantage than that of making them retreat a little; but in the fourth, while the two armies were fighting furiously, Moctezuma, with the courageous troops he had placed in ambush, fell with such impetus upon the rear guard of the rebels that he threw them into disorder and forced them to abandon the field and flee to the city. He pursued them also, and perceiving that they meant to fortify themselves in the great temple, forestalled them by occupying it, and burned the tower of that sanctuary. At such a blow the rebels were so dismayed that, leaving the city, they fled to the mountains that lie south of Coyoacán; but even there they were pressed by the royal troops for more than thirty miles, until on a mountain west of Cuauhnahuac the fugitives, weary and with no hope of escaping, threw down their arms in token of surrender and gave themselves up to the discretion of the victors.

> Con questa vittoria restò Irzcoatl Padrone di tutto lo stato de' Tepanechi , € Motezuma pieno di gloria, E' da fac maraviglia , dicono gli Storici , che la maggior parte de’ prigioni fartisi in quella guerra di Cojohuacan apparteneva a Motezuma, ed a tre bravi uffiziali Acolhui ; poichè tutti e quattro sull' esempio degli antichi Messicani nella guerra contro i Xochimilchi , s' erano convenuti di cagliar una ciocca di capellia tutti quei che prendessero , e nella maggior parte di essi trovosli. un tal contraflegno.,

By this victory Itzcoatl remained master of the whole state of the Tepanecs, and Moctezuma full of glory. It is a marvel, say the historians, that the greater part of the prisoners taken in that war of Coyoacán belonged to Moctezuma and to three brave Acolhua officers; for all four, following the example of the ancient Mexicans in the war against the Xochimilcas, had agreed to cut a lock of hair from all those they took, and on the greater part of them such a mark was found.

§ 3. in the war against the Mexicans, whether through some secret incliMonarchy of Tacuba, and alliance of the nation that he bore them or through aversion to his uncle Maxtla.

three kings. Itzcoatl summoned him to Mexico and made him king of Tlacopan, or Tacuba, a considerable city of the Tepanecs, and of all the places that lay to the west, including the country of Mazahuacan; but

Coyoacán, Azcapotzalco, Mixcoac, and other Tepanec cities remained immediately subject to the crown of Mexico. That crown was given to

Totoquihuatzin on condition of serving the king of Mexico with all his troops whenever he should require it, assigning to him for this purpose the fifth part of the spoils that might be taken from the enemy. Similarly Nezahualcoyotl was put in possession of the throne of

Acolhuacan on condition of having to assist the Mexicans in war, and therefore the third part of the booty was assigned to him, after first deducting that of the king of Tacuba, the other two thirds remaining to the Mexican king. Besides this, both kings were created honorary electors of the king of Mexico, (b) which honor was reduced merely to ratifying the election made by four Mexican nobles, who were the true electors. The king of Mexico bound himself reciprocally to assist each of those two kings wherever there might be need. This alliance of the three kings, which was maintained firm and unaltered for almost a century, was the cause of the rapid conquests which the

Mexicans afterwards made. This was not the only master stroke of

King Itzcoatl’s policy: he also rewarded advantageously all those who had distinguished themselves in the war, not making so much account of birth

Bk. IV. the services they rendered. Thus the hope of reward animated them to the most heroic enterprises, being sure that their glory and their advantages did not depend upon certain accidents of fortune, but upon the merit of their own actions. Such a policy was for the most part adopted by the later kings, with great benefit to the state. This famous alliance being established, Itzcoatl went with King Nezahualcoyotl to Texcoco to crown him with his own hand. This ceremony was celebrated with the greatest solemnity in 1426. Thereupon the king of Mexico returned to his court, and the king of Acolhuacan applied himself with the greatest diligence to reforming his own.

The kingdom of Acolhuacan was not so well regulated as

§ 4. Techotlalatzin had left it. The domination of the Tepanecs and the Singular regulations revolutions that had occurred in those twenty years had altered the of King

Nezahualcoyotl. government of the peoples, weakened the vigor of the laws, and in great part spoiled the customs. Nezahualcoyotl, who besides the love he bore to his nation was endowed with singular prudence, made such regulations for the reform of the kingdom that it was soon seen more flourishing than under any other of his predecessors. He gave a new form to the councils already established by his grandfather. He conferred the offices on the most suitable persons. There was a council for purely civil causes, and besides others there sat in it five lords who in his adversities had been constantly faithful to him. There was another council for criminal causes, over which presided two princes, his brothers, of the highest integrity. The Council of War was composed of the most famous captains, among whom the first place was held by the lord of Teotihuacan, son-in-law of the king and one of the thirteen grandees of the kingdom. The council for the royal revenues consisted of the king’s stewards and of the chief merchants of the court. There were three principal stewards, who had charge of the tributes and of the other revenues of the king. He established assemblies in the manner of academies for their poetry, for astronomy, for music,

History of Mexico, Vol. I.                  Ff [p. 226] for painting, for history, and for the art of divination, and he sum‐

Bk. IV.

moned to the court the most renowned professors of the kingdom, who assembled on certain days to communicate to one another their lights and their inventions; and for each of the aforesaid sciences and arts, imperfect though they were, he founded schools at the court. As to the mechanical arts, he divided the city of Texcoco into thirty and more parts, and assigned to each art its own, to the exclusion of the others, so that in one place were the goldsmiths, in another the sculptors, in another the weavers, and so with the rest. For the promotion of religion he built new temples, created ministers for the worship of their gods, gave them houses, and assigned revenues both for their sustenance and for the other expenses to be incurred in the festivals and in the sacrifices. To increase the splendor of his court he constructed great buildings within and outside the city, and planted new gardens and woods, which in part were preserved many years after the conquest, and some vestiges of that magnificence are seen to this day.

Some were of the opinion to submit voluntarily to the dominion of the Mexicans, since they must in the end be overwhelmed by their power; but the opinion of the others prevailed, who thought it better to declare war on them before they should become more formidable through new conquests. As soon as the king of Mexico learned their resolution, he put on foot a good army under the command of the celebrated Moctezuma, and notified the king of Tacuba to come with his troops. Bk. IV. withstand their attack, the citizens fled to the mountains; but being besieged there also by the Mexicans, they finally surrendered. Moctezuma was received by the Xochimilca priests with music of little flutes and small drums, having dispatched so important an expedition in only eleven days. The king of Mexico presently betook himself to take possession of that city, which was, as we have already indicated, the greatest of the Valley of Mexico after the courts; there he was recognized and acclaimed king, received the obedience of those new subjects, and promised to love them as a father and to take care in the future of their interests.

The misfortune of the Xochimilcas was not enough to frighten the people of Cuitlahuac; indeed, the advantageous situation of their city, founded on a little island of Lake Chalco, encouraged them to provoke the Mexicans to war. Itzcoatl wished to fall upon them with all the forces of Mexico; but Moctezuma offered to humble their pride with smaller forces, and therefore levied some companies of young men, especially of those who were brought up in the seminaries of Mexico; and having exercised them in arms, and instructed them in the order and manner which they were to observe in that war, he prepared a proportionate number of boats and went with such a flotilla against the people of Cuitlahuac. We are wholly ignorant of the particular circumstances of this expedition; but we know that after seven days the city was taken and subjected to the obedience of the king of Mexico, and that the young men returned laden with spoils and brought with them a good number of prisoners to be sacrificed to the god of war. Nor is the precise year known in which this war was made, any more than the time of that of Cuauhnahuac, though the latter seems to have been made toward the end of the reign of Itzcoatl.

Mexicans by Ocuillan on the west side, the Tepanecs by

Tlatzacapechco on the north side, and the Texcocans together with the people of Xiuhtepec by Tlalquitenanco on the east and south sides. The people of Cuauhnahuac, trusting in the natural strength of the city, chose to await the assault. The first to deliver it were the

Tepanecs, who were vigorously repulsed; but the other troops arriving immediately, the citizens were forced to surrender and to submit to the king of Mexico, to whom they paid annually from that time forward tribute in cotton, in paper, and in other commodities, as we shall say elsewhere. By the conquest of that great, pleasant, and strong city, which was the capital of the Tlahuicas, a great part of that country remained under the dominion of the Mexican king; and soon after there were added to these conquests those of Cuauhtitlan and of

Toltitlan, considerable cities, fifteen miles north of Mexico; but we are wholly ignorant of their circumstances.

In this manner a city which a little before had been tributary to the Tepanecs, and not much esteemed by the other nations, found itself in little more than twelve years in a state to command those very ones who had dominated it, and the peoples who thought [p. 229] themselves superior. So much does the valor and wisdom of its Head matter to the happiness of a nation! The great Itzcoatl died at last, af‐ Bk. IV. ter so glorious a reign and at a very advanced age, in 1436 of the common era. He was a king justly celebrated by the Mexicans for his singular qualities and for the incomparable services he rendered them. He served the nation for more than thirty years in the office of General, and governed it for nearly thirteen as sovereign. Besides having freed it from the domination of the Tepanecs, enlarged its dominions, restored the royal family of the Chichimecs to the throne of Acolhuacan, enriched his court with the spoils of the conquered cities, and laid, in the triple alliance that he established, the foundations of its future greatness, he also ennobled it with new buildings. Among others, after the conquest of Cuitlahuac he built a temple to the goddess Cihuacoatl, and soon after another to Huitzilopochtli. The Mexicans celebrated his funeral rites with extraordinary solemnity and with the greatest demonstrations of grief, and laid his ashes in the same tomb as those of his predecessors.

The four electors had no need to deliberate in the election of the § 6. new king; for, since no brother of the deceased kings survived, the Moctezuma         I, fifth

king of Mexico. election had to fall upon one of the nephews of Itzcoatl; and no one was truly found more worthy than Moctezuma Ilhuicamina, the son of Huitzilihuitl, no less for his virtues than for the important services he had rendered his nation. He was therefore elected with general applause, and notice of this was given at once to the two allied kings, who not only ratified the election but even celebrated it with great praises of the one elected, and sent him presents worthy of his greatness and of their esteem. After the customary ceremonies and the congratulatory speeches of the priests, the nobles, and the soldiers, there were great rejoicings, with banquets, dances, and illuminations. But before coming to the coronation, whether by a law established by the nation or by his own will, he went out to war to take prisoners from among the enemy to be sacrificed at this great ceremony. It seems that the new war against Chalco broke out while it was being built. The Chalcas, besides the injuries already done to Moctezuma, provoked his anger anew by a cruel and horrible outrage that deserved the execration of all posterity. It happened, then, that two royal princes of Texcoco, while hunting in the mountains that overlook the plains of Chalco, engrossed in this diversion and separated from their retinue, with only three Mexican lords, fell in with a squad of Chalca soldiers, who, believing that they were doing a great service to the cruel passions of their master, made them prisoners and led them to Chalco. The barbarous lord of that city, who was probably the same Toteotzin who had so ill-treated

[p. 231]

> menato Motezuma , senza riguardo veruno all’ alto carattere ==de’ prigionieri, e fenza timore de’ funesti efferti della sua Lu. 1y inumana risoluzione, fece subito morir tutti e cinque; ed acciocchè nona mancasse mai a' suoi occhi uno spettacolo, in cui la sua crudeltà fi potesse dilertare , fece salare e feccare: i loro cadaveri; e poi che furono ben asciutti , gli mise in una sala della fu “casa , affinchè gli ferviflero per sostener le fiaccole di pino , con cui fi faceva lume la notte»

Moctezuma, without any regard for the high rank of the prisoners, and without fear of the baneful effects of his inhuman resolution, im‐ Bk. IV. mediately put all five to death; and so that there might never be lacking before his eyes a spectacle in which his cruelty could take delight, he had their bodies salted and dried; and when they were quite dry he placed them in a hall of his house, so that they might serve to hold up the pine torches with which light was made at night.

The report of so horrible an event spread at once through the whole land. The king of Texcoco, whose heart was pierced by this news, asked help of the allied kings to avenge the death of his sons. Moctezuma decided that the Texcocan army should attack the city of Chalco by land, while he and the king of Tacuba with their troops would attack it by water; and to bring this about he assembled an incredible number of boats, capable of transporting so many men, and he wished to command this flotilla in person. The Chalcas, in spite of so great a multitude of enemies, made a vigorous resistance; for besides being warriors by nature, this time despair increased their courage. The lord of that state himself, although he was so old that he could not walk on his own feet, had himself carried in a litter to encourage his subjects by his presence and his voice. Nevertheless they were utterly defeated, the city was sacked, and its lord was punished with the extreme penalty for his atrocious crimes. The booty was divided among the three kings, according to the agreement made under King Itzcoatl; but the city, with all that state, remained from then on subject to the king of Mexico. This victory, according to what the historians say, was owed in great part to the courage of Axoquentzin, the young son of Nezahualcoyotl.

This famous king, although from his youth he had had several wives, and by them many sons, had until then granted the honor of queen to none, since they were all

§ 8. Marriage of the king married Matlalcihuatzin, daughter of the king of Tacuba, a young of Acolhuacan to a princess of Tacuba. woman, beautiful and modest, who was conducted to Texcoco by her

father and by the king of Mexico. Great rejoicings were held for this marriage for eighty days; and after a year there was born of that marriage a son, whom they named Nezahualpilli, who was, as we shall see below, the heir to that crown. Soon after, other very noisy rejoicings were held there for the completion of the building of the Hueitecpan, or Great Palace, to whose magnificence the Spaniards were witnesses.

These rejoicings, at which the two allied kings were also present, ended with a most sumptuous banquet, to which the nobility of the three courts was invited. At this banquet Nezahualcoyotl had his musicians sing, to the sound of instruments, an ode composed by himself, which began, Xochitl mamani in ahuehuetitlan; its subject was to remind those present of the brevity of life, and of all the pleasures of mortals, in the swiftness with which a beautiful flower withers. The pathetic warnings of this song drew tears from those present, to whom love of life made the memory of death the more distressing.

IV. and enmity between the Mexicans and the Tlatelolcas that they remained for years without communicating with one another, except for some commoners who went furtively to the markets. Under the reign of Moctezuma, Cuauhtlatoa resumed his perverse designs; but this time they did not go unpunished; for Moctezuma, being warned, forestalled the blow by a furious assault that he made upon Tlatelolco, in which he had that restless petty king put to death, although his city did not then remain subject to the dominion of the Mexican. The Tlatelolcas elected as king the brave Moquihuix, in whose election the king of Mexico himself doubtless had a hand.

Conquests of went to the province of the Cohuixcas, south of Mexico, to avenge Moctezuma. the death that those peoples had inflicted upon certain Mexicans. In this glorious expedition he added to his crown the states of Huaxtepec, Yauhtepec, Tepoztlan, Yacapichtla, Totolapan, Tlalcozauhtitlan, Chilapan, which is more than a hundred and fifty miles distant from the court, Coixco, Oztomantla, Tlachmallac, and several others; and returning toward the west he conquered Tzompahuacan, leaving from then on subject to the dominion of the king of Mexico both the great country of the Cohuixcas, who had been the authors of those deaths, and many other states near that country, which perhaps by such insults had provoked his anger. On his return to the court he enlarged the temple of Huitzilopochtli and adorned it with the spoils of those peoples. All these conquests were made by him in the first nine years of his reign.

The dike was nine miles in length and eleven braccia in width, and was composed of two parallel palisades, the space between which was filled with stone and sand. The greatest difficulty was found in having to work within the lake, and especially in some places of considerable depth; but it was overcome by the skill of the Director and the constancy of the workmen. This dike was in truth most useful to the city, though it did not suffice to free it entirely from inundations:

1451, besides the weather having been unfavorable, there was scarcely any grain to sow, since almost all of it had been consumed because Bk. IV. of the scantiness of the earlier harvests; so that in 1452 the need of the peoples was so great that, the generosity of the king and of the lords, who opened their granaries for the benefit of their subjects, not being enough to relieve it, they were reduced to buying what they needed with their own liberty. Moctezuma, unable to raise his subjects out of their misery, permitted them to go off to other countries to procure their food; but knowing that some made slaves of themselves for the sustenance of only two or three days, he published an edict in which he commanded that no woman be sold for less than four hundred ears of maize, and no man for less than five hundred. But nothing sufficed to avoid the pernicious effects of the dearth. Some of those who went to seek relief in other countries died of hunger in the roads. Others, who sold themselves elsewhere, never returned to their homeland. The greater part of the Mexican common people sustained themselves, like their ancestors, on aquatic birds and marsh plants, and on the insects and little fish that they caught in the same lake. The following year was not so bad, and finally in 1454, which was a secular year, there was a most abundant harvest, not only of maize but also of legumes and of every sort of fruit.

IV. dered to Moctezuma, who not only became master of the city and state of Coaixtlahuacan, but, going on, took possession of Tochtepec, Tzapotlan, Tototlan, and Chinantla, and in the two following years of Cosamaloapan and Cuauhtochco. The cause of these wars was the same that gave rise to many others, namely that the inhabitants of those places had killed, in time of peace, some Mexican merchants or couriers.

More difficult and more famous was the expedition undertaken in 1457 against Cuetlachtlan, or Cotaxtla. This province, situated, as we have already said, on the coast of the Gulf of Mexico, and founded, or at least inhabited, by the Olmecs, who had been driven out by the Tlaxcalans, was very populous. We likewise do not know the cause of this war; but we do know that the people of Cotaxtla, foreseeing the storm that hung over them, called to their aid the Huexotzincas and the Tlaxcalans. These, being gravely resentful of the defeat of Coaixtlahuacan, and wishing to avenge themselves, not only offered to help them, but also persuaded the Cholulans, their neighbors, to enter the same confederation. These three republics sent numerous troops to Cotaxtla to await the enemy there. Moctezuma for his part raised a large and brilliant army, in which the flower of the Mexican, Acolhua, Tlatelolca, and Tepanec nobility had enlisted. Besides other personages there were in this army Axayacatl, General, Tizoc, and Ahuitzotl, all three brothers and of the royal house of Mexico, who successively occupied that throne after Moctezuma their cousin. There were likewise the lords of Colhuacan and of Tenayuca; but the most noteworthy by his rank was Moquihuix, king of Tlatelolco, successor of the unfortunate Cuauhtlatoa. When this army left Mexico, the news of the confederation of the three republics with the people of Cotaxtla had not yet arrived; as soon as Moctezuma learned of it, he sent his generals couriers

[p. 238] with the order not to advance further, but to return at once to the court. The Bk. IV. generals went into deliberation: some were of the opinion that the sov‐

ereign’s orders should be obeyed without reply; others said that there was no obligation to submit to an order that would do so grave a prejudice to their honor, since their nobility would be discredited and abased if they ever shunned fighting on so opportune an occasion to show their bravery. The first opinion nevertheless prevailed, as the safer; but as they were about to march toward Mexico, King Moquihuix said to them: “Let those return to whom courage suffices to turn their backs on the enemy, while I with my

Tlatelolcas alone will win the honor of the victory.” This resolution of

Moquihuix stung and fired the other generals in such a way that all determined to face the danger. At last the battle was fought, in which, although the people of Cotaxtla fought courageously, they were nonetheless defeated with their allies. Of these the greater part remained on the field, both of the one and of the other; six thousand two hundred prisoners were taken, who a little later were sacrificed in Mexico at the festival of the dedication of the

Quauhxicalco, or of the religious edifice destined to preserve the skulls of the victims. All that province then remained subject to the king of Mexico, who established a garrison there to keep those peoples in obedience to the crown.

So great a victory was owed principally to the courage of King Moquihuix, and down to our own times a Mexican ode or song (e), composed then in his praise, has been preserved. Moctezuma, more pleased at the happy outcome of the war than offended at the disobedience to his orders, rewarded the king of Tlatelolco by giving him in marriage a cousin of his, sister of the aforesaid princes Axayacatl, Tizoc, and Ahuitzotl.

scripts and paintings of his most valuable museum. [p. 239] of punishment, not only for the rebellion but also for other new crimes. At this time they had the rashness to take prisoner a brother Bk. IV. of King Moctezuma himself, who was, as we believe, lord of Ehecatepec, together with other Mexicans. Such an attempt, carried out upon a person so closely bound in blood to their sovereign, seems to have been a means devised by them to withdraw from the dominion of the Mexicans and make the city of Chalco a rival of that of Mexico; for they wished to make that lord king of Chalco, and often, though in vain, proposed it to him. He, seeing them obstinate in their resolution, told them that he accepted the crown offered to him; and in order that the act of his exaltation might be more solemn, he wished a very tall tree to be planted in the marketplace, and a scaffold to be made upon it, from which he could be seen by all. Everything was done as he required, and, gathering the Mexicans around the tree, he climbed upon the scaffold with a nosegay of flowers in his hand; and from that height, in view of an immense throng of people, he spoke to his own thus: “You know well, brave Mexicans, that the Chalcas wish to crown me king; but may it not please our god that I should betray our country: rather I wish to teach you by my example to prize the fidelity owed to it more than life itself.” And having said this he hurled himself from the scaffold. An act truly barbarous, but quite in conformity with the ideas that the ancients had of magnanimity, and so much the less blameworthy than that of Cato and of others celebrated by antiquity as the motive was nobler and the spirit of the Mexican greater. This resolution so inflamed the anger of the Chalcas that they at once fell upon the other Mexicans and killed them with lance thrusts. The following night they chanced to hear the melancholy cry of an owl, and, as men given to superstition, they took it for a bad omen of their imminent ruin. Nor were they mistaken in their presentiment of their misfortune; for Moctezuma, gravely angered by their rebellion and by their enormous outrages, immediately proclaimed the

Huexotzinco and in Atlixco. The city of Chalco was sacked. To the fury of vengeance there succeeded in Moctezuma, as is wont in noble hearts, compassion for the afflicted. He published a general pardon for all the fugitives, and especially in favor of the old men, the women, and the children, inviting them to return without fear to their homeland; and, not content with this, he sent his troops to scour the mountains to gather up those unfortunate people who, fleeing from men, had sought refuge among the beasts. Thus many returned, who were distributed in Amaquemecan, in Tlalmanalco, and in other places; but some, either from distrust of the pardon or from despair, abandoned themselves to death in the mountains. A part of the countryside of Chalco was divided by Moctezuma among the captains who had distinguished themselves most in the war.

After this expedition the Mexicans conquered Tamazollan,

Piaztlan, Xilotepec, Acatlan, and other places. By these rapid conquests Moctezuma so enlarged his dominions that to the east they extended as far as the Gulf of Mexico, to the southeast as far as the center of the great country of the Mixtecs, to the south as far as

Chilapan, and beyond, to the west as far as the Valley of Toluca, to the northwest as far as the center of the country of the Otomis, and to the north as far as the end of the Valley of Mexico.

But in attending to war, this famous king did not neglect what pertained to political government and to religion. He published new laws, increased the splendor of his court, and introduced there a certain ceremonial unknown to his predecessors. He built a great temple to the god of war, instituted [p. 241] many rites, and increased the number of the priests. The interpreter

Bk. IV. of the Mendoza collection adds that Moctezuma was sober, and singularly severe in punishing drunkenness, and that by his justice, his prudence, and the goodness of his manners he made himself feared and respected by his subjects. Finally, after a glorious reign of twenty-eight years and some months, he died, lamented by all, in 1464. His funeral rites were celebrated with so much the greater pomp as the magnificence of the court and the power of the nation were already greater.

Before dying he convoked the chief nobility of the court, and

§ 14. made them a speech to exhort them to concord, and to beg the elec‐ Axayacatl, sixth king of Mexico. tors to elect after his days Axayacatl, whom he judged the man most fit to promote the glory of the Mexicans. The electors, whether out of deference to the opinion of a king so deserving of the nation, or because they themselves knew the merit of Axayacatl, elected him, preferring him to Tizoc, his elder brother. Axayacatl was the son of Tezozomoc, who had been brother of the three kings who preceded Moctezuma and, like them, son of King Acamapichtli.

After the festivals of the election the new king went out to war to procure, following the example of his predecessor, victims to be sacrificed at his coronation. He made his expedition against the province of Tehuantepec, situated on the coast of the Pacific Ocean, about four hundred miles southeast of Mexico. The people of Tehuantepec had prepared themselves well, and allied themselves with their neighbors, to oppose the attempts of the Mexicans. In the furious battle that was fought there, Axayacatl, who commanded as General, pretended to flee in order to lead the enemy into an ambush. The people of Tehuantepec were pursuing the Mexicans, already singing the victory, when suddenly they found themselves attacked in the rear by a part of the Mexican army that came out of the ambush, and in front by those who had been fleeing, who turned against them; so that, harried from both sides, they were utterly defeated

In 1469 died Totoquihuatzin, first king of Tacuba, who in the forty years and more that he held that little kingdom was constantly faithful to the kings of Mexico, and served them very well in almost all the wars that they undertook against the enemies of the state. His son Chimalpopoca succeeded him in the kingdom, very like him no less in courage than in fidelity.

§ 15.

Far more regrettable was the loss that the Mexicans suffered in Death and eulogy of 1470 in the death of the great king of Acolhuacan, Nezahualcoyotl. King Nezahualcoyotl.

This king was one of the most renowned heroes of ancient America.

His courage, which in his youth was rather rashness, however great it was, was yet among the less notable endowments of his soul. His fortitude and his constancy were truly admirable in those thirteen years in which he lived deprived of the crown and persecuted by the usurper. His rectitude in the administration of justice was inflexible. To make his nation more civilized, and to correct the disorders introduced into the kingdom in the time of the Tyrants, he published eighty laws, which were afterward compiled by his most illustrious [p. 243] descendant Don Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl in his manuscript History of the Chichimec Lords. He established that no case, civil or Bk. IV. criminal, could be prolonged beyond eighty days, that is, four Mexican months. Every eighty days a great assembly was held in the royal palace, where all the judges and all the accused came together. The cases that had not been concluded in the preceding four months were infallibly concluded on that day, and the accused who were convicted of any crime immediately and irremissibly suffered the penalty proportioned to their crime in the presence of that numerous assembly. For different crimes he prescribed different penalties, and some he punished with the utmost rigor, especially adultery, sodomy, theft, homicide, drunkenness, and treason against the country. If we believe the Texcocan historians, he had four of his sons put to death for being guilty of incest with their stepmothers.

Yet his clemency toward the wretched was singular. In that kingdom it was forbidden, on pain of death, to take anything from another’s field; and this law was so rigorous that stealing seven ears of maize was enough to incur the penalty. Nezahualcoyotl, in order to provide in some way for needy travelers without detriment to the law, commanded that on both sides of the main roads maize and other seeds should be sown, of whose fruits the needy might make use. A great part of his revenues he spent for the poor, particularly the aged, the sick, and widows. To prevent the destruction of the forests he prescribed limits to the woodcutters, and forbade them to pass beyond them under heavy penalties. Wishing to know whether such an order was exactly observed, he went out one day in disguise with another prince, his brother, and betook himself to the foot of the neighboring mountains, where the limits prescribed by him lay. There he found a boy occupied in gathering shavings that had been left from the wood cut, and asked him why he did not enter the forest to make firewood. Because the king, answered the boy, has forbidden us to cross these limits, and if

He had a great zeal for the faithful administration of justice, and so that no one, under the pretext of necessity, might let himself be corrupted by any of the litigating parties, he established that all his ministers and judges should be furnished from the royal treasury with sustenance, clothing, and everything needful according to the rank and quality of the person. So great was what he spent annually on his family and house, on the sustenance of the ministers and magistrates, and on the relief of the poor, that it would be altogether incredible, nor should I have the courage to write it, if it were not established for us by the original paintings seen and examined by the first apostolic friars who were engaged in the conversion of those peoples, and confirmed by the testimony of a great-grandson of that same king, who, converted to the faith of Christ, received in baptism the name of Don Antonio Pimentel. The progress made by this celebrated king in the arts and in the sciences was as great as can be made by a great mind that has neither books in which to study nor masters from whom to learn. He was skilled in the poetry of those nations, and made various compositions that were universally applauded. In the sixteenth century the sixty hymns composed by him in praise of the Creator of Heaven were famous even among the Spaniards. Two of his odes or songs, rendered into Spanish verse by his descendant Don Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, have been preserved down to our own times. (h) One of them was composed by him some time after the ruin of Azcapotzalco. Its subject, not unlike that of the other of which we have already made mention, is to lament the instability of human greatness in the person of the Tyrant Tezozomoc, who, like a great and thick tree, had spread his roots through so many countries and extended his green branches so far as to shade all the lands of the empire; but at last, worm-eaten and spoiled, fell to the ground without any hope of recovering his former greenness.

(g) The fourteen cities charged with the provision of the first half of the year were Texcoco, Huexotla, Coatlichan, Atenco, Chiauhtla, Tezoyocan, Papalotla, Tepetlaoztoc, Acolman, Tepechpan, Xaltocan, Chimalhuacan, Iztapalocan, and Coatepec. The other fifteen were Otompan, Aztaquemecan, Teotihuacan, Cempoallan, Axapochco, Tlalanapan, Tepepolco, Tizayocan, Ahuatepec, Oztoticpac, Cuauhtlatzinco, Cojoac, Oztotlatlauhcan, Achichillacachocan, and Tetliztacac.

(h) The Chevalier Boturini had these two odes of Nezahualcoyotl among his precious antiquities. I wish I had them too, so that I might publish them in this History.

But in nothing did Nezahualcoyotl delight so much as in the study of Bk. IV.

> (3) Tutti i sopraddetti aneddoti sono Mati prefi da’ preziosi manuscricri di Don Ferdinando d' Alba. Egli come quarta nipote di quel Re , potè ricever a bocca molti riscontri da' suoi Padri, ed Avi,

nature. He also acquired several astronomical notions by the frequent observation that he made of the course of the stars. He applied himself likewise to knowing the plants and the animals, and because he could not keep in his court those that were proper to a different clime, he had all the vegetables and animals of the land of Anahuac painted from life in his palaces; of which paintings the celebrated Dr.

Hernández bears witness, who saw them and made use of them in part. Paintings truly far more useful and more worthy of a royal palace than those that represent the wicked mythology of the

Greeks. He curiously investigated the causes of the effects that he admired in nature, and this continual observation made him recognize the folly of idolatry. To his sons he said privately that, in outwardly adoring the idols to conform with the people, they should detest in their minds that worship, worthy of scorn, because it was directed to insensible creatures; that he acknowledged no other God than the

Creator of Heaven, and that he did not forbid idolatry in his kingdom, as he would wish, so as not to be blamed for wanting to contradict the doctrine of his ancestors. He prohibited sacrifices of human victims; but, perceiving afterward how difficult it is to turn a nation away from its ancient ideas in matters of religion, he returned to permitting them, but commanding under heavy penalties that no others should ever be sacrificed than prisoners of war. He built in honor of the Creator of Heaven a lofty tower of nine stories. The last story was dark, with a small vault painted on the inside with blue and adorned with gold moldings. There always resided in this tower men charged with sounding, at certain hours of the day, plates of very fine metal, at the sound of which the king knelt to make his prayer to the Creator of Heaven, and in honor of that God he made at a certain time of the year a fast. Bk. IV. his people, so illustrated his court that in the future it was considered the homeland of the arts and the center of civilization. Texcoco was the city where the Mexican language was spoken with the greatest polish and perfection, where the best artisans were found, and where poets, orators, and historians were most abundant. (k) Hence the Mexicans and other peoples took many laws: wherefore it might be said that Texcoco had been the Athens, and Nezahualcoyotl the Solon, of Anahuac.

In his last illness, having had all his sons come into his presence, he declared as his heir and successor in the kingdom of Acolhuacan Nezahualpilli, who, although he was the youngest of all, was nevertheless preferred to the others, both for having been born of Queen Matlalcihuatzin and for his well-known rectitude and his singular talent. He charged his eldest son Acapipioltzin to aid the new king with his counsel until he should learn the difficult art of governing. To Nezahualpilli he warmly recommended love of his brothers, care of his subjects, and zeal for justice. Finally, to prevent any disorder that the news of his death might cause, he commanded that it be concealed from the people, as far as possible, until Nezahualpilli should be secure in the peaceful possession of the crown. The princes received with tears the last counsels of their father, and, coming out into the audience hall, where the nobility awaited them, Nezahualpilli was acclaimed king of Acolhuacan, Acapipioltzin declaring that this was the will of their father, who, having a long journey to make, wished first to name his successor. All gave obedience to the new king, and the next morning Nezahualcoyotl died, in the forty-fourth year of his reign and about the eightieth of his age. His sons kept his death secret, and hid

Nevertheless the common people remained persuaded that that great king had been transported to the company of the gods as a reward for his virtues.

§ 16.    Not long after the exaltation of Nezahualpilli there occurred the

Conquest of Tlatelolco, and death memorable war of the Mexicans with their neighbors and rivals the of King Moquihuix.

Tlatelolcas. The king of Tlatelolco, Moquihuix, unable to bear the glory of the Mexican, used every means to obscure it. He was married, as we have already said, to a sister of King Axayacatl, given to him by Moctezuma as a reward for the famous victory won over the people of Cotaxtla. On this unfortunate lady he often vented his rage against his brother-in-law, and, not content with this, he secretly sought to ally himself with other states that bore the yoke of the

Mexicans unwillingly. These were the people of Chalco, of Xilotepec, of Toltitlan, of Tenayuca, of Mexicaltzinco, of Huitzilopochco, of

Xochimilco, of Cuitlahuac, and of Mixquic, who agreed to attack the

Mexicans in the rear after the Tlatelolcas had begun the battle. The people of Cuauhpanco, moreover, the Huexotzincas, and the

Matlatzincas, whose help he had also implored, were to incorporate their troops with those of the Tlatelolcas for the defense of the city.

The queen learned of these negotiations, and, now from the hatred that she bore her husband, now from love of her brother and her country, she warned Axayacatl of everything, that he might avoid so serious a blow, which would have made his throne totter.

Moquihuix, assured of the help of the confederates, convoked the nobles of his court to encourage them to the undertaking. An old and authoritative priest, called Poyahuitl, raised his voice in the assembly, and in the name of all offered to fight courageously against the enemies of the country: then [p. 249] to encourage them still further, he washed the altar of the sacrifices

Indi a pochi giorni avvisò i Confederati , acciocché foflero ben dilposti a soccorergli , tosto che cominciafle l'artacco . Il giorno seguente queste ambasciate fece Moquibuix la ceremonia d' armar le sue truppe, ed indi portolsli al tempio di Huirtzilopochtli per implorar l' ajuto di lui , dove - tornarono a prender quella abominabile bevanda , che diede a loro Pojahuitl nel primo congresso, e tutti i Soldati pafsarono ad uno ad uno dinanzi all'Idolo, facendogli una profonda riverenza. Appena terminata questa ceremonia entrò nella piazza del Mercato una compagnia d' arditi Messicani , uccidendo tutti quanti incontravano; ma sopravvenendo subito le truppe Tlatelolche, gli scacciarono, e fecero alcuni prigionieri , i quali fsurono lenza indugio sacrificati in un tempio appellato T!lillan. Quello steflo giorno sul tramontar del Sole ebbero algune donne Tlatelolche I’ ardire d' inonolcrarsi nelle strade di

Bk. IV. and gave that water, tinged with human blood, to the king and to all the captains to drink; with it, they said, they felt their courage grow, and I do not doubt that it had grown the better to practice cruelty. Meanwhile the queen, impatient of the ill treatment she suffered and frightened by the perils of the war, left her husband and betook herself to Mexico with four children, to put herself under the shelter of her brother. This she could do easily because of the very short distance between the two cities. Such a novelty so increased the mutual ill feeling of the Mexicans and the Tlatelolcas that wherever they met they insulted one another with words, came to blows, and killed one another.

As the time for making war was now drawing near, Moquihuix, together with his captains and many of the confederates, held a solemn sacrifice on the mountain least distant from the city, in order to obtain the protection of their gods; and there the day was fixed on which war was to be declared on the Mexicans. A few days later he gave notice to the confederates, so that they might be well prepared to come to his aid as soon as the attack began. Xiloman, lord of Colhuacan, wished first to assail the Mexicans and then, feigning flight, to provoke them to pursue him, so that the Tlatelolcas might attack them from behind. The day after these embassies Moquihuix performed the ceremony of arming his troops, and then betook himself to the temple of Huitzilopochtli to implore his help; there they returned to drink that abominable draught which Poyahuitl had given them at the first assembly, and all the soldiers passed one by one before the idol, making it a deep reverence. No sooner was this ceremony over than a company of bold Mexicans entered the market square, killing everyone they met; but the Tlatelolca troops, coming up at once, drove them out and took some prisoners, who were sacrificed without delay in a temple called Tlillan. That same day, at sunset, some Tlatelolca women had the boldness to advance into the streets of

That same night the Tlatelolcas took up arms, and in the morning, at first light, they began the attack on Mexico. They were in the hottest of the fray when Xiloman arrived with his Colhuas; but seeing that the king of Tlatelolco had begun to fight without waiting for him, and without heeding his counsel, he withdrew in indignation, and, wishing to do the Mexicans some harm, had certain canals closed to prevent any relief that might reach them by water; but they were soon reopened by order of Axayacatl. All that day they fought with indescribable ardor on both sides, until night forced the

Tlatelolcas to withdraw. The Mexicans burned the houses of the city that were nearest to Tlatelolco, perhaps because they hampered them in the fighting; but in setting the fire twenty of them were taken prisoner by the enemy and immediately sacrificed.

Axayacatl that night distributed his army in all the streets that led to Tlatelolco, and at daybreak they began to march from every side toward the market square, which was to be the point of their union.

The Tlatelolcas, seeing themselves attacked on every side, were falling back toward that great square, to unite all their forces there and be able to resist still better; but on arriving at that place they found themselves more hampered by their own multitude. The shouts with which King Moquihuix tried from the top of the great temple to encourage his men were of no avail. The Tlatelolcas were wounded and killed, and those who fell vented their rage against the king with insults: “Come down from there,” they said to him, “and take up arms, you coward; for it is not the part of brave men to stand calmly watching those who fight and lose their lives in defense of their homeland.”

Meanwhile the Mexicans advanced as far as the stairway of the temple and, climbing it, reached the upper court, from which Moquihuix encouraged his people and defended himself like a desperate man; but a Mexican captain named Quetzalhua threw him down the stairs with a shove, (l) and some soldiers, taking the corpse on their arms, presented it to Axayacatl, who, opening its chest, tore out the heart. A horrible act, but performed without horror, being too common in their sacrifices.

Thus ended the brave Moquihuix, and with him the little monarchy of the Tlatelolcas, governed by four kings in the space of about a hundred and eighteen years. The Tlatelolcas, seeing their king dead, at once fell into disorder and tried to save their lives by flight, passing through the midst of their enemies; but four hundred and sixty were left dead in that square, and among them some officers of note. After this conquest the city of Tlatelolco was perfectly united to that of Mexico, and was no longer considered a distinct city, but as a part, or rather a suburb, of that court, as it is at present. The king of Mexico always kept a governor there, and the Tlatelolcas, besides the tribute of maize, clothing, arms, and armor that they paid annually to the crown, were obliged to rebuild the temple of Huitznahuac whenever it should be needed.

(l) The Interpreter of the Mendoza Collection says that Moquihuix, having lost the battle, fled to the top of the temple and then threw himself down, because he could not bear the insults of a priest; but the account of the other historians seems to us more in keeping with the character of that king. [p. 252] the historians say that, having arrived to the relief of the Tlatelolcas

Bk. IV. when Moquihuix was already dead and the war ended, they went back without doing anything. As soon as Axayacatl saw himself victorious, he condemned to the extreme penalty Poyahuitl and Ehecatzitzimitl, both Tlatelolcas, for having been the ones who had most warmly stirred up their fellow citizens against the Mexicans, and shortly afterward he put to death the lords of Xochimilco, Cuitlahuac,

Colhuacan, Huitzilopochco, and others, for having confederated with his enemies.

§ 17.     To avenge himself next on the Matlatzincas, a numerous and powNew conquests, and erful nation settled in the Valley of Toluca and not yet subject to the death of Axayacatl.

Mexicans, he declared war on them, and setting out from Mexico together with the two allied kings, he took in passing the places of

Atlapolco and Xalatlauhco, and then in the same valley conquered

Toluca, Tetenanco, Metepec, Tzinacantepec, Calimaya, and other places in the southern part of the valley, the nation remaining from then on tributary to the crown of Mexico. After some time he returned to the same province to conquer also the northern part of the valley, today called the Valley of Ixtlahuaca, and chiefly Xiquipilco, a city and considerable state of the Otomis, whose lord, named

Tlilcuezpalin, was famous for his bravery. Axayacatl, who still boasted of his courage, wished to fight a duel with him in the battle that he offered to the people of Xiquipilco; but the outcome was disastrous to Axayacatl himself; for he received a severe wound in the thigh, and two Otomi captains, coming upon him, threw him to the ground with several blows and would have taken him prisoner, had not certain young Mexicans, seeing their king in such grave danger, courageously saved his liberty and his life. In spite of such a misfortune, the

Mexicans gained a complete victory, and took, according to their historians, eleven thousand and sixty prisoners, among them

Tlilcuezpalin himself and those two captains who had assailed the king. By this glorious victory Axayacatl added to the crown

Xiquipilco, Xocotitlan, Atlacomulco, and all the other places of that pleasant valley that he still lacked.

Indi rivolgendofi verso Levante s' impadronì d' Ocuilla, e di Malacatepec, La morte sopravvenutagli nel decimoterzo anno del suo regno, che su il 1477, dell’ era volgare, interruppe il corso delle sue vittorie. Fu assai guerriere , e severo nel nunire i trasgreflori delle leggi dal suo Antecesflore pubblicate . Lascid da parecchie mogli un' gran numero di figliuoli, fra i quali il celebre Motezuma II.,di cui fra poco ragioneremo.

Bk. IV. one of his legs for the rest of his life, he gave a great banquet to the allied kings and to the Mexican grandees, at which he put to death Tlilcuezpalin and the two aforesaid Otomi captains. The carrying out of a punishment amid the delights of a banquet did not seem inopportune to those men; for, accustomed to shed human blood, they had changed their natural horror into recreation. So great is the force of custom, and so easy is it for our minds to make the most horrible objects familiar to themselves!

(m) Non sappiamo , dove fosse la sua prima spedizione, dì Mec. per procurarsi delle vittime neceffarie per la sua incoronazio- fico, ne, IL fuo regno fu breve, ed ofcaro. Nondimeno nella dipintura decima della raccolta di Mendoza fi rappresentano quattordici Città da lui sortomesfe, fra lequali vi sono Toluca ,e Tecaxic, che per eslerlì ribellate alla Corona , bisognò riconquista.

In the last years of his reign, finding the limits of the empire too narrow on the west side, he went out again on campaign through the Valley of Toluca and, passing beyond the mountains, conquered Tochpan and Tlaximaloyan, this place being from then on the frontier of the kingdom of Michoacán. Then, turning toward the east, he took possession of Ocuillan and Malacatepec. Death, which came upon him in the thirteenth year of his reign, which was 1477 of the common era, interrupted the course of his victories. He was very warlike, and severe in punishing those who transgressed the laws published by his predecessor. He left by several wives a great number of sons, among whom was the famous Moctezuma II, of whom we shall shortly speak.

§ 19.

In the time of this king there occurred the war between the War between the Texcocans and the Huexotzincas. That war had its origin in the ambiTexcocans and the

Huexotzincas. tion of the princes, brothers of King Nezahualpilli, who, though they showed themselves content at the beginning with the exaltation of their younger brother, the memory of their dead father having afterward cooled, and no longer able to bear seeing themselves subject to one whom they believed they ought to command by right of age, plotted a secret conspiracy against him. For the execution of their perverse designs they first invited the Chalcas, who were the readiest for such misdeeds; but having failed in all the means they had employed, they solicited for the same end the Huexotzincas.

Nezahualpilli, informed of such a conspiracy, equipped without delay a good army and marched to go against the Huexotzincas. The general of that state had ascertained all the marks of King Nezahualpilli, in order to direct all his blows against him, and had even promised rewards to anyone who should deliver him over to him alive or dead.

There was someone who made it known to the king; whereupon he, before entering the battle, exchanged his garments and insignia for those of one of his captains. This unfortunate officer, having been taken for the king himself, was at once overwhelmed by the multitude and killed. While they were venting their rage upon him,

Nezahualpilli fell upon the Huexotzinca general and killed him, not without grave risk of being killed himself by the soldiers who came to the aid of their general. The Texcocans, who had made the same mistake as the Huexotzincas, not being aware of the change of garments, had begun to lose heart; but now, recognizing him, they rushed to his defense, and after having routed his enemies, they sacked the city of

Already at that time the king of Texcoco had several wives of very Marriage of King

Nezahualpilli, with noble houses; but none had been declared queen by him, since he was two Mexican ladies. reserving that honor for one whom he meant to take from the royal family of Mexico. He asked her of King Tizoc, and the latter gave him a niece of his, daughter of Tzotzocatzin. This marriage was celebrated in Texcoco with a great concourse of the nobility of the two courts. This lady had a sister endowed with singular beauty, who was called Xocotzin. They loved each other so much that, being unable to part, the new queen obtained from her father permission to take her sister with her to Texcoco. By frequent sight of her, and by conversing often with her, the king became so enamored of his fair sister-in-law that he resolved to marry her and to raise her also to the dignity of queen. This second marriage was, according to what the historians say, the most solemn and the most magnificent ever seen in that country. Not long afterward the king had by the first queen a son named Cacamatzin, who was his successor in the crown and, taken prisoner afterward by the Spaniards, died wretchedly. By the other he had Huexotzincatzin, (*) of whom we shall speak shortly, Coanacochtzin, who was also king of Acolhuacan and some time after the conquest by the Spaniards was hanged by the Conqueror Cortés, and Ixtlilxochitl, who allied himself with the Spaniards

§ 21. tories were plotting the death of the king of Mexico. Techotlalla, lord Tragic death of King

Tizoc. of Iztapalapan, either resentful over some displeasure received or impatient of Tizoc’s domination, conceived the wicked design of making an attempt on his life, and would reveal it to no one except to such as seemed to him capable of carrying it out. He and Maxtlaton, lord of Tlachco, agreed on the manner of executing so dangerous a crime. The historians do not agree on this point. Some say that they made use of certain witches, and that these by sorcery took his life; but this seems to me a popular fable. Others affirm that they found a way of giving him poison. However that may be, it is certain that their plot succeeded. Tizoc was killed in the fifth year of his reign, in

1482 of the common era. He was a circumspect man, grave and severe, like his predecessors and successors, in the punishment of offenders. Since in his time the power and opulence of that crown were already so great, he undertook to build for the tutelary god of the nation a temple that in size and magnificence should surpass all the temples of that country, and to this end he had prepared infinite materials and had even begun the building, when death came to upset his designs.

The Mexicans, well aware that the death of their king had not been natural, wished to avenge it before proceeding to a new election.

Their inquiries were so thorough that in a short time they discovered the authors of the attempt and put them to death in the great square

Mexico. and begun. It was resumed with the greatest activity, an incredible number of workmen taking part in it, and it was finished in four years. While work was going on at this undertaking, the king often went out to war, and all the enemies who were taken prisoner were reserved for the festival of the Dedication. The wars of these four years were against the Mazahuas, a few miles to the west, who had rebelled against the crown of Tacuba, against the Zapotecs, three hundred miles to the southeast, and against several other peoples. When the building was finished, the king invited to the festival of the Dedication the two allied kings and all the nobility of both kingdoms. The concourse was the largest ever seen in Mexico (n); for people came to be present at so celebrated a ceremony even from the most distant places. The festival lasted four days, during which all the prisoners taken in the four preceding years were sacrificed on the upper court of the temple. The historians do not agree concerning the number of the victims. Torquemada says that there were seventy-two thousand three hundred and forty-four. Others affirm that there were sixty-four thousand and sixty. To carry out such horrible sacrifices with greater display, they arranged the victims in two rows, each about a mile and a half long, which began in the streets of

Thus this king passed his reign in continual wars until 1496, in which year the war against Atlixco took place. The entry of the Mexican army into this valley was so sudden that the first notice the people of Atlixco had of it was that which they received through their eyes on seeing them enter. They took up arms at once for their defense; but not finding themselves with forces sufficient to resist for long, they asked help of the Huexotzincas, their neighbors. When the ambassadors of Atlixco arrived at Huexotzinco, a famous captain named Toltecatl, whose great courage was in no way inferior to the extraordinary strength of his arm, was playing ball. As soon as he learned the news of the Mexican army, he left the game to go to Atlixco with the auxiliary troops, and, entering the battle unarmed, to display his bravery and to show the contempt he felt for his enemies, he struck down with his fists the first Mexican who presented himself, and took his arms, with which he made great slaughter. The Mexicans, unable to overcome the resistance of their enemies, abandoned the field and returned to Mexico covered with ignominy. The Huexotzincas, to reward the singular prowess of Toltecatl, made him head of their republic. This had been subjected to the dominion of the Mexicans, whose arms they had provoked with their insults; but since the conquered do not bear the yoke of the conqueror except when they cannot shake it off, every time the Huexotzincas found themselves with forces sufficient to resist, they rebelled, and the same happened with the greater part of the provinces subjected by force of arms to the crown of Mexico; whence it was necessary that the Mexican army should be in continual motion to reconquer what the king was losing. Toltecatl accepted the office conferred on him; but

Kk2 [p. 260] scarcely had a year passed when he was obliged to give up his office

Bk. IV. and his country. The priests and other ministers of the temples, abusing their authority, entered the houses of private persons and carried off the maize and the turkeys that were there, and committed other excesses unbecoming to their dignity. Toltecatl wished to put a stop to it; but the priests took up arms. The people partly sided with them, and partly opposed their violence, and between these two factions a war broke out, which, like all other civil wars, caused very grave evils. Toltecatl, weary of ruling so unruly a people, or fearing to perish in the tempest, withdrew from the city with other nobles and, crossing the mountains, betook himself to Tlalmanalco. The governor of this city gave prompt notice of it to the king of Mexico, and he at once put to death all those fugitives in punishment of their rebellion, and had their bodies carried to Huexotzinco to frighten the rebels.

§ 25.     In 1498 it seemed to the king of Mexico that for lack of water the New inundation of

Mexico.  navigation  of the lake had become difficult, and he wished to increase that water with the other from the spring of Huitzilopochco, which the people of Coyoacán used, and he summoned Tzotzomatzin, lord of Coyoacán, to give him his orders. Tzotzomatzin represented to him that that spring was not perennial: that at times the water failed, and at times came in such abundance that it might cause some damage to the court. Ahuitzotl, thinking that Tzotzomatzin’s reasons were mere pretexts to excuse himself from doing what had been commanded him, insisted on his first order; and seeing that man persist in the difficulty he had put forward, he dismissed him in anger, and afterward had him put to death. This is usually the reward of good counsels, when princes obstinate in some caprice will not listen to the sincere remonstrances of their faithful subjects. Ahuitzotl, unwilling by any means to abandon his project, had a great and ample aqueduct

With such solemnity the water arrived at Mexico; but it was not long before the general joy was changed into weeping; for the rains of that year having been extraordinarily abundant, the water of the lake rose so much that it flooded the city, all the streets were full of boats, and some houses collapsed. One day, the king being in a lower room of his palace, the water entered it so suddenly and in such quantity that, hastening in his fear to go out by the door, which was low, he gave himself such a violent blow on the head that after some time it caused his death. Afflicted by the evils of the inundation and by the clamors of the people, he called to his aid the king of Acolhuacan, who without delay had the dike repaired that, on the counsel of his father Nezahualcoyotl, had been built in the reign of Moctezuma.

Scarcely were the Mexicans freed from the evil of the inundation when in the following year they had to suffer that of the scarcity of grain, the maize having been spoiled by the excessive abundance of water; but in this same year they had the good fortune to discover in the valley of Mexico a quarry of tetzontli, which has been so useful for the buildings of that great city. The king at once began to use this kind of stone in the temples, and in imitation of him private persons in their houses. Besides this the king had all

He spent the last two years of his life in frequent wars, such as

§ 26. those      of Izquixochitlan, Amatlan, Tlacuilollan, Xaltepec, New conquests, and

death of King  Tehuantepec,     and Huexotla in the Huaxteca. Tliltototl, a Mexican

Ahuitzotl. general, the war of Izquixochitlan being over, carried his victorious arms as far as Cuauhtemallan, or Guatemala, more than nine hundred miles southeast of the court, in which expedition he performed, according to what the historians say, prodigies of courage; but no one relates the particular deeds of so renowned a general, nor do we know whether all that great tract of land remained subject to the crown of

Mexico.

Finally, in the year 1502, after about twenty years of reign,

Ahuitzotl died of an illness caused by the blow to the head already mentioned. He was a very warlike man, and one of the kings who most enlarged the dominions of the crown. When he died, the

Mexicans possessed almost all that they had at the arrival of the

Spaniards. Besides courage he had two other royal virtues that made him famous among his countrymen, namely magnificence and liberality. He so embellished Mexico with new and magnificent buildings that it had already become the finest city of the New World. When he received the tributes of the provinces, he would assemble the people in a certain place in the city and distribute provisions and clothing personally to the needy. He rewarded his captains and soldiers who distinguished themselves in war, and the ministers and officials of the crown who served him faithfully, with gold, silver, gems, and beautiful feathers. These virtues were obscured by some vices; for he was capricious, vindictive, and sometimes cruel, and so given to war that he seemed to hate peace; whence the name of Ahuitzotl is used proverbially even among the Spaniards of that kingdom to signify a man who with his molestations and vexations does not let another live. IV. night was this entertainment lacking in the palace; which must have been prejudicial to the public good, since it robbed him of a great part of the time and care that he ought to have given to the affairs of the kingdom. Nor did women occupy his mind any less. His predecessors had had many wives, thinking that their authority and greatness appeared the greater the greater the number of persons devoted to their pleasures. Ahuitzotl, having so greatly enlarged the dominions and increased the power of the crown, wished to show the superiority of his greatness over that of his predecessors in the excessive number of his wives. Such was the state of the court of Mexico at the beginning of the sixteenth century, of that century so fertile in great events, in which that kingdom was to change its face and the whole New World was to be turned upside down.

ceeded to the election of the new sovereign. No brother of the preceding kings was still living; so that, according to the law of the kingdom, one of his nephews, sons of his predecessors, had to succeed the dead king. These were many; for of the sons of Axayacatl there were living Moctezuma, (a) Cuitláhuac, Matlatzincatl,

Era uomo raciturno , e molto considerato non meno nelle sue azioni , che nelle sue parole, ed ogni volta che parlava nel Real Configlio , del qual'era membro , fi faceva sentir con rispetto. Diedesi parte dell' elezione a' Re alleati, e costoro fi portarono inconcanente a quella Corte A fare i lor complimenti. Motezuma di ciò consapevole fi ritirò al tempio , come per proteltarsi indegno di tant’ onore . Andò colì la Nobiltà per avvisarlo della sua elezione, e trovollo, per quel che dicono gli Storici, spazzando il pavimento del tempio , Fu condotto con grand’ accompagnamento a palagio , dove gli Elettori gl’ intimarono solennemente la elezione fatta della persona di lui per occupare il trono di Messico. Indi ritornò al tempio per far le solite ceremonie ; è terminate che furono', ricevette nel trono l’ubbidienza della Nobili, ed ascoltò l'aringhe gratulatorie degli Oratori, La prima fu quella di Nezabualpilli Re d' Acolhuacan , la quale presen. tiamo qu) a' Leggivori tale , quale ce la conservarono i Mes. sicani .

(*) Besides the bravery that he had shown in several battles, in the exercise of the office of general, he was also a priest, and for his gravity Bk. V. and circumspection, and for his religion, he was much revered. He was a taciturn man and very considerate no less in his actions than in his words, and every time he spoke in the royal council, of which he was a member, he made himself heard with respect. Notice of the election was given to the allied kings, and they betook themselves at once to that court to pay their compliments. Moctezuma, aware of this, withdrew to the temple, as if to protest himself unworthy of so great an honor. The nobility went there to inform him of his election, and found him, according to what the historians say, sweeping the pavement of the temple. He was conducted with a great retinue to the palace, where the electors solemnly announced to him the election that had been made of his person to occupy the throne of Mexico. He then returned to the temple to perform the customary ceremonies; and when they were over, he received on the throne the obedience of the nobility and listened to the congratulatory speeches of the orators. The first was that of Nezahualpilli, king of Acolhuacan, which we present here to the readers just as the Mexicans have preserved it for us.

They have indeed reason to celebrate it; for the kingdom of Mexico has attained such an extent that to bear so great a weight neither a lesser fortitude than that of your invincible heart would suffice, nor a lesser wisdom than that which we admire in you. I see clearly how great is the love that Almighty God bears this nation; for He has enlightened it, so that it might know how to choose what

Rejoice, then, O blessed land, that a prince has fallen to your lot who will be your support, and by his mercy will be a father and a brother to his subjects. You have in fact a king who will not take occasion of his superiority to give himself to softness and to lie stretched on his bed, abandoned to pastimes and delights; rather, in the sweetest repose the care he will have of you will disquiet his heart and rouse him, nor will he find relish in the most delicate food, for his anxiety for your welfare. And you, most noble prince and powerful lord, take courage, and trust that the Creator of Heaven, who has raised you to so eminent a dignity, will give you strength to fulfill the obligations attached to it. He who has been so liberal toward you until now will not deny you his precious gifts, having himself raised you to the throne, in which I wish you many and very happy years.”

He thought next of making war to procure the victims that were to be sacrificed at his coronation. This misfortune fell upon the people of Atlixco, who a little before had rebelled against the crown. The king therefore went out from the court with the flower of the nobility, among whom went also his brothers and cousins. In this war the Mexicans lost some brave officers; but nevertheless they put the rebels back under their former yoke, and Moctezuma returned victorious, bringing with him the unfortunate prisoners he needed for his coronation. This ceremony was celebrated with such a display of games, dances, theatrical performances, and illuminations, and with such abundance and richness of tributes sent from the provinces of the kingdom, that even foreigners never before seen in Mexico came to see it, and the very enemies of the Mexicans, such as the Tlaxcalans and the Michoacans, disguised themselves in order to be present as spectators; but Moctezuma, having learned of it, with royal generosity had them lodged and entertained, and also had some terraces fitted up from which they could observe that great ceremony at their ease.

Matrone, che vegliavano sulla loro coni dotta ; poichè erano troppo geloli que’ Re, e qualunque disordinez che vi fosse in palagio, quantunque leggiero, il punivano con. rigore . Di queste donne prendeva il Re per se stesso quelle, che gli piacevano, (c) e l'altre servivano per ricompensare i servizj de' suoi Vailalli . Tutti i Feudatarj della Corona doveano risedere alcuni mesi dell’ anno-nella Corte, e nel ritornar a' loro stati ,. vi lasciavano i loro figliuoli, ovvero i loro fratelli , come ottaggi richiesti dal Re per af ficurarsi della loro fedeltà: onde lor bisognava aver casa ia Melslico . Ll2 [p. 268] of a different mind, and disapproved the conduct of his predecessors, Bk. V. on the pretext that the commoners served according to their station,

> (ce), Alcuui Storici affermano, che Motezuma ebbe infieme gravide ceneinquanca delle sue mogli; ma questo È affatto incredibile,

and that in all their actions they displayed the baseness of their birth and of their upbringing. Prompted by this maxim, he stripped the commoners of all the offices they held, both in his royal household and at court, declaring them incapable of obtaining any in the future.

A prudent old man who had been his tutor represented to him that such a resolution might estrange the minds of the common people from his person; but nothing sufficed to turn him from the course he had resolved upon.

The whole service of his royal palace was performed by persons of rank. Besides those who always lived there, who were very many, six hundred feudatory lords and nobles entered every morning to pay him court. These spent the whole day in the antechambers, where servants were not allowed to enter, talking in low voices and awaiting the orders of their sovereign. The servants who accompanied these lords were so many that they filled the three courtyards of the palace, and many remained in the street. No smaller was the number of the women who lived there, ladies, maidservants, and slaves. All this numerous flock lived shut up within a kind of seraglio, under the care of some noble matrons, who watched over their conduct; for those kings were exceedingly jealous, and punished with rigor any disorder in the palace, however slight. From these women the king took for himself those who pleased him, (c) and the others served to reward the services of his vassals. All the feudatories of the crown had to reside some months of the year at court, and on returning to their states they left there their sons or their brothers, as hostages required by the king to assure himself of their fidelity; hence they had to keep a house in Mexico.

> Effetto ancora del dispotismo di Motezuma fu il cere.==== moniale, che introdufle nella Corte . Nefluno poteva entrar Lu, V. in palazzo, o per servire al Re, o per trattar con lui qualche affare , senza \calzar@ prima nella porta. A niuno era permesso di comparire innanzi al Re in abito superbo; perchè fi stimava mancanza di rispetto alla Maeltà: ficchè i più gran Signori ( eccetto gli stretti consanguinei del Re ) fi spogliavano della veste ricca, che portavano , o almeno la coprivano con altra ordinaria ,, per mostrare la loro umiltà, Tutti nell’ entrare nella Sala d' udienza, e prima di parlare al Re, facevano tre inchini, dicendo nel primo, Signore , nel’ secondo , Mio Signore, e nel terzo, Gran Signore « (d) Parlavano baffo, e col capo chino ,e riceveano la risposta, che il Re lor dava per mezzo de’ suoi segretarj, sì attentamente, e sì umilmente, come se fofle un oracolo. Nel licenziars, niuno voltava le spalle al trono -

Another effect of Moctezuma’s despotism was the ceremonial that he introduced at court. No one could enter the palace, whether to Bk. V. serve the king or to transact some business with him, without first taking off his shoes at the door. No one was permitted to appear before the king in splendid dress, because it was thought a want of respect toward Majesty; so that the greatest lords (except the king’s close kinsmen) stripped off the rich garment they wore, or at least covered it with another, plain one, to show their humility. All, on entering the audience hall, and before speaking to the king, made three bows, saying at the first, Lord, at the second, My Lord, and at the third, Great Lord. (d) They spoke low and with bowed heads, and received the answer that the king gave them through his secretaries as attentively and as humbly as if it had been an oracle. In taking leave, no one turned his back to the throne.

The same audience hall served him for his dinner: the table was a large cushion, and the chair a low stool. The tablecloths, napkins, and towels were of cotton, but very fine, white, and spotless. The dishes were of the fine majolica of Cholula; but none of these things served him more than once, for he immediately gave it to one of the nobles. The cups in which chocolate and the other drinks of cacao were prepared for him were of gold, or of handsome sea shell, or certain natural vessels curiously varnished, of which we shall speak elsewhere. He also had gold plates, but he did not use them except in the temple at certain festivals. The dishes were so many and so varied that the Spaniards who saw them were amazed. The conqueror Cortés says that they covered the floor of a great hall, and that there were presented to Moctezuma plates of every kind of game, fish, fruit, and herbs of that country. Three or four hundred young nobles in good order carried this dinner;
