nied by its own chafing dish. The king indicated with a little rod that he held in his hand the dishes he wanted, and all the rest he distributed among the nobles who were in the antechambers. Before sitting down, four of his wives, the most beautiful of his seraglio, offered him water to wash his hands; they remained standing there the whole time the dinner lasted, together with six of his principal ministers and the steward.

As soon as the king sat down to table, the steward closed the door of the hall, so that none of the other nobles should see him eat. The ministers kept at a distance and observed a deep silence, except when they had to reply to what the king said to them. The steward and the four women served him the dishes, besides two others who brought him the maize bread kneaded with eggs. Often he listened to music while dining, and amused himself with the jests of certain deformed men whom he kept for grandeur. He showed great pleasure in hearing them, and said that among their jests they were wont to tell him some important truth. When the dinner was over he took tobacco mixed with liquidambar in a pipe, or reed, handsomely varnished, and with that smoke he brought on sleep.

After sleeping a little, leaning on the same stool, he gave audience, in which he listened attentively to all that was proposed to him, encouraged those who from agitation could not speak, and answered all through his ministers or secretaries. After the audience there was music, for he took great delight in hearing sung the glorious deeds of his ancestors. At other times he amused himself by watching various games, of which we shall speak elsewhere. When he went out of the house he was carried on the shoulders of the nobles in an open litter under a rich canopy, with a numerous train of courtiers, and wherever he passed all stopped with eyes closed, as if they feared to be dazzled by the splendor [p. 271] of Majesty. When he dismounted from the litter to go on foot, carpets were spread so that he should not touch the ground with his Bk. V. feet.

Le sale e le camere di queste case erano tante , che , comes teltifica il suddetto Conquistatore, avrebbon poruto ia esla alloggiarsi due gran Principî con tutto il loro seguito. Questa celebre cala era situata nel luogo, dove oggidì è il Convento grande di S. Francesco.

of the palace of his ordinary residence was a vast building of stone and lime, palaces houses.

and royal which had twenty doors opening on the square and the streets, three great courtyards, and in one of them a handsome fountain, several halls, and more than a hundred rooms. Some of the chambers had their walls faced with marble and other precious stones. The beams were of cedar, cypress, and other excellent woods, well worked and carved. Among the halls there was one so large that, according to an eyewitness and a careful one (*), three thousand men could stand in it. Besides this palace he had others, within and outside the capital. In Mexico, besides the seraglio of his wives, there were dwellings for his councilors and ministers, and for all the officials of his household and of his court, and also for lodging foreign lords who happened to come there, and especially the two allied kings.

He had two houses in Mexico for animals: one for the birds other than birds of prey, and the other for the birds of prey, for the quadrupeds, and for the reptiles. In the first there were many rooms, and corridors supported on columns of marble, each of a single piece. These corridors looked upon a garden, where amid the foliage of a grove of trees ten ponds were laid out, some of fresh water for the aquatic river birds, and the others of brackish water for those of the sea. In the rest of the house there were all the other species of birds, which were so many and so different that the Spaniards who saw them were amazed, and could not persuade

themselves

(*) The Anonymous Conqueror, in his valuable account. He tells us further that, having entered that great palace four times, and having gone round it until he was worn out, he could not see all of it. [p. 272] themselves that any species was lacking of all that exist in the world. Bk. V.

To each was supplied the same food on which it fed in its time of liberty, now seeds, now fruits, now insects. For the birds alone that live on fish, ten Castilian weights of fish were consumed every day (as the conqueror Cortés bears witness in his letters to Charles V), that is, more than three hundred Roman pounds. Three hundred men, according to the same Conqueror, were employed solely in the care of these birds, besides their physicians, who observed their diseases and applied the suitable remedies. Of those three hundred some procured their food, others distributed it, others had charge of the eggs and of their hatching, and others, finally, plucked the birds at a certain season; for besides the pleasure that the king took in seeing so great a multitude of animals gathered together, he took chief care of the feathers, no less for the famous mosaic images, of which we shall speak in their place, than for the other works that were made of them. The halls and rooms of these houses were so many that, as the aforesaid Conqueror testifies, two great princes could have lodged in them with all their retinue. This celebrated house stood on the site where the great convent of San Francisco is today.

> 1 altra cala per le fiere destinata aveva un grande, e bel cortile lastricato a scacchi, ed era divisa.in molti appartamenti In uno d' essi v' erano tutti gli uccelli di rapina dall Aquila Reale infino all’ Acertello, e d' ogni spezie molti individui 2 Quetti uccelli erano compartiti secondo le loro spezie in molta stanze sotterranee, che aveano più di sette piedi di profon. dit, e più di diciafsette di lunghezza, € di larghezza . La merà d' ogni stanza era coperta di buone lastre, ed eranvi delle stanghe affissz al muro, acciocchè vi potessero dormire e difevderli dalla pioggia, L' altra metà era soltanto coperta da una pelosìa con altre stanghe, dove godeffsero del sole . Pel sostentamento di questi-uccelli fi ammazzavano ogni giorno iosino a cinquecento gallinaccj , Nella stessa casa v' erano pon [p. 273] safe basse con un gran numero di gabbie forti di legno, dove ==stavano rinchiusi i Leoni, le Tigri, i Lupi, i Cojorti , i Gatti Liu-Vfalvatici ; e tutte l’ altre spezie di ficre, le quali fi cibavano di Cervi, di Conigli, di Lepri, di Techichi , e d'altri animali , e degl' intestini degli uomini sacrificati .

The other house, intended for the wild beasts, had a large and handsome courtyard paved in checkerboard pattern, and was divided into many apartments. In one of them were all the birds of prey, from the royal eagle down to the kestrel, and of every species many individuals. These birds were distributed according to their species in many underground chambers, which were more than seven feet deep and more than seventeen long and wide. Half of each chamber was covered with good slabs, and there were perches fixed to the wall, so that they could sleep there and shelter from the rain. The other half was covered only by a lattice with other perches, where they might enjoy the sun. For the sustenance of these birds as many as five hundred turkeys were killed every day. In the same house there were many halls [p. 273] low halls with a great number of strong wooden cages, in which were shut up the lions, the tigers, the wolves, the coyotes, the wild cats, Bk. V. and all the other species of wild beasts, which were fed on deer, rabbits, hares, techichi, and other animals, and on the entrails of the men who were sacrificed.

> Nè solamente manteneva il Re di Messico tutte quelle spezie d' animali, che altri Principî tengono per grandezza; ma eziandio quelli, che per la lor natura pajono esenti della schiavitù, come i Coccodrilli, e le Serpi , Le Serpi di parecchie spezie erano dentro a certe botti, o vali grandi; 1 coccodrilli in vivai circondati da muro . Vi erano parimente moltissimi vivai per i pesci, de' quali ne sussistono ancora due belli , da noi veduti nel palagio di Chapoltepec due miglia da Messico.

Nor did the king of Mexico keep only those species of animals that other princes keep for grandeur, but even those which by their nature seem exempt from servitude, such as crocodiles and serpents. The serpents of several species were kept in certain casks or large vessels, the crocodiles in ponds enclosed by a wall. There were likewise very many ponds for fish, of which two handsome ones still survive, seen by us in the palace of Chapultepec, two miles from Mexico.

> Non contento Motezuma di tener ne’ suoi palagi opni sorte d' animali, avea ancor ivi radunati tutti gli uomini irregolari, che o pel colore del pelo, o della pelle, o per qualche altra deformità nelle membra , erano divenuti fingolari nella loro spezie, Vanità in vero profittevole ; mentre assicurava il mantenimento a tanti miserabili, e gli liberava dagli insulti inumani degli alcci uomini, E va

Not content with keeping in his palaces every sort of animal, Moctezuma had also gathered there all the abnormal men who, whether by the color of their hair or of their skin or by some other deformity of the limbs, had become singular in their kind. A truly profitable vanity, since it secured the maintenance of so many wretched persons and freed them from the inhuman insults of other men.

Un di questi boschi era in una isoletta del lago, conosciuta presentemente dagli Spagnuoli coli nome di Peton .

In all his palaces he had most beautiful gardens, in which there was every kind of precious flower, fragrant herb, and medicinal plant. He had also woods enclosed by walls and supplied with abundant game, where he was accustomed to amuse himself. One of these woods was on a little island of the lake, known at present to the Spaniards by the name of Peñón.

Of all the aforesaid palaces, gardens, and woods nothing remains but the wood of Chapultepec, which the Spanish viceroys have preserved for their recreation. All the others were wrecked by the conquerors. They demolished the most magnificent edifices of Mexican antiquity, now from an indiscreet zeal for religion, now from vengeance, now to make use of the materials. They abandoned the cultivation of the royal gardens, cut down the woods, and reduced that land to such a state that nowadays the magnificence of those kings could not be believed, if

Both the palaces and all the aforesaid pleasure places were kept extremely clean, even those where he never went; for there was nothing of which he boasted more than cleanliness in his person and in all his things. Every day he bathed, and therefore there were baths in all his palaces. Every day he changed four garments, and the one that he had

§ 4. The good and the once laid aside he did not use again, but destined it to be given as a gift bad in Moctezuma. to the nobles who served him and to the soldiers who bore themselves

well in war. Every morning he employed, according to some historians, more than a thousand men in sweeping and sprinkling the streets of the city.

In one of the royal houses there was a great armory, where he had every sort of arms, offensive and defensive, in use among those nations, and insignia and military ornaments. In the making of these implements he kept employed a surprising number of artisans; as also for other works he had very many goldsmiths, mosaic workers, marble workers, painters, and others. A whole street was devoted solely to dancers, intended for his amusement.

His zeal for religion was not inferior to his magnificence. He built several temples to his gods, and offered them frequent sacrifices, observing exactly the established rites and ceremonies. He took great care that all the temples, and especially the greatest one of Mexico, should be well served and exceedingly clean; but the vain fear of the auguries and of the supposed oracles of those wicked deities utterly cowed his spirit.

He was extremely zealous for the observance of his orders and of the laws of the kingdom, and was inexorable in punishing transgressors. He often tested, through a third person and with gifts, the rectitude of his magistrates, and if he ever found anyone guilty, he punished him without remission, even though he belonged to the most conspicuous nobility.

He was an implacable enemy of idleness, and to banish it [p. 275] as far as possible from his dominions, he sought to keep his subjects

V. constantly occupied: the soldiers in continual exercises of war, and the others either in the cultivation of the fields, or in the construction of new buildings, or in other public works; and even the beggars, that they should not be altogether idle, he required to contribute a certain quantity of those filthy insects that are the nurslings of squalor and the companions of misery.

> Questa oppressione, in ‘cui teneva i suoi vassalli , i so.

This oppression in which he held his vassals, the excessive burdens that he had laid upon them, his haughtiness and his pride, and his too great severity in punishing alienated their minds; but otherwise he won their love by liberality, both in providing for the needs of his peoples and in rewarding the services of his captains and ministers. Among the other things worthy of being celebrated with the highest praises, and of being imitated by all princes, he designated the city of Colhuacan as a hospital for all those invalids who, after having faithfully served the crown in military or political employments, needed, whether on account of their age or of their infirmities, to be cared for. There, at the expense of the royal treasury, their support and their cure were attended to. Such were the qualities, partly good and partly bad, of the celebrated Moctezuma, which it seemed to us fitting to set before the readers here, before relating the series of events that befell him.

At the beginning of his reign he put to death Malinalli, lord of Tlachquiauhco, for having rebelled against the crown of Mexico; he brought that state back under his obedience, and conquered that of Achiotlan. Soon afterward another war broke out, more serious and dangerous, in which he was not so fortunate.

Tlaxcalans wished to take possession of the maritime provinces of the

> Erank ricoverati nella verra di Thscalla moltislumi vasfalli della Gorona di Messico , massimamente de' Chalchesi, e degli Otomiti di Xaltocan, che fi salvarono dalla rovina delle loro patrie nelle guerre già accennate , Questi portavano un odio capitale a' Messicani a cagione de' mali. da loro ricevuti, e però parvero a' Tlascallesi gli uomini più idonei ad opporsi vigorosamente a" tentativi de' loro nemici: non s' ingannarono; perchè in fatti non trovarono in altri maggior resistenza i Messicani, che in que’ fuorusciti ,. spezialmente. negli Oromiri , di cui & componeva la puernigione delle frontiere, è quali servirono fedelmente alla Repubblica, e da efla furono rimuneraci con luminosi impieghi.

Gulf of Mexico, and that by their commerce with those provinces they increased their power and wealth every day, and were stirring up the minds of the peoples. The commerce of the Tlaxcalans, of which the Huexotzincas complained, was quite justified and necessary; for besides the fact that the people of those coasts were originally in great part from Tlaxcala, and the one and the other considered themselves kinsmen, the Tlaxcalans needed to provide themselves with the cacao, the cotton, and the salt that they lacked. Nevertheless the representations of the Huexotzincas and of the other rivals of Tlaxcala so moved the minds of the Mexicans that, beginning with

Moctezuma I, all the kings of Mexico treated the Tlaxcalans as the greatest enemies of their empire, and always kept strong garrisons on the frontiers of Tlaxcala, to prevent those people from trading with the maritime provinces.

The Tlaxcalans, finding themselves deprived of freedom in trade, and consequently of the acquisition of things necessary to life, resolved to send an embassy to the Mexican nobility (probably in the time of King Axayacatl), complaining of the wrong done them through the sinister reports of their rivals. The Mexicans, insolent from their prosperity, replied that the king of Mexico was universal lord of the world, and that all mortals were his vassals, and as such the Tlaxcalans ought to give him obedience and acknowledge him with tribute, after the example of the other nations; but if they refused to submit, they would perish without fail, their cities would be utterly ruined, and their country would be inhabited by other peoples. To so arrogant and so foolish a reply the ambassadors answered with these courageous words: “Most powerful lords, Tlaxcala owes you no homage; nor, since their ancestors came out of the northern countries to dwell in this land, have the Tlaxcalans ever acknowledged any prince with tribute. They have always preserved [p. 277] their liberty, and, not being accustomed to the servitude to which you claim to reduce them, rather than surrender to your power they will Bk. V. shed more blood than their ancestors shed in the famous battle of Poyauhtlan.”

The Tlaxcalans, distressed by the arrogant and ambitious pretension of the Mexicans, and despairing of being able to induce them to a reasonable agreement, thought seriously of fortifying their frontiers still further to prevent any invasion. They had before surrounded the lands of the republic with great ditches, and had placed good garrisons on the frontiers; now, in view of the threats of the Mexicans, they increased their fortifications, augmenting the troops of the garrisons, and building that famous wall of six miles which barred the entry to enemies on the east side, from which quarter greater danger threatened them. Often they were attacked by the Huexotzincas, the Cholulans, the people of Itzocan, the people of Tecamachalco, and other states neighboring or little distant from Tlaxcala; but they could never take from the republic a palm of land, thanks to the supreme vigilance of the Tlaxcalans and the courage with which they opposed the invaders.

Very many vassals of the crown of Mexico had taken refuge in the land of Tlaxcala, especially Chalcas and Otomis of Xaltocan, who had saved themselves from the ruin of their homelands in the wars already mentioned. These bore a deadly hatred to the Mexicans on account of the evils they had received from them, and therefore seemed to the Tlaxcalans the men best fitted to oppose vigorously the attempts of their enemies; nor were they mistaken; for in fact the Mexicans found greater resistance in no others than in those exiles, especially in the Otomis, of whom the garrison of the frontiers was composed, who served the republic faithfully, and were rewarded by it with distinguished posts.

During all the time that Axayacatl and his successors reigned, the Tlaxcalans remained deprived of commerce with the maritime provinces; hence salt failed the people to such a degree that they became accustomed to eating their food without such a seasoning

secret correspondence with certain Mexican lords, provided themselves with everything necessary, without the commoners of either side knowing it. No one is unaware that in general calamities it is the poor who bear the whole weight of the tribulation, while the well-to-do find in their wealth the means of escaping it, or at least of softening it.

Now Moctezuma, unable to endure that the little republic of

Tlaxcala should refuse to render him the obedience and the adoration that so many peoples paid him, even those most distant from the court, ordered, at the beginning of his reign, that the states neighboring Tlaxcala should make ready their troops and attack that republic on every side. The Huexotzincas, confederated with the Cholulans, soon raised troops under the command of Tecayahuatzin, head of the state of Huexotzinco, but trusting more to their cunning than to their forces, they tried first, with gifts and promises, to draw to their side the people of Hueyotlipan, a city of the republic situated on the frontier of the kingdom of Acolhuacan, and the Otomis, who guarded the other frontiers; but neither the one nor the other would bind themselves; indeed they declared that they were prepared to die in defense of their republic. Whereupon the Huexotzincas, being compelled to resort to force, entered the lands of Tlaxcala with such fury that, the garrison of the frontier not sufficing to hold them back, they advanced, making a great slaughter, as far as Xiloxochitla, a place only three miles distant from the capital. There Tizatlacatzin, a celebrated

Tlaxcalan captain, put up a great resistance against them; but in the end he died, overcome by the multitude of the enemy; who, finding themselves so near the capital, were so afraid of the vengeance of the

Tlaxcalans that they returned from there precipitately to their own lands. This was the beginning of the continual battles and hostilities that there were between those two states until the arrival of the

The Tlaxcalans remained so enraged against the Huexotzincas that, no longer willing to confine themselves within their own state to defend it, as they had done before, they often went out to attack their enemies. Once they assaulted them along the foot of the mountains that lie to the west of Huexotzinco (*), and pressed them in such a way that, the Huexotzincas not being able to resist, they asked help of Moctezuma, who immediately sent an army under the command of his eldest son. This army marched along the southern slope of the volcano Popocatepetl, where it was swelled by the troops of Chietlan and Itzocan, and thence by way of Cuauhquechollan entered the valley of Atlixco. The Tlaxcalans, aware of the route the Mexicans were taking, determined to forestall them and fall upon them before they could unite with the Huexotzincas. So sudden was their assault that the Mexicans were defeated, and the Tlaxcalans, taking advantage of their disorder, made a great slaughter of them. Among the dead fell the prince-general himself, to whom perhaps so important an office had been given rather to add this honor to the splendor of his birth than out of regard for his skill in the art of war. The rest of the army took to flight, and the victors, laden with spoils, returned to Tlaxcala. It is surprising that they did not fall immediately upon the city of Huexotzinco, when they might have hoped that it would at once surrender; but perhaps their victory was not so complete as to leave them without the loss of many of their own in the battle, and they thought it better to enjoy then the fruits of the victory, to return afterward to the war with greater forces. In fact they returned; but they were repulsed by the Huexotzincas, who had meanwhile fortified themselves, and went back to Tlaxcala without

As for King Moctezuma, he felt an inexpressible grief at the death of his eldest son and at the defeat of his army; therefore, to avenge himself, he had another army immediately made ready in the provinces surrounding Tlaxcala, to blockade the whole republic; but the

Tlaxcalans, well foreseeing the hostility of the Mexicans, had fortified themselves extraordinarily and had increased the garrisons everywhere. There was vigorous fighting on the one side and on the other; but at last the royal troops were repulsed, leaving no little wealth in the hands of their enemies. The republic celebrated this victory with great rejoicings, and rewarded the Otomis, to whom it was chiefly due, raising the most distinguished of them to the dignity of Texctli, which was held among them in the highest esteem, and giving to the chiefs of that nation as wives some daughters of the noblest

Tlaxcalans.

There is no doubt that if the kings of Mexico had engaged seriously against the Tlaxcalans, they would at length have subjected them to the crown; for however great the forces of the republic, however seasoned its troops, and however strong its places, it was nevertheless by far inferior in power and in strength to the Mexicans. Hence what the historians affirm seems to me quite probable, that the kings of

Mexico purposely left the republic of Tlaxcala in existence, scarcely sixty miles distant from that capital, having conquered the more distant provinces, both so that the Mexican troops might have somewhere to exercise their courage, and also, and chiefly, to have a place where they could easily procure victims for their sacrifices. Both of these they obtained in the frequent assaults that they made on the places of Tlaxcala.

Among the Tlaxcalan victims, one very memorable in the Mexican histories [p. 281] was a most famous general called Tlahuicole, (e) in whom it was not known which was greater, the courage or the surprising strength of Bk. V. his body. The Maquahuitl, or Mexican sword, with which he fought was so heavy that a man of ordinary strength could hardly lift it from § 6. the ground. His name was the terror of the enemies of the republic, Tlahuicole, celebrat‐

> Szroria del Messico Tom. I. Nn pre-=

ed general of the and wherever he appeared with his weapon, all fled. This man, then, Tlaxcalans. in an assault that the Huexotzincas made on a garrison of Otomis, rashly placed himself, in the greatest heat of the fray, in a marshy place, where, not being able to move as nimbly as he wished, he was taken prisoner, shut up in a strong cage, and then carried to Mexico and presented to Moctezuma. This king, who knew how to esteem merit even in his enemies, instead of putting him to death generously granted him the liberty of returning to his native land; but the arrogant Tlaxcalan would not accept the favor, on the pretext that, having been taken prisoner, he had not the heart to present himself with such ignominy to his countrymen. He said that he wished to die, like the other prisoners, in honor of their gods. Moctezuma, seeing him so reluctant to return to his native land, and not wishing besides to deprive the world of so celebrated a man, kept him at court in the hope of making him a friend of the Mexicans and of making use of him for the benefit of the crown. Meanwhile war broke out with the Michoacans, the cause and circumstances of which we do not know at all, and Moctezuma committed to Tlahuicole himself the command of the army that he sent to Tlaximaloyan, the frontier, as we have already said, of the kingdom of Michoacán. Tlahuicole responded advantageously to the confidence placed in him; for although he could not dislodge the Michoacans from the place where they had fortified themselves, he nevertheless took many of them prisoner, and took from them a good quantity of gold and silver. Bk. V. he offered him the illustrious office of Tlacatecatl, or general of the

Mexican forces. To this the Tlaxcalan replied courageously that he would not be a traitor to his country, and that he wished absolutely to die, provided it were in the gladiatorial sacrifice, which, being destined for the most distinguished prisoners, would be more honorable for him. This celebrated general remained three years in Mexico with one of his wives, who had gone there from Tlaxcala to live with him.

It may be believed that the Mexicans themselves contrived this, so that he might leave them a glorious posterity, which would ennoble by its prowess the court and the kingdom of Mexico. At length the king, seeing the obstinacy with which he refused whatever proposal was made to him, yielded to his barbarous wishes, and fixed the day of the sacrifice. Eight days before, the Mexicans began to celebrate it with dances, and when the term was completed, in the presence of the king, of the nobility, and of an immense crowd of people, they set the Tlaxcalan prisoner, tied by one foot, on the Temalacatl, or great round stone, where such sacrifices were made. There came out one by one, to fight with him, several courageous men, of whom he killed, as they say, eight, and wounded as many as twenty, until, falling half dead to the ground from a violent blow received on the head, he was carried before the idol of Huitzilopochtli, and there the priests opened his breast and tore out his heart, and threw the corpse down the stairs of the temple according to the established rite. So ended this famous general, whose courage and whose loyalty to his country

§ 7. would have raised him to the class of heroes, had he been guided by Famine in the provinces of the empire,

the lights of true religion. and public works at     At the time when the war against the Tlaxcalans was being waged,

court.

a famine was suffered in some provinces of the Mexican empire, caused by a drought of two years. All the grain that private persons had having been consumed, the king had occasion to exercise his liberality; he therefore opened all his granaries, and distributed [p. 283] among his subjects all the maize that there was; but this not sufficing to remedy their need, he permitted, in imitation of Moctezuma I, Bk. V. their going off to other countries to procure their sustenance. The following year (1505), having had an abundant harvest, the Mexicans went out to war against Cuauhtemallan, a province more than nine hundred miles distant from Mexico toward the southeast. While this war was in progress, caused probably by some hostility committed by the people of Guatemala against the subjects of the crown, the building of a temple erected in honor of the goddess Centeotl was completed in Mexico, whose most solemn dedication was celebrated with the sacrifices of the prisoners taken in that war.

They had also by this time widened the road on the lake from Chapultepec to Mexico, and rebuilt the aqueduct that was upon the same road; but the joy they felt at the completion of so great a work was disturbed by the burning of the tower of another temple, called Zomolli, caused by lightning. The inhabitants of that part of the city which was farther from that temple, and particularly the Tlatelolcas, not having noticed the lightning, persuaded themselves that such a fire had been started by enemies who had come suddenly upon the city; whereupon they at once took up arms to defend it, and ran in crowds toward the temple. Moctezuma conceived such anger at that disturbance, persuading himself that it had been a mere pretext of the Tlatelolcas to stir up some sedition (for there was perpetual distrust of them), that he deprived them of all the public offices they held, and even forbade them to appear at court, neither the protestations they made of their innocence nor the prayers with which they implored the royal clemency then sufficing to turn him from such a resolution; but as soon as that first fire of his wrath died down, he restored them to their offices and to his favor.

§ 8. Mexicans who were in the garrisons of Huaxyacac and of other

Rebellion of the places. As soon as Moctezuma had news of this rebellion, he sent

Mixtecs and the

Zapotecs. against them a large army composed of Mexicans, Texcocans, and

The rebels were completely defeated, very many of them taken prisoner with their leaders, and their cities sacked. The army returned to Mexico laden with spoils, the prisoners were sacrificed, and the state of Tzotzollan was given to Cozcacuauhtli, brother of Nahuixochitl, for having been faithful to the crown, putting the obligation of a subject before the ties of blood; but Cetecpatl was not sacrificed until he had disclosed all the accomplices of the rebellion and the designs of the rebels.

§ 9.     Soon after this expedition some dispute or other arose between Dispute between the

Huexotzincas and the Huexotzincas and the Cholulans, their neighbors and friends, the Cholulans. and, committing the decision to arms, they fought a pitched battle.

The Cholulans, as more practiced in the exercise of religion, of commerce, and of the arts than in that of war, were soon beaten and forced to retire to their city, to which the enemy pursued them, killed some of their people, and burned some of their houses. No sooner had the Huexotzincas obtained such a victory than they repented of it, because of the punishment that threatened them; hence, to avoid it, they sent to King Moctezuma two distinguished persons, called

> [p. 285]

Tolimpanecatl and Tzoncoztli, seeking to justify themselves and to blame the Cholulans. These ambassadors, whether to make the courage of their fellow citizens appear greater or for any other motive, so exaggerated the slaughter of the Cholulans that they made the king believe that all had perished, and that those few who had saved their lives had abandoned the city. Moctezuma, on hearing this report, was exceedingly grieved by it, and feared the vengeance of the god Quetzalcoatl, whose sanctuary, which was among the most celebrated and [p. 285] most revered in all that land, he believed to have been profaned by

> più riveriti di tutta. quella terra, credeva profanato dagli ===

Bk. V. the Huexotzincas. Having therefore taken counsel with the two allied kings, he sent to Cholula some persons of his court to inform themselves fully of the whole affair, and having found it very different from what the Huexotzincas had told him, he conceived such indignation at having been deceived by them that he at once dispatched an army, ordering the general to punish them severely if they should not give fitting satisfaction. The Huexotzincas, sensing the storm that was about to burst upon them, came out drawn up in battle array to receive the Mexicans; but the Mexican general advanced toward them to set forth his commission in these words: “Our lord Moctezuma, who has his court in the midst of the water, Nezahualpilli, who commands on the shores of the lake, and Totoquihuatzin, who reigns at the foot of the mountains, order us to tell you that, having learned from your ambassadors that you have ruined Cholula and killed its inhabitants, they have felt the utmost grief, and are compelled to avenge so great an outrage against the venerable sanctuary of Quetzalcoatl.” The Huexotzincas protested that the report of their ambassadors was too exaggerated and false, and that therefore a body so respectable as that of the city of Huexotzinco could not be the author of it, and they offered to satisfy all three kings by the punishment of the guilty. Then, having caused the aforesaid ambassadors to be brought there, and having cut off their ears and nose (which was the penalty established against those who told lies harmful to the public), they handed them over to the general. Thus they avoided the evils of war, which otherwise would have been inevitable.                 § 10.

I, and in the other secular years. This one, which was the most

Bk. V. solemn, was also the last that the Mexicans celebrated. A very great number of prisoners was sacrificed in it, others being reserved for the festival of the Dedication of the Tzompantli, which was, as we shall say elsewhere, a building near the great temple, where the skulls of the victims were kept strung up.

§ 11. Presages of the war    This secular year seems to have passed without war, but in 1507 with the Spaniards. the Mexicans made the expedition against Tzollan and Mictlan, states

of the Mixtecs, whose inhabitants fled to the mountains to save themselves, and the Mexicans had no other advantage than that of taking prisoner a few Mixtecs who had remained in their houses.

Then they went to subjugate those of Cuauhquechollan who had rebelled, in which war Prince Cuitláhuac, general of the army, displayed his courage. Some brave captains of the Mexicans died in this expedition; but they brought the rebels back under the yoke nonetheless, and took three thousand two hundred prisoners, who were sacrificed, part in the festival Tlacaxipehualiztli, which was held in the second

Mexican month, and part at the Dedication of the sanctuary Zomolli, which after the aforementioned fire had been rebuilt with greater magnificence.

The following year the royal army of the Mexicans, Texcocans, and

Tepanecs marched out against the remote province of Amatlan. As they were marching over a very high mountain, a furious north wind with snow came upon them, which wrought a very great slaughter in the army, for some, being accustomed to a mild climate and going almost naked, died of cold; and others were crushed by the trees that the wind tore up. Of the rest of the army, which continued its journey weakened as far as Amatlan, the greater part died in the battle.

> Queste: ed altre calamità, aggiunte alla apparizione d' upa: cometa in quello stesso tempo nel Gielo , misero, in, gran coîternazione rutti que” Popoli . Motezuma , il quale era troppo superstizioso per poter guardar con indifterenza, yalle [p. 287] fenomeno , consultò sopra ciò i suoi Asftrologi; ma non {a-==—pendo questi indovinarne la significazione , la richiese dal Re Lu. Questi Re, avvegnachè parenti fossero fra loro, e perpetuamente alleati , non i viveano in molta armonia, dacchè il Re d’Acolhuacan fece morire, siccome fra poco vedremo , il suo figliuolo Huexotzincatzin , non curando le preghiere di Motezuma, il quale come Zio di quel Principe, s' interpose per lui. Era giù molto tempo, che non fi tractavano più con quella frequenza, e con quella confidenza con cui dfolevano; ma questa volta il vano terrore, che ingombrò l' animo ‘di Motezuma lo {pinle a prevalersì della scienza del Re Nezahualpilli: ‘onde lo pregò di portarli a Melslico per deliberare insieme sopra tal affare, che premeva del pia a tutti e due. Andò Nezahualpilli, e dopo aver conferito prolissamente con Motezuma, fu di parere, per uel che dicono gli Storici, che la Cometa annunziava le uture disgrazie di que' regni -per l'arrivo di nuove genti, Ma non piacendo «otal interpretazione a Motezuma , Neza» hualpilli lo sfidò al giuoco del pallone, ch' era frequentislimo anche fra gli steM Re, e sS'accordarono, che se il Re di Melslico vinceva la partita , quello d’ Acolhuacan rinunzierebbe alla sua interpretazione, stimandola falsa ; ma fe vinceva Nezahualpilli ,, Motezuma dovrebbe riconoscerla vera, ed abbracciarla, Sciocchezza veramente ridicola di quegli uomini nel credere dipendente la verità d'una predizione dalla de> strezza del giuocatore, 0 dalla fortuna del giuoco; ma pure men perniciola di quella degli amichi Europei , che compro» mettevano nella barbarie del duello, e nella incertezza del» le armi la verità, l’'innocenza,-e l'onore, Restò Nezahualpilli vittorioso nel giuoco, e Motezuma sconsolato per la perdita, è per la confermazione di sì cattivo pronesticamento . Nondimeno volle tentare altra strada, sperando trovare una predizione più favorevole , che si comtrappesafle con quella del Re d' Acolhbuacan, € colla disprazia del giuoco. Fece dunque consyltar un famosissimo Alstrologo, molto versato [p. 288] =——= nelle superstizioni della Divinazione ; colla quale avea rén: Liu. V. duto tanto celebre. il suo nome in quella terra, ed erasi conciliata sì grande autorità, che senza uscir di casa era consulrato come un oracolo dagli stessi Re. Egli fapenda senz’ alrro ciò ch’ era avvenuto fra i due Re, in vece di dare una sisposta gradevole al suo Sovrano, o almeno equivoca ,! come fagno per lo più tali pronoîticatori, confermò la funesta predizion del Tezcucano . Sdegnossì tanto Motezuma della risposta , cha in ricompensa fece rovinargli la cala, restando ll’ infelice indovino sepolto fra le rovine del suo {santuario . ‘ Questi, ed altri simili pronosticamenti della caduta di quell' Imperio lì -vedono nelle pitture degli Americani , 8 nelle Storie degli Spagnuoli. Sono troppo loncano da persua -

These and other calamities, added to the appearance of a comet in the sky at that same time, threw all those peoples into great consternation. Moctezuma, who was too superstitious to be able to regard with indifference such [p. 287] a phenomenon, consulted his astrologers about it; but these not knowing how to divine its meaning, he asked it of the king of Bk. V. Acolhuacan, who was also given to astrology and divination. These kings, although they were related to each other and perpetually allied, did not however live in much harmony, ever since the king of Acolhuacan had put to death, as we shall soon see, his son Huexotzincatzin, heedless of the entreaties of Moctezuma, who, as uncle of that prince, had interceded for him. It had already been a long time since they had dealt with each other with that frequency and that confidence with which they used to; but this time the vain terror that weighed upon Moctezuma’s mind impelled him to avail himself of the learning of King Nezahualpilli; hence he begged him to come to Mexico to deliberate together on that matter, which pressed equally upon both. Nezahualpilli went, and after conferring at length with Moctezuma, was of the opinion, according to what the historians say, that the comet announced the future misfortunes of those kingdoms through the arrival of new peoples. But this interpretation not pleasing Moctezuma, Nezahualpilli challenged him to the ball game, which was very frequent even among the kings themselves, and they agreed that if the king of Mexico won the match, the king of Acolhuacan would renounce his interpretation, esteeming it false; but if Nezahualpilli won, Moctezuma should acknowledge it as true and embrace it. A truly ridiculous folly of those men, to believe that the truth of a prediction depended on the dexterity of the player or on the fortune of the game; but yet less pernicious than that of the ancient Europeans, who committed to the barbarity of the duel and the uncertainty of arms truth, innocence, and honor. Nezahualpilli remained victorious in the game, and Moctezuma disconsolate at the loss and at the confirmation of so evil a prognostication. Nevertheless he wished to try another way, hoping to find a more favorable prediction that might counterbalance that of the king of Acolhuacan and the misfortune at the game. He therefore had a most famous astrologer consulted, well versed

[p. 288] in the superstitions of divination, by which he had made his name so Bk. V.

celebrated in that land, and had won for himself such great authority that, without leaving his house, he was consulted like an oracle by the kings themselves. Knowing without any doubt what had passed between the two kings, instead of giving his sovereign a pleasing answer, or at least an equivocal one, as such prognosticators for the most part do, he confirmed the fatal prediction of the Texcocan. Moctezuma was so angered by the answer that, in recompense, he had his house pulled down, and the unfortunate diviner remained buried among the ruins of his sanctuary.

> - dermi, che tutro ciò, chs scritto troviamo sopra sì fatto argomento, degno fia della nostra feda; ma neppur fi può dabitare della tradizione, che v' era fra gli Americani di dovere arrivare a quel regno delle nuove genti aflai diverse da’ proprj abitatori, che xs’ impadronirebbe:ro di turta la ter- 7a. Non Y' è stata nel paese d' Anahuac veruna Nazion dirozzata, O mezzo dirozzata , che non abbia fatto fede di co ral tradizione, © colle loro testimonianze verbali, o colk proprie loro Storie. Non è possibile indovinare la prima orîgine di questa tradizione tanto universale; ma nel Secolo XV., ed anche nel XIV. dappoichè colla invenzione della bussola non temevano più gli domini di perder di vista la terra, e gli Europei stimolati dall’ ambizione , e dalla insaziabil fame dell’ oro aveano cominciato a rendersi famigliari i perigli dell’ Oceano, quel maligno spirito , capital nemico del genére umano , che gira inceffantemente per “ructa la rerra spiando le azionidei Mortali, porè facilmente congettura» re i progressi degli Europei , la ettà del nuovo Mondo, ed una parte de' grandi avvenimenti , che’ ivi erano per accadere : e mon è inverifimile , che’ gli predicessle a Nazioni consacrate al suo culto , per confermarle colla stessa predizione dell' avvenire nella erronea persuasione della sua pretesa divinità, Ma fe il Demonio pronolticaya le - ae cala[p. 289] zalamità per ingannar que' miserabili Popoli, il pietosisimo== =Dio le annunziava per disporre i loro spiriti al Vangeio. Lu. V, L'avvenimento , che fon per raccontare in conferma di quefta verità , fu pubblico, e strepitoso, accaduto in presenza di due Re, e della Nobiltà Meslicana . Trovosk altresì rappresentato in alcune dipinture di quelle Nazioni, e fe ne mandò alla Corte di Spagna un attestato giuridico. (*),

These and other like prognostications of the fall of that empire are to be seen in the paintings of the Americans and in the histories of the Spaniards. I am far from persuading myself that everything we find written on such a subject is worthy of our belief; but neither can one doubt the tradition that existed among the Americans, that there were to arrive in that kingdom new peoples very different from its own inhabitants, who would take possession of the whole land. There was no civilized or half-civilized nation in the country of Anahuac that did not bear witness to this tradition, either by their verbal testimony or by their own histories. It is not possible to guess the first origin of so universal a tradition; but in the fifteenth century, and even in the fourteenth, after the invention of the compass had freed men from the fear of losing sight of land, and the Europeans, spurred on by ambition and by the insatiable hunger for gold, had begun to make the perils of the Ocean familiar to themselves, that malignant spirit, the capital enemy of mankind, who goes ceaselessly about the whole earth spying on the actions of mortals, could easily conjecture the progress of the Europeans, the discovery of the New World, and a part of the great events that were to take place there; and it is not improbable that he predicted them to nations consecrated to his worship, in order to confirm them, by that same prediction of the future, in the erroneous persuasion of his pretended divinity. But if the Devil prognosticated the future [p. 289] calamities in order to deceive those wretched peoples, the most merciful God announced them in order to dispose their spirits to the Bk. V. Gospel. The event that I am about to relate in confirmation of this truth was public and sensational, having occurred in the presence of two kings and of the Mexican nobility. It is also found represented in some paintings of those nations, and a juridical attestation of it was sent to the court of Spain. (*)

Papantzin, a Mexican princess and sister of King Moctezuma, had § 12.

> Storia del Messico Tom. I. O0o se

Memorable occurmarried the governor of Tlatelolco, and after his death remained in rence concerning a his palace until the year 1509, when she too died of an illness. Her Mexican princess. funeral was celebrated with a magnificence corresponding to the splendor of her birth, the king her brother and all the Mexican and Tlatelolca nobility attending. Her body was buried in a subterranean cave or grotto that was in the garden of the same palace, near a pond where she used to bathe, and the entrance of the cave was closed with a stone of no great weight. The following day a little girl of five or six years took it into her head to go from her mother’s apartment to that of the deceased’s steward, which lay on the other side of the garden, and in passing she saw the princess seated on the steps of the pond, and heard herself called by her with the word Cocoton, (f) which they use in speaking tenderly to children. The little girl, not being capable at her age of reflecting on the death of the princess, and thinking that she had come to bathe, as she was accustomed to do, approached without fear, and the princess sent her to call the wife of her steward. She went to call her; but the woman, smiling and caressing her, said to her: “My daughter, Papantzin is already dead, and yesterday we buried her.” But as the girl insisted, and even pulled her by the huepilli, or woman’s shift, she, more to please her than because she believed

(f) Cocoton is almost the same as “little girl”; but it expresses somewhat more tenderness. [p. 290] what was said to her, followed her; but scarcely had she come in sight Bk. V. of the princess when she was seized with such horror that she fell to

> Ss. 13. Fenomeni nota-bili.

the ground in a swoon. The girl told her mother, and she, with two other companions, ran to help the woman; but on seeing the princess they were so frightened that they were on the point of fainting, had not the princess herself comforted them, assuring them that she was now alive. She had her steward summoned through them, and charged him to go and carry this news to the king her brother; but he did not dare to do so, for he feared that the king, thinking the news a fable, would punish him as a liar without examining it, with his usual severity. Go, then, to Texcoco, the princess said to him, and beg King

> benchè alcuni adulatori per rafferenarlo , procurarono persuadergli, che la malattia, che avea patito la Principesla , le avea stravolto il cervello. Non volle tornar più a lei, per non fentir un'altra volta i malinconici presag, della rovina del suo Imperio . La Principessa visse poi molti anni in somma ritiratezza ed astinenza . Fu la prima, che nell' anno 1524 ricevette in Tlatelolco il sacro battesimo, e fi chiami fin d'allora Donna Maria Papantzin . Negli anni in cui {& pravvisse alla sua rigenerazione , fu un perfetto modello di virtù cristiana, e la sua morte corrispose alla sua vira, ed alla sua maravigliofa vocazione al Crittianesimo . (g)

Nezahualpilli in my name to come and find me. The steward obeyed, and the king, informed by him, went at once to Tlatelolco. When he arrived there, the princess had entered a room of the palace. The king greeted her, full of amazement, and she begged him to go to Mexico and tell the king her brother that she was alive and had need to see him in order to disclose to him certain things of the highest importance. The king went to Mexico to carry out the commission; but

> Oltre a questo memorabile successo accadde nel 1510; l’ improvviso, e violento incendio delle torri del tempio maggior di Mesffico in una notte serena , senza potersi mai indovinar la cagione, e nell’ anno antecedente una sì rapida e sì straordinaria agitazione delle acque del lago , che rovinarono -alcune case di Messico , non eflendovi nè vento , pè tremuoto , nè altra cagione naturale, a cui potesse ascriversi sì raro fenomeno. Si dice ancora , che nel 1511.-{i videro rappresentati nell' aria degli uomini armati , che combattevano fra loro, e s' ammazzavano . Questi , ed altri & mili fenomeni raccontati dall’ Acosta, dal Torquemada , € da altri, fi trovarono esattamente descritti nelle Storie Messicane , ed Acolhue. Non è pur inverisimile , che avendo Dio annunziato con sì fatti prodigj l’ eccidio d’ alcune Città, ficcome in parte ci consta dalla Sacra Scrittura , € in parte dalla testimonianza di Gioseffo, d' Eusebio Cesariense , d’ Orofio, e d' altri Autori, adoperasle ancora la medesima providenza nello scompiglio generale d' un Mondo intero, ch’ è senza dubbio l'avvenimento più raro e più notabile di tutti quanti si leggono nelle Storie umane .

Moctezuma could scarcely give credence to what he heard.

> La costernazione messa da sì funesti presag} nell’ animo di Mot ezuma , non lo distornò da' pensieri di guerra, Molte

Nevertheless, in order not to fail in the respect due to so authoritative an ambassador, he went with him, and with many of the Mexican nobility, to Tlatelolco, and, entering the hall where the princess was, asked her whether she was his sister. “I am indeed, lord,” replied the princess, “your sister Papan, whom you buried the day before yesterday; I am truly alive, and I wish to make known to you what I have seen, because it concerns you.” This said, the two kings sat down, all the others remaining standing, amazed at what they saw.

Then the princess continued to speak thus: “After I died, or, if you will not believe that I was dead, after I was left deprived of motion and of the senses, I suddenly found myself in an extended plain, the end of which could be seen on no side. In the middle of it I observed a [p. 291] road, which I then saw divide into various paths, and on one side there ran a great river, whose waters made a frightful noise; and as I Bk. V. wished to throw myself into the river to cross to the opposite bank by swimming, I saw before me a handsome youth of good stature, dressed in a long robe, white as snow and shining like the sun, furnished with wings of beautiful feathers, and bearing on his forehead this sign (in saying this the princess made the sign of the cross with her first two fingers); and, taking me by the hand, he said to me: Stay; for it is not yet time to cross this river. God loves you greatly, though you do not know him. Then he led me along the river, on whose bank I saw very many human skulls and bones, and I heard such lamentable groans that they moved me to compassion. Then, turning my eyes to the river, I saw upstream some large boats, and in them certain men of a color and dress very different from ours. They were white and bearded, and carried standards in their hands and helmets on their heads. God, the youth then said to me, God wills that you live, so that you may be a witness of the revolutions that are to come to pass in these kingdoms. The groans that you heard among those bones are those of the souls of your ancestors, who are and always will be tormented for their crimes. The men whom you see coming in the boats are those who by force of arms will make themselves masters of all these kingdoms, and with them will come also the knowledge of the true God, Creator of heaven and earth. As soon as the war is ended and the bath is proclaimed by which sins are washed away, be the first to receive it, and guide your countrymen by your example. This said, the youth vanished, and I, called back to life, rose from the place where I lay, lifted the stone from the sepulcher, and went out into the garden, where I was found by my servants.”

Moctezuma was stunned on hearing such an account, and, with his mind disturbed by a great throng of thoughts, he rose and went out at once to betake himself to a palace of his set apart for the time of mourning, without saying a word to his sister, or to the king of Texcoco, or to any of those who accompanied him,

Oo2 [p. 292] although some flatterers, in order to reassure him, tried to persuade

Bk. V.

him that the illness the princess had suffered had unhinged her brain.

He did not wish to go back to her again, so as not to hear once more the melancholy presages of the ruin of his empire. The princess afterwards lived many years in the utmost seclusion and abstinence. She was the first who, in the year 1524, received holy baptism at

Tlatelolco, and from that time on she was called Doña María

Papantzin. In the years that she survived her regeneration she was a perfect model of Christian virtue, and her death corresponded to her life and to her marvelous vocation to Christianity. (g)

§ 13.     Besides this memorable occurrence there happened in 1510 the Remarkable sudden and violent burning of the towers of the great temple of phenomena.

Mexico on a clear night, without its cause ever being guessed, and in the preceding year so rapid and so extraordinary an agitation of the waters of the lake that it ruined some houses of Mexico, there being neither wind, nor earthquake, nor any other natural cause to which so rare a phenomenon could be ascribed. It is said also that in 1511

armed men were seen represented in the air, fighting among themselves and killing one another. These and other like phenomena, related by Acosta, by Torquemada, and by others, were found exactly described in the Mexican and Acolhua histories. Nor is it improbable that God, having announced by such prodigies the destruction of some cities, as is known to us partly from Holy Scripture and partly from the testimony of Josephus, of Eusebius of Caesarea, of Orosius, and of other authors, should employ the same providence in the general overthrow of an entire world, which is without doubt the rarest and most notable event of all those that are read of in human histories.

The consternation caused in the mind of Moctezuma by such dismal presages did not turn him from thoughts of war. Many expeditions

After having had it polished and curiously carved, he commanded that it be carried solemnly to Mexico. A great multitude gathered to drag it; but in crossing a bridge of beams that lay over a canal at the entrance of the city, it broke the beams with its enormous weight and fell into the canal, dragging with it some men, and among them the high priest, who was walking before it incensing it. This misfortune greatly grieved the king and the people; but without abandoning the undertaking they drew the stone out of the water with the utmost labor and carried it to the temple, where it was dedicated with the sacrifice of all the prisoners who had been reserved for this great festival, which was truly one of the most solemn that the Mexicans celebrated. To it the king summoned the principal nobility of his whole kingdom, and he spent great treasures on the gifts that he made to the nobles and to the commoners. This same year there was also celebrated the dedication of the temple of Tlamatzinco, and of that of the Quauhxicalco, of which we shall speak elsewhere. The victims sacrificed at the dedication of these two buildings and at that of the altar of the sacrifices were, according to what the historians say, twelve thousand two hundred and ten.

To furnish so great a number of victims it was necessary to wage war continually. In 1511 the Yopis rebelled, and wished to kill the whole garrison of Mexicans that was at Tlacotepec; but their design having been opportunely discovered, they were punished, and two hundred of them were led as prisoners to the capital. Every province, every place conquered became a new enemy of the conquerors, which, impatient of the yoke to which it was not accustomed, and irritated by the violence, awaited nothing but some good occasion to avenge itself and to restore itself to its former liberty. The happiness of a kingdom does not consist in the extent of its dominions, nor even in the multitude of its vassals; indeed it never approaches its end so closely as when, by reason of its vast and immoderate extent, it can maintain neither the necessary union among its parts nor the vigor that is needed to resist the multitude of its enemies.

After six months of this private life he returned to the capital, ordered his dear Xocotzin to withdraw with her children to the palace called Tecpilpan, and shut himself up in the one that was his ordinary residence, without letting himself be seen by anyone save some of his confidants, with the design of concealing his death in imitation of his father. In fact neither the time nor the other circumstances of his death were ever known. It is known only that he died in 1516, and that before dying he commanded the confidants whom he employed to burn his body secretly. Hence it came about that the common people, and even a good many nobles, remained persuaded that he was not dead, but had gone to the kingdom of Amaquemecan, whence his ancestors had their origin, as he had often said he wished to do.

This king was of the same opinion in matters of religion as his great father Nezahualcoyotl. He despised in his mind the worship of idols, although outwardly he conformed with the people. He likewise imitated his father in zeal for the laws and in severity of justice, of which he gave a rare example in the last years of his reign. There was a law that forbade, under pain of death, the speaking of indecent words in the royal palace. This law was violated by one of the princes his sons, named Huexotzincatzin, whom he loved more than all the others, no less for his character and for the virtues that were already shining in his youth than for his being the first-born among the sons he had by his favorite Xocotzin; but the prince’s words had been rather the effect of youthful thoughtlessness than of any wicked purpose. The king learned of it from one of his concubines, to whom such words had been said. He asked her whether this had occurred before other persons, and, having learned that the prince’s tutors had been present, he withdrew to an apartment of the palace that was set aside for occasions of mourning. There he had the tutors summoned to examine them. They, fearing

[p. 296] to be severely punished if they concealed the truth, testified to it Bk. V.

frankly; but at the same time they endeavored to excuse the prince, saying that he neither knew the person to whom he was speaking nor had the words been obscene. But in spite of their representations he ordered at once that the prince be arrested, and on the same day pronounced against him the sentence of death. The whole court was dismayed at so rigorous a sentence; the nobility interceded with prayers and tears, and the prince’s own mother, trusting in the great love the king bore her, presented herself to him weeping, and, to move him the more to compassion, brought her children with her. But neither reasons, nor prayers, nor tears sufficed to bend the king. “My son,” he said, “has violated the law. If I pardon him, it will be said that the laws are not made for everyone. Let my subjects know that to no one will transgression be pardoned, since I do not pardon it in the son whom I love most.” The queen, pierced by the keenest grief and despairing of being able to overcome the king’s firmness, said to him:

“Since for so slight a cause you have driven from your heart all the affections of a father and of a husband, and wish to make yourself the executioner of your own son, what is left to you but to give death also to me and to these tender princes whom I have borne you?” The king then, with a grave look, commanded her to withdraw, since there was no longer any remedy. The queen went away disconsolate to her apartment, and there, in the company of some ladies who went to console her, abandoned herself to weeping. Meanwhile those who were charged with the prince’s execution kept delaying, so that, with time, zeal for justice being relaxed, there might be room for paternal love and for clemency; but the king, perceiving their intention, commanded that it be carried out at once, as in fact it was, to the general sorrow of the whole kingdom, and to the very great displeasure of

King Moctezuma, not only because of the kinship that he had with the prince, but also because the entreaties he had interposed that the sentence be revoked had been disregarded.

[p. 297]

After the execution had been carried out, the king shut himself up in

Bk. V. a hall for the space of forty days, without letting himself be seen by anyone, in order to give full vent there to his grief, and he had the doors of his son’s apartment walled up, so as to remove from his eyes that incentive to sorrow.

This severity in punishing transgressors was counterbalanced by the compassion that he showed for the misery of his subjects. There was in his palace a window that looked on the marketplace, covered by a lattice, from which he observed, without being seen, the people who gathered there; and when he saw some poorly dressed woman he had her called, and, having informed himself of her way of life and of her need, he provided her with what was necessary for her and for all her children, if she had any. Every day he gave alms in his palace to all the infirm and the orphans. There was in Texcoco a hospital for all those who in war had lost their eyes, or in any other way had been made useless for the exercise of arms, and there they were maintained at the king’s expense according to their condition, and often visited by the king himself. On such works he spent a great part of his revenues.

The intelligence of this king has been much celebrated by the historians of that kingdom. He proposed to himself to imitate, both in his studies and in his conduct of life, the example of his father, and in fact he was very like him. With him the glory of the Chichimec kings may be said to have ended; for the discord that arose among his sons diminished the splendor of the court, weakened the forces of the state, and disposed it to its final ruin. Nezahualpilli did not declare who was to succeed him on the throne, as all his predecessors had done. We likewise do not know the motive of such negligence, which proved so pernicious to the kingdom of Acolhuacan.                        § 16.

Prince Cacamatzin; since, besides his prudence and his courage, he was the first-born of the first Mexican princess whom the deceased king had married. All the other councilors adhered to this opinion, which was so just, and was that of so authoritative a person. The princes, who were awaiting in a neighboring hall the resolution of the council, were asked to enter in order to hear it. When all had entered, the principal seat was given to Cacamatzin, who was a young man of twenty-two years, and at his sides sat his brothers Coanacochtzin, of twenty, and Ixtlilxochitl, of nineteen years. Then that elder who had been the first to speak rose, and declared the resolution of the council, in which that of the kingdom was pledged, to give the crown to

Cacamatzin by reason of the right of primogeniture. Ixtlilxochitl, who was an ambitious and enterprising young man, opposed it, saying that if the king had really been dead he would doubtless have named his successor; that his not having done so was an unmistakable sign that he was alive, and that, the lawful sovereign being alive, it was a presumption on the part of the subjects to name a successor. The councilors, knowing well the disposition of Ixtlilxochitl, did not dare to contradict him openly; but they begged Coanacochtzin to say what he thought. This prince praised and confirmed the determination of the council, and pointed out the inconveniences that were to follow if the execution were delayed. Ixtlilxochitl contradicted him, charging him with levity and thoughtlessness, since he did not perceive that in embracing such a course he favored the designs of Moctezuma, who was too much inclined toward Cacamatzin, and was working to put him on the throne, hoping to have in him a king of wax, to whom he could give whatever form he pleased. “It is not reasonable, my brother,” replied Coanacochtzin, “to oppose so wise and so just a resolution. Do you not observe that if Cacamatzin were not king, [p. 299] to me, not to you, would the crown be due?” “It is true,” said Ixtlilxochitl then, “that if in the succession only age is to be consid‐ Bk. V. ered, the crown is due to Cacamatzin, and, he failing, to you; but if regard is had, as is just, to courage, it is due to me rather than to you or to Cacamatzin.” The councilors, seeing that the anger of the princes was growing ever hotter, imposed silence on both and dismissed the assembly.

The two princes went to their mother, Queen Xocotzin, to continue their dispute, and Cacamatzin, accompanied by many nobles, went at once to Mexico to inform Moctezuma of what had happened and to ask his help. Moctezuma, who, besides the love he bore him, saw the right of that prince and the consent of the nation, advised him to place in safety, before anything else, the royal treasure, and promised him to settle the quarrel with his brother, and to employ the Mexican arms in his favor if negotiations should not prove sufficient.

As soon as Ixtlilxochitl learned of the departure of Cacamatzin, and foresaw the consequences of his recourse to Moctezuma, he left the court with all his partisans, and went off to the domains that his tutors had in the mountains of Metztitlan. Coanacochtzin promptly gave notice to Cacamatzin to return without delay to Texcoco, and to take advantage of so opportune an occasion to be crowned. Cacamatzin took the salutary counsel of his brother, and went to that court accompanied by Cuitláhuac, brother of Moctezuma and lord of Iztapalapan, and by many Mexican nobles. Cuitláhuac, without losing time, convoked the Texcocan nobility in the Hueitecpan, or great palace of the kings of Acolhuacan, and presented to them Prince Cacamatzin, that he might be recognized by them as lawful sovereign. All accepted him, and the day was then fixed for the ceremony of the coronation; but it was prevented by the news that arrived at the court, that Prince Ixtlilxochitl was descending from the mountains of Metztitlan at the head of a large army,

Cacamatzin, under the pretext of zeal for the honor and liberty of the

Chichimec and Acolhua nations: that it was an unworthy and very dangerous thing to obey a king so pliant to the will of him of Mexico; that the Mexicans, forgetting how much they owed to the Acolhuas, wished to add to their iniquitous usurpations that of the kingdom of

Acolhuacan; that he for his part was determined to employ all the courage that God had given him in defending his country from the tyranny of Moctezuma. With such reasons, suggested to him probably by his tutors, he so inflamed the minds of those lords that all offered to help him with all their forces, and in fact they raised so many troops that, when the prince came down from the mountains, his army amounted, by what they say, to more than a hundred thousand men. In all the places through which he passed he was well received, either from fear of his power or from inclination to favor his pretensions. From Tepepulco he sent an embassy to the people of Otompan, ordering them to render him obedience as to their own king; but they answered that, King Nezahualpilli being dead, they recognized no other master than Cacamatzin, who had been peacefully accepted in the capital and was already in possession of the throne of Acolhuacan.

This answer irritated Ixtlilxochitl, and made him march headlong against that city. The people of Otompan came out to meet him in battle order; but although they offered some resistance to the enemy army, they were nevertheless defeated, and their city was taken by the prince. Among the dead fell the lord of Otompan himself, and this very circumstance hastened the victory for the prince.

This occurrence put Cacamatzin and all his court in great disquiet; whence, fearing that the enemy might wish even to besiege the capital, he sought to fortify himself; but the prince, content to see himself respected and feared, did not move [p. 301] then from Otompan; but he posted guards on the roads with orders

Bk. V. to do harm to no one, not to hinder the passage of private persons who might wish to go from the capital to any other place, and to show respect to persons of the first rank who might pass there. Cacamatzin, seeing the forces and the resolution of his brother, and thinking it a lesser evil to sacrifice a part, though a large one, of the kingdom than to lose it all, sent him, with the consent of Coanacochtzin, an embassy to make some accommodation with him. He sent to tell him that he might keep, if he wished, all the dominions of the mountains, since he himself was content with the capital and the states of the plains; that he wished also to share with his brother Coanacochtzin the revenues of the kingdom; but at the same time he begged him to renounce every other pretension and to disturb no more the public tranquillity. The ambassadors were two personages of the royal blood of Acolhuacan, for whom Ixtlilxochitl had great respect. This prince replied that his brothers might do whatever they pleased; that it was pleasing to him that Cacamatzin should be in possession of the kingdom of Acolhuacan; that he was plotting nothing against them, nor against the state; that he maintained that army for no other purpose than to oppose the ambitious designs of the Mexicans, who had caused the gravest vexations and suspicions to his father Nezahualpilli; that if the kingdom was divided at that time for the common interest of the nation, he hoped to see it united again another time; that above all they should take care not to fall into the snares of the crafty Moctezuma. Nor was Ixtlilxochitl mistaken in his distrust of Moctezuma; for in fact that king was the very one who gave the unfortunate Cacamatzin, as we shall see, into the hands of the Spaniards, in spite of the love he bore him.

By the agreement made with his brother, Cacamatzin remained in peaceful possession of the crown of Acolhuacan, but with his dominions much diminished, since what he had ceded was a considerable part of the kingdom. Ixtlilxochitl kept his troops always in motion, and often let himself be seen with his army in the neighborhood of Mexico, defying Moctezuma

already begun to die down with the years, and domestic delights had weakened his spirit; nor would it have been prudent to expose himself to such a conflict with so resolute a young man, who by secret negotiations had already drawn to his side a great part of the Mexican provinces. Nevertheless the Mexicans often fought with that army, being now defeated, now victorious. In one of those skirmishes a relative of the king of Mexico was taken, who had gone out to the war with the resolution of making that prince prisoner and bringing him bound to Mexico, and had so promised Moctezuma. Ixtlilxochitl learned of this arrogant promise, and, to avenge himself, having had him bound and covered with dry cane, had him burned alive in sight of the whole army.

> Nel decorso della nostra storia faremo vedere , quanta parte ebbe questo inquieto Principe nella felicità degli Spagnuoli, i quali a questo tempo cominciarono a lasciarsi vedere sulle coste del Golfo Messicano; ma prima d'’intraprendere la narrazione d'una guerra, che mise turti que’ regai in Ucompiglio , è d' uopo far conoscere la Religione, il Go: verno, le arti, ed i costumi de' Meslicani .

In the course of our history we shall show how large a part this restless prince had in the good fortune of the Spaniards, who at this time began to let themselves be seen on the coasts of the Gulf of

Mexico; but before undertaking the narration of a war that threw all those kingdoms into confusion, it is necessary to make known the religion, the government, the arts, and the customs of the Mexicans.
